name: Aberrant Regeneration of the Third Cranial Nerve
symptoms: Abnormal eyelid movements with eye movement (pseudo-von Graefe: lid elevation on downgaze/adduction).
Pupil constriction on attempted adduction or downgaze (pseudo-Argyll Robertson).
Diplopia from incomplete recovery of extraocular muscle function.
History of prior CN III palsy (typically compressive) weeks to months earlier.
findings: ## Pseudo-von Graefe sign (signature finding)

• The affected upper eye lid retracts when the patient looks down or adducts the eye, instead of falling normally. The opposite of true von Graefe's (lid-lag on downgaze in thyroid eye disease) — hence "pseudo."
## Pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupil (light-near dissociation)

• The pupil on the affected side constricts on attempted adduction or downgaze (fibres meant for medial rectus / inferior rectus have re-routed to the sphincter), producing apparent "light-near dissociation" — poor light reflex but constriction with near effort. Unlike true Argyll Robertson, this is unilateral and accompanied by other synkineses.
## Other synkineses

• Adduction of the eye on attempted elevation or depression; limitation of both elevation and depression (partial residual CN III weakness in the involved muscles); absent optokinetic response; retracted globe with certain gazes; and in severe cases gaze-evoked lid oscillation.
## Critical clinical rule

• Aberrant regeneration does no occur after microvascular CN III palsy. The nerve sheath is preserved in ischemic lesions, so regenerating axons return to their original endings. Aberrancy requires axonal + sheath disruption (i.e. compressive/traumatic lesion). Clinical discovery of aberrant regeneration therefore implies: (1) prior compressive CN III palsy (PCOM aneurysm, tumour, trauma, cavernous sinus lesion) now partially recovered, or (2) congenital CN III palsy (up to two-thirds show aberrancy), or (3) Primary aberrant regeneration — the alarming scenario below.
## Primary aberrant regeneration

• Aberrant signs WITHOUT any history of preceding CN III palsy. This is a DO-NOT-MISS finding — it reflects a slowly enlarging parasellar / cavernous sinus lesion (intracavernous carotid aneurysm, cavernous sinus meningioma, schwannoma, pituitary macroadenoma) that damages individual nerve fascicles so gradually that overt CN III palsy never develops but synkinetic regeneration proceeds. Primary aberrant CN III regeneration mandates urgent contrast MRI + MRA of the brain and cavernous sinus.
etiology: ## Mechanism
• Misdirection of regenerating CN III fibers to alternate CN III–controlled muscles (e.g., inferior-rectus fibers re-routed to the iris sphincter or levator).
## Congenital CN III palsy
• Aberrancy seen in up to two-thirds of congenital CN III palsy cases.
## Acquired CN III palsy (most common)
• Recovery from trauma or compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
• Never occurs after a microvascular/ischemic CN III palsy — sheath is preserved, axons regenerate correctly.
## Primary aberrant regeneration (no preceding palsy)
• Almost always indicates a slowly enlarging parasellar / cavernous-sinus lesion.
• Intracavernous carotid aneurysm, cavernous-sinus meningioma, schwannoma, or pituitary macroadenoma.
• Mandates urgent contrast MRI + MRA.
redFlags: Aberrant regeneration without preceding CN III palsy → intracavernous aneurysm or tumor; urgent MRI/MRA.
Primary aberrant regeneration → almost always non-ischemic, compressive cause; surgical consideration.
New oculomotor synkinesis months after apparent recovery → tumor compression.
Pupillary involvement with aberrant regeneration → exclude aneurysm.
investigations: ## After congenital CN III palsy
• None additional — pattern is from birth and stable.
## After acquired CN III palsy
• Document the workup of the prior CN III palsy if previously obtained (imaging, vascular study, etc.).
• If aberrant regeneration develops in a patient previously diagnosed as "ischemic" CN III palsy → re-image; the original etiology must have been compressive.
## Primary aberrant regeneration (no preceding palsy)
• All patients require neuroimaging to rule out a slowly enlarging compressive lesion or aneurysm.
• MRI brain with contrast, thin cuts through the cavernous sinus + MRA of the circle of Willis.
• If MRA equivocal and aneurysm suspicion high → CT angiography or catheter angiography.
actionSteps: Detailed neuro-ophthalmic exam documenting all aberrant findings.
MRI/MRA brain with contrast to exclude aneurysm, tumor, or cavernous sinus lesion.
Neurosurgical evaluation if compressive lesion identified.
No specific ocular therapy; observe if benign cause identified.
treatment: ## Underlying disease
• Treat the causative compressive lesion (aneurysm clipping/coiling, tumor resection, pituitary management).
• No specific ocular therapy; aberrant regeneration itself is not reversible.
## Diplopia management
• Defer surgical strabismus correction until the deviation is stable for ≥6 months.
• Prisms for small stable vertical/horizontal deviations.
• Strabismus surgery for larger angles once stable.
## Ptosis repair
• Defer until lid position is stable (≥6 months of stable measurements).
• Levator resection or frontalis sling depending on residual levator function.
• Counsel that the synkinetic lid movements will not be eliminated by surgery.
followUp: MRI/MRA brain and orbits — aberrant regeneration implies compressive lesion (aneurysm, meningioma, schwannoma, pituitary) not microvascular.
Neurosurgical referral if compressive lesion identified.
Strabismus/prism management for persistent diplopia; usually surgery deferred until pattern stable (~6 months).
Rule out congenital aberrant regeneration (present from birth, distinct pattern) in children.
differentials: Synkinesis from aberrant facial nerve regeneration
pearl: Lid elevation on adduction or pupillary constriction on downgaze after a CN III palsy is aberrant regeneration — this is a compressive lesion fingerprint and mandates MRI/MRA, never seen with microvascular etiology.
willsRef: Wills Eye §10.6 (Aberrant Regeneration of the Third Cranial Nerve)

name: Acanthamoeba keratitis
symptoms: Severe ocular pain — characteristically out of proportion to clinical findings (hallmark).
Foreign body sensation, redness, and photophobia.
Chronic course: symptoms often persist for several weeks before correct diagnosis.
findings: ## Early (epithelial)
• Epitheliitis with pseudodendrites and epithelial ridges.
• Whorls and diffuse subepithelial microcysts.
## Intermediate
• Radial keratoneuritis: Perineural inflammation along corneal nerves (earliest pathognomonic finding).
• Subepithelial infiltrates.
## Late (3–8 weeks)
• Ring-shaped stromal infiltrate (Wessely ring): Pathognomonic in advanced cases.
• Corneal vascularization and potential perforation.
## Anterior segment
• Eyelid swelling and circumcorneal conjunctival injection.
• Anterior chamber cell and flare with minimal discharge.
etiology: ## Causative agent
• Free-living protozoan (Acanthamoeba spp.) found in tap water, soil, and swimming pools.
• Exists as trophozoites and highly resistant cysts (resistant to most topical agents).
## Risk factors
• Contact lens wear (dominant factor): Especially with tap-water rinsing or swimming in lenses.
• Non-contact lens cases: Ocular trauma involving soil or water exposure.
redFlags: Contact lens wearer + severe pain out of proportion to exam findings.
Ring infiltrate, pseudodendrites, or perineuritis in a non-responsive keratitis.
Misdiagnosis as HSV: Steroid use without amoebicidal coverage accelerates damage.
Diagnosis delay >2–3 weeks significantly worsens visual prognosis.
investigations: ## Smears and staining
• Corneal scrapings for Gram, Giemsa, PAS, and Calcofluor white stains.
## Culture
• Non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay.
• Culture of contact lenses and storage cases.
## Imaging and biopsy
• Confocal microscopy: May show double-walled cysts in vivo.
• Corneal biopsy: Indicated if clinical suspicion is high but cultures are negative.
actionSteps: Perform corneal scraping for culture (non-nutrient agar + E. coli) and confocal microscopy.
Initiate intensive topical biguanides alternating hourly.
Urgent referral to a cornea specialist.
Strictly avoid prescribing topical anesthetics for home use.
treatment: ## Topical biguanides (first-line)
• Polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) 0.02% q1h.
• Chlorhexidine 0.02% q1h.
## Topical diamidines
• Propamidine isethionate 0.1% drops q1h.
• Dibromopropamidine isethionate 0.15% ointment.
## Systemic therapy
• Oral Antifungals: Itraconazole (400mg load, then 100-200mg daily), Voriconazole, or Ketoconazole.
• Oral Miltefosine: 50mg BID/TID for 4 weeks (Monitor BMP, LFTs, and pregnancy status).
## Adjunctive & surgical
• Avoid topical steroids until confirmed amoebicidal kill.
• Penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) for medical failure or perforation.
followUp: • Acute: Daily to every-other-day exams.
• Maintenance: Slow taper over 6–12 months as clinical response allows.
• Monitoring: Watch for ring infiltrates, scleritis, limbitis, cataract, and glaucoma.
pearl: Severe pain + ring infiltrate + CL wearer exposed to water = Acanthamoeba. Often misdiagnosed as HSV due to pseudodendrites; radial keratoneuritis is the earliest pathognomonic finding.

name: Acquired Cataract
symptoms: ## Visual decline
• Slowly progressive, painless blurring or vision loss over months to years.
• May be unilateral or bilateral.
## Glare & photophobia
• Significant in bright sunlight or from oncoming headlights at night.
## Color & contrast
• Reduced contrast sensitivity and altered color perception (yellowing).
• No true dyschromatopsia (unlike optic neuropathies).
## Morphology-specific
• Nuclear: Blurs distance > near.
• PSC: Profound glare and difficulty reading (near vision worse).
• Cortical: Glare is the dominant complaint.
findings: ## Core findings
• Any opacification/discoloration of the crystalline lens; diagnosed on slit-lamp.
• Screening finding: Dimming or disruption of the red reflex on retinoscopy.
## The RAPD rule
• Cataract alone does not cause an RAPD.
• If RAPD is present: Search for optic nerve or extensive retinal pathology before surgery.
## Morphology types
• Nuclear sclerotic (NS): Yellow-to-brown central lens discoloration. Causes "second sight" (myopic shift allowing patients to read without glasses).
• Posterior subcapsular (PSC): Plaque-like granular opacity on the posterior capsule; "snowflake" shadow on retroillumination. Symptoms may paradoxically improve with dilation.
• Cortical: Radial/spoke-like wedge opacities; vacuoles and water clefts on slit-lamp.
## Diagnostic subtypes
• Sunflower: Copper deposition; pathognomonic for Wilson disease.
• Christmas-tree: Iridescent multicolored opacities; classic for Myotonic Dystrophy.
• Oil-droplet: Central opacity on retroillumination; classic for Galactosemia.
• Snowflake: White AS/PSC opacities; associated with acute juvenile diabetes.
• Glaukomflecken: Gray-white anterior subcapsular opacities from prior acute angle-closure.
• Rosette / Vossius ring: Trauma-induced opacities and pigment imprints.
## Advanced stages
• Mature: Totally white lens.
• Hypermature / Morgagnian: Liquefied cortex; nucleus may sink in the capsular bag.
• Intumescent: Swollen lens; high risk for phacomorphic angle-closure.
## Pre-surgical evaluation
• Slit-lamp grading (LOCS III) and endothelial health (guttata).
• Assessment of zonular status (pseudoexfoliation, phacodonesis) and pupil size.
• Macular OCT to exclude comorbidities (AMD, ERM, DME).
• Biometry: IOL Master/Lenstar for axial length, K, and ACD.
etiology: ## Primary cause
• Age-related degeneration (most common).
## Trauma
• Penetrating or blunt injury (rosette cataract), electric/lightning injury, or copper IOFB.
## Toxic / drug-induced
• Steroids: Any route (topical, oral, inhaled, IVT); dose-dependent.
• Long-term miotics or phenothiazines.
## Ocular co-morbidities
• Chronic anterior uveitis, prior vitrectomy, radiation, or retinitis pigmentosa.
## Metabolic & systemic
• Diabetes: Early onset or acute snowflake cataracts.
• Wilson disease (sunflower) or myotonic dystrophy (christmas-tree).
• Hypocalcemia (iridescent cortical changes) or galactosemia (oil-droplet).
• Syndromic: Down syndrome, NF2 (PSC), atopic dermatitis (anterior shield).
redFlags: ## Rapid or unilateral progression
• In young patients: Rule out diabetes, steroid use, trauma, or uveitis.
• Unilateral: Rule out intraocular tumor or occult hemorrhage; obtain B-scan if view is obscured.
## Pediatric PSC
• Promptly rule out steroid exposure, NF2, or chronic uveitis.
## Secondary glaucoma
• Mature/intumescent lens leading to phacomorphic angle-closure or phacolytic glaucoma.
## Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis
• Triad: Stellate KPs, iris heterochromia/atrophy, and rapid PSC; no posterior synechiae.
## Steroid risks
• Fluocinolone implants: ~43% cataract and ~75% IOP-elevation rate at 2 years.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• BCVA (distance/near), manifest refraction, and pupillary exam.
• Glare testing: Essential when BCVA is ≥20/30 but patient reports functional decline.
## Dilated exam
• Slit-lamp for LOCS III grading, zonular health, and dilation quality.
• Fundus exam: Exclude macular/optic nerve disease limiting visual potential.
## Imaging & biometry
• B-scan ultrasonography: Required if fundus view is obscured.
• Macular OCT: To exclude AMD, ERM, or DME.
• IOL Master/Lenstar: For IOL power calculation.
• Endothelial cell count: If corneal guttata are present.
actionSteps: Confirm functional impact on daily life (driving, reading, work).
Perform macular OCT/B-scan to ensure vision loss is solely attributable to cataract.
Obtain pre-operative biometry and discuss IOL options (monofocal, toric, EDOF).
Address comorbidities (corneal disease, glaucoma) before proceeding to surgery.
Plan for phacoemulsification with foldable IOL.
treatment: ## Surgical indications
• Symptomatic visual disability affecting daily activities.
• Lens-induced disease (phacolytic/phacomorphic glaucoma, uveitis).
• Requirement for fundus view to treat other pathologies (e.g., diabetic retinopathy).
## Procedure
• Modern small-incision phacoemulsification with foldable IOL insertion.
• Usually outpatient, ~15 mins, >95% success rate in suitable eyes.
## IOL options
• Monofocal: Fixed for distance or near.
• Toric: Corrects regular astigmatism.
• Multifocal / EDOF: Provides extended range; requires counseling on dysphotopsia.
followUp: ## Pre-operative
• Update refraction; monitor annually until visually significant.
• Discussion of surgery when functional needs are no longer met.
## Post-operative
• Standard schedule: Day 1, week 1, and month 1.
• Final refraction and IOL performance assessment at 1 month.
pearl: Cataract surgery is refractive surgery — biometry, IOL selection, and patient expectations are as critical as surgical technique. Dissatisfaction usually stems from unmet refractive goals rather than complications.

name: Acute Conjunctivitis
symptoms: ## General
• Red eye (conjunctival hyperemia) and foreign body sensation.
• Eyelids sticking or crusting on awakening.
• Duration <4 weeks (otherwise consider chronic conjunctivitis).
## Viral (adenovirus)
• Itching, burning, tearing, and gritty sensation.
• Recent URI or sick contact; often starts unilateral then involves fellow eye.
## Bacterial
• Mucopurulent yellow-green discharge with minimal itching.
## Allergic
• Bilateral itching (hallmark symptom).
• Watery discharge and history of allergies.
## Chlamydial & gonococcal
• Chlamydial: Chronic (>3 weeks) unilateral discharge in sexually active adult.
• Gonococcal: Hyperacute (12–24h) copious purulent discharge, chemosis, and lid edema.
findings: ## Viral (adenovirus / EKC)
• Follicular reaction on lower tarsus (pale dome-shaped nodules).
• Tender ipsilateral preauricular lymph node (nearly pathognomonic).
• Watery/serous discharge (crusted but not purulent on awakening).
• EKC specific: Fine intraepithelial microcysts (early); subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) appearing 1–2 weeks later; tarsal pseudomembranes in severe cases.
## Bacterial
• Papillary reaction (cobblestone upper tarsus).
• Mucopurulent yellow-green discharge; eyelids matted shut.
• Preauricular lymph node absent (key bedside discriminator from viral).
## Special etiologies
• Herpes simplex: Unilateral follicles, preauricular node, and vesicular periocular/lid-margin lesions.
• Hyperacute gonococcal: Copious purulent discharge, marked chemosis, and rapid risk of corneal ulceration/perforation.
• Chlamydial (adult inclusion): Chronic unilateral follicular reaction in a sexually active adult.
etiology: ## Viral
• Adenovirus (most common overall): Serotypes 3, 4, 7 (pharyngoconjunctival fever); Serotypes 8, 19, 37 (epidemic keratoconjunctivitis).
• Herpes simplex: Primary infection in children/young adults.
## Bacterial
• Pediatric: H. influenzae (often with otitis media), S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis.
• Adult: S. aureus (associated with blepharitis), S. epidermidis.
• Hyperacute: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (most aggressive) or N. meningitidis.
## Chlamydial & neonatal
• Chlamydia (Serotypes D–K): Chronic follicular conjunctivitis in sexually active adults.
• Neonatal timeline: Day 1 (chemical), Days 2–5 (gonococcal), Days 5–14 (chlamydial).
## Allergic
• Seasonal or perennial; bilateral itching is pathognomonic.
redFlags: ## Clinical emergencies
• Hyperacute purulent discharge (<24h) → treat as gonococcal (perforation risk).
• Unilateral follicular conjunctivitis >3 weeks → chlamydial until proven otherwise.
• Vesicular lid lesions or dendritic keratitis → herpes simplex (steroids contraindicated).
• Progressive vision loss, corneal infiltrate, or hypopyon → rule out bacterial keratitis or endophthalmitis.
## Infection control
• EKC is highly contagious for 10–14 days; survives on surfaces for weeks.
• Dedicated exam rooms and immediate tonometer/slit-lamp disinfection required.
## Patient instructions
• Stay home from work/school; no shared towels, pillows, or makeup.
• Rigorous hand hygiene and discard any eye drops used during illness.
investigations: ## Clinical evaluation
• History and slit-lamp exam are primary; look for follicles vs. papillae.
• Palpate for preauricular lymphadenopathy.
• Fluorescein staining to check for corneal involvement (SPK, dendrites, ulcer).
## Lab testing
• Gram stain/culture (Chocolate/Thayer-Martin) for hyperacute purulent discharge.
• PCR/NAAT of conjunctival scrapings for suspected chlamydial cases.
• STI workup and partner referral for confirmed gonococcal or chlamydial cases.
actionSteps: Differentiate viral, bacterial, and allergic etiologies by history and physical signs.
Test for gonorrhea (Gram stain) if hyperacute purulent discharge is present.
Prescribe systemic antibiotics and treat partners for gonococcal or chlamydial cases.
Institute strict contact precautions and supportive care for viral/EKC cases.
Refer to ophthalmology if corneal involvement or vision loss occurs.
treatment: ## Viral / EKC
• Supportive: PF artificial tears 4–8×/day and cool compresses.
• Peel pseudomembranes to prevent symblepharon.
• Topical steroids (loteprednol 0.5% QID) only for membranes or visually significant SEIs.
## Bacterial
• Topical trimethoprim/polymyxin B or fluoroquinolone QID for 5–7 days.
• Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for H. influenzae to prevent systemic spread.
## Gonococcal & chlamydial
• Gonococcal: Ceftriaxone 1g IM single dose + Azithromycin 1g PO (for co-existing chlamydia).
• Chlamydial: Azithromycin 1g PO once OR Doxycycline 100mg BID for 7 days.
• Saline irrigation until discharge resolves in gonococcal cases.
## Allergic
• Antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizers (olopatadine, alcaftadine, ketotifen).
• Mild topical steroids (loteprednol 0.2% QID) for severe cases.
## Special conditions
• HSV: Oral acyclovir; no topical steroids without antiviral cover.
• Pediculosis: Mechanical removal of lice/eggs + erythromycin ointment to lid margins TID.
followUp: • Viral/EKC: 2–3 weeks (sooner if using topical steroids).
• Bacterial (nongonococcal): Every 2–3 days initially, then 5–7 days when stable.
• Gonococcal: Daily until improvement, then every 2–3 days.
• On topical steroids: Monitor IOP and taper slowly.
pearl: The key question in red eye is "does the cornea stain?" — pure conjunctivitis has a clear cornea; a staining cornea means keratitis, ulcer, or HSV and requires a completely different treatment path.

name: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Sudden onset of severe eye pain and frontal headache.
• Blurred vision and colored halos around lights.
• Systemic symptoms: Nausea and vomiting (often misdiagnosed as GI illness or migraine).
findings: ## Primary diagnostic signs
• Acutely elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), often 40–80 mmHg.
• Closed angle on gonioscopy in the involved eye.
• Fixed, mid-dilated pupil with a shallow anterior chamber.
## Anterior segment
• Microcystic corneal edema and conjunctival injection (ciliary flush).
• AC cell and flare or iridescent particles.
## Signs of prior attacks
• Glaukomflecken: Small anterior subcapsular lens opacities.
• Iris stromal atrophy.
## Fellow eye
• Narrow or occludable angle (strong anatomic predisposition).
etiology: ## Pupillary block (most common)
• Anteriorly bowed iris against the lens blocks aqueous flow through the pupil.
## Anatomic predisposition
• Shallow AC, narrow angle, short axial length, thick lens, and hyperopia.
• Demographic risks: Advanced age, Asian ancestry, and female sex.
## Precipitants
• Pharmacologic pupil dilation or dim light.
• Medications: Anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, or topiramate (ciliary body swelling).
## Secondary causes
• Plateau iris syndrome, neovascularization, or lens-related issues (phacomorphic/phacolytic).
• Inflammation or posterior segment tumors.
redFlags: • IOP >40 mmHg with corneal edema: Retinal ganglion cell loss progresses within hours.
• Systemic misdiagnosis: Headache, nausea, and vomiting mistaken for migraine or GI distress.
• Fellow eye risk: 40–80% lifetime attack risk mandates prophylactic LPI.
• Vision loss: Ipsilateral amaurotic pupil suggests CRAO complication.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Slit-lamp: Note pupil reactivity, AC depth, lens thickness, and corneal clarity.
• Gonioscopy: Both eyes essential; use topical hyperosmolar agents (glycerin) to clear edema for a better view.
• IOP: Immediate measurement of both eyes.
## Fundus exam
• Look for optic nerve cupping, CRVO, or spontaneous arterial pulsations.
## Imaging
• B-scan ultrasound or UBM if secondary angle closure is suspected.
actionSteps: • Perform immediate IOP measurement and gonioscopy in both eyes.
• Initiate intensive topical medical therapy (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, CAIs, miotics).
• Administer systemic acetazolamide (IV or PO) if IOP is refractory.
• Arrange YAG laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) once the attack is broken and cornea is clear.
treatment: ## Immediate topical therapy
• Beta-blocker: Timolol 0.5% (caution with asthma/COPD).
• Alpha-2 agonist: Brimonidine 1%.
• Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: Dorzolamide 2%.
• Miotic: Pilocarpine 1%.
• Steroid: Prednisolone acetate 1% to reduce inflammation and edema.
• Protocol: 3 rounds of drops separated by 15 minutes.
## Systemic therapy
• Acetazolamide: 500 mg IV or 250–500 mg PO.
• Osmotic agents: Mannitol 1–2 g/kg IV over 45 minutes if refractory (check renal/cardiac status).
## Adjuncts
• Compression gonioscopy: May mechanically open the angle and break the attack.
• AC paracentesis: For immediate IOP reduction in severe refractory cases.
## Definitive treatment
• YAG laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI): The definitive treatment for pupillary block.
• Prophylactic LPI: Required for the fellow eye due to high lifetime risk.
• Lens extraction: For phacomorphic cases once the eye is quiet.
followUp: ## Post-attack
• Recheck IOP at 1 hour post-treatment.
• Evaluate for definitive LPI within 1–5 days once inflammation subsides.
## Long-term
• Baseline visual fields and optic nerve imaging.
• Monitor for chronic angle-closure development.
• Educate patient on avoiding precipitating medications (anticholinergics).
pearl: Acute angle-closure is an emergency often masked by systemic symptoms. Nausea and vomiting can lead to a GI misdiagnosis; always check pupils and IOP in patients with severe headache. Fellow eye LPI is mandatory.

name: Adie (Tonic) Pupil
symptoms: • Difference in pupil size (anisocoria) noticed by patient or others.
• Blurred near vision due to accommodative paresis.
• Photophobia.
• Often asymptomatic.
findings: ## Demographics & presentation
• Classic patient: Young, healthy adult women (ages 20–40).
• Presentation: Acute or subacute unilateral mydriasis; up to 20% become bilateral over time.
## Pupil exam
• Large (mydriatic) and irregular pupil with minimal to no direct light reflex.
• Vermiform (worm-like) movements: Pathognomonic sectoral palsy of the iris sphincter visible at the slit lamp.
## Near response & hallmark
• Light-near dissociation: Poor response to light but present (though slow) response to near.
• Tonic behavior: Slow, sustained constriction with accommodation and very slow redilation when returning to distance viewing.
## Pharmacologic testing
• Denervation supersensitivity: Instill dilute pilocarpine (0.125% or 0.1%) in both eyes.
• Adie pupil constricts briskly within 10–15 minutes; the normal pupil does not react.
## Natural history
• "Little old Adie's": Over years, the pupil progressively becomes smaller (miotic) due to reinnervation and supersensitivity.
• Accommodative paresis: Common at onset; requires assessment for a temporary reading add.
## Systemic associations
• Holmes-Adie syndrome: Tonic pupil + diminished or absent deep-tendon reflexes (usually lower extremity).
• Ross syndrome: Tonic pupil + absent reflexes + segmental anhidrosis (patchy loss of sweating).
etiology: ## Mechanism
• Postganglionic parasympathetic denervation caused by damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves.
## Causes
• Idiopathic (most common): Presumed post-viral inflammation.
• Secondary: Orbital trauma, orbital surgery, or varicella zoster virus (VZV).
• Rare: Early syphilis, paraneoplastic syndromes, giant cell arteritis (GCA), sarcoidosis, Sjögren syndrome, or neurologic Lyme disease.
redFlags: • Sudden unilateral mydriasis without ptosis or diplopia suggests a benign Adie pupil.
• Presence of ptosis or extraocular muscle weakness suggests a CN III palsy (requires urgent imaging for aneurysm).
• Bilateral simultaneous tonic pupils in a young patient warrant an autonomic neuropathy or paraneoplastic workup.
• Tonic pupil in an older adult or with constitutional symptoms requires investigation for GCA or malignancy.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Slit-lamp exam to identify vermiform sectoral iris palsy.
• Assessment of tonic near response and light-near dissociation.
• Systemic check: Test deep-tendon reflexes.
## Pharmacologic confirmation
• Dilute pilocarpine test (0.125%): Constriction of the affected pupil confirms the diagnosis.
## Systemic workup (if atypical)
• Unilateral Adie in a young patient: No further testing; reassurance.
• Bilateral or atypical cases: Consider testing for syphilis (RPR/FTA-ABS), sarcoidosis (ACE), Sjögren syndrome, or paraneoplastic markers.
actionSteps: Perform dilute pilocarpine (0.125%) test to confirm postganglionic denervation.
Assess deep-tendon reflexes to check for Holmes-Adie syndrome.
Provide reassurance; the condition is typically benign and idiopathic.
Exclude CN III palsy by ensuring normal motility and absence of ptosis.
treatment: ## General management
• Reassurance: Most cases are benign and require no intervention.
• Near-vision blur: Prescribe a reading add if accommodative paresis is symptomatic.
## Symptomatic relief
• Photophobia: Dilute pilocarpine 0.125% BID can be used to constrict the pupil.
• Tinted lenses: May help with glare.
## Referrals
• Neurology referral: Indicated for bilateral cases, autonomic symptoms (Ross syndrome), or atypical neurologic findings.
followUp: • No routine imaging is required for typical unilateral presentations.
• Periodic monitoring for the development of bilateral involvement or chronic miosis.
• Long-term management focuses on reading correction as needed.
differentials: CN III palsy (presents with ptosis and motility deficits)
Pharmacologic mydriasis (does not react to 1% pilocarpine)
Argyll Robertson pupils (typically bilateral, miotic, and associated with neurosyphilis)
Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome (associated with upgaze palsy and convergence-retraction nystagmus)
pearl: A large tonic pupil with light-near dissociation in a young woman is almost always Adie's. Confirm with dilute (0.125%) pilocarpine and check deep-tendon reflexes for Holmes-Adie syndrome.

name: Amaurosis Fugax / Transient Visual Loss
symptoms: • Monocular visual loss lasting seconds to minutes (occasionally up to 1–2 hours).
• Complete return to normal vision between episodes.
findings: ## Ocular findings
• Often normal between episodes.
• Visible embolus within a retinal arteriole (Hollenhorst, calcific, or platelet-fibrin).
• Signs of ocular ischemic syndrome (OIS).
## Neurologic findings
• Associated TIA features: Contralateral arm or leg weakness, dysarthria, or aphasia.
etiology: ## Embolic (most common)
• Carotid artery atherosclerosis: The most common source.
• Cardiac: Valvular disease, atrial fibrillation, or endocarditis.
• Aortic arch atherosclerosis.
## Hypoperfusion
• Arteriosclerotic disease anywhere along the aorta-to-globe path.
• Often precipitated by postural changes or cardiac arrhythmias.
## Other causes
• Giant cell arteritis (GCA): Must consider in patients age ≥55.
• Hypercoagulable or hyperviscosity states.
• Rare: Vasospasm or gaze-evoked loss (intraorbital mass compressing the nerve or vessel).
redFlags: • Treat as a TIA: Up to 10% stroke risk within 90 days; 2–5% risk within 48 hours.
• Visible Hollenhorst plaque: Strong indicator of a carotid source.
• Age ≥55 with new monocular loss: Rule out GCA immediately with ESR and CRP.
• Symptomatic carotid stenosis >70%: High risk for stroke; mandates urgent intervention.
investigations: ## Emergent TIA workup
• Emergent stroke-center or ER referral (AHA classifies amaurosis fugax as a TIA).
• Neurology consultation and MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging.
## Ocular examination
• Confrontation visual fields and dilated fundus exam to identify emboli or OIS signs.
## Cardiovascular & imaging
• Carotid duplex Doppler ultrasound (or MRA/CTA).
• ECG and echocardiogram.
• Orbital color Doppler ultrasound (if retrolaminar stenosis is suspected).
## Laboratory testing
• CBC with differential (rule out polycythemia/thrombocytosis), fasting glucose, HbA1c, and lipid profile.
• If age ≥55: Stat ESR, CRP, and platelet count (rule out GCA).
actionSteps: Refer emergently to a stroke center for same-day workup.
Obtain carotid Doppler, ECG, echocardiogram, and brain imaging (CT/MRI).
Initiate antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel) while the workup is in progress.
Consult vascular surgery if symptomatic stenosis >50–70% is identified.
treatment: ## Antiplatelet therapy
• Aspirin 81–325 mg daily or Clopidogrel 75 mg daily (start while workup is ongoing).
## Vascular & cardiac management
• Carotid disease: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) or stenting for high-grade stenosis; medical therapy for low-grade.
• Cardiac disease: Anticoagulation (heparin/warfarin/DOAC) for atrial fibrillation or thrombus.
## Systemic & lifestyle
• High-dose corticosteroids if GCA is confirmed.
• Risk-factor modification: Statin therapy, smoking cessation, and BP/DM control.
• Calcium channel blockers only if vasospasm is confirmed after excluding embolic sources.
followUp: ## Stroke prevention
• Coordinate longitudinal care with neurology, cardiology, and PCP.
• Re-image carotids if symptoms recur.
## Ophthalmic monitoring
• Re-evaluate if new symptoms develop; monitor for permanent retinal artery occlusion.
## Patient education
• Educate on returning immediately for new visual symptoms or focal neurologic signs.
pearl: Amaurosis fugax is an ocular TIA. The risk of a permanent stroke within 48 hours is 2–5%. The ABCD2 score applies. Carotid endarterectomy is indicated if stenosis is >70%. Never dismiss a transient visual episode.

name: Angioid Streaks
symptoms: • Frequently asymptomatic in early stages.
• Decreased central vision or metamorphopsia if choroidal neovascularization (CNV) develops.
• Sudden, profound vision loss following minor blunt ocular trauma.
findings: ## Pathophysiology
• Crack-like dehiscences in a thickened, calcified, and brittle Bruch membrane.
• Linear breaks radiating from the peripapillary region caused by normal ocular pulsations.
## Clinical appearance
• Bilateral, jagged, reddish-brown to gray linear bands radiating from a peripapillary ring (spoke-wheel pattern).
• Peau d'orange: Orange-peel mottling of the temporal mid-periphery (indicates diffuse Bruch thickening).
• Salmon spots: Peripheral chorioretinal scars from prior small subretinal hemorrhages.
• Optic disc drusen (commonly associated with pseudoxanthoma elasticum).
## Systemic associations (pepsi mnemonic)
• P: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (most common; skin "plucked-chicken" appearance, GI bleeding, atherosclerosis).
• E: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility).
• P: Paget disease of bone (enlarged skull, elevated alkaline phosphatase).
• S: Sickle cell disease and other hemoglobinopathies (thalassemia, spherocytosis).
• I: Idiopathic (approximately 50% of cases).
## Complications
• Choroidal neovascularization (CNV): Develops in 70–80% of patients; typically Type 2 with high risk of disciform scarring.
• Traumatic Bruch rupture: Minor trauma can cause catastrophic subretinal hemorrhage.
## Imaging
• Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): More sensitive than ophthalmoscopy; shows diffuse damage beyond visible streaks.
• Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Early hyperfluorescence (window defects) and late staining; detects active CNV.
• OCT / OCTA: Essential for monitoring subretinal fluid and detecting non-exudative CNV.
etiology: ## Genetic & metabolic
• Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE): ABCC6 gene mutation; involves skin flexures and vascular calcification.
• Paget disease of bone: Late-stage manifestation; associated with bone remodeling and hearing loss.
• Hemoglobinopathies: Sickle cell, thalassemia, and hereditary spherocytosis.
## Connective tissue
• Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: Collagen abnormality leading to fragile tissues.
## Other
• Idiopathic: No identifiable systemic cause in half of the population.
• Rare: Acromegaly, hemochromatosis, lead poisoning, and senile elastosis.
redFlags: • Central distortion or new scotoma: Suggests active maculopathy or CNV.
• History of blunt trauma: High risk for extensive Bruch rupture even with trivial force.
• Systemic symptoms: GI bleeding or cardiovascular disease (especially in PXE).
• Peripheral neovascularization: May require panretinal photocoagulation.
investigations: ## Ocular evaluation
• Dilated fundus exam with macular biomicroscopy.
• OCT: Perform at every visit to screen for subretinal/intraretinal fluid.
• FAF and OCTA: Preferred for diagnosis and non-invasive surveillance.
## Systemic workup
• Skin biopsy (Verhoeff stain) if PXE is suspected.
• Hemoglobin electrophoresis (especially in patients of African descent).
• Serum alkaline phosphatase and urinary calcium (rule out Paget disease).
• Cardiology and GI referral for patients confirmed with PXE.
actionSteps: Obtain systemic workup for PXE, Paget disease, and sickle cell disease.
Counsel patient to avoid contact sports and wear polycarbonate safety lenses at all times.
Initiate anti-VEGF therapy immediately for active macular CNV.
Provide Amsler grid for daily home monitoring.
treatment: ## CNV management
• Intravitreal anti-VEGF (aflibercept, ranibizumab, or bevacizumab) is first-line therapy.
• Avoid PDT or focal laser due to poor outcomes and increased scarring.
## Trauma prevention
• Mandatory use of polycarbonate safety eyewear.
• Strict avoidance of contact sports and high-impact activities.
## Systemic management
• Referral to internist or specialist (genetics, cardiology, dermatology) for underlying conditions.
followUp: • Regular OCT monitoring: Required at every visit for CNV surveillance.
• Immediate urgent follow-up for any new symptoms of distortion or vision drop.
• Periodic systemic review to manage cardiovascular or skeletal complications.
differentials: Lacquer cracks (pathologic myopia; radiate from staphyloma)
Traumatic choroidal rupture (concentric to optic disc)
pearl: Angioid streaks are a "biopsy of the body" found in the eye. Remember the PEPSI mnemonic: pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Ehlers-Danlos, Paget disease, sickle cell, and idiopathic.

name: Aphakic Bullous Keratopathy/Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy
symptoms: • Decreased visual acuity.
• Ocular pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation.
• Photophobia and redness.
• History of prior cataract surgery in the affected eye.
findings: ## Corneal signs
• Corneal edema in an aphakic or pseudophakic eye.
• Presence of epithelial bullae and Descemet folds.
• Subepithelial haze, scarring, or neovascularization (chronic disease).
## Associated signs
• Cystoid macular edema (CME) frequently coexists.
• Pre-existing endothelial guttae (Fuchs dystrophy) may be present in either eye.
• Retained lens fragments or malpositioned intraocular lens (IOL).
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Endothelial cell density falls below critical threshold (~500 cells/mm²).
• Failure of pump-leak equilibrium leads to stromal and epithelial edema.
## Surgical trauma
• Prolonged phacoemulsification time or mechanical trauma (iris prolapse, vitreous loss).
• Complicated ACIOL placement or retained lens fragments.
## Mechanical contact
• ACIOL risk: Rigid PMMA haptics chronically abrading endothelium.
• Vitreous-cornea touch or subluxed IOL contacting the endothelium.
## Pre-existing & chronic factors
• Endothelial compromise (Fuchs guttae, prior surgery, uveitis, glaucoma).
• UGH syndrome: Chronic inflammation from IOL malposition accelerates cell loss.
redFlags: • Painful bullae: Requires bandage contact lens and hypertonic saline.
• Vitreous-cornea touch: Mandates anterior vitrectomy plus keratoplasty.
• Recurrent infection: Risk with bandage lenses; requires prophylactic antibiotics.
• Concurrent CME: Must be addressed to optimize visual potential after surgery.
investigations: ## Slit lamp exam
• Fluorescein staining: To detect ruptured bullae or denuded epithelium.
• IOL/Vitreous assessment: Look for malposition or vitreous-cornea touch.
• Fellow eye: Screen for Fuchs endothelial dystrophy.
## Ancillary testing
• IOP measurement: Manage associated glaucoma.
• Macular OCT: To exclude or document concurrent CME (may be limited by haze).
actionSteps: Initiate hypertonic saline (5% drops/ointment) for symptomatic edema.
Apply bandage contact lens with prophylactic topical antibiotics for pain.
Refer for endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK/DSAEK) if vision is limited.
Prepare for anterior vitrectomy if vitreous contact is present.
treatment: ## Medical management
• Sodium chloride 5% drops QID and ointment QHS.
• Lower IOP if elevated.
• Avoid prostaglandins and epinephrine derivatives (CME risk).
## Management of ruptured bullae
• Topical antibiotics (erythromycin/bacitracin q2h) and cycloplegics (cyclopentolate 1% TID).
• Bandage soft contact lens for comfort.
• Chronic pain: Anterior stromal micropuncture or excimer PTK.
## Surgical intervention
• Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK/DSAEK): First-line definitive surgery.
• Penetrating keratoplasty (PK): Reserved for cases with significant stromal scarring.
• Combined procedures: IOL repositioning/exchange or vitrectomy as required.
followUp: • Ruptured bullae: Every 1–3 days until improvement; then every 5–7 days until healed.
• Routine: Every 1–6 months depending on symptom severity.
pearl: A hazy cornea in the setting of an IOL is pseudophakic bullous keratopathy. Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK/DSAEK) is the definitive treatment and restores vision more effectively than full-thickness PK.
willsRef: Wills Eye §4.27 (Aphakic Bullous Keratopathy/Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy)

name: Argyll Robertson Pupils
symptoms: • Usually asymptomatic; often an incidental finding on examination.
• Concurrent neurologic symptoms: Sensory ataxia, gait disturbance, or dementia (suggests tabes dorsalis or general paresis).
findings: ## The classic triad
• Small pupils: Typically <3 mm in ambient light.
• Irregular and miotic: Often "pinpoint" or notched with loss of fine iris detail.
• Light-near dissociation: Absent or sluggish constriction to bright light with brisk, normal constriction to near (accommodation-convergence).
## Diagnostic rules
• Intact vision: True Argyll Robertson (AR) requires intact afferent visual function; failure to react to light in a blind eye is a simple afferent pupillary defect, not AR.
• Bilateralism: Almost always bilateral, though often asymmetric. Unilateral cases suggest alternate etiologies.
• Poor dilation: Pupils remain stubbornly small in the dark (blunted sympathetic response) and respond poorly to mydriatic drops.
## Anatomic localization
• Rostral dorsal midbrain (pretectal/periaqueductal area).
• Damage interrupts light-reflex fibers before they reach Edinger-Westphal nuclei, while sparing the more ventral near-response pathway.
## Clinical significance
• Pathognomonic for neurosyphilis: Specifically tabes dorsalis and late/tertiary CNS syphilis.
• Fixed deficit: Pupil findings do not reverse with penicillin treatment; they represent a permanent midbrain scar.
etiology: ## Neurosyphilis (tertiary disease)
• Tabes dorsalis, general paresis, or meningovascular syphilis.
• Increased prevalence in HIV-coinfected populations.
## Pathways involved
• Interruption of the dorsal light-reflex fibers in the midbrain.
• Sparing of the ventral accommodation-convergence fibers.
redFlags: • Bilateral miotic pupils with light-near dissociation: mandates immediate syphilis serology (RPR, FTA-ABS).
• AR pupils are a clinical marker of CNS involvement: mandates lumbar puncture regardless of RPR titer.
• HIV coinfection: requires aggressive evaluation for neurosyphilis.
• Atypical features (unilateral or mydriatic): reconsider differentials like Adie pupil or Parinaud syndrome.
investigations: ## Pupillary evaluation
• Slit-lamp exam: assess iris detail and confirm sectoral stability.
• Near response testing: ask patient to shift focus from a distant target to a near finger.
## Ocular screening
• Slit lamp: check for interstitial keratitis (late syphilis stigma).
• Dilated fundus: look for luetic chorioretinitis, "salt-and-pepper" retinopathy, or optic atrophy.
## Laboratory testing
• Treponemal-specific assays: FTA-ABS or TP-PA.
• Non-treponemal assays: RPR or VDRL.
• HIV testing (mandatory).
## Lumbar puncture
• Required for all suspected neurosyphilis cases.
• CSF analysis: cell count, protein levels, and CSF-VDRL.
actionSteps: Obtain syphilis serology (RPR, FTA-ABS) and HIV testing.
Perform lumbar puncture if serology is positive to evaluate for neurosyphilis.
Refer to infectious disease for IV penicillin G therapy.
Coordinate neurology evaluation for tabes dorsalis or cognitive decline.
treatment: ## Neurosyphilis regimen
• IV aqueous penicillin G: 18–24 million units/day for 10–14 days.
• Penicillin desensitization: preferred over alternatives if patient is allergic.
## Monitoring
• Serologic titers (RPR): follow quarterly; expect a fourfold decline within 6–12 months.
• Pupil monitoring: educate patient that pupillary findings are unlikely to reverse.
followUp: • Coordination with infectious disease and neurology for longitudinal care.
• Repeat RPR testing post-treatment to confirm therapeutic response.
• No specific ocular treatment needed for the pupils themselves.
differentials: • Adie (tonic) pupil: typically dilated/mydriatic, not miotic.
• Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome: associated with upgaze palsy and convergence-retraction nystagmus.
• Severe bilateral afferent visual loss (optic nerve/retinal disease).
• Sarcoidosis or amyloidosis involving the pretectum.
pearl: Small, irregular, miotic pupils that accommodate but do not react to light are the signature of neurosyphilis. This finding mandates CSF analysis and IV penicillin regardless of the RPR titer.

name: Band Keratopathy
symptoms: • Decreased vision (if deposits cross the visual axis).
• Foreign body sensation and irritation.
• Visible whitening of the cornea (cosmetic concern).
• Recurrent erosions if the calcium plaque fractures.
• May be asymptomatic in early stages.
findings: ## Morphology
• Horizontal gray-white opaque band of calcium hydroxyapatite deposits.
• Located at the level of the Bowman layer and anterior stroma.
• Restricted to the interpalpebral fissure (CO₂ evaporation raises local pH, favoring precipitation).
• "Swiss-cheese" appearance: Lucid round holes within the band representing corneal nerve penetration sites.
## Progression
• Begins as peripheral opacities at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions.
• Spreads centripetally to form a complete horizontal band.
• "Lucid interval": A thin strip of clear cornea separates the band from the limbus (limbal vessels buffer pH).
## Ocular associations
• Chronic uveitis: Especially JIA-associated uveitis (classic pediatric finding).
• Chronic corneal edema / bullous keratopathy.
• Silicone oil in the anterior chamber.
• Phthisis bulbi and end-stage glaucoma.
• Interstitial keratitis (ghost vessels).
etiology: ## Ocular causes (most common)
• Chronic inflammation (uveitis) or surface disease.
• Chronic corneal edema.
• Phthisis bulbi.
• Silicone oil retention after retinal surgery.
• Prolonged use of phosphate-buffered eye drops.
## Systemic causes (hypercalcemia/hyperphosphatemia)
• Hyperparathyroidism.
• Vitamin D intoxication.
• Sarcoidosis.
• Renal failure (hyperphosphatemia).
• Multiple myeloma and metastatic bone disease.
• Milk-alkali syndrome.
• Paget disease of bone.
redFlags: • Chronic uveitis (especially JIA): Inflammation must be controlled before surgical chelation.
• Systemic hypercalcemia: Requires medical workup to address potentially serious underlying renal or parathyroid disease.
• Rapidly progressive disease in young patients: Rule out toxic exposure or phosphate-drop overuse.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to document the extent of the plaque and identify associated ocular disease.
• Assess both eyes (often bilateral in systemic disease).
## Systemic workup (if no ocular cause)
• Serum calcium (corrected for albumin), ionized calcium, and phosphate.
• Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and 25-OH Vitamin D.
• Renal function tests (BUN, creatinine).
• ACE and lysozyme (if sarcoidosis suspected).
• SPEP (if multiple myeloma suspected).
actionSteps: Identify and treat the underlying cause (e.g., control uveitis or systemic hypercalcemia).
Initiate conservative therapy with lubricants for mild irritation.
Perform EDTA chelation for vision-limiting or severely symptomatic plaques.
Maintain long-term surveillance for recurrence or associated complications.
treatment: ## Conservative management
• Mild cases: Preservative-free artificial tears and ointments.
• Recurrent erosions: Bandage soft contact lens and prophylactic topical antibiotics.
## Surgical (EDTA chelation)
• Indications: Visual obstruction or persistent foreign body sensation.
• Procedure: Epithelial debridement followed by application of 3–4% disodium EDTA until calcium clears.
• Post-op care: Antibiotic ointment, cycloplegics, and bandage contact lens until epithelialized.
## Adjunctive therapy
• Excimer laser PTK: Used for residual stromal scarring or to manage recurrent erosions.
followUp: ## Post-surgical
• Every few days until the epithelial defect heals.
## Long-term
• Every 3–12 months depending on symptoms and stability.
• Monitor for recurrence (common if underlying cause persists); chelation can be repeated.
pearl: Calcium deposits in the Bowman layer point to either chronic intraocular inflammation (think JIA) or systemic hypercalcemia. Chelation with EDTA clears the cornea but does not address the underlying systemic or ocular trigger.

name: Behçet Disease
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Sudden onset of bilateral decreased vision.
• Floaters and photophobia.
• Mild to moderate ocular pain.
findings: ## Disease overview
• Relapsing-remitting multisystem vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes.
• Classic demographic: "Silk Road" ancestry (Middle Eastern, Mediterranean, Central Asian, Japanese).
• Typically affects young adults (ages 20–40); more severe in men.
• Strong association with HLA-B51.
## Diagnostic criteria (international study group)
• Mandatory requirement: Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers (≥3 episodes in 12 months).
• Plus at least two of the following:
• Recurrent genital ulcers (heal with scarring).
• Ocular lesions (uveitis or retinal vasculitis).
• Skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, or acneiform papules).
• Positive pathergy test (papule formation 24–48 hours after sterile needle stick).
## Ocular features
• Bilateral, simultaneous, non-granulomatous panuveitis.
• Shifting hypopyon: Anterior chamber pus that moves with head position (hallmark sign).
• Occlusive retinal vasculitis: Affects both arteries and veins simultaneously.
• Ischemic signs: Retinal hemorrhages, branch vessel occlusions, and capillary nonperfusion.
• Complications: Cystoid macular edema (CME), vitreous hemorrhage, neovascular glaucoma, and optic atrophy.
• Prognosis: High risk of blindness within 5 years if not aggressively treated.
## Systemic features
• Vascular: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary artery aneurysms (major cause of death).
• Neurologic (Neuro-Behçet): Meningoencephalitis and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
• GI: Ulcerations throughout the tract mimicking inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
• Articular: Seronegative non-erosive arthritis of the knees and ankles.
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Idiopathic systemic vasculitis with a genetic predisposition (HLA-B51).
• Characterized by neutrophil hyperreactivity and widespread vascular inflammation.
## Ancestry
• High prevalence in populations along the historic Silk Road trading route.
redFlags: • Shifting hypopyon in a young patient of Mediterranean or Middle Eastern descent.
• Occlusive retinal vasculitis: Requires immediate systemic immunosuppression (steroids alone are insufficient).
• Hemoptysis: May indicate a life-threatening pulmonary artery aneurysm.
• Neuro-Behçet symptoms: Any new neuropsychiatric changes or focal neurologic deficits.
investigations: ## Infectious rule-out
• Syphilis serology (RPR/FTA-ABS) and TB screening (PPD or IGRA).
• Chest X-ray or CT (to rule out sarcoidosis and TB).
• Serum ACE and lysozyme.
## Immunologic & genetic
• HLA-B51: Supportive evidence, especially in endemic populations.
• Pathergy test: Skin hypersensitivity reaction to minor trauma.
## Clinical monitoring
• ESR and CRP: Often elevated during systemic flares.
actionSteps: Initiate urgent systemic immunosuppression (steroids + steroid-sparing agents).
Refer to rheumatology, dermatology, and neurology for multidisciplinary management.
Document baseline retinal status with photography and fluorescein angiography.
Counsel patient on the high risk of bilateral involvement and systemic vascular events.
treatment: ## Pharmacotherapy
• Systemic corticosteroids: Used as bridging therapy for acute flares.
• Anti-TNF agents (First-line for posterior uveitis): Infliximab or adalimumab.
• Steroid-sparing agents: Azathioprine, cyclosporine, or interferon-alpha.
## Complication management
• Manage neovascularization with panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).
• Aggressive control of intraocular pressure if secondary glaucoma develops.
## Long-term care
• Multidisciplinary coordination between ophthalmology and rheumatology.
• Lifelong surveillance is mandatory due to the relapsing-remitting nature.
followUp: • Active disease: Monthly examinations and lab monitoring.
• Stable disease: Every 3 months.
• Vigilance: Monitor for new vascular or neurologic symptoms at every visit.
pearl: A shifting hypopyon with occlusive retinal vasculitis in a young patient of Silk Road descent is Behçet until proven otherwise. HLA-B51 supports the diagnosis, and early use of anti-TNF biologics has transformed the prognosis.

name: Best Disease (Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy)
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Decreased central visual acuity.
• Metamorphopsia or central scotoma.
• Frequently asymptomatic; often identified during routine exams or family screening.
findings: ## Hallmark morphology
• Round, yellow-orange "egg-yolk" (vitelliform) subretinal foveal deposit.
• Typically 1–2 disc diameters in size and bilateral.
• Material consists of lipofuscin situated between the photoreceptor outer segments and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
## Five clinical stages
• Stage 1 (previtelliform): Normal fundus but abnormal EOG (identifies carriers).
• Stage 2 (vitelliform): Classic "egg-yolk intact" lesion; vision often remains 20/20–20/40.
• Stage 3 (pseudohypopyon): Yellow material layers inferiorly within subretinal fluid.
• Stage 4 (vitelliruptive): "Scrambled egg" appearance as material breaks up; vision begins to decline.
• Stage 5 (atrophic/cicatricial): Macular atrophy or fibrosis; mimics dry AMD. Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) develops in ~20%.
## Electrophysiologic signature
• EOG: Markedly abnormal with an Arden ratio <1.5 (hallmark sign).
• ERG: Normal full-field response (photoreceptor function is preserved).
• Diagnostic triad: Abnormal EOG + normal ERG + vitelliform lesion.
## Imaging characteristics
• OCT: Hyperreflective subretinal material between the neurosensory retina and RPE.
• FAF: Intense hyperautofluorescence of the "yolk" (fresh lipofuscin); fades with atrophy.
## Genetics and associations
• Autosomal dominant with variable penetrance (BEST1/VMD2 mutation).
• Associated with short axial length (hyperopia) and increased risk of angle-closure glaucoma.
## Differential: adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform (AOFVD)
• Presents later (4th–6th decade) with smaller lesions (1/3 disc diameter).
• Characterized by a normal EOG and often PRPH2 mutations.
etiology: ## Genetic basis
• Bestrophin-1 mutation (BEST1/VMD2 gene).
• Affects a calcium-activated chloride channel on the basolateral RPE membrane.
## Pathomechanism
• RPE dysfunction leads to lipofuscin accumulation between the RPE and photoreceptors.
• Progressive stages lead from lipofuscin "yolk" deposits to eventual macular atrophy or scarring.
redFlags: • Sudden vision drop or metamorphopsia in stages 2–5: Indicates secondary CNV.
• Abnormal EOG Arden ratio (<1.5) with normal ERG: Confirms diagnosis.
• Family history of macular disease: Warrants cascade screening of relatives.
• Shallow anterior chambers: High risk for angle-closure glaucoma.
investigations: ## Functional testing
• EOG: Essential to confirm Arden ratio <1.5.
• ERG: Full-field testing to confirm normal photoreceptor function.
## Structural imaging
• OCT: To monitor for subretinal fluid or CNV development.
• FAF: To evaluate lipofuscin distribution and lesion activity.
## Genetic confirmation
• BEST1 gene mutation analysis.
actionSteps: Perform EOG to establish Arden ratio and genetic testing for BEST1.
Initiate annual monitoring for asymptomatic patients or early vitelliform stages.
Provide Amsler grid for home monitoring to detect CNV early.
Conduct family screening and provide genetic counseling.
Refer for anti-VEGF therapy if CNV is identified.
treatment: ## Management strategy
• Observation: Standard for early stages with stable vision.
• Vision rehabilitation: Low-vision aids for advanced atrophic disease.
## Complication care
• Intravitreal anti-VEGF (aflibercept, ranibizumab, or bevacizumab): First-line for secondary CNV.
• No current medical or surgical therapy alters the natural history of the dystrophy.
followUp: • Annual examinations including OCT, FAF, and visual acuity checks.
• Urgent follow-up for any new metamorphopsia (Amsler grid monitoring).
• Lifelong surveillance for secondary glaucoma and CNV.
pearl: The definitive signature of Best disease is a markedly reduced Arden ratio on EOG (<1.5) despite a normal full-field ERG, paired with the classic "egg-yolk" foveal lesion.

name: Blebitis
symptoms: • Red eye and mucous discharge localized to the bleb area (early).
• Aching pain, photophobia, and decreased vision (late).
• History of prior trabeculectomy or filtering surgery (months to years ago).
findings: ## "White-on-red" appearance (pathognomonic)
• Milky white, opaque filtering bleb (inflammatory material) contrasted against intensely hyperemic conjunctiva.
• High diagnostic value: Distinguishes blebitis from simple conjunctivitis in a glaucoma patient.
## Bleb characteristics
• Microhypopyon may be visible within bleb loculations under high magnification.
• Purulent material may collect inside the bleb or leak through a Seidel-positive microperforation.
• Seidel test: Mandatory check to identify the portal of bacterial entry.
• Intraocular pressure (IOP): Usually low or normal due to active aqueous outflow through the infected bleb.
## Wills bleb-infection grading
• Grade 1 (Blebitis proper): Infected bleb and conjunctival injection only; quiet anterior chamber (AC), no vitritis.
• Grade 2: Grade 1 findings plus AC cells/flare ± hypopyon; no vitritis.
• Grade 3 (Bleb-associated endophthalmitis): Grade 1 findings plus vitreous involvement (vitritis).
## Substrate and risk
• Most common substrate: Avascular, thin, or cystic blebs (frequently associated with mitomycin-C use).
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Localized infection of a filtering bleb following glaucoma surgery.
• Primary organisms: Streptococci (S. pneumoniae), Staphylococci, and H. influenzae.
## Predisposing factors
• Late bleb leaks, contact lens wear, and chronic topical antibiotic use.
• Thin, avascular bleb morphology (mitomycin-C augmentation).
redFlags: • White milky bleb + AC reaction + vision loss → bleb-associated endophthalmitis.
• Late-onset infections (months/years post-op) are often fulminant Streptococcus.
• Any trabeculectomy patient with a red eye requires urgent assessment.
• Delaying treatment (even by hours) significantly worsens visual prognosis.
investigations: ## Slit-lamp biomicroscopy
• High-magnification check for microhypopyon within bleb loculations.
• Seidel test: To identify bleb leaks/portals of entry.
• Vitreous assessment: To rule out Grade 3 endophthalmitis.
## Microbiology
• Culture the bleb surface and any leaking discharge.
• Anterior chamber tap for culture in Grade 2 or higher disease.
## Imaging
• B-scan ultrasound: If posterior view is obscured and vitritis is suspected.
actionSteps: Initiate intensive topical fortified antibiotics immediately; the window to prevent endophthalmitis is measured in hours.
Escalate to tap-and-inject (intravitreal antibiotics) if AC or vitreous involvement is present (Grade 2–3).
Obtain cultures from the bleb surface and any active leakage.
Add cycloplegics (atropine 1% or cyclopentolate 1%) for comfort and to prevent synechiae.
Stop topical aqueous suppressants and admit to hospital if medication adherence is uncertain.
Coordinate urgent co-management with glaucoma and vitreoretinal specialists.
treatment: ## Grade 1 (blebitis)
• Fortified Vancomycin (25–50 mg/mL) alternating with fortified Ceftazidime (50 mg/mL) every 30 minutes for 24 hours.
• Loading dose: One drop of each every 5 minutes for 4 doses.
• Alternative: Fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin or besifloxacin) every 1 hour.
## Grade 2 (AC involvement)
• Same topical regimen as Grade 1 plus cycloplegics.
• Add oral fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin 400 mg daily or ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID).
• Maintain a very low threshold for escalation to tap-and-inject.
## Grade 3 (endophthalmitis)
• Immediate vitreous tap and intravitreal injection (vancomycin 1 mg + ceftazidime 2.25 mg).
• Early pars plana vitrectomy is strongly preferred; bleb-associated cases are often fulminant.
followUp: ## Monitoring
• Daily examination until the infection is resolving.
• Hospitalization is often indicated for hourly drop administration.
## Escalation triggers
• Any clinical worsening at 6–12 hours mandates escalation to tap-and-inject.
• Discovery of new vitritis triggers full endophthalmitis protocol.
pearl: A "white milky" bleb set against an angry red conjunctiva is blebitis—intensive topicals can save the eye, but if untreated, the infection enters the eye within hours.

name: Blepharitis/Meibomitis
symptoms: ## Ocular discomfort
• Itching, burning, and foreign body sensation.
• Chronic tearing and mild ocular pain.
## Eyelid signs
• Redness (erythema) of the eyelid margins.
• Crusting around the lashes upon awakening.
## Timing
• Symptoms typically worse on awakening (helps distinguish from dry eye syndrome, which often worsens later in the day).
findings: ## Lid margin & lashes
• Crusting, scurf (collarettes), and cylindrical sleeves around the lashes.
• Cylindrical collarettes ("cylindrical dandruff"): Waxy cuffs at the lash base, pathognomonic for Demodex blepharitis.
• Meibomian gland findings: Capped, plugged, or obstructed orifices with turbid, "toothpaste-like" secretions upon expression.
• Telangiectasia of the posterior lid margin.
## Anterior segment
• Conjunctival injection and swollen, erythematous eyelids.
• Superficial punctate keratitis (SPK) and mild mucous discharge.
## Corneal sequelae
• Marginal corneal infiltrates (staph hypersensitivity).
• Corneal pannus, phlyctenules, or neovascularization (especially in rosacea).
## Systemic signs
• Rosacea: Facial telangiectasia, malar flushing, papules, or rhinophyma.
• Seborrhea: Scalp dandruff or greasy skin.
etiology: ## Anterior blepharitis (lash line)
• Staphylococcal: Toxin-mediated inflammation; associated with collarettes and type III/IV hypersensitivity (marginal infiltrates).
• Seborrheic: Associated with seborrheic dermatitis; characterized by greasy scurf.
## Posterior blepharitis (MGD)
• Meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD): Obstruction and altered lipid composition leading to evaporative dry eye.
## Demodex blepharitis
• Mite infestation (D. folliculorum in follicles; D. brevis in glands).
• Diagnosis confirmed by pathognomonic cylindrical collarettes or microscopy.
## Associated conditions
• Ocular Rosacea: Strong association with MGD and corneal inflammatory signs.
• Chalazion/Hordeolum: Acute manifestations of chronic gland obstruction or staph infection.
redFlags: • Unilateral, chronic, or recurrent "chalazion" at the same site: Mandates full-thickness biopsy to rule out sebaceous gland carcinoma (masquerade tumor).
• Rosacea with corneal phlyctenules: Requires aggressive systemic intervention.
• Staph hypersensitivity with marginal ulcers: Requires combined steroid/antibiotic therapy.
• Refractory pediatric blepharitis: Consider Demodex as a potential cause.
investigations: ## Slit-lamp exam
• Detailed inspection of lid margins for telangiectasia, meibomian plugging, and cylindrical dandruff.
• Evaluation of tear break-up time (TBUT) and corneal staining patterns.
## Ancillary testing
• Meibography: To quantify meibomian gland dropout or distortion.
• Microscopy: Epilation of lashes to confirm Demodex mites if clinical suspicion is high.
• Culture: Reserved for refractory or atypical cases to rule out resistant staph.
actionSteps: Initiate daily lid hygiene (warm compresses, lid massage, and scrubs).
Apply topical antibiotic ointment (erythromycin or bacitracin) to lid margins at bedtime.
Consider oral doxycycline (50–100 mg BID) for rosacea or moderate-to-severe MGD.
Treat Demodex with lotilaner 0.25% or tea tree oil if cylindrical collarettes are present.
treatment: ## Lid hygiene (cornerstone)
• Warm compresses (5–10 min BID–QID) followed by lid massage.
• Eyelid scrubs (commercial wipes or diluted baby shampoo) twice daily.
## Topical medications
• Antibiotics: Erythromycin ointment or azithromycin gel q.h.s.
• Antibiotic/Steroid combinations: Tobramycin/dexamethasone BID–TID for refractory meibomitis (monitor IOP).
• Surface inflammation: Cyclosporine or lifitegrast for associated dry eye.
## Oral antibiotics
• Doxycycline: 100 mg daily for 1–2 weeks, then tapered for 3–6 months (anti-MMP/anti-lipase effect).
• Alternatives: Oral azithromycin or low-dose isotretinoin for refractory rosacea.
## Demodex-specific therapy
• Lotilaner 0.25% (Xdemvy) BID for 6 weeks (direct mite kill via GABA-Cl inhibition).
• Tea tree oil: 50% weekly in-office or daily terpinen-4-ol scrubs.
## Procedural options
• Thermal pulsation (LipiFlow), Intense Pulsed Light (IPL), or manual gland expression.
followUp: • Chronic management: Reinforce that symptoms are managed, not eliminated.
• Routine: Every 3–6 months to adjust therapy and reinforce hygiene.
• Aggressive monitoring for secondary dry eye and corneal complications.
differentials: Dry eye syndrome (symptoms typically worsen later in day)
Sebaceous gland carcinoma (if unilateral and refractory)
pearl: Blepharitis is a chronic condition; emphasize to the patient that treatment manages symptoms rather than providing a cure. Always biopsy unilateral refractory blepharitis to rule out sebaceous gland carcinoma. Cylindrical collarettes are pathognomonic for Demodex.

name: Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Sectoral blind spot or visual field defect (usually unilateral).
• Painless vision loss if the macula is involved.
• Often asymptomatic if the occlusion is peripheral.
• Acute or subacute onset; frequently noticed upon awakening.
findings: ## Clinical appearance
• Wedge-shaped sector of superficial flame-shaped (NFL) and dot/blot hemorrhages.
• Hemorrhages respect the horizontal raphe; the apex points to the site of occlusion.
• Most common location is the superotemporal quadrant (~60%).
• Dilated, tortuous downstream veins with cotton-wool spots (precapillary microinfarction).
• Chronic signs: Hard exudates, leaking microaneurysms, and collateral shunt vessels.
## Pathophysiology
• Occurs at an arteriovenous (A/V) crossing where an atherosclerotic artery compresses a vein sharing the same adventitial sheath.
• Mechanical compression + turbulent flow + stasis leads to thrombus formation.
## Macular edema (ME)
• Most common cause of vision loss; occurs in ~60% of symptomatic cases.
• Confirmed on OCT by cystoid spaces or serous detachment.
• Disorganization of retinal inner layers (DRIL) correlates with a poor visual prognosis.
## Ischemia & neovascularization
• Ischemic threshold: ≥5 disc diameters of capillary non-perfusion on widefield FA.
• Neovascularization (NVE): 40% risk in ischemic cases, typically at the border of perfused retina.
• High risk of vitreous hemorrhage (~60%) if NVE is left untreated.
etiology: ## Primary mechanism
• Arteriovenous (A/V) crossing compression (thickened artery compresses underlying vein).
## Systemic risk factors
• Hypertension (single strongest association).
• Diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia.
• Glaucoma (associated with disc-level vascular architecture changes).
• Smoking.
## Atypical presentations
• If young (<50), bilateral, or recurrent: Consider hyperviscosity (myeloma, polycythemia), antiphospholipid syndrome, or inflammatory vasculitis.
redFlags: • Macular edema with vision loss: Requires prompt anti-VEGF or steroid intervention.
• Retinal neovascularization (NVE): High risk for vitreous hemorrhage; requires sector PRP.
• Bilateral or young patient: High suspicion for systemic hypercoagulable or inflammatory disease.
• Sudden worsening of vision: Rule out conversion to ischemic status or new macular edema.
investigations: ## Ocular imaging
• OCT: Quantify macular edema and assess ellipsoid zone integrity.
• Widefield fluorescein angiography (FA): Identify the 5 DD ischemic threshold and locate NVE.
• OCT angiography: Non-invasive monitoring of capillary perfusion.
## Systemic workup
• Blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and lipid profile.
• CBC, platelets, and PT/PTT.
## Specialized testing (young/atypical cases)
• Antiphospholipid antibodies, homocysteine, and ANA/ESR/CRP.
• SPEP/IPEP (rule out Waldenström or myeloma).
• Carotid Doppler if concurrent neurologic symptoms are present.
actionSteps: Perform BP check and order labs (lipids, glucose, CBC).
Obtain OCT to evaluate for macular edema.
Order widefield FA to determine ischemia and check for neovascularization.
Initiate anti-VEGF therapy or steroids for vision-threatening macular edema.
Apply sector PRP for active retinal neovascularization.
treatment: ## Macular edema management
• Anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab): Gold standard/first-line therapy.
• Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex): Effective alternative, especially in pseudophakic eyes.
• Grid laser: Now secondary to anti-VEGF; used for non-center-involving edema.
## Neovascularization management
• Sector panretinal photocoagulation (PRP): Target the non-perfused territory identified on FA.
• Anti-VEGF: Adjunct to clear vitreous hemorrhage and facilitate laser delivery.
## Systemic management
• Aggressive control of hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
• Smoking cessation.
followUp: • Schedule: Monthly for 6 months, then every 3 months for 2 years.
• Monitoring: Repeat OCT for macular edema and dilated exam for peripheral NVE.
• Transition: Move to treat-and-extend anti-VEGF protocols once macular edema is stabilized.
differentials: Retinal artery macroaneurysm (localized hemorrhage and exudates)
Branch retinal artery occlusion (retinal whitening, minimal hemorrhage)
pearl: The superotemporal quadrant is most commonly involved due to high A/V crossing density. While the prognosis is generally better than CRVO (~50% reach 20/40), macular edema is the primary vision threat and warrants early anti-VEGF treatment.

name: Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Abrupt, unilateral, painless visual change.
• Sectoral visual field loss corresponding to the affected area.
• May report preceding episodes of amaurosis fugax.
findings: ## Retinal appearance
• Superficial whitening and opacification along the distribution of the affected branch artery.
• Retinal edema within the ischemic sector.
• Possible cotton-wool spots in the involved area.
## Vascular changes
• Narrowed branch retinal artery with "boxcarring" or segmentation of the blood column.
• Presence of emboli: Hollenhorst (bright, yellow-white cholesterol crystals), calcific, or platelet-fibrin.
etiology: ## Primary mechanism
• Embolic occlusion of a retinal arteriole branch.
## Source of emboli
• Carotid atherosclerosis: The most common source.
• Cardiac sources: Valvular disease, endocarditis, or atrial fibrillation.
• Aortic arch atherosclerosis.
## Systemic risk factors
• Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and smoking.
• Less common: Vasculitis (GCA, SLE), hypercoagulable states, or sickle cell disease.
redFlags: ## Stroke equivalency
• BRAO is a retinal stroke equivalent; mandates immediate investigation for an embolic source.
• Hollenhorst plaque at a bifurcation strongly indicates a carotid source; requires urgent Doppler.
• Bilateral or recurrent BRAOs suggest cardiac embolism or Susac syndrome.
• Patients age ≥55: Must rule out giant cell arteritis (GCA) with stat labs.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Dilated fundus exam to identify sectoral retinal whitening and emboli.
• Macular OCT: Focal inner retinal hyperreflectivity (acute) followed by inner layer thinning (chronic).
• Fluorescein angiography (FA): Shows delayed arterial filling in the affected branch.
## Systemic workup
• Carotid Doppler/CTA and echocardiography to identify the embolic source.
• Cardiovascular risk assessment: Blood pressure, lipids, and HbA1c.
• If age ≥55: Stat ESR, CRP, and platelet count.
• Consider hypercoagulability panel in young or recurrent cases.
actionSteps: Refer emergently to an ED or stroke center for a full systemic workup.
Obtain carotid Doppler, ECG, and echocardiogram within 24 hours.
Screen for GCA (ESR/CRP) in all patients age ≥55.
Initiate antiplatelet therapy as per stroke-prevention guidelines following imaging.
treatment: ## Systemic management
• No proven acute ocular treatment; focus is on systemic workup and secondary stroke prevention.
• Optimize cardiovascular risk factors (BP, lipids, glucose control).
## Complication care
• Anti-VEGF therapy for macular edema if vision is affected.
• Sector laser photocoagulation if retinal neovascularization develops (rare).
• Low-vision rehabilitation for persistent visual field defects.
followUp: ## Coordination
• Longitudinal follow-up with PCP, cardiology, and the stroke team for risk modification.
## Ophthalmic schedule
• Re-examine at 1 week, then monthly for 3 months.
• Monitor for rare complications like neovascularization.
pearl: BRAO = embolic stroke until proven otherwise. Hollenhorst plaques (bright, yellow-white cholesterol crystals at vessel bifurcations) are pathognomonic for carotid emboli. Full cardiovascular workup is mandatory — same risk of stroke as CRAO.

name: Candida Retinitis/Endophthalmitis
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Decreased vision and floaters.
• Ocular pain.
• Often bilateral involvement.
## Clinical context
• Recent hospitalization or major abdominal/GI surgery (e.g., perforated viscus, pancreatitis).
• Immunocompromised state (e.g., malignancy, transplant, HIV, chemotherapy).
• Presence of indwelling lines/catheters (hyperalimentation, hemodialysis, PICC/TPN).
• History of intravenous (IV) drug use.
findings: ## Pathophysiology
• Hematogenous seeding of Candida (usually C. albicans) from candidemia.
• Fungi reach the eye via choroidal vasculature as septic emboli.
## Stage 1 — chorioretinitis
• Isolated fluffy, creamy-white to yellow-white deep retinal/chorioretinal lesions.
• Typically 1/4–1 disc diameter in size, scattered around the posterior pole.
• Minimal or no vitritis; treatable with systemic antifungals alone.
## Stage 2 — endophthalmitis
• Lesions break through the internal limiting membrane (ILM) into the vitreous.
• Pathognomonic "string of pearls" or "cotton balls": Fluffy fungal aggregates on vitreous strands.
• Associated vitritis, AC cell/flare, and hypopyon.
• Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers (Roth-spot-like).
## IDSA screening guideline
• Every patient with candidemia requires a dilated fundus exam within 1 week of positive blood culture.
• Repeat exam at 2 weeks if the initial check is negative.
• Screening is mandatory regardless of symptoms, as ocular involvement is often asymptomatic.
## Risk groups
• Patients on long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics or total parenteral nutrition (TPN).
• Premature neonates (NICU patients).
• Patients with burns, prolonged neutropenia, or diabetes.
etiology: ## Causative organisms
• Candida species: C. albicans (most common), glabrata, parapsilosis, krusei, or tropicalis.
## Primary mechanisms
• Hematogenous spread from candidemia seeding the choroid and retina.
## Risk factors
• Indwelling central venous or hemodialysis catheters.
• Intravenous drug use.
• Prolonged hospitalization and broad-spectrum antibiotic use.
• Major abdominal/GI surgery with contamination.
redFlags: • Candidemia mandates a dilated fundus exam within 1 week (asymptomatic screening).
• Fluffy white retinal lesions + vitritis + "string of pearls" = Candida endophthalmitis.
• Echinocandins (caspofungin, etc.) have poor ocular penetration and are inadequate as monotherapy for endophthalmitis.
• Delaying treatment can lead to permanent vision loss even if systemic infection is managed.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Skin check for IV drug injection track marks.
• Serial dilated funduscopic exams (initial within 72 hours, repeat at 2 weeks).
## Microbiology
• Blood, urine, and catheter-tip fungal cultures.
• Vitreous biopsy with smear, culture, and PCR (definitive diagnosis).
• Note: Blood cultures may be negative at the time ocular findings appear.
## Imaging & labs
• B-scan ultrasound: Identifies vitritis and fungal balls if the posterior view is obscured.
• OCT: Shows hyperreflective inner retinal or vitreous infiltrates.
• Baseline CBC, renal function, and liver function tests.
actionSteps: Obtain blood/urine cultures and remove all indwelling catheters/lines.
Consult infectious disease (ID) for co-management of disseminated infection.
Initiate systemic oral or IV antifungals (fluconazole or voriconazole).
Administer intravitreal antifungals (amphotericin B or voriconazole) if vitritis is present.
Arrange urgent pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) for severe vitritis or diagnostic specimen collection.
treatment: ## Chorioretinitis (no vitritis)
• Systemic therapy alone is usually sufficient.
• Fluconazole (for C. albicans) or Voriconazole (broad coverage, excellent ocular penetration).
## Endophthalmitis (with vitritis)
• Combined systemic and intravitreal antifungal therapy.
• Intravitreal: Amphotericin B (5–10 µg/0.1 mL) or Voriconazole (50–100 µg/0.1 mL).
• Urgent PPV for diagnostic specimen, clearing opacities, or poor medical response.
## Duration & source control
• Minimum 4–6 weeks of therapy; often extends to 3 months.
• Mandatory removal of all offending indwelling hardware/catheters.
followUp: ## Monitoring
• Weekly examinations for the first month, then monthly until resolution (2–3 months).
• Coordination with ID to monitor for other metastatic foci of infection.
• Surveillance of the fellow eye and repeat blood cultures to confirm clearance.
differentials: Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis (rapid progression, high pain)
Toxoplasmosis (headlight in fog near pigmented scar)
pearl: A fluffy chorioretinal lesion in a patient with candidemia is Candida chorioretinitis — systemic fluconazole or voriconazole often suffices if there is no vitritis; vitritis needs intravitreal antifungals and often vitrectomy.

name: Cavernous Sinus and Associated Syndromes (Multiple Ocular Motor Nerve Palsies)
symptoms: • Diplopia (secondary to multiple ocular motor nerve palsies).
• Eyelid droop (ptosis).
• Pain or numbness in the forehead (V1) or cheek (V2).
• Proptosis and chemosis.
• Headache or altered mental status.
• Pulsatile "whooshing" sound (characteristic of fistula).
findings: ## Localization principles
• The cavernous sinus is the only site where CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI, and sympathetics can be injured by a single lesion.
• Signature sign: Unilateral CN VI palsy + Horner syndrome (sympathetics travel briefly with CN VI here).
• V1/V2 involvement: Ipsilateral forehead/cheek numbness distinguishes cavernous sinus disease from orbital disease (orbit does not involve V2).
## Anatomic syndromes
• Superior Orbital Fissure (SOF): Multiple cranial nerve palsies without V2 involvement.
• Orbital Apex: SOF pattern + Optic Neuropathy (decreased acuity, APD, and proptosis).
## Carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF)
• Dilated "corkscrew" episcleral vessels and pulsatile proptosis.
• Barrow Type A: High-flow (direct ICA); sudden onset, often post-traumatic.
• Barrow Types B/C/D: Low-flow (dural branches); insidious onset, often in hypertensive women over 50.
• Audible bruit over the globe or temple.
• Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) due to raised episcleral venous pressure.
## Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis
• Life-threatening infection (often S. aureus) spreading from the face, sinuses, or orbit.
