• Rapidly becomes bilateral; presents with fever, malignant proptosis, and altered consciousness.
## Mucormycosis (zygomycosis)
• Acute, painful ophthalmoplegia in immunocompromised or diabetic (DKA) patients.
• Black necrotic eschar on the nasal turbinates or palate is pathognomonic.
## Pituitary apoplexy
• Sudden headache, bilateral ophthalmoplegia, and bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression).
• Associated with hypotension and acute cortisol deficiency.
## Tolosa-Hunt syndrome
• Idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus or SOF.
• Painful ophthalmoplegia with a dramatic response to steroids (<48 hours).
etiology: ## Vascular
• Carotid-cavernous fistula (direct or dural).
• Intracavernous ICA aneurysm (rupture leads to CCF).
• Cavernous sinus thrombosis (septic or aseptic).
## Neoplastic
• Local invasion: Pituitary adenoma, meningioma, craniopharyngioma.
• Perineural spread: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma.
• Distant metastasis: Breast, lung, or lymphoma.
## Inflammatory & infectious
• Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous inflammation).
• Fungal: Mucormycosis (associated with DKA/immunosuppression).
• Viral: Varicella zoster virus (can produce palsies and light-near dissociated pupils).
• Systemic: Sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and IgG4-related disease.
redFlags: • Painful ophthalmoplegia + proptosis + fever → septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.
• Acute painful ophthalmoplegia in DKA patient → mucormycosis; requires emergent ENT consult.
• Sudden "thunderclap" headache + bilateral palsies → pituitary apoplexy; requires stat MRI and steroids.
• Pulsatile proptosis + bruit → carotid-cavernous fistula.
• Multiple palsies involving V1/V2 → mandates urgent neuroimaging of the cavernous sinus.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Ocular exam: Motility, pupils (look for Horner or light-near dissociation), and exophthalmometry.
• Physical exam: Auscultate globe/temple for bruit; inspect nasal/palatal mucosa for eschar.
• Sensory check: V1 and V2 distribution (forehead and cheek).
## Imaging
• MRI brain and cavernous sinus (thin cuts) with gadolinium (gold standard).
• MRV/CT venogram: If cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected.
• MRA/CTA: For aneurysm or fistula evaluation.
• Orbital color Doppler: Checks for reversed flow in the superior ophthalmic vein (fistula).
• Catheter angiography: Definitive diagnosis and treatment for fistulas.
## Laboratory
• CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood cultures (if septic thrombosis suspected).
• Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and electrolytes (if mucormycosis suspected).
• ANA, ANCA, and ACE for inflammatory/vasculitis screening.
actionSteps: Order emergent MRI/MRA of the brain and orbits with attention to the cavernous sinus.
Obtain stat ENT consult and nasal endoscopy if mucormycosis is suspected.
Initiate high-dose systemic steroids and neurosurgical consult for pituitary apoplexy.
Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and anticoagulation for septic thrombosis.
Refer to interventional neuroradiology for CCF embolization.
treatment: ## Septic thrombosis & mucormycosis
• CST: Long-term IV antibiotics (covering S. aureus) and anticoagulation.
• Mucormycosis: Emergent surgical debridement (often exenteration) and IV liposomal amphotericin B.
## Vascular lesions
• CCF: Endovascular embolization is the definitive treatment.
• Aneurysm: Neurosurgical or endovascular repair.
## Inflammatory & neoplastic
• Tolosa-Hunt: High-dose oral steroids with slow taper.
• Pituitary apoplexy: Immediate IV steroids and neurosurgical decompression.
• Tumors: Biopsy, oncology referral, and potentially radiation therapy.
## Supportive care
• Manage exposure keratopathy (lubricants, moisture chambers, tarsorrhaphy).
• Prisms or strabismus surgery for stable diplopia.
• Medical management of secondary glaucoma.
followUp: • Weekly to monthly monitoring during the acute phase depending on etiology.
• Chronic surveillance for recurrence (Tolosa-Hunt) or progression (tumor).
• Coordination with neurosurgery, neurology, and infectious disease specialists.
• Long-term management of intraocular pressure and diplopia.
differentials: Myasthenia gravis (no sensory loss, pupil spared)
pearl: Painful ophthalmoplegia with V1/V2 numbness and a fixed pupil in a diabetic patient is mucormycosis until proven otherwise. A unilateral CN VI palsy paired with Horner syndrome localized specifically to the cavernous sinus.

name: Central Serous Chorioretinopathy
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Central scotoma, blurred or dim vision (acuity 20/20 to 20/200).
• Metamorphopsia: Distorted vision.
• Micropsia: Objects appear smaller than actual size.
• Acquired hyperopia due to anterior displacement of the retina.
• Faded color perception and reduced contrast sensitivity.
## Laterality
• Usually unilateral at onset.
• Bilateral involvement is more common in older patients and may be asymptomatic.
findings: ## Demographics
• Typically young to middle-aged men (ages 20–50; M:F ≈ 6:1).
• Often associated with a "Type A" personality (driven, competitive, stressed).
• Note: Suspect wet AMD or choroidal tumor in patients over 60 or women.
## Clinical exam
• Localized, dome-shaped serous detachment of the neurosensory retina in the macula.
• Absence of subretinal blood or hard exudates (presence suggests CNV).
• Possible associated serous pigment epithelial detachments (PEDs).
• Focal RPE mottling may indicate prior episodes.
## Imaging (OCT & angiogaphy)
• OCT: Subretinal fluid (hypo-reflective dome) and thickened choroid (pachychoroid).
• EDI-OCT: Choroidal thickness often >390 μm (normal ~260 μm).
• Fluorescein Angiography: "Inkblot" (common) or "smokestack" (10–20%, pathognomonic) leakage patterns.
• ICG Angiography: Shows diffuse choroidal hyperpermeability.
• OCTA: Essential in older/atypical patients to rule out secondary CNV.
## Clinical course
• Acute: 80–90% of episodes resolve spontaneously within 3–4 months.
• Chronic: Fluid persisting beyond 3–4 months leads to progressive outer-retinal atrophy.
• Recurrence: Occurs in 30–50% of cases.
etiology: ## Primary mechanism
• Choroidal hyperpermeability and RPE dysfunction.
• Part of the "pachychoroid spectrum" of retinal disorders.
## Exogenous steroids (critical risk)
• Odds ratio for exposure is ~37; includes all routes (oral, inhaled, nasal spray, topical creams, intra-articular).
• Steroid discontinuation is the most vital management step.
## Lifestyle and systemic factors
• High endogenous cortisol (stress, Cushing syndrome).
• Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): Up to 61% of CSCR patients; screen with STOP-BANG.
• Pregnancy: Typically occurs in the third trimester; resolves postpartum.
• Other: Sympathomimetics, PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil), and methamphetamine.
redFlags: • Chronic fluid (>3 months): Risk of permanent photoreceptor loss and RPE decompensation.
• Recent steroid use: Must be tapered or discontinued immediately.
• CSCR in patients over 50: High risk for occult CNV; mandates OCTA/ICG.
• Subretinal blood or hard exudates: Rule out neovascular AMD or polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV).
investigations: ## Clinical and bedside
• Amsler grid: To map and monitor the area of visual distortion.
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: Use 60/90-D lens to evaluate for fluid, PEDs, or optic pits.
• Dilated fundus exam: Rule out peripheral RRD or choroidal tumors.
## Multimodality imaging
• OCT: Demonstrate subretinal fluid and monitor for resolution.
• OCTA: Mandatory for older patients to distinguish chronic CSCR from secondary CNV.
• FA/ICG: For diagnostic uncertainty or to localize a leak before laser treatment.
## Systemic screening
• STOP-BANG questionnaire: To screen for obstructive sleep apnea.
• Cortisol levels: If Cushing syndrome is clinically suspected.
actionSteps: Perform a meticulous history for steroid use (nasal, topical, or inhaled).
Discontinue or taper any exogenous corticosteroids if medically feasible.
Obtain baseline OCT and consider OCTA for patients >50 years old.
Observe for 3–4 months in acute cases, as most resolve spontaneously.
Treat sleep apnea if identified via screening.
treatment: ## Observation (first-line)
• Standard for the first 3–4 months of an acute episode.
• Focus on removing triggers (steroids, stress, caffeine).
## Intervention for chronic/recurrent disease
• Photodynamic therapy (PDT): Half-dose/half-fluence verteporfin is the gold standard (superior to anti-VEGF).
• Micropulse (subthreshold) diode laser: To the site of the leak.
• Conventional focal laser: Restricted to extrafoveal leaks identified on FA.
## Pharmacologic and secondary management
• Anti-VEGF: Indicated if secondary CNV develops.
• Mineralocorticoid antagonists (eplerenone/spironolactone): Randomised trials (VICI/SPECTRA) showed no benefit over placebo; not recommended as primary therapy.
• Adjuncts: Rifampin or melatonin (limited evidence).
followUp: • Acute: Monitor every 4–6 weeks until fluid resolves.
• Chronic (>3 months): Transition to active treatment (PDT/laser).
• Surveillance: Multimodal imaging at each visit for chronic/recurrent cases to detect RPE atrophy or secondary CNV.
• Home monitoring: Provide Amsler grid for daily use.
pearl: Always ask about steroid use by all routes (nasal sprays, skin creams, inhalers)—steroids have an odds ratio of 37 for CSCR. Mineralocorticoid antagonists (eplerenone) are ineffective despite their theoretical rationale. Half-dose PDT is the gold standard for chronic cases.

name: Chemical Burn
symptoms: • Acute severe pain, burning, and tearing.
• Intense photophobia and blurred vision following a chemical splash.
• History of exposure to specific agents (e.g., bleach, oven cleaner, ammonia, battery acid, lime, or plaster).
findings: ## Corneal epithelial status
• Ranges from scattered superficial punctate keratopathy (SPK) to total epithelial sloughing.
• Focal or diffuse epithelial loss.
## Limbal stem cells
• Limbal ischemia (blanching of perilimbal vessels): The key prognostic sign.
• Mild burns show no significant blanching; severe burns show extensive ischemia.
## Ocular surface & anterior segment
• Conjunctival epithelial defects, chemosis, hyperemia, and hemorrhages.
• Mild eyelid edema and anterior chamber (AC) reaction.
• First- and second-degree periocular skin burns with potential lash loss.
etiology: ## Alkali burns (most dangerous)
• Agents: Ammonia, lye, lime, magnesium hydroxide, and plaster.
• Mechanism: Saponify lipid membranes, allowing deep and rapid penetration.
## Acid burns
• Agents: Sulfuric, hydrofluoric, and hydrochloric acids.
• Mechanism: Cause coagulation necrosis, which typically limits deeper penetration.
• Exception: Hydrofluoric acid behaves like an alkali and penetrates deeply.
## Severity classification
• Assessed by Roper-Hall or Dua classification systems.
• Based on the degree of limbal stem-cell ischemia and corneal clarity.
• Stem cell loss leads to chronic surface failure, conjunctivalization, and neovascularization.
redFlags: • Alkali burns: Continue to damage the eye long after exposure due to deep penetration.
• Limbal ischemia: Blanching at presentation predicts a poor visual prognosis.
• Grade IV burns: Opaque cornea with no view of iris; high risk of perforation and blindness.
• Priority rule: Immediate irrigation must start before checking pH or performing an exam.
investigations: ## Immediate assessment
• Litmus paper check: Wait 5–10 minutes after irrigation stops before checking pH (normal 7.0–7.4).
## Clinical examination
• Slit lamp exam with fluorescein staining only after irrigation is complete.
• Eyelid eversion: Crucial to search for retained caustic particulate matter in the fornices.
• Diagramming: Document all epithelial defects and ulcerations.
## Tonometry
• IOP measurement: Use Tono-Pen, pneumotonometer, or rebound tonometer if the cornea is distorted.
• Gentle palpation if instruments are unavailable.
## Grading
• Formally document the Roper-Hall or Dua grade to guide management.
actionSteps: Initiate immediate copious irrigation with saline or Ringer lactate for at least 30 minutes.
Continue irrigation until the ocular surface pH is neutral (7.0–7.4).
Evert eyelids and sweep fornices to remove all caustic particles.
Assess visual acuity and IOP only after pH normalization.
Refer promptly to ophthalmology after initial stabilization.
treatment: ## Acute irrigation protocol
• Copious irrigation with saline or Ringer lactate; tap water is a valid emergency alternative.
• Never attempt to neutralize an alkali with an acid (or vice versa) due to thermal injury risk.
• Use IV tubing connected to the irrigating solution and an eyelid speculum.
• Sweep fornices with a moistened cotton-tipped applicator to remove necrotic tissue or particles.
## Medical management
• Cycloplegics: Cyclopentolate 1–2% or homatropine 5% for pain and inflammation; avoid phenylephrine.
• Lubrication: Frequent (q1–2h) preservative-free artificial tears.
• Antibiotics: Topical fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim/polymyxin B q.i.d.; erythromycin ointment for large defects.
• Steroids: Prednisolone acetate 1% (up to q1–2h) for the first 7–14 days; must taper early to prevent melting.
## Adjunctive systemic therapy
• Collagenolysis prevention: Doxycycline 100 mg b.i.d. and Vitamin C 1,000 mg daily.
• Ascorbate 10% topical q1h for alkali burns (caution in renal patients).
• Acetylcysteine 10–20% (collagenase inhibitor) if healing is poor.
## IOP control
• Use oral acetazolamide (250 mg q.i.d.) or topical beta-blockers.
• Avoid alpha-agonists (due to vasoconstriction).
## Surgical & advanced care
• Amniotic membrane (e.g., ProKera) or scleral shells for severe burns.
• Emergency patch graft or tissue adhesive for corneal melting/perforation.
• Long-term: Limbal stem cell transplantation (LSCT) if surface fails to re-epithelialize.
followUp: ## Acute phase
• Daily follow-up until the corneal epithelium is fully healed.
• Monitor IOP, corneal clarity, and signs of stromal melting closely.
## Maintenance phase
• Taper topical steroids strictly after 10–14 days; switch to medroxyprogesterone 1% if needed.
• Twice-daily fornix sweeping to lyse forming symblepharon.
## Long-term monitoring
• Watch for corneal neovascularization, dry eye, and limbal stem-cell failure.
• Chronic lubrication and potential tarsorrhaphy for persistent surface disease.
pearl: Alkali burns are an ophthalmic emergency that keeps damaging the eye after exposure. Limbal ischemia (blanching) is the single most important prognostic sign. Always evert the lids to find hidden caustic particles.

name: Chloroquine/Hydroxychloroquine Toxicity
symptoms: • Often asymptomatic in early stages (detected only on screening).
• Decreased central vision and abnormal color vision (late-stage).
• Reported paracentral scotomas.
• Reduced dark adaptation.
findings: ## Bull's-eye maculopathy (late-stage)
• Annular ring of parafoveal RPE atrophy surrounding a preserved foveal island.
• Represents end-stage, irreversible anatomic injury and photoreceptor loss.
## Structural signs (sd-OCT & faf)
• "Flying-saucer sign": Parafoveal loss of the ellipsoid zone (EZ) with preservation beneath the fovea, making the central EZ look like a hovering saucer.
• Outer nuclear layer thinning typically precedes EZ loss.
• Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): Early perifoveal hyperautofluorescence (RPE stress) progressing to hypoautofluorescence (atrophy).
## Functional signs (vf & mferg)
• 10-2 Humphrey Visual Field: Earliest detectable finding is a reproducible paracentral scotoma (2°–8° from fixation).
• Multifocal ERG (mfERG): Depressed central/paracentral responses; often abnormal before VF or OCT changes.
## Ethnicity-dependent patterns
• White/European patients: Toxicity concentrates in the parafovea (2°–8° ring).
• Asian patients: Toxicity often affects the pericentral/mid-peripheral retina (8°–15° ring).
• Clinical note: 10-2 VF may miss Asian-pattern toxicity; use 24-2 or 30-2 and wider-field OCT.
## Corneal verticillata (vortex keratopathy)
• Golden-brown intraepithelial whorls radiating from below the pupillary axis.
• Marker of drug exposure only; non-sight-threatening and reversible upon cessation.
## Risk factors
• Duration of use >5 years.
• Dose >5 mg/kg of real (not ideal) body weight per day.
• Renal insufficiency (decreased drug clearance).
• Concomitant Tamoxifen use (synergistic toxicity).
• Pre-existing macular or retinal disease.
etiology: ## Mechanism
• Chronic use of hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) or chloroquine.
• Drug binds to melanin in the RPE, causing chronic lysosomal dysfunction and eventual photoreceptor damage.
## Progression
• Damage is not reversible and may continue to progress after drug discontinuation due to slow release from RPE melanin.
redFlags: • Parafoveal EZ thinning or disruption on OCT: Indicates early toxicity.
• Reproducible paracentral scotoma on 10-2 VF: Toxicity present even if fundus looks normal.
• Daily dose >5 mg/kg real body weight: Significantly increases toxicity risk.
• Renal failure: Requires more frequent screening and lower dosing.
investigations: ## Baseline evaluation (within 1 year of start)
• BCVA and dilated fundus exam.
• Baseline 10-2 VF (24-2 for Asians) and SD-OCT.
• Fundus photography for longitudinal comparison.
## Annual screening (begin at year 5)
• Primary tests: Automated 10-2 VF and SD-OCT.
• Asian patients: Use 24-2 or 30-2 VF and wide-angle OCT scans.
• Adjuncts: mfERG (most sensitive functional test) and FAF.
• Protocol: Confirm any abnormality with a second test/modality before diagnosing toxicity.
actionSteps: Perform baseline screening within 12 months of starting therapy.
Calculate daily dose based on real body weight (target ≤5 mg/kg/day).
Initiate annual screening with VF and SD-OCT after 5 years of use.
If toxicity is suspected, confirm with a second modality (e.g., mfERG or FAF).
Coordinate drug discontinuation with the prescribing rheumatologist if toxicity is confirmed.
treatment: ## Medication management
• Discontinue the offending drug in coordination with rheumatology.
• Switch to an alternative disease-modifying agent.
## Dose optimization (prevention)
• Maintain dose ≤5 mg/kg real body weight/day.
• Adjust for renal impairment and avoid Tamoxifen if possible.
## Supportive care
• Counsel patient that vision may continue to decline slightly after stopping the drug.
• Provide low-vision rehabilitation for advanced cases.
followUp: • Routine screening: Annual exams starting at year 5 (or sooner if high-risk factors present).
• Post-toxicity: Continue serial OCT and VF monitoring to track potential progression after cessation.
pearl: Toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent. Always dose by real body weight (≤5 mg/kg). The screening goal is to catch outer-retinal changes on OCT or VF long before the classic "bull's-eye" becomes visible on exam.

name: Chorioretinitis Sclopetaria
symptoms: • Severe visual loss (severity depends on proximity to the macula).
• History of high-velocity projectile injury near the orbit (e.g., bullet, shrapnel, or bb).
findings: ## Chorioretinal appearance
• Full-thickness rupture of both the retina and choroid, exposing the underlying bare white sclera.
• Typically presents in a claw-like configuration of atrophy and pigmentary changes.
## Hemorrhage
• Extensive subretinal, intraretinal, and vitreous hemorrhage is common in the acute phase.
• Hemorrhage eventually resorbs and is replaced by dense white fibrous tissue.
## Associated signs
• Presence of an intraorbital foreign body.
• Vitreous base avulsion or peripheral retinal dialysis.
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Caused by a high-velocity non-penetrating projectile passing near the globe.
• Concussive shockwave: The soft tissues transmit a force that deforms the sclera; the inelastic choroid and retina stretch beyond their limit and tear, while the scleral shell remains intact.
• This is a closed-globe injury by definition.
## Scar formation
• Over weeks, a robust fibroglial scar covers the exposed sclera.
• The resulting chorioretinal adhesion is so strong that the long-term risk of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is paradoxically very low.
## Concurrent injuries
• Optic nerve avulsion or transection (look for hemorrhagic excavation of the disc).
• Commotio retinae and traumatic macular holes.
• Choroidal rupture (crescent-shaped breaks concentric to the optic nerve).
redFlags: • Ruptured globe: High-velocity trauma may cause an occult scleral break; always rule this out first.
• Obscured view: If hemorrhage prevents a fundus exam, perform a B-scan ultrasound to exclude a retinal detachment.
• Optic nerve injury: A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) out of proportion to retinal findings suggests nerve avulsion.
• Delayed complications: Monitor for secondary choroidal neovascularization in the months following injury.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Dilated fundus exam: Identify the extent of retinal/choroidal disruption and underlying bare sclera.
• External exam: Carefully inspect the conjunctiva and sclera for signs of a penetrating injury.
• Periphery check: Look for retinal tears or dialysis in the far periphery.
## Imaging
• CT orbit (1-mm sections): Essential to locate intraorbital foreign bodies and assess the integrity of the globe and optic nerve.
• B-scan ultrasound: To evaluate the posterior segment if the view is blocked by blood.
actionSteps: Place a rigid eye shield immediately and avoid any pressure on the globe until rupture is ruled out.
Perform orbital CT to identify foreign bodies and rule out occult globe perforation.
Obtain a B-scan ultrasound if the retina cannot be visualized due to vitreous hemorrhage.
Observe acutely; surgical intervention is generally not indicated unless complications arise.
treatment: ## Primary management
• Observation: There is no effective acute surgical or medical treatment for the retinochoroidal tears.
## Complication care
• Retinal detachment: Require standard repair (vitrectomy or scleral buckle).
• Non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage: Consider pars plana vitrectomy after several weeks.
• Late issues: Manage epiretinal membranes or tractional detachments with vitreoretinal surgery.
followUp: • Acute: Every 1–2 weeks to monitor for early retinal detachment.
• Maintenance: Monthly for 3 months, then every 6 months for 2 years.
• Long-term: Annual monitoring for macular holes or traumatic choroidal neovascularization.
pearl: Sclopetaria appears catastrophic on exam, but because the forces rupture the tissue faster than they can pull on it, the risk of retinal detachment is low. The exposed sclera heals with a dense scar that "staples" the retina down.

name: Choroidal Effusion/Detachment
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Decreased vision or asymptomatic (common in serous cases).
• Significant vision loss if the detachment involves the macula or extends posteriorly.
## Hemorrhagic features
• Sudden onset of red eye.
• Moderate-to-severe ocular pain.
findings: ## Hallmark appearance
• Smooth, bullous, lobular elevations of the peripheral retina and choroid.
• Serous: Orange-brown hue; Hemorrhagic: Dark reddish-brown hue.
• Lobular configuration (four quadrants) separated by vortex vein ampullae distinguishes this from retinal detachment.
## Classic clinical signs
• Ora serrata visible without scleral depression: The detached choroid displaces the peripheral retina anteriorly.
• "Kissing choroidals": Large lobules touch centrally in the vitreous cavity; apposing retinas may suffer secondary damage.
## Serous detachment
• Low intraocular pressure (IOP), often <6 mmHg (hypotony).
• Shallow anterior chamber (AC) with mild cell and flare.
• Positive transillumination (fluid allows light to pass).
## Hemorrhagic detachment
• Variable IOP (may be elevated) with acute pain.
• Negative transillumination (blood blocks light).
• Associated with rapid onset, typically intra- or postoperatively.
## B-scan ultrasound
• Confirms suprachoroidal fluid between the choroid and sclera.
• Distinguishes serous (echolucent/black) from hemorrhagic (hyperechoic/white) material.
• Detects the "T-sign" in Tenon’s space if posterior scleritis is present.
etiology: ## Serous causes
• Postoperative: Wound leak, over-filtering blebs, or cyclodialysis clefts.
• Inflammatory: Posterior uveitis or scleritis.
• Traumatic: Associated with globe rupture or scleral perforation.
• Other: Nanophthalmos, uveal effusion syndrome, or carotid-cavernous fistula.
## Hemorrhagic causes
• Intraoperative: Anterior displacement of ocular contents causing rupture of short posterior ciliary arteries.
• Spontaneous: Associated with corneal ulcer perforation, uncontrolled hypertension, or anticoagulation use.
redFlags: • Appositional ("kissing") retinas: Mandates urgent surgical drainage to prevent permanent damage.
• Postoperative flat AC with hypotony: Requires immediate management to protect the cornea and lens.
• Spontaneous hemorrhagic detachment: Rule out underlying intraocular tumor (melanoma).
• Nanophthalmic eyes: High risk for uveal effusion; requires specialized surgical approaches.
investigations: ## Clinical examination
• Slit-lamp: Perform Seidel test to identify wound/bleb leaks.
• Gonioscopy: Inspect the angle for a cyclodialysis cleft.
• Dilated fundus exam: Check for concomitant retinal detachment or underlying tumors.
## Imaging
• B-scan ultrasound: Essential to differentiate serous vs. hemorrhagic and track resolution.
• Transillumination: To help distinguish fluid from solid masses or blood.
actionSteps: Perform B-scan ultrasound to distinguish serous from hemorrhagic fluid.
Initiate topical steroids and cycloplegics (atropine) to stabilize the eye.
Identify and treat the source of hypotony (e.g., repair wound leaks or close clefts).
Arrange for surgical drainage if retinas are appositional or the AC remains persistently flat.
treatment: ## Medical management
• Topical cycloplegic: Atropine 1% TID to deepen the AC and rotate the ciliary body.
• Topical steroid: Prednisolone acetate 1% (4–6×/day) to reduce inflammation.
• Systemic: Consider oral steroids if the cause is primary inflammatory disease.
## Underlying cause
• Repair wound leaks or revise filtering blebs.
• Close cyclodialysis clefts via laser or surgery.
## Surgical drainage
• Indications: Persistent kissing choroidals, appositional retina, or corneal decompensation from lens-cornea touch.
followUp: • Schedule: Monthly until complete resolution.
• Monitoring: Serial B-scans to document fluid reduction.
• Vigilance: Watch for secondary glaucoma as the detachment resolves and aqueous production recovers.
differentials: Melanoma of the ciliary body or choroid
pearl: Kissing choroidals with a flat AC after surgery are usually driven by hypotony. Management focuses on deepening the chamber and fixing the leak; drainage is reserved for persistent appositional retinas.

name: Choroidal Nevus and Malignant Melanoma of the Choroid
symptoms: • Usually asymptomatic; often an incidental finding during a dilated exam.
• Photopsias (flashes) if associated subretinal fluid is present.
• Decreased visual acuity if the lesion is subfoveal or causes complications.
• Floaters or visual field defects (rare).
findings: ## Choroidal nevus
• Most common intraocular tumor (present in 5–10% of adults).
• Appearance: Flat or minimally elevated (<2 mm thick); pigmented or amelanotic; oval or round.
• Overlying drusen: A benign marker of chronicity and stability.
## Choroidal melanoma
• Most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults.
• Shape: Dome-shaped pigmented mass; may rupture Bruch membrane to form a pathognomonic mushroom or collar-button configuration.
• Surface features: Orange lipofuscin (hyperautofluorescent) and surrounding subretinal fluid indicating activity.
## Ultrasound signatures
• B-scan: Acoustic hollowness (low-to-medium internal reflectivity), choroidal excavation (scooped dip beneath tumor), and orbital shadowing.
• A-scan: Initial high spike followed by a descending angle with low-medium internal reflectivity.
## Imaging (OCT & faf)
• OCT (EDI): Highly sensitive for detecting small amounts of subretinal fluid (a critical risk factor) and overlying retinal changes.
• FAF: Orange pigment (lipofuscin) appears hyperautofluorescent; drusen over nevi appear relatively hypoautofluorescent.
## Risk assessment (tfsom-uhhd mnemonic)
• T — Thickness >2 mm (measured by B-scan).
• F — subretinal Fluid (detected by OCT).
• S — Symptoms (vision loss, flashes, or floaters).
• O — Orange pigment (lipofuscin; hyperAF).
• M — Margin within 3 mm of the optic disc.
• U — Ultrasound hollowness (low internal reflectivity).
• H — Halo absent (presence of a halo suggests benignity).
• D — Drusen absent (presence of drusen suggests benignity).
• Growth risk (5-year): 0 factors ≈ 3%; 3 factors ≈ 25%; ≥5 factors ≈ >50%.
## Metastatic biology
• Hematogenous spread occurs primarily to the liver (>90% of cases).
• Prognostication (GEP): Class 1A (best, ~2% risk), Class 1B (intermediate), Class 2 (highest risk, ~50% at 5 years).
etiology: ## General
• Choroidal nevus: Benign melanocytic proliferation.
• Choroidal melanoma: Primary intraocular malignancy often arising from a pre-existing nevus.
## Transformation risk
• Risk factors for malignancy: Thickness >2 mm, subretinal fluid, symptoms, orange pigment, margin near disc, and absence of drusen/halo.
## Patient risk factors
• Fair skin, light irides, and oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota; 1/400 lifetime risk).
• Dysplastic-nevus syndrome and germline BAP1 mutations.
## Genetic markers
• Monosomy 3, 8q gain, and BAP1 loss correlate with high metastatic risk.
redFlags: • Any "tfsom-uhhd" risk factors: Presence of two or more warrants urgent oncology referral.
• Rapid growth or new internal vascularization.
• Hepatomegaly or abnormal LFTs at diagnosis: Suggests existing metastatic disease.
• Class 2 gene expression profile or monosomy 3: Indicates 50% metastatic risk at 5 years.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Dilated fundus examination with 20D lens; detailed clinical drawing.
• Baseline color fundus photography to track diameter and growth.
## Multimodal imaging
• B-scan and A-scan ultrasound: To determine thickness and acoustic reflectivity.
• EDI-OCT: To detect subtle subretinal fluid and retinal disruption.
• Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF): To identify orange pigment (lipofuscin).
## Systemic & biopsy
• Fine-needle aspiration: For cytogenetics/GEP prognostication (selected cases).
• Metastatic workup: LFTs, LDH, and liver MRI (preferred) or ultrasound every 6–12 months.
actionSteps: Document the lesion with fundus photography, OCT, FAF, and B-scan.
Apply the "tfsom-uhhd" criteria to categorize the lesion as benign, suspicious, or malignant.
Observe benign-appearing nevi with repeat exams in 3–4 months, then annually.
Refer all suspicious or growing lesions immediately to an ocular oncologist.
treatment: ## Nevus management
• Serial observation with multimodal imaging to confirm stability.
## Melanoma treatment
• Plaque brachytherapy (I-125 or Ru-106): First-line for globe preservation in most small-to-medium tumors.
• Proton-beam or stereotactic radiotherapy: Used for juxtapapillary lesions.
• Enucleation: Reserved for large tumors or eyes with no visual potential.
• Exenteration: Indicated only for cases with orbital extension.
## Adjuvant therapy
• Intravitreal anti-VEGF: Every 4 months for 2 years post-radiation to minimize radiation retinopathy.
## Metastatic surveillance
• Lifelong monitoring of the liver (LFTs, LDH, MRI) every 6–12 months.
followUp: ## Low-risk nevus
• Annual dilated exam with photography and OCT.
## Suspicious lesion
• Re-examination every 3–6 months; referral if growth or fluid develops.
## Post-melanoma treatment
• Serial ophthalmic exams to monitor for CME, neovascular glaucoma, or radiation retinopathy.
• Lifelong systemic oncology follow-up; liver is the primary site of metastasis (>90%).
• Intensified surveillance for patients with Class 2 GEP or BAP1 loss.
pearl: The "tfsom-dim" (or uhhd) mnemonic flags a nevus at risk: thickness, fluid, symptoms, orange pigment, margin near disc, diameter, and absent drusen/halo. Two or more features warrant oncology referral.
willsRef: Wills Eye §11.36 (Choroidal Nevus and Malignant Melanoma of the Choroid)

name: Chronic Angle Closure Glaucoma
symptoms: • Usually asymptomatic until the disease is in an advanced stage.
• Progressive visual field loss or decreased visual acuity in late cases.
• Intermittent blurred vision, headaches, or mild eye pain (subclinical attacks).
findings: ## Epidemiology
• A leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, particularly in East and South Asian populations.
• Frequently as common as primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) but often missed due to lack of symptoms.
• Mandatory finding: Requires gonioscopy on every new glaucoma workup.
## Gonioscopy (hallmark signs)
• Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS): Iris adhesions to the trabecular meshwork blocking angle structures.
• "Creeping" closure: Gradual, asymptomatic advancement of the iris root over the meshwork.
• Synechial progression: Often begins superiorly and moves inferiorly.
• Indentation gonioscopy: The key to distinguishing reversible appositional contact from permanent synechial closure.
## Structural & functional damage
• Glaucomatous optic nerve damage and visual field defects analogous to POAG.
• Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), which may be asymmetric.
## The Eagle trial (2016)
• For patients ≥50 with PACG/PAC and IOP >30 mmHg, clear-lens extraction was more effective than LPI.
• Demonstrated superior IOP control and improved quality-of-life scores.
etiology: ## Primary mechanism
• Gradual angle narrowing from prolonged appositional closure or repeated subclinical attacks.
## Secondary causes
• Formation of PAS following a flat anterior chamber (due to trauma, surgery, or hypotony).
## Risk factors
• Highest prevalence in East Asian, South Asian, and African populations.
• Anatomical predisposition (shallow AC, high iris insertion).
redFlags: • PAS progression despite a patent LPI: May require surgical goniosynechialysis.
• Acute-on-chronic presentation: Sudden pressure spikes on an already narrowed angle.
• Fellow eye status: 50% risk of closure within 5 years without prophylactic LPI.
• Silent progression: Advanced visual field loss is often the first symptom reported by the patient.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Bilateral indentation gonioscopy to assess the extent of synechial vs. appositional closure.
• Comprehensive baseline glaucoma workup including IOP and pachymetry.
## Imaging
• Anterior segment OCT or UBM: To identify plateau iris configuration.
• A-scan biometry: Necessary if planning clear-lens extraction.
## Optic nerve & field monitoring
• Standard automated perimetry (24-2 or 10-2) and OCT RNFL.
• Baseline optic disc photography.
actionSteps: Perform indentation gonioscopy in both eyes to map PAS.
Arrange laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) for appositional components.
Initiate topical IOP-lowering therapy.
Consider early clear-lens extraction as definitive treatment for patients ≥50.
treatment: ## Laser procedures
• Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI): Standard first-line for pupillary block; will not reopen fibrotic PAS.
• Laser iridoplasty: Temporizing measure to reduce new PAS formation.
• Laser trabeculoplasty (ALT/SLT): Strictly contraindicated; may worsen angle scarring.
## Surgical options
• Clear-lens extraction (lensectomy): Increasingly used as definitive therapy (EAGLE trial).
• Goniosynechialysis: Surgical iris pulling to open PAS <6 months in duration.
• Incisional surgery: Trabeculectomy or tube shunt for advanced, medically refractory cases.
## Contraindications
• MIGS: Generally avoided due to poor angle visualization.
followUp: • Prophylactic LPI: Required for the fellow eye to prevent acute or chronic closure.
• Monitoring: Every 3–4 months with gonioscopy, IOP, visual fields, and OCT.
• Post-LPI assessment: Monitor for plateau iris syndrome if the angle remains narrow despite a patent iridotomy.
pearl: Chronic angle closure is a "silent blinder" that hides in plain sight. Indentation gonioscopy is the only way to catch appositional closure before permanent synechiae form. Clear-lens extraction is now often considered first-line for patients over 50.

name: Chronic Conjunctivitis
symptoms: • Persistent red eye (conjunctival hyperemia) lasting >4 weeks.
• Conjunctival discharge and foreign body sensation.
• Eyelids sticking together upon awakening.
findings: ## General characteristics
• Persistent follicular or papillary conjunctival reaction (>3–4 weeks).
• Possible superior corneal pannus, palpable preauricular nodes, or peripheral subepithelial infiltrates.
## Adult inclusion conjunctivitis (chlamydial)
• Unilateral chronic follicular reaction with stringy mucoid discharge.
• Presence of a palpable preauricular node in a sexually active adult.
• Often misdiagnosed as refractory bacterial or viral conjunctivitis.
## Molluscum contagiosum
• Small, dome-shaped, pearly-white umbilicated nodules on the lid margin.
• Causes a secondary toxic follicular conjunctivitis due to viral shedding.
## Trachoma (c. trachomatis serotypes a–c)
• Leading infectious cause of blindness; endemic in regions with low sanitation.
• Superior tarsal follicles lead to cicatricial scarring, entropion, and trichiasis.
• Pathognomonic Herbert pits: Scarred follicles at the limbus.
## Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome
• Unilateral granulomatous/follicular conjunctivitis with prominent ipsilateral lymphadenopathy.
• Most common trigger: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae).
## Masquerade syndromes
• Sebaceous gland carcinoma: Chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis in elderly patients (requires biopsy).
• Conjunctival lymphoma: Characterized by "salmon-patch" lesions.
etiology: ## Infectious
• Chlamydia (Adult Inclusion D–K or Trachoma A–C).
• Molluscum contagiosum, Microsporidia, or Bartonella.
## Non-infectious / toxic
• Drug-Induced: Chronic use of drops with BAK, brimonidine, or antivirals (especially trifluridine).
• Mechanical: Trichiasis, floppy eyelid syndrome, or retained foreign bodies.
## Allergic & atopic
• Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC): Giant "cobblestone" papillae and Horner-Trantas dots.
• Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC): Associated with atopic dermatitis; high risk for fibrosis.
## Masquerade
• Sebaceous carcinoma, OSSN/CIN, or ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (MMP).
redFlags: • Unilateral conjunctivitis >3 weeks: Must rule out molluscum, chlamydia, or sebaceous gland carcinoma.
• New symblepharon formation: High suspicion for mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP).
• Blood-stained discharge: Suggests potential granulomatous disease or tumor.
• Extensive molluscum lesions in an adult: Mandatory HIV testing.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Evert eyelids to inspect tarsal conjunctiva for follicles, papillae, and scarring.
• Check for lid-margin nodules (molluscum) and meibomian gland health.
## Laboratory testing
• Chlamydia: PCR/NAAT of a conjunctival swab (most sensitive).
• Giemsa stain: Look for basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.
• Microsporidia: Confocal microscopy or conjunctival scrapings.
## Biopsy
• Mandatory for suspicious unilateral upper-lid disease to rule out sebaceous gland carcinoma.
• Indicated for suspected lymphoma or pemphigoid (with DIF).
actionSteps: Obtain a detailed history regarding sexual partners, pet contact, and topical medication use.
Collect conjunctival scrapings for PCR or culture before applying fluorescein.
Perform a full eyelid and fornix exam to identify mechanical or viral triggers.
Refer for biopsy if the presentation is unilateral, chronic, and unresponsive to standard therapy.
treatment: ## Chlamydial (adult inclusion)
• Oral Azithromycin (1 g single dose) or Doxycycline (100 mg BID × 7 days).
• Treat sexual partners simultaneously to prevent reinfection.
## Trachoma
• WHO SAFE strategy: Surgery (for trichiasis), Antibiotics (Azithromycin), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement.
## Molluscum contagiosum
• Surgical excision or cryotherapy of the lid-margin lesion; conjunctivitis resolves post-removal.
## Toxic / drug-induced
• Discontinue the offending topical agent; resolution typically occurs within 2–4 weeks.
## Microsporidia
• Topical fumagillin or PHMB; coordinate care with an infectious disease specialist if HIV+.
followUp: • Chlamydial: 2–3 weeks with primary care coordination for STI screening.
• Molluscum: Every 2–4 weeks until the ocular surface clears.
• Chronic condition monitoring: Reinforce lid hygiene and monitor for scarring in AKC/MMP cases.
pearl: Chronic follicular conjunctivitis in a sexually active adult is adult inclusion conjunctivitis until proven otherwise. Success requires oral antibiotics for both the patient and their partners, not just topical drops.

name: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia
symptoms: • Slowly progressive, symmetric drooping of the eyelids (ptosis).
• Gradually reduced eye movements (ophthalmoplegia) over many years.
• Diplopia is RARE because the progression is symmetric (distinguishes it from Myasthenia Gravis).
• Chin-up head posture due to severe bilateral ptosis.
• No diurnal variation or fatigability.
• Possible systemic features: hearing loss, dysphagia, exercise intolerance, or ataxia.
findings: ## Cardinal clinical pattern
• Bilateral, symmetric ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia.
• "Fixed" character: No fluctuation or fatigability (negative ice-pack and rest tests).
• Eyes may become essentially "frozen" in advanced disease.
## Ptosis features
• Chronic chin-up head posture with prominent forehead rhytids from sustained frontalis over-action.
• Functional disability is often modest because downgaze is typically preserved.
## Muscular & pupil signs
• Orbicularis oculi weakness is usually present (indicates a generalized myopathy).
• Pupils are NORMAL (smooth muscle is spared); abnormal pupils should prompt an alternative diagnosis.
• VOR (doll’s head) and Bell’s phenomenon are lost as the disease progresses.
## Kearns–sayre syndrome (KSS)
• Triad: CPEO + pigmentary retinopathy + cardiac conduction defect.
• Onset before age 20; usually sporadic.
• Retinal sign: Diffuse "salt-and-pepper" RPE mottling in the mid-periphery (vision usually remains good).
• Mandatory finding: Heart block (first-degree to complete) can be silent and fatal.
## Mitochondrial histology
• Muscle biopsy (orbicularis or deltoid) shows "ragged-red fibers" on modified Gomori trichrome staining.
• Cytochrome-c-oxidase (COX) negative fibers.
etiology: ## Mitochondrial genetics
• Caused by mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) deletions or point mutations affecting muscle energy metabolism.
• Inheritance: Often maternal (mtDNA), but autosomal dominant forms (e.g., POLG mutations) exist.
## Pathophysiology
• Chronic energy failure leads to progressive degeneration of the extraocular muscles.
redFlags: • Kearns–Sayre Triad: CPEO + pigmentary retinopathy + heart block. Sudden death can occur from complete heart block.
• EKG is MANDATORY: Every CPEO patient requires an initial EKG and cardiology referral, regardless of age or symptoms.
• Surgical risk: Aggressive levator resection is contraindicated; poor lid closure and impaired Bell’s phenomenon lead to severe exposure keratopathy.
• Mitochondrial toxicity: Avoid Valproate (fatal liver failure risk in POLG disease), Metformin (lactic acidosis), and statins.
investigations: ## Clinical & screening
• Mandatory EKG: Screen for AV block or bifascicular block immediately at diagnosis.
• Dilated fundus exam: Check for salt-and-pepper retinopathy.
• Orbicularis strength test: Weakness strongly supports CPEO over Myasthenia Gravis.
## Laboratory & metabolic
• Serum lactate and pyruvate levels.
• CSF analysis: Elevated protein (>100 mg/dL) is characteristic of Kearns–Sayre syndrome.
## Genetic & histologic
• mtDNA analysis: Large single deletions or point mutations.
• Muscle biopsy: To identify ragged-red fibers if genetic testing is inconclusive.
## Exclusion of myasthenia
• Order anti-AChR and anti-MuSK antibodies; consider ice-pack or rest tests.
actionSteps: Obtain an emergent EKG to screen for life-threatening cardiac conduction defects.
Refer to cardiology for Holter monitoring and potential prophylactic pacemaker.
Conduct mtDNA analysis and consider a muscle biopsy for definitive diagnosis.
Provide genetic counseling, especially if a maternal inheritance pattern is suspected.
Consult ENT or neurology if dysphagia or systemic weakness is reported.
treatment: ## Surgical management
• Frontalis sling: For severe ptosis limiting vision; must be conservative to prevent exposure keratopathy.
• Leave 1–2 mm of residual ptosis to protect the ocular surface.
• Aggressive overnight lubrication is required postoperatively.
## Supportive care
• Prism glasses or strabismus surgery: For the rare cases of primary-gaze diplopia.
• Coenzyme Q10 and ubiquinol supplementation (may have limited benefit).
## Systemic coordination
• Multidisciplinary care involving cardiology, endocrinology (screen for diabetes/hypoparathyroidism), and genetics.
followUp: • Annual EKG: To monitor for late-onset conduction disease.
• Endocrine screening: Annual fasting glucose and TSH.
• Ocular surface monitoring: Regular checks for exposure keratopathy, especially after ptosis surgery.
differentials: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (dysphagia + ptosis; older onset)
Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (axial rigidity, vertical gaze palsy)
Thyroid Eye Disease (retraction, proptosis, restrictive motility)
pearl: Symmetric, "frozen" eyes with bilateral ptosis and no diplopia is CPEO. Because heart block can be silent and fatal, an EKG is a mandatory part of the eye exam.

name: CMV Retinitis
symptoms: • Progressive unilateral or bilateral vision loss.
• New floaters or "blind spots" (scotomas).
• Often asymptomatic in early peripheral disease; high-risk patients require routine screening.
findings: ## Classic triad ("pizza fundus")
• Retinitis: White, granular, full-thickness retinal necrosis.
• Hemorrhage: Scattered "brushfire" hemorrhages within or at the leading edge of necrosis.
• Mild Vitritis: Usually minimal in severely immunosuppressed patients.
## Progression & anatomy
• Expansion: Necrosis typically follows vascular arcades, advancing at ~250 µm/week.
• Frosted-branch angiitis: Intense perivascular sheathing occasionally seen in active disease.
• Zone 1: Involvement within 3000 µm of the fovea or 1500 µm of the optic nerve (highest vision threat).
## Chronic & recovery signs
• Atrophy: Healed lesions leave "burnt-out" atrophic retina with RPE mottling.
• Retinal Detachment: High risk (30–40%) due to multiple necrotic retinal breaks.
• Immune Recovery Uveitis (IRU): Increased vitritis, CME, or ERM after starting ART as the immune system reactivates.
etiology: ## Host factors
• Reactivation of latent Cytomegalovirus (CMV) during profound cellular immunodeficiency.
• Classic setting: AIDS with CD4 count <50 cells/µL.
• Modern settings: Hematologic malignancies, bone marrow/solid organ transplant, or intensive chemotherapy.
redFlags: • CD4 <50 cells/µL: Mandatory dilated fundus exam every 3 months for screening.
• Zone 1 Lesions: Threaten the fovea or optic disc; require immediate intravitreal therapy.
• Bilateral involvement: Indicates high systemic viral load and high risk of disseminated CMV disease.
• Flashes/Floaters in healing phase: High suspicion for CMV-related rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Dilated fundus exam with peripheral depressed ophthalmoscopy.
• Wide-field fundus photography to document lesion borders for progression tracking.
## Laboratory testing
• HIV status and CD4+ T-lymphocyte count.
• CMV PCR (Aqueous/Vitreous): Diagnostic gold standard if the clinical appearance is atypical.
• Plasma CMV PCR: Useful for monitoring systemic burden but does not confirm retinitis.
## Systemic screening
• Evaluation for extraocular CMV: GI (colitis), pulmonary (pneumonitis), or hepatic involvement.
actionSteps: Consult Infectious Disease/HIV specialists immediately for systemic antiviral management.
Initiate or optimize Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) in AIDS patients.
Administer intravitreal ganciclovir/foscarnet for vision-threatening (Zone 1) disease.
Schedule weekly follow-ups during the induction phase to ensure stabilization.
treatment: ## Systemic therapy (induction & maintenance)
• Valganciclovir: 900 mg PO BID for 3 weeks (induction), followed by 900 mg daily (maintenance).
• IV Ganciclovir: 5 mg/kg BID for severe disease or patients with poor GI absorption.
• Maintenance duration: Continue until CD4 >100 cells/µL for at least 3–6 months on ART.
## Intravitreal therapy
• Indications: Zone 1 disease or failure of systemic therapy.
• Agents: Ganciclovir (2 mg/0.1 mL) or Foscarnet (2.4 mg/0.1 mL) twice weekly initially.
## Surgical intervention
• Pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade for CMV-associated retinal detachment.
followUp: • Induction phase: Weekly dilated examinations.
• Maintenance phase: Monthly examinations until immune recovery is documented.
• Post-recovery: Every 3–6 months if CD4 remains stable >100.
differentials: Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN): HSV/VZV; more rapid, peripheral, and associated with severe vitritis.
Progressive Outer Retinal Necrosis (PORN): VZV in AIDS; deep retinal whitening with minimal vitritis.
Toxoplasmic Retinochoroiditis: Typically focal with an adjacent pigmented scar.
Syphilitic Chorioretinitis: "The Great Masquerader"; usually multifocal or placoid.
Primary Intraocular Lymphoma: Creamy sub-RPE infiltrates in older patients.
pearl: "Pizza fundus" (white necrosis + brushfire hemorrhage) in an immunocompromised patient is CMV retinitis until proven otherwise. While oral valganciclovir is the standard, immune reconstitution via ART is the only definitive way to arrest the disease.

name: Commotio Retinae
symptoms: • Decreased central or peripheral vision, depending on the site of impact.
• Can be asymptomatic if localized outside the macula.
• Positive history of recent blunt ocular trauma.
findings: ## Ophthalmoscopic appearance
• Confluent, well-demarcated area of gray-white retinal opacification at or directly opposite the site of impact.
• Retinal blood vessels course normally and undisturbed over the area of whitening (distinguishes it from ischemic CRAO).
## Berlin'S EDEMA
• The specific eponym used when commotio retinae involves the macula/posterior pole.
• May present with a "cherry-red spot" mimicking a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).
## Pathophysiologic signature
• Despite the term "edema," this is NOT true extracellular fluid accumulation.
• The retinal whitening is caused by fragmentation and disruption of the photoreceptor outer segments and intracellular RPE swelling.
## Associated traumatic findings
• Commotio rarely occurs in isolation following significant trauma.
• Must look for: Choroidal rupture, traumatic macular hole, hyphema, and peripheral retinal tears/dialyses at the vitreous base.
etiology: ## Mechanism of injury
• Blunt concussive force to the globe generates a shockwave transmitted to the posterior segment.
• The shockwave physically disrupts the fragile photoreceptor outer segments and RPE cell layer.
## Healing and recovery
• The disrupted outer segments typically regenerate, allowing the retinal whitening to fade and vision to improve over days to weeks.
• Severe forces can cause permanent photoreceptor loss or delayed RPE atrophy.
redFlags: • Central vision loss that fails to improve: Indicates permanent photoreceptor damage or a developing traumatic macular hole.
• Concurrent choroidal rupture: High risk for secondary choroidal neovascularization (CNV) months to years later.
• Peripheral commotio without a full peripheral exam: A missed retinal tear or dialysis leading to retinal detachment.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Complete comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation including dilated fundoscopy.
• 360° scleral depressed examination of the peripheral retina to rule out tears/dialysis.
• CAUTION: Defer scleral depression if there is a ruptured globe, active hyphema, microhyphema, or severe iritis.
## Macular OCT
• Key diagnostic tool: Confirms the absence of true retinal edema.
• Demonstrates focal disruption or fragmentation of the ellipsoid zone (IS/OS junction), confirming outer segment damage.
actionSteps: Rule out globe rupture or hyphema before proceeding with extensive manipulation.
Perform a dilated fundus exam with scleral depression to identify any retinal breaks.
Obtain a macular OCT to document the extent of photoreceptor disruption.
Reassure the patient that the condition is often self-limiting, but schedule close follow-up.
treatment: ## Primary management
• Supportive observation is the only indicated management.
• Because there is no true extracellular edema, therapies such as topical NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or dehydrating agents offer ZERO benefit.
## Management of complications
• Retinal tears or dialyses: Require immediate prophylactic laser retinopexy or cryotherapy to prevent detachment.
• Traumatic macular hole: May require pars plana vitrectomy if it fails to close spontaneously.
followUp: • Initial follow-up: Repeat dilated exam with scleral depression at 1–2 weeks to check for delayed retinal breaks.
• Macular monitoring: Repeat OCT at 1 month and 3 months if the fovea was involved, to track ellipsoid zone recovery or RPE atrophy.
• Long-term: Monitor patients with concurrent choroidal rupture for signs of CNV.
pearl: Commotio retinae is photoreceptor outer-segment disruption, not true edema. Steroids and NSAIDs are useless. While the commotio itself usually resolves, the mandatory task is to search for the hidden complications: peripheral retinal tears and choroidal ruptures.

name: Cone Dystrophies
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Slowly progressive central visual loss, typically manifesting in the first three decades.
• Hemeralopia ("Day Blindness"): A diagnostic hallmark where vision is significantly worse in bright light; patients often function better at dusk or in shaded environments.
• Severe photophobia and squinting in bright ambient light.
• Acquired Dyschromatopsia: Loss of color vision, often following a red-green axis before progressing to blue-yellow.
• Note: Children are frequently mislabeled as "malingering" because refraction does not improve vision and the fundus can appear normal early on.
findings: ## Hallmark morphology
• Bull's-eye Maculopathy: A ring of RPE atrophy surrounding a preserved central foveal island.
• Temporal optic disc pallor and spotty perifoveal pigment clumping.
• Tapetal-like macular sheen (metallic or polychromatic) in specific genetic variants.
## Electrophysiologic signature (the "gold standard")
• Full-Field ERG: Photopic (cone) and 30-Hz flicker responses are markedly reduced or extinguished.
• Scotopic (rod) responses remain normal (the mirror image of Retinitis Pigmentosa).
## Imaging & structural changes
• SD-OCT: Centered foveal disruption and eventual loss of the ellipsoid zone (EZ). Outer nuclear layer (ONL) thinning often precedes visible fundus atrophy.
• FAF: Characterized by a hyperautofluorescent ring (stressed RPE) surrounding a hypoautofluorescent center (atrophy).
• Nystagmus: Common in congenital or infancy-onset forms (e.g., achromatopsia).
etiology: ## Genetic basis
• Autosomal Dominant (Most Common): Mutations in *GUCY2D*, *PRPH2*, or *RP1L1*.
• Autosomal Recessive: *ABCA4* (often overlaps with Stargardt disease features).
• X-linked: *RPGR* (often progresses to a cone-rod dystrophy pattern).
## Stable variants
• Achromatopsia: Complete lack of cone function (*CNGA3*, *CNGB3*); characterized by pendular nystagmus and total color blindness from birth.
• Blue-Cone Monochromacy: X-linked deletion of *OPN1LW/MW* gene clusters.
redFlags: • Progressive central loss + photophobia in a child: Mandates immediate ERG to differentiate from functional loss.
• Concurrent neurologic signs (ataxia): Consider syndromic mitochondrial or spinocerebellar etiologies.
• Sudden "day blindness": Differentiates cone loss from rod-driven diseases like RP.
• Family history: Requires genetic counseling and cascade screening of first-degree relatives.
investigations: ## Diagnostic workup
• Full-Field ERG: Essential to confirm organic cone dysfunction.
• Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue Test: To quantify the extent of acquired dyschromatopsia.
• SD-OCT and FAF: For structural mapping of the "bull's-eye" and monitoring progression.
• Genetic Testing: Now standard of care to guide prognosis and identify eligibility for emerging gene therapy trials (e.g., *CNGB3*).
actionSteps: Order a full-field ERG to objectively distinguish cone vs. cone-rod dystrophy.
Perform genetic testing for definitive genotyping (especially *ABCA4*, *GUCY2D*).
Prescribe UV-blocking, heavily tinted sunglasses (magenta or red tints often preferred) for photophobia.
Refer for low-vision rehabilitation and vocational counseling early in the disease course.
treatment: ## Supportive management
• Optical Aids: Tinted lenses or specialized contact lenses to mitigate photophobia and maximize contrast.
• Low-Vision Rehab: Eccentric viewing training and high-power magnifiers.
• Miotics: Weak pilocarpine (0.5%) may occasionally be used to reduce photophobia via miosis.
## Curative outlook
• No current FDA-approved disease-modifying therapy exists, though gene therapy trials for achromatopsia are active.
followUp: • Annual examinations to monitor visual acuity, refraction (acquired myopia), and ERG progression.
• Monitor for "cone-rod" conversion: Test rod function and peripheral visual fields if symptoms change.
• Psychological and educational support for pediatric patients.
differentials: Stargardt Disease: Differentiated by yellow pisciform "flecks" and a "silent choroid" on FA.
Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) Toxicity: The most critical acquired mimic. Always rule out antimalarial use in any patient with a bull's-eye pattern.
Benign Concentric Annular Macular Dystrophy: Stable or very slowly progressive; better visual acuity.
Batten Disease: Consider in children with concurrent neurologic decline and seizure history.
Functional (Non-organic) Vision Loss: Disproven by abnormal ERG/OCT findings.
pearl: The clinical triad of photophobia, central vision loss, and acquired color deficits in a young patient is cone dystrophy until proven otherwise. A normal-appearing fundus in the early stages does NOT rule out the diagnosis—trust the ERG.

name: Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction
symptoms: • Onset typically within the first 3 months of life.
• Persistent tearing (epiphora) and crusting of the medial lashes.
• Recurrent mucoid or mucopurulent discharge.
• Erythema of the medial canthal skin.
• Development of an increased tear meniscus.
findings: ## Natural history
• >90% of cases resolve spontaneously within the first 12 months of life.
• Observation and conservative management are the preferred first-line approaches.
## Exam characteristics
• Wet-appearing eye with tears overflowing the lid margin.
• Mucoid or mucopurulent reflux from the punctum upon lacrimal sac palpation.
• Generally quiet, white eye without conjunctival injection.
## Diagnostic tests
• Dye Disappearance Test (DDT): Fluorescein remains pooled on the affected side after 5 minutes; confirms obstruction.
## Clinical variants
• Congenital Dacryocele (Amniotocele): Tense bluish cystic swelling at the medial canthus; neonatal emergency if bilateral due to potential airway obstruction (intranasal cysts).
• Infant Dacryocystitis: Red, tender, warm mass over the sac with fever; requires urgent systemic antibiotics.
## Critical mimic: congenital glaucoma
• Must be ruled out in every tearing infant.
• Associated with megalocornea (>12 mm), corneal cloudiness, Haab striae, and photophobia.
etiology: ## Primary mechanism
• Failure of the membrane to canalize at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct (the Valve of Hasner).
## Secondary factors
• Bony stenosis of the canal (craniofacial syndromes).
• Punctal or canalicular agenesis.
• Concurrent intranasal cysts (dacryocele).
redFlags: • Dacryocystitis: Red, swollen sac with fever; risk of orbital cellulitis or meningitis.
• Neonatal Dacryocele: Possible respiratory distress from intranasal extension.
• Corneal Changes: Megalocornea or cloudiness suggests congenital glaucoma, not NLDO.
• Failed Probing: Persistent symptoms after 12 months require escalation to intubation.
investigations: ## Primary evaluation
• Slit-lamp/External exam: Measure corneal diameters and check for Haab striae.
• Palpation: Check for purulent reflux from the puncta.
• Dye Disappearance Test: To objectively confirm poor drainage.
## Specialized workup
• ENT evaluation: If a dacryocele or intranasal cyst is suspected.
• IOP measurement: To exclude congenital glaucoma.
actionSteps: Instruct parents on the Crigler massage technique (downward hydrostatic pressure).
Order a Dye Disappearance Test to confirm the obstruction.
Monitor closely for signs of dacryocystitis (redness, warmth, fever).
Schedule probing and irrigation if the condition persists beyond 12 months of age.
treatment: ## Conservative (first 12 months)
• Crigler Massage: Digital downward pressure over the lacrimal sac 2–3 times daily.
• Topical Antibiotics: Erythromycin or Polytrim for symptomatic mucopurulent discharge.
## Surgical intervention
• Nasolacrimal Duct Probing: Standard treatment if unresolved by 12 months; success rate 80–90%.
• Silicone Intubation: Used for failed probing or complex canalicular anatomy.
• Balloon Dacryoplasty: For refractory cases.
• Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR): Reserved for severe, persistent cases or bony abnormalities.
followUp: • Every 2–3 months to reinforce massage technique and monitor for infection.
• Urgent visit for any signs of acute dacryocystitis.
• Post-probing check at 1 week to ensure resolution of symptoms.
differentials: Congenital Glaucoma (look for megalocornea and photophobia)
pearl: Tearing in a baby that resolves by year one is almost always a membrane at the Valve of Hasner. Massage is the answer until 12 months, but always rule out congenital glaucoma first.

name: Congenital Ptosis
symptoms: • Drooping of one or both eyelids present at birth or in early infancy.
• Compensatory chin-up head posture (to see beneath the ptotic lid).
• Marcus Gunn jaw-winking: Synkinetic elevation of the lid with jaw movement or sucking.
• Associated concerns: Strabismus or decreased vision (amblyopia).
findings: ## Key measurements
• Margin-Reflex Distance 1 (MRD1): Distance from the corneal light reflex to the upper lid margin (ptosis if <2 mm).
• Levator Function: Lid excursion from extreme downgaze to upgaze while fixing the brow (poor <4 mm; normal >12 mm).
• Upper Lid Crease: Often absent or elevated due to levator fibrosis.
## Pathognomonic signs
• Lid Lag on Downgaze: The ptotic lid hangs HIGHER than the normal lid when looking down (indicates non-contractile fibrosis).
• Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking: Aberrant innervation between CN V (motor to pterygoids) and CN III (levator). The lid "winks" up with jaw opening or lateral excursion.
## BPES tetrad
• Blepharophimosis-Ptosis-Epicanthus Inversus Syndrome (BPES):
1. Severe ptosis with poor levator function.
2. Short horizontal fissures (blepharophimosis).
3. Epicanthus inversus (skin fold arising from the lower lid).
4. Telecanthus.
## Amblyogenic indications (operate <1 year)
• Visual axis occlusion by the lid margin.
• Induced anisometropic astigmatism (>1.5 D).
• Abnormal chin-up head posture causing strabismus or neck issues.
etiology: ## Primary pathology
• Levator Fibrosis: Striated muscle is replaced by fibrous or fatty tissue, preventing both full contraction (elevation) and full relaxation (causing lid lag in downgaze).
## Urgent neurogenic causes
• Pediatric Horner Syndrome: Ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis. A pediatric emergency until neuroblastoma is ruled out.
• CN III Palsy: Ptosis with associated motility deficits (check pupils).
redFlags: • Visual axis occlusion: High risk for irreversible deprivation amblyopia; requires surgery before age 1.
• Anisometropic astigmatism: The weight of the lid can "mold" the cornea, requiring refraction and patching.
• New-onset anisocoria: If the pupil on the ptotic side is smaller, urgently rule out neuroblastoma.
• Progressive ptosis: Rule out Myasthenia Gravis or mitochondrial myopathy (CPEO).
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Visual acuity and cycloplegic refraction (screen for amblyopia/astigmatism).
• Ocular motility and assessment of Bell phenomenon.
## Quantitative lid exam
• MRD1, palpebral fissure height, and levator function.
• Check for Marcus Gunn jaw-winking by asking the child to chew or suck on a bottle.
## Urgent systemic workup (if Horner suspected)
• Urinary catecholamines (VMA/HVA).
• MRI of the chest, abdomen, neck, and brain to screen for neuroblastoma.
actionSteps: Perform a full pediatric ophthalmic exam including cycloplegic refraction.
Document levator function to guide surgical procedure choice.
Evaluate for "amblyopia triggers" (axis occlusion or high astigmatism).
Consult oculoplastics for early intervention if the visual axis is threatened.
Rule out Horner syndrome/neuroblastoma if anisocoria is present.
treatment: ## Surgical selection
• Levator Function <4 mm: Frontalis suspension (Sling) using silicone, fascia lata, or Gore-Tex.
• Levator Function >4 mm: Levator resection or advancement.
## Specific syndromes
• Marcus Gunn: Often requires bilateral levator excision + frontalis suspension to eliminate the "wink."
• BPES: Always requires frontalis suspension due to poor levator function; telecanthus may require separate repair.
## Amblyopia management
• Aggressive patching and refractive correction often needed even after successful ptosis repair.
followUp: • Urgent (<1 year old): If the lid is covering the pupil.
• Routine elective: Usually repaired at age 3–5 (before school) to allow for more accurate measurements.
• Chronic: Regular screening for refractive changes and amblyopia until age 9–10.
differentials: Pseudoptosis (e.g., from microphthalmos or contralateral lid retraction)
pearl: Ptosis that covers the pupil is an amblyopia emergency. Unlike acquired ptosis, congenital ptosis shows "lid lag" on downgaze—if the lid stays high when looking down, the levator is fibrotic.

name: Congenital/Infantile Glaucoma
symptoms: ## Classic Presentation
• Epiphora (excessive tearing), photophobia, and blepharospasm in an infant.
• Parents may note a "cloudy" appearance to the eye or general irritability.
## Advanced or Late Signs
• Noticeably enlarged eye (buphthalmos).
• Progressive myopia or unexplained vision loss in older children.
• Asymptomatic IOP elevation in cases without early corneal changes.
findings: ## The Classic Triad
• Corneal Clouding: Stromal and epithelial edema resulting from acute IOP rise.
• Buphthalmos: "Ox eye" appearance caused by the elastic infant sclera stretching under pressure (usually before age 3).
• Haab Striae: Pathognomonic horizontal or concentric breaks in Descemet membrane.
## Diagnostic Thresholds
• Horizontal Corneal Diameter: >12 mm before age 1, or >13 mm at any age is highly suspicious.
• IOP: Typically >21 mmHg; note that most anesthetic agents (except ketamine) lower IOP, potentially masking the true severity during EUA.
• Optic Nerve: Progressive cupping; uniquely, early cupping can reverse in infants if IOP is controlled promptly.
## Anatomy & Gonioscopy
• Goniodysgenesis: High iris insertion (anterior to the scleral spur) with a translucent membrane covering the angle.
• Bilateral in ~80% of primary cases but often presents with significant asymmetry.
• Look for secondary signs like corectopia or heterochromia in syndromic forms.
etiology: ## Primary Congenital Glaucoma
• Isolated incomplete differentiation of the trabecular meshwork during embryogenesis.
## Secondary & Syndromic
• Aphakic Glaucoma: The most common form of pediatric glaucoma; a lifelong risk after cataract surgery.
• Sturge–Weber Syndrome: Associated with ipsilateral port-wine stains and leptomeningeal angiomatosis.
• Anterior Segment Dysgenesis: Axenfeld–Rieger spectrum, Peters anomaly, or aniridia.
• Systemic/Other: Neurofibromatosis (NF1), Lowe syndrome, congenital rubella, or Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP).
redFlags: • The Triad: Epiphora + Photophobia + Blepharospasm = Glaucoma until proven otherwise.
• Haab Striae vs. Trauma: Horizontal breaks = Glaucoma; Vertical/Oblique breaks = Forceps birth trauma.
• Brimonidine Warning: Strictly contraindicated in infants due to the risk of lethal CNS depression and apnea.
• Shifting Myopia: Rapidly progressing myopia in an infant is a clinical proxy for uncontrolled IOP.
investigations: ## Office Assessment
• Measurement of horizontal corneal diameter with calipers.
• IOP check and retinoscopy (axial length surrogate).
• Portable slit-lamp exam to evaluate for Descemet breaks.
## Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA)
• Mandatory for definitive diagnosis and surgical planning.
• Comprehensive check: Corneal diameter, IOP, gonioscopy, and axial length (A-scan).
• Normal Axial Length: ~17 mm at birth, increasing to ~20 mm by age 1; excess growth indicates pressure-driven stretching.
actionSteps: • Arrange an urgent Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA).
• Document baseline horizontal corneal diameter and axial length.
• Initiate temporizing medical therapy (topical beta-blockers or CAIs).
• Prepare for definitive surgical intervention (angle surgery).
treatment: ## Definitive Surgical Therapy
• Goniotomy: Preferred first-line if the cornea is clear enough for visualization.
• Trabeculotomy: Indicated when corneal clouding prevents a clear view of the angle.
• Refractory Cases: Glaucoma drainage devices (tubes) or cyclophotocoagulation.
## Medical (Temporizing Only)
• Oral Acetazolamide: 15–30 mg/kg/day (most effective pre-surgical medical bridge).
• Topical Agents: Timolol (0.25% in infants) or Dorzolamide.
• Strict Avoidance: Never use brimonidine in children under age 2.
followUp: • Immediate: Frequent EUA and office checks post-surgery.
• Long-Term: Lifelong surveillance is mandatory; recurrence can happen decades later.
• Amblyopia: Aggressive treatment of refractive error and amblyopia is as critical as IOP control for the final visual outcome.
differentials: • Megalocornea: Large cornea but normal IOP, no striae, and normal optic nerves.
• Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction: Tearing without photophobia or corneal clouding.
• Forceps Trauma: Vertical corneal breaks; history of difficult delivery.
• CHED: Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (bilateral corneal edema without high IOP).
pearl: Epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm in a baby is congenital glaucoma, not a "clogged tear duct." If the cornea looks large or cloudy, check the IOP—and whatever you do, keep the brimonidine far away from the nursery. Remember that horizontal Descemet breaks (Haab striae) equal glaucoma, while vertical breaks equal birth trauma.

name: Conjunctival Laceration
symptoms: • Ocular pain and redness.
• Persistent foreign body sensation.
• Clear history of blunt or sharp trauma.
findings: ## Clinical appearance
• Fluorescein-staining linear defect of the bulbar conjunctiva.
• Edges may be rolled or retracted, potentially exposing the bare white sclera.
• Surrounding subconjunctival hemorrhage and chemosis are common.
## Management by size
• Small Lacerations (<1 cm): Usually heal spontaneously within days with prophylactic antibiotics; no sutures required.
• Large Lacerations (>1–2 cm): Mandate careful exploration to rule out underlying injury.
## The "occult" open globe
• Bullous Hemorrhage: Thick, elevated, 360° subconjunctival hemorrhage is a major red flag for occult scleral rupture.
• Peaked pupil, marked hypotony, or visible dark uveal tissue within the wound confirms an open globe.
etiology: ## Mechanisms
• Sharp trauma (fingernails, twigs, glass) or blunt concussive forces.
• Iatrogenic: Post-surgical complications (strabismus or pterygium surgery) or contact lens insertion trauma.
## Clinical concern
• Chemosis and blood can easily hide a globe perforation—the mobile conjunctiva must be manipulated to inspect the underlying scleral bed.
redFlags: • Bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage: High suspicion for underlying scleral laceration.
• Dark uveal tissue: Indicates a full-thickness prolapse/rupture.
• Retained organic material: High risk of infection; necessitates aggressive debridement and broad-spectrum coverage.
• Canalicular involvement: Lacerations near the medial canthus require intubation within 24–48 hours.
investigations: ## Ocular exploration
• Slit-lamp exam: Use proparacaine and a sterile cotton-tipped applicator to gently shift the mobile conjunctiva.
• Scleral inspection: Inspect the entire area of sclera beneath the defect to ensure it is intact.
• Seidel test: To rule out aqueous leak if the injury is near the limbus.
## Imaging
• CT Orbit (1-mm sections): Without contrast to rule out intraocular or intraorbital foreign bodies (IOFB).
• B-scan ultrasound: Only if the globe is confirmed to be closed and the posterior segment view is obscured.
## Surgical exploration
• General anesthesia exploration in the OR if a scleral rupture cannot be ruled out at the bedside.
actionSteps: Instill topical anesthesia and explore the sclera beneath the laceration using a sterile swab.
Perform a Seidel test if the laceration is near the limbal area.
Obtain a CT scan if the mechanism suggests a high-velocity foreign body.
For lacerations <1 cm: Start topical antibiotics and observe.
For lacerations >1 cm or gaping: Arrange for primary surgical closure (e.g., 8-0 Vicryl).
treatment: ## Medical therapy
• Topical antibiotic (e.g., Polytrim or a Fluoroquinolone) QID for 7 days.
• Tetanus prophylaxis as indicated by immunization history.
## Surgical repair
• Indications: Gaping wounds, lacerations >1 cm, or anatomic restoration needs.
• Technique: 8-0 or 9-0 Vicryl sutures with buried knots.
• Crucial: Never close a conjunctival laceration until the underlying sclera is confirmed intact.
followUp: • Re-examine in 24–48 hours to ensure no signs of missed globe rupture or infection.
• Small lacerations typically re-epithelialize within 48–72 hours.
• Large repairs: Follow up in 1 week to check suture integrity and wound healing.
pearl: A bullous or 360° subconjunctival hemorrhage after trauma is an occult scleral rupture until proven otherwise. Always manipulate the mobile conjunctiva to see the bare sclera underneath.

name: Conjunctival Tumors
symptoms: Visible growth or mass on the conjunctiva.
Foreign-body sensation or irritation.
Changes in pigmentation, size, or vascularity.
Vision changes (rare; usually from corneal encroachment or induced astigmatism).
findings: ## Conjunctival nevus (benign)
• Pigmented bulbar lesion near the limbus.
• Hallmark: intralesional cysts (clear, fluid-filled microcysts).
• Note: lesions in the palpebral conjunctiva or fornix are atypical and suspicious.
## OSSN / squamous cell carcinoma
• Gelatinous pink-gray or leukoplakic (white) lesion at the interpalpebral limbus.
• Signature finding: prominent "corkscrew" feeder vessels.
• Stains with Rose Bengal due to defective surface glycoproteins.
## Primary acquired melanosis (PAM)
• Flat, unilateral, patchy golden-brown pigmentation in fair-skinned adults.
• Requires biopsy to distinguish PAM without atypia (benign) from PAM with atypia (high malignant potential).
## Conjunctival melanoma
• Raised, nodular, pigmented or pink (amelanotic) mass with intrinsic vascularity.
• Often arises from PAM with atypia; exhibits rapid growth and feeder vessels.
## Conjunctival lymphoma
• Salmon-pink patch, typically in the fornix.
• Often bilateral (25%); most are MALT (extranodal marginal zone) lymphomas.
## Other lesions
• Pyogenic granuloma: friable red vascular nodule; bleeds easily.
• Papilloma: cauliflower-like lesion; HPV-related (pedunculated in children, sessile/dysplastic in adults).
• Dermoid/Dermolipoma: congenital limbal dome-shaped lesion; may have hair follicles.
• Kaposi sarcoma: violaceous lesion mimicking chronic hemorrhage; associated with HIV.
etiology: ## Risk factors
• UV light exposure: primary driver for OSSN and melanoma.
• Immunosuppression: HIV or transplant status markedly increases OSSN risk.
• Viral: HPV 16/18 implicated in papillomas and some OSSN.
## Precursors
• PAM with atypia: main precursor for conjunctival melanoma.
• Systemic disease: lymphoma may be a local manifestation of systemic disease.
redFlags: Rapid enlargement or new elevation of a pigmented lesion.
Prominent "corkscrew" feeder or sentinel vessels.
Lesion crossing from the limbus onto the cornea.
Ulceration, symblepharon, or fixation to deep tissue (suggests invasion).
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Slit-lamp photography to document size, pigment, and vascular patterns.
• AS-OCT or UBM to assess depth of invasion.
## Biopsy
• Excisional or incisional biopsy (with map biopsies) for histopathology.
• Lymphoma biopsy must be sent fresh/non-fixed for flow cytometry.
## Systemic workup
• Melanoma: full-body skin exam and liver imaging.
• Lymphoma: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and bone marrow biopsy.
• OSSN in young patients: HIV testing.
actionSteps: Document baseline with high-magnification slit-lamp photography.
Perform AS-OCT/UBM for suspicious depth.
Arrange urgent biopsy for any enlarging, vascular, or nodular lesion.
Coordinate systemic staging if melanoma or lymphoma is confirmed.
treatment: ## Benign nevus
• Observation with serial photography every 6–12 months.
• Excision only if growth occurs or for cosmesis.
## OSSN / CIN
• Complete "no-touch" excision with cryotherapy to margins.
• Adjuvant topical chemotherapy: Interferon alpha-2b, 5-FU, or Mitomycin C.
## Conjunctival melanoma
• Wide excisional biopsy; avoid tumor seeding.
• Supplemental cryotherapy to margins and absolute alcohol for corneal involvement.
• Adjuvant topical chemotherapy (MMC or Interferon).
## Lymphoid tumors
• Excision for localized MALT lymphoma.
• Low-dose radiation or chemotherapy/Rituximab for systemic or incomplete excision cases.
## Miscellaneous
• Kaposi Sarcoma: highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART); excision or irradiation if needed.
• Pyogenic Granuloma: excision with cautery.
• Papilloma: observation in children; excision/cryotherapy for adults.
followUp: ## Monitoring
• Benign lesions: every 6–12 months.
• OSSN (post-op): every 3 months for 2 years.
• Melanoma (post-op): every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months (lifelong).
## Systemic coordination
• Oncology-led follow-up for lymphoma and melanoma staging.
pearl: Pigmented lesions with feeder vessels or rapid growth are melanoma until proven otherwise. Benign nevi are usually static, flat at the limbus, and contain clear epithelial inclusion cysts.

name: Contact Dermatitis
symptoms: Sudden onset periorbital rash
Intense pruritus (itching)
Eyelid swelling
findings: ## Cutaneous
• Periorbital edema and erythema
• Vesicles, scaling, and crusting
• Lichenification (skin thickening) in chronic cases
## Ocular
• Watery discharge
• Conjunctival chemosis or papillary reaction
etiology: ## Immune mechanism
• Type IV delayed cell-mediated hypersensitivity: reaction occurs 48–72 hours after re-exposure (distinguish from Type I immediate allergy).
• Atopic diathesis: patients with asthma or hay fever are at higher risk due to compromised skin barriers.
## Ophthalmic culprits
• Benzalkonium chloride (BAK): most common preservative; high risk in chronic glaucoma patients.
