• Neomycin: aminoglycoside in triple-antibiotic ointments; up to 10% sensitization rate.
• Others: aminoglycosides (tobramycin, gentamicin), brimonidine (often delayed onset), apraclonidine, atropine, trifluridine, and thimerosal.
## Non-ophthalmic triggers
• Cosmetics: nickel (eyelash curlers), paraphenylenediamine (hair dye), fragrances, formaldehyde.
• "Nail-to-lid" transfer: nail polish or acrylics transferred by fingers to the eyes.
## Irritant VS allergic
• Irritant: direct cytotoxicity from soaps/detergents (non-immune).
• Allergic: immune-mediated; requires patch testing for confirmation.
redFlags: Corneal involvement with periorbital swelling → stop agent; check for infection; consider topical steroid.
Associated atopic dermatitis with keratoconus or cataract → monitor for ocular sequelae.
Severe bilateral reaction → evaluate for systemic contact allergens (cosmetics, preservatives).
Chronic relapsing course → dermatology referral for patch testing.
investigations: ## Clinical history
• Review all topical agents: eye drops (BAK, neomycin), cosmetics, nail products, and hair dyes.
## Examination
• Slit-lamp exam to assess periocular skin, conjunctival chemosis, and papillary reaction.
## Diagnostic testing
• Trial of discontinuation: monitor for resolution within days of stopping suspected agent.
• Patch testing: T.R.U.E. test or expanded ophthalmic panel (Gold Standard for recurrent cases).
actionSteps: Identify and eliminate the offending agent immediately.
Prescribe short-course low-potency topical steroid (hydrocortisone 1%) for skin.
Start oral antihistamines for pruritus relief.
Refer to dermatology if condition is recurrent or chronic.
treatment: ## Allergen avoidance
• Discontinue suspected triggers (neomycin, BAK-preserved drops, cosmetics, nickel).
## Skin & surface care
• Cool compresses for symptomatic relief.
• Preservative-free artificial tears for ocular surface irritation.
## Pharmacotherapy
• Topical: hydrocortisone 1% ointment to eyelid skin for 1–2 weeks.
• Systemic: oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine) for itching.
followUp: Expect resolution within 1–2 weeks of allergen discontinuation.
Limit topical steroid use to a short course to avoid ocular side effects.
Patient education: emphasize common triggers (BAK, neomycin) and "nail-to-lid" transfer.
pearl: Periocular dermatitis in a "raccoon" pattern usually implies a topical allergen; neomycin, BAK, and nail polish are the most frequent culprits.

name: Contact Lens–Induced Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis
symptoms: Itching (intense, often worse after lens removal).
Mucous discharge.
Contact lens intolerance or increased awareness.
Excessive lens movement on blink.
findings: ## Exam technique
• Upper lid eversion is mandatory; signs are localized to the upper tarsal conjunctiva.
## Tarsal signs
• Giant papillae (≥1 mm diameter); macropapillae (>2 mm).
• Cobblestone appearance: discrete, raised, flat-topped fibrovascular papillae.
• Central vascular tuft within each papilla.
• Sparing of inferior tarsus (distinguishes from trachoma/vernal).
## Lens & lid changes
• Protein, lipid, or calcium deposits on the lens surface.
• Mucous strands on the lens or tarsus.
• High-riding lens (pushed superiorly by papillae during blink).
• Pseudoptosis (late sign from chronic inflammation and lid edema).
## Corneal status
• Usually normal or mild superior SPK.
• Any corneal infiltrate mandates culture to rule out microbial keratitis.
etiology: ## Mechanisms
• Mechanical: Repeated friction of the lens edge against the upper tarsus.
• Immune: Type I and IV hypersensitivity to denatured proteins (lysozyme, albumin) on the lens surface.
## Risk factors
• Extended-wear and hydrogel lenses (higher protein binding than silicone hydrogel).
• Older lens material and non-daily replacement schedules.
• Preservative sensitivity (thimerosal, chlorhexidine, BAK).
## Non-lens triggers
• Ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, extruded scleral buckles, or glaucoma shunt tubes.
redFlags: Persistent GPC despite lens cessation → switch to daily disposables or scleral lenses.
Corneal infiltrate or worsening SPK → rule out microbial keratitis; culture if suspicious.
Bilateral severe symptoms with atopy → systemic allergy workup.
Tarsal scarring or symblepharon → oculoplastic evaluation.
investigations: ## Slit lamp
• Upper lid eversion to document papilla size and tarsal extent.
• Inspection for lens deposits and mucous strands.
## Ocular surface
• Fluorescein staining for SPK or epithelial defects.
• Culture of any suspicious corneal infiltrates.
actionSteps: Discontinue lens wear for 2–4 weeks during the acute phase.
Initiate topical mast-cell stabilizers or combination drops.
Refit with daily-disposable or RGP/scleral lenses upon resolution.
Educate on hygiene: avoid overwear and use preservative-free solutions.
treatment: ## Lens management
• Preferred: Switch to daily-disposable soft lenses.
• Alternative: Rigid gas-permeable (RGP) or scleral lenses.
• Hygiene: Use hydrogen peroxide disinfection or preservative-free saline.
## Topical therapy
• Mast cell stabilizer/antihistamine (e.g., olopatadine, bepotastine, ketotifen) BID.
• Severe cases: Low-potency topical steroid (loteprednol 0.5%, fluorometholone 0.1%) QID × 2 weeks.
• Rule: No lens wear while on topical steroids.
## Steroid-sparing / chronic
• Topical cyclosporine (0.05% or 0.09%) or Lifitegrast 5%.
followUp: ## Initial
• Reassess in 2–4 weeks.
## Resuming wear
• Return to lens wear only once tarsal papillae and symptoms have resolved.
• Counsel on replacement schedules and avoiding extended wear.
pearl: GPC is a disease of "lenses and deposits"—switching to daily disposables often resolves what months of mast-cell stabilizers cannot.
willsRef: Wills Eye §4.21 (Contact Lens–Induced Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis)

name: Corneal Abrasion
symptoms: Sharp ocular pain.
Photophobia.
Foreign body sensation.
Tearing and discomfort with blinking.
Blurred vision.
History of mechanical trauma (scratch, hit, or contact lens use).
findings: ## Corneal findings
• Epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein.
• Absence of underlying corneal opacification (opacification suggests infection or inflammation).
## Associated signs
• Conjunctival injection.
• Eyelid edema.
• Mild anterior chamber (AC) reaction.
etiology: ## Mechanical trauma
• Fingernails, tree branches, paper, makeup brushes, or contact lenses.
• Residual defect following foreign-body removal.
## Recurrent erosion syndrome
• Spontaneous epithelial breakdown upon awakening due to weak basement-membrane adhesion (from prior trauma or EBMD).
## Contact lens risks
• High risk for bacterial ulcer, specifically Pseudomonas; must be treated as keratitis until proven otherwise.
redFlags: Contact lens wearer → never patch; must cover for Pseudomonas; culture if infiltrate appears.
Vegetable matter or soil contamination → high risk for fungal or gram-negative infection; low threshold for scraping.
Non-healing defect (>5 days) → consider recurrent erosion, neurotrophic keratopathy, or occult infection.
Associated hyphema or iritis → rule out open globe or occult intraocular foreign body (IOFB).
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Slit-lamp exam with fluorescein dye.
• Document size (height × width) and diagram the location of the defect.
## Critical checks
• Evert eyelids to rule out retained foreign bodies (especially with vertical/linear abrasions).
• Inspect for stromal infiltrates or opacification (infection signs).
• Assess AC reaction and check for hyphema.
• Rule out corneal laceration or penetrating trauma.
actionSteps: Apply topical antibiotics (erythromycin or moxifloxacin) QID until healed.
Contact lens wearers: ensure Pseudomonas coverage (fluoroquinolone); DO NOT patch.
Provide oral analgesia and consider topical cycloplegics for photophobia.
Recheck in 24 hours; refer to cornea specialist if infiltrate develops or healing stalls at 48–72h.
treatment: ## Antibiotic coverage
• Standard: Erythromycin, bacitracin, or Polytrim ointment/drops QID.
• Organic/Vegetable trauma: Fluoroquinolone drops (moxifloxacin, ofloxacin) or ciprofloxacin ointment ≥ QID.
• Contact lens wearer: Mandatory antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone; NO patching.
## Pain management
• Topical NSAIDs: Ketorolac 0.4–0.5% QID for 3 days (avoid in chronic surface disease).
• Cycloplegics: Use for significant photophobia; avoid long-acting agents in small defects.
• Oral meds: Acetaminophen or systemic NSAIDs.
• Warning: NEVER prescribe topical anesthetics for home use (risks corneal melt and delayed healing).
## Mechanical management
• Debride loose or hanging epithelial flaps with a cotton-tipped applicator.
• Bandage soft contact lens (BCL): May improve comfort in large defects.
• Steroids: Strictly avoided while epithelial defect is active.
followUp: Recheck in 24 hours if symptoms are severe; otherwise follow until healed (usually 2–4 days).
Check for retained subtarsal foreign bodies at every visit via lid eversion.
Contact lens wearers: Close monitoring for ulcer development; no patching.
Recurrent erosion: Consider hypertonic NaCl 5% ointment at night or BCL for refractory cases.
pearl: Never prescribe topical anesthetics for home use; they cause corneal melt. Never patch a contact lens wearer; it facilitates Pseudomonas infection.

name: Corneal and Conjunctival Foreign Bodies
symptoms: Foreign body sensation.
Tearing and redness.
Pain.
findings: ## FB and rust ring
• Presence of conjunctival or corneal foreign body on slit lamp.
• Rust ring (iron/steel): begins within 3–4 hours; fully developed by 12–24 hours.
## Subtarsal FB signs
• Vertical linear corneal abrasions or "ice-skating rink" SPK pattern.
• Mandates single or double upper-lid eversion to inspect the tarsal conjunctiva and superior fornix.
## Associated signs
• Conjunctival injection and lid edema.
• Mild anterior chamber (AC) reaction.
• Small reactive/sterile infiltrate may surround an embedded FB.
## High-velocity red flags (suggest occult IOFB)
• Microhyphema or pupil peaking/irregularity.
• Iris transillumination defects or lens capsule perforation.
• Shallow or asymmetrically deep AC; low IOP in the affected eye.
• Any Seidel-positive wound.
etiology: ## Mechanisms
• Metal grinding or hammering: highest risk for intraocular foreign body (IOFB).
• Organic matter, glass, or insect parts: common in the superior fornix.
## Complications
• Retained iron leads to rust ring formation.
• Organic material carries a high risk of fungal keratitis.
redFlags: High-velocity injury (metal-on-metal) → occult IOFB; obtain CT orbits.
Seidel-positive wound with iris prolapse → open globe; use shield and prepare for surgery.
Vegetable/organic material → high fungal risk; requires prolonged monitoring.
Persisting rust ring → remove with burr at 24 hours to prevent scarring.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Document visual acuity before any procedure.
• Slit-lamp exam: assess FB depth, entry sites, and AC reaction.
• Check for pupil peaking, iris tears, or lens opacities.
• Measure IOP: look for asymmetrically low pressure.
## Lid eversion
• Evert eyelids and inspect fornices (Desmarres retractor for double eversion if necessary).
• Inspect conjunctival lacerations to rule out underlying scleral perforation.
## Imaging and dilation
• Perform dilated fundus exam to rule out posterior segment IOFB.
• CT orbits (1-mm thin cuts; axial, coronal, and parasagittal): preferred for IOFB.
• B-scan or UBM: if the view is hazy or to localize scleral wounds.
• WARNING: avoid MRI if a metallic FB is possible.
actionSteps: ## Mandatory exam
• Always evert the upper lid in cases of vertical corneal scratches.
• Perform DFE and CT orbits for any high-velocity mechanism (grinding/hammering).
## Removal strategy
• Remove FB under topical anesthesia with a 25-gauge needle or Algerbrush.
• Rust ring: if deep/central, wait 24 hours for it to soften before removal to minimize scarring.
## Medical management
• Start topical antibiotics (fluoroquinolone or polymyxin-trimethoprim) × 3–5 days.
• Update tetanus status for metallic or soil-contaminated injuries.
• Refer to cornea specialist if infiltrate persists or epithelial defect >48 hours.
treatment: ## Corneal FB
• Remove with FB spud, jeweler's forceps, or needle at the slit lamp.
• For multiple superficial FBs, consider saline irrigation.
• Diagram the dimensions of the resulting epithelial defect.
## Conjunctival FB
• Remove with a cotton-tipped applicator or irrigation under topical anesthesia.
## Pharmaceuticals
• Topical antibiotic prophylaxis until the epithelium heals.
• Update tetanus immunization.
followUp: Recheck in 24 hours to confirm healing and ensure no retained material.
Second visit at 24–48 hours if residual rust ring requires removal.
Continue antibiotics until the epithelium is fully healed.
Counsel on the use of safety eyewear.
pearl: Always evert the upper lid; a hidden subtarsal foreign body will continue to scratch the cornea despite optimal drops and a "normal" primary gaze exam.
willsRef: Wills Eye §3.3 (Corneal and Conjunctival Foreign Bodies)

name: Corneal Dystrophies
symptoms: ## Clinical triad
• Bilateral, symmetric, and slowly progressive (distinguishes from degeneration or keratitis).
## Visual symptoms
• Painless, progressive vision loss (chief complaint in stromal and endothelial types).
• Glare and haloes around lights due to light scatter from opacities or edema.
• Morning blurred vision that clears throughout the day (classic for Fuchs endothelial dystrophy).
## Recurrent erosions
• Episodes of acute pain, photophobia, and tearing upon waking (common in EBMD, Meesmann, Reis–Bücklers, lattice, and granular).
## Onset windows
• Congenital: CHED.
• 1st Decade: Macular.
• 1st–2nd Decade: Lattice, Granular.
• 3rd–4th Decade: EBMD.
• 5th–7th Decade: Fuchs.
findings: ## Epithelial layer
• EBMD (Map–Dot–Fingerprint): subtle patterns in basal epithelium; highlighted with retroillumination or by drying the cornea.
• Meesmann: fine intraepithelial cysts across the entire cornea; best seen on retroillumination.
• Reis–Bücklers: reticular gray-white subepithelial opacities at the level of Bowman layer; painful recurrent erosions.
## Stromal layer
• Granular (TGFBI): discrete white "crumb-like" opacities in central anterior stroma; spares the limbus (Hyaline/Masson trichrome).
• Lattice (TGFBI): branching refractile linear deposits (Amyloid/Congo red).
• Macular (CHST6): diffuse cloudy stroma with poorly-defined opacities extending to the limbus; most visually devastating (Mucopolysaccharide/Alcian blue).
• Schnyder: central crystalline deposits and stromal lipid; associated with systemic hyperlipidemia.
## Endothelial layer
• Fuchs: central endothelial guttae ("beaten-metal" appearance on specular reflection); progresses to stromal edema and bullae.
• Posterior Polymorphous (PPMD): bands, vesicles, or geographic patterns at the endothelium.
• Congenital Hereditary Endothelial Dystrophy (CHED): ground-glass corneal clouding present at birth.
## Unifying negative findings
• NO conjunctival injection, NO vascularization, and NO active infiltrate (presence suggests keratitis or scarring).
etiology: ## Genetics
• Autosomal Dominant (most common): EBMD, Granular, Lattice, Fuchs, PPMD, Reis–Bücklers.
• Autosomal Recessive: Macular dystrophy, CHED.
## Specific genes
• TGFBI (5q31): Granular, Lattice, Reis–Bücklers.
• CHST6: Macular (keratan sulfate synthesis defect).
• COL8A2 / TCF4: Fuchs.
redFlags: Bilateral edema in an infant → consider CHED vs congenital glaucoma; requires urgent pediatric referral.
Progressive central clouding in children → high risk for amblyopia; requires aggressive management.
Middle-aged Fuchs patient with rapid visual decline → impending corneal decompensation.
Recurrent erosion with hypopyon or worsening pain → suspect superimposed microbial keratitis.
investigations: ## Clinical tools
• Slit lamp exam: identify lesion depth (epithelial vs stromal vs endothelial).
• Retroillumination: highlights EBMD, Meesmann, and guttae.
• Pachymetry: maps corneal thickness; >640 μm suggests significant edema.
## Specialized imaging
• Specular microscopy: quantifies endothelial cell density (normal >2000 cells/mm²).
• Anterior Segment OCT / Pentacam: maps opacity depth to guide PTK treatment.
## Systemic & genetic
• Fasting lipid panel: mandatory for Schnyder dystrophy.
• Genetic testing: for diagnosis confirmation or family planning.
actionTitle: Identify the layer; manage erosions and edema
actionSteps: Classify the dystrophy by corneal layer (epithelial, stromal, or endothelial).
Manage acute erosions with lubrication, cycloplegics, and antibiotic ointment.
Obtain baseline specular microscopy and pachymetry for all endothelial dystrophies.
Coordinate genetic counseling and screen first-degree relatives if indicated.
treatment: ## Recurrent erosion ladder
• Lubrication: PF artificial tears and ointment qhs.
• Hypertonic saline: 5% NaCl (Muro 128) qid + ointment qhs.
• Procedural: Bandage contact lens (6–8 weeks) → epithelial debridement/micropuncture → excimer PTK.
## Endothelial management (Fuchs)
• Mild edema: topical hypertonic saline.
• Visually significant edema: DMEK (Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty) or DSAEK.
• Triple procedure: combined Phaco/IOL and DMEK for borderline cell counts.
## Stromal & congenital management
• Anterior stromal opacities: excimer PTK.
• Deep/diffuse disease: DALK (deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty) or PK.
• Macular dystrophy: typically requires PK due to full-thickness limbus-to-limbus involvement.
• CHED: PK in infancy to prevent amblyopia.
followUp: Asymptomatic/Stable: annual slit lamp exam with photography.
Post-erosion: check in 1–2 weeks; continue nighttime ointment for months after healing.
Post-keratoplasty: daily initially, tapering to monthly through the first year.
pearl: Remember "MARILYN MONROE Always Gained Her Men's Lovers And Comebacks": MAcular = Mucopolysaccharide (Alcian blue); Granular = Hyaline (Masson trichrome); LAttice = Amyloid (Congo red). Morning blur is pathognomonic for Fuchs.

name: Corneal Graft Rejection
symptoms: Decreased vision (often the first sign).
Mild pain, redness, and photophobia.
History of corneal transplantation (months to years prior).
May be asymptomatic; detected during routine follow-up.
findings: ## Endothelial rejection
• Khodadoust line (pathognomonic): A line of keratic precipitates (KPs) sweeping across the donor endothelium.
• Keratic precipitates localized specifically to the donor endothelium.
• Stromal and/or epithelial edema.
## Stromal rejection
• Krachmer spots: Subepithelial infiltrates.
• Localized stromal neovascularization.
## Epithelial rejection
• Irregularly elevated epithelial rejection line.
## Other clinical signs
• Circumcorneal conjunctival injection.
• Anterior chamber (AC) inflammation (cell and flare).
• Neovascularization extending to or onto the graft.
• Broken or loose graft sutures.
etiology: ## Immune mechanism
• Host immune response against donor corneal antigens; endothelial rejection is the most visually threatening form.
## Risk factors
• Prior graft failure, corneal neovascularization, or large/eccentric grafts.
• Active inflammation at time of surgery or pediatric recipient.
## Triggers
• Loose/broken sutures or suture-related neovascularization.
• Intercurrent illness, trauma, recent surgery, or non-compliance with steroid regimen.
redFlags: Khodadoust line → active endothelial rejection; requires aggressive therapy within 24 hours.
New stromal edema, subepithelial infiltrates, or AC reaction in a grafted eye.
Sudden decreased vision or redness in a transplant patient → rejection until proven otherwise.
Treatment delay >1–2 weeks significantly reduces the chance of graft survival.
investigations: ## Clinical history
• Time since transplant and original surgical indication (e.g., HSV).
• Current medication compliance and recent changes in steroid frequency.
## Slit-lamp exam
• Search for the Khodadoust line and localized KPs.
• Document Krachmer spots, edema, and neovascularization.
• Evaluate suture integrity and check for signs of infection.
## Microbiology
• If suture infection is suspected: Remove suture and send for smears/cultures.
actionSteps: Initiate intensive topical Prednisolone acetate 1% every 1–2 hours while awake.
Consider systemic steroids (Oral Prednisone 60–100 mg/day) for severe endothelial rejection.
Arrange urgent corneal specialist follow-up within 1–3 days.
Discuss long-term/lifetime low-dose steroid maintenance for high-risk grafts.
treatment: ## Endothelial rejection (intensive)
• Topical: Prednisolone acetate 1% q1h or Difluprednate 0.05% q2h while awake.
• Ointment: Dexamethasone 0.1% at bedtime.
• Systemic: Oral Prednisone 40–80 mg daily (tapered based on response).
• Hospitalization: For high-risk/severe cases, consider IV Methylprednisolone 500 mg (1–3 doses).
## Epithelial & stromal rejection
• Topical steroids: Required, though typically less frequent than for endothelial forms.
## Adjunctive care
• Cycloplegia: Cyclopentolate 1% tid for comfort and AC inflammation.
• IOP Control: Manage elevated intraocular pressure as needed.
• Immunosuppression: Topical Cyclosporine (0.05–2%) as an adjunct for treatment or prevention.
## Special considerations
• Suture Infection: Remove suture, culture, and start intensive antibiotics; reduce steroid frequency.
• HSV History: Start or increase suppressive oral antiviral therapy.
followUp: Early re-examination within 1–3 days to assess KPs, edema, and AC reaction.
Very slow steroid taper (weeks to months) once rejection has reversed.
Lifelong maintenance of low-dose topical steroids for high-risk grafts.
Patient education: Instruct to return immediately for "RSVP" symptoms (Redness, Sensitivity to light, Vision loss, Pain).
differentials: Epithelial downgrowth (scalloped border, non-responsive to steroids)
Elevated IOP with secondary epithelial edema
pearl: Corneal graft rejection is an ophthalmic emergency. The Khodadoust line (endothelial KPs) is pathognomonic. Intensive steroids started within 24 hours can often reverse the process and salvage the graft.

name: Corneal Refractive Surgery Complications
symptoms: ## Early (1–14 days)
• Decreasing visual acuity.
• Increased pain.
## Late (2 weeks – several months)
• Decreasing visual acuity.
• Severe glare and monocular diplopia.
• Dry-eye symptoms (burning, foreign body sensation).
findings: ## DLK (sands of the Sahara)
• Fine granular white cells in the LASIK flap interface (typically days 1–5).
• Sterile, non-infectious; lacks epithelial defects or significant conjunctival injection.
• Stages 3–4: central confluent cells with vision loss; requires flap lift and irrigation.
## Epithelial ingrowth
• Pearly gray-white nests or fronds under the flap edge.
• May cause flap edge elevation, irregular astigmatism, or stromal melt.
## Post-LASIK ectasia
• Progressive inferior corneal steepening and thinning.
• Results in increasing irregular astigmatism.
## PISK (pressure-induced stromal keratitis)
• Interface fluid resulting from steroid-induced intraocular pressure (IOP) rise.
• Mimics DLK appearance.
• Critical check: central IOP readings are falsely low; must measure IOP peripheral to the flap edge.
## Flap complications
• Dislocation: usually occurs within the first 24 hours.
• Striae/Microstriae: fine folds in the flap that may be visually significant.
• Buttonholes or free caps (incomplete or detached flaps).
## Post-PRK findings
• Corneal haze: subepithelial scarring (prevented by intraoperative Mitomycin-C).
• Delayed epithelial healing or refractive regression.
## Ocular surface
• Dry eye/neurotrophic keratopathy: most common complication due to transected corneal nerves.
etiology: ## Inflammatory & immune
• DLK: sterile response to interface contaminants (debris, meibum, endotoxins, glove powder).
• PISK: transudation of aqueous into the interface due to steroid-induced OHT.
• Corneal haze: aggressive wound healing response following PRK.
## Mechanical & anatomical
• Epithelial Ingrowth: displacement of cells during surgery or migration through poor edge apposition.
• Ectasia: excessive stromal ablation (residual bed <250–300 μm) or unrecognized preoperative keratoconus.
• Dry Eye: disruption of the homeostatic reflex due to corneal nerve transection.
redFlags: Post-LASIK ectasia (progressive thinning) → must perform cross-linking; no further ablation.
Flap dislocation or significant striae → urgent surgical repositioning required.
Stage 3–4 DLK → requires immediate aggressive steroids and interface irrigation.
Interface infection → mandates flap lift for culture; must cover atypical mycobacteria and fungi.
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Slit-lamp evaluation with fluorescein to assess the flap interface and epithelium.
• Refraction: perform hard contact lens overrefraction to identify irregular astigmatism.
## Tonometry
• Use Tono-Pen/Applanation; measure peripherally if PISK is suspected.
## Imaging
• Corneal topography/tomography (e.g., Pentacam) to evaluate for ectasia or irregular astigmatism.
• Schirmer testing for severe dry eye symptoms.
actionSteps: Identify complication type via slit-lamp and topography.
For DLK: start intensive topical steroids; prepare for flap lift if stage 3–4.
For PISK: stop topical steroids immediately and initiate IOP-lowering drops.
For Ectasia: plan corneal cross-linking (CXL) and fit for scleral lenses.
For flap striae: perform flap lift and refloat within 24 hours if visually significant.
treatment: ## DLK management
• Intensive Prednisolone acetate 1% every hour.
• Severe cases: lift flap and irrigate the interface to remove inflammatory cells.
## PISK management
• Discontinue topical steroids rapidly.
• Initiate ocular hypotensive (IOP-lowering) medications.
## Epithelial ingrowth
• Observation for peripheral, non-progressive cases.
• Surgical debridement/scrape for progressive or vision-threatening growth.
## Ectasia & haze
• Ectasia: corneal cross-linking (CXL); visual rehab with scleral lenses.
• PRK Haze: increase steroid frequency; consider PTK with Mitomycin-C for severe cases.
## Flap repair
• Dislocation/Striae: lift, irrigate, and refloat the flap.
• Lost flap: manage as a large epithelial defect.
followUp: Standard: day 1, week 1, and month 1 post-op.
DLK/PISK/Infection: daily monitoring until resolution.
Ectasia: serial topography every 3–6 months.
Dry Eye: assess at 3 and 6 months (most improve within 12 months).
pearl: Post-LASIK ectasia mimics keratoconus on topography; the treatment is early cross-linking and specialty contact lenses, never more laser ablation.

name: Corneal Ulcer
symptoms: ## Clinical presentation
• Rapid-onset severe eye pain and redness.
• Intense photophobia and foreign-body sensation.
• Mucopurulent or purulent discharge (eyelids may stick together).
• Blurred vision (severity depends on proximity to the visual axis).
## Risk factors
• Contact lens wear (overnight wear, poor hygiene) is the dominant modern risk.
• Recent trauma, dry eye, or exposure keratopathy.
• Chronic epithelial disease or prolonged topical steroid use.
findings: ## Primary signs
• Gray-white stromal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect (stains with fluorescein).
• Conjunctival hyperemia and ciliary flush.
• Anterior chamber (AC) cell and flare; hypopyon (layered pus) in severe cases.
• Stromal edema and Descemet folds surrounding the infiltrate.
## Etiology-specific clues
• Fungal: feathery edges, satellite lesions, or endothelial plaques.
• Acanthamoeba: ring infiltrate, perineuritis, and pain out of proportion to exam.
• Bacterial (Gram-positive): thick mucopurulent discharge.
## Complications & severity
• Pseudomonas: characteristic "soupy" mucoid stromal melt; can perforate within 24–48 hours.
• Descemetocele: extreme thinning where only Descemet membrane remains.
• Perforation: full-thickness corneal breach.
etiology: ## Bacterial
• Pseudomonas aeruginosa (high-risk in contact lens wearers).
• Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, and Moraxella (associated with malnutrition/alcoholism).
## Fungal
• Fusarium (common after vegetative/plant trauma).
• Aspergillus and Candida (common in chronic epithelial disease).
## Acanthamoeba
• Associated with contact lens wear and water exposure (pools, showers, hot tubs).
## Non-infectious / sterile
• Neurotrophic keratopathy (CN V lesions).
• Autoimmune peripheral melt (Rheumatoid Arthritis, GPA).
redFlags: Central ulcer >2 mm or vision <20/400 → urgent cornea specialist referral.
Rapidly progressing Pseudomonas melt → risk of perforation within 24–48 hours.
Descemetocele or clinical perforation → requires immediate surgical repair (glue or graft).
Misdiagnosing Acanthamoeba as HSV → steroids will accelerate tissue destruction.
investigations: ## Slit-lamp assessment
• Measure infiltrate size and epithelial defect dimensions exactly.
• Assess corneal thinning and depth of involvement using a narrow beam.
## Microbiology (scraping)
• Mandatory for ulcers >2 mm, central/sight-threatening, or treatment-resistant.
• Gram stain, Giemsa, KOH prep.
• Cultures: blood, chocolate, and Sabouraud agars.
• Culture contact lenses and lens cases if available.
## Specialized imaging
• Confocal microscopy for suspected Acanthamoeba or fungal infections.
actionSteps: ## Initial actions
• Discontinue contact lens wear immediately.
• Perform corneal scraping for stain and culture before starting antibiotics.
## Antibiotic regimen
• Vision-threatening/Central/Large (>2 mm): fortified Vancomycin (25–50 mg/mL) alternating with fortified Tobramycin (14 mg/mL) or Cefazolin (50 mg/mL) every 30–60 minutes around the clock.
• Small/Peripheral/Non-vision-threatening: fluoroquinolone monotherapy (Moxifloxacin or Gatifloxacin).
## Critical contraindications
• Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated until the organism is identified and a clear positive clinical response is confirmed.
• Premature steroid use can accelerate melting and worsen fungal/Acanthamoeba infections.
## Adjunctive care
• Start cycloplegics for pain management and to prevent synechiae.
• Daily re-examination is required until the ulcer is stabilized.
pearl: Pseudomonas in contact lens wearers is a "melt-down" emergency—it can perforate within 48 hours. Fungal ulcers typically feature feathery borders and satellite lesions. Never add steroids to the regimen until the infection is under control and the organism is known.

name: Cortical Blindness
symptoms: Bilateral complete or severe loss of vision.
Anton syndrome: patient may deny blindness (visual anosognosia).
Riddoch phenomenon: ability to perceive moving targets but not stationary ones.
findings: ## Diagnostic triad
• Severely reduced visual acuity bilaterally (may reach NLP).
• Normal-appearing fundus and optic discs (initially and long-term).
• Intact pupillary light reflexes (signals post-geniculate lesion; midbrain reflex arc is preserved).
## Clinical phenomena
• Riddoch phenomenon: statokinetic dissociation (moving targets perceived, stationary targets not).
• Blindsight: involuntary forced-choice discrimination despite lack of conscious vision.
• Incomplete cortical blindness: distance acuity may be better than near acuity due to small surviving macular islands.
## Anton syndrome
• Visual anosognosia (denial of blindness).
• Confabulation of visual descriptions (e.g., describing absent relatives).
• Results from bilateral occipital infarcts extending into visual association cortex.
## Balint syndrome
• Simultanagnosia: perceives only one object at a time.
• Optic ataxia: misreaching under visual guidance.
• Oculomotor apraxia: inability to voluntarily direct gaze to a target.
## Differential etiologies
• Vascular: embolic bilateral PCA infarct ("top of the basilar"), cardioembolic, or hypotensive watershed infarct.
• PRES: associated with hypertension, eclampsia, or immunosuppressant toxicity.
• Neurodegenerative: Posterior Cortical Atrophy (Benson syndrome) showing progressive visuospatial dysfunction.
• Rare: Heidenhain variant of CJD (blindness + dementia + myoclonus), MELAS, or trauma contusions.
## Imaging characteristics
• MRI with DWI: test of choice; detects acute infarct within minutes.
• FLAIR: identifies white-matter edema in PRES.
• Gadolinium: reveals tumors, metastases, or demyelination.
• Note: non-contrast CT may miss acute lesions; a normal CT does not exclude the diagnosis.
etiology: ## Vascular (most common)
• Bilateral occipital lobe infarctions (e.g., top-of-the-basilar embolic or cardioembolic events).
## Inflammatory & toxic
• Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES).
• Toxic exposures or amniotic fluid embolus (postpartum).
## Neoplastic & degenerative
• Occipital tumors or metastases.
• Neurodegenerative atrophy (Alzheimer variant).
redFlags: Acute bilateral vision loss with intact pupils → suggests bilateral PCA infarct; emergent stroke workup required.
Anton syndrome → high risk of injury due to denial; mandates supervised ambulation.
Progressive cortical visual dysfunction → consider tumor or neurodegenerative disease (Benson syndrome).
PRES with hypertension → emergent blood pressure control required.
investigations: ## Ocular assessment
• Comprehensive exam to document intact pupils and normal fundus.
• Visual acuity testing at distance (may reveal preserved macular islands).
• Rule out nonphysiologic (functional) visual loss.
## Systemic workup
• Urgent neuroimaging: MRI with DWI/FLAIR/contrast (preferred over CT).
• Cardiovascular: ECG, telemetry (rule out Afib), and echocardiogram.
• Vascular: Carotid and vertebral artery imaging.
• Clinical: Blood pressure and glycemic control.
actionSteps: Order emergent MRI with DWI and initiate a full stroke workup.
Obtain neurology consultation and admit for evaluation if symptoms are acute (<72h).
Identify and treat underlying cause (e.g., hypertension in PRES, embolic source in stroke).
Initiate safety planning and caregiver education (especially for Anton syndrome).
treatment: ## Acute management
• Hospitalization for neurologic observation and evaluation of stroke etiologies.
• Management of systemic triggers (BP control, eclampsia management).
## Rehabilitation
• Low-vision occupational therapy and rehabilitation.
• Orientation and mobility training.
• Family counseling regarding visual anosognosia (Anton syndrome).
followUp: Co-management with neurology and stroke teams.
Serial visual assessment to monitor potential partial recovery over weeks/months.
Neuropsychology involvement for patients with Anton syndrome.
pearl: Normal pupils and a normal fundus in a blind patient point directly to the occipital cortex—MRI is the diagnostic test, not the dilated exam.

name: Cotton–Wool Spot
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic (incidental finding on dilated exam).
Visual acuity is typically normal.
Rarely presents as a paracentral scotoma if located immediately adjacent to the fovea.
findings: ## Appearance
• Small, fluffy, white superficial retinal lesion.
• Feathery or indistinct margins.
• Typically ≤1 optic disc diameter in size.
• Located in the posterior pole (within 3 disc diameters of the optic nerve).
## Pathophysiology
• Focal microinfarct of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).
• Caused by occlusion of a terminal precapillary arteriole.
• Ischemia halts axoplasmic flow, leading to accumulation of "cytoid bodies."
• Note: This is swollen axoplasm, NOT an extracellular exudate (unlike yellow/waxy hard exudates).
## Clinical pattern-matching
• Single CWS (No known DM/HTN): Red flag for HIV, SLE, carotid disease, or GCA.
• Multiple CWS (≥6): Suggests diffuse ischemia (e.g., ischemic RVO, malignant HTN, severe DR).
• Diabetes: Accompanied by microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, and hard exudates.
• Hypertension: Accompanied by flame hemorrhages, AV nicking, and arteriolar narrowing.
• Endocarditis/Leukemia: Often presents with Roth spots.
## Imaging
• Acute OCT: Hyper-reflective band in the RNFL/GCL with underlying shadowing.
• Chronic OCT: Permanent focal RNFL thinning/atrophy.
• OCT-Angiography: Triangular zone of capillary dropout with apex toward the disc.
etiology: ## Common systemic causes
• Diabetes Mellitus: Most common etiology.
• Hypertension: Acute (malignant) or chronic.
• Retinal Vein Occlusion: Significant CWS count (≥6) indicates ischemic variety.
## Vasculitic & autoimmune
• Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (most common collagen vascular cause).
• Giant Cell Arteritis (if age ≥55 with disc pallor/jaw claudication).
• Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener).
## Infectious
• HIV Retinopathy: Early ocular manifestation; presents as posterior pole CWS.
• Others: Subacute bacterial endocarditis, Toxoplasmosis, Lyme disease.
## Hematologic & other
• Anemia, Leukemia, or Hypercoagulable states.
• Purtscher / Pseudo-Purtscher retinopathy (bilateral peripapillary CWS).
• Radiation Retinopathy: Resembles diabetic retinopathy; threshold ~1500–3000 cGy.
• Interferon therapy.
redFlags: Multiple CWS in a young patient → warrants urgent workup for HIV, lupus, or leukemia.
CWS combined with optic disc edema → consider hypertensive emergency or GCA.
CWS combined with Roth spots → suspect subacute bacterial endocarditis.
Isolated CWS in a healthy patient → warrants carotid Doppler or cardiac evaluation for emboli.
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• Dilated fundus exam (DFE) with 60/90D lens and indirect ophthalmoscopy.
• Evaluate for concurrent hemorrhages, vasculitis, or vascular occlusions.
## Systemic screening
• Mandatory: Blood pressure, Fasting Glucose/HbA1c, and CBC.
## Targeted workup
• Infectious: HIV testing.
• GCA (if ≥55): ESR, CRP, and platelet count.
• Embolic: Carotid Doppler and Echocardiogram.
• Rheum: ANA and ANCA (especially in young patients or multiple CWS).
actionSteps: Screen for undiagnosed systemic disease: BP, HbA1c, HIV, and CBC.
Optimize control of known diabetes or hypertension.
Obtain ESR/CRP immediately if GCA symptoms (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness) are present.
Coordinate with primary care or infectious disease for underlying management.
treatment: ## Systemic management
• Treat the underlying condition; CWS is a clinical sign, not a primary ocular disease.
• Optimize blood pressure, glucose, and lipid profiles.
• Adjust HAART for HIV retinopathy or manage rheumatologic triggers.
## Ocular management
• No specific ocular treatment is required for the CWS itself.
• Individual lesions typically fade over 4–12 weeks.
followUp: Hypertensive/Diabetic with isolated CWS: Systemic optimization and follow-up in 3–6 months.
Unexplained CWS: Comprehensive systemic workup required.
Evaluate for retinopathy progression or new ischemic signs at each visit.
differentials: Myelinated nerve fibers (stable, feathery striations radiating from disc)
pearl: A cotton-wool spot is a microinfarct of the nerve fiber layer. While often benign in diabetics, multiple CWS in a non-diabetic patient demand a workup for HIV, vasculitis, or embolic disease.

name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
symptoms: Unilateral, painless, acute vision loss (occurs over seconds).
Severe vision loss: counting fingers to light perception in 94% of cases.
May have a history of amaurosis fugax (transient visual loss).
findings: ## Acute signs
• Marked afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) on the affected side.
• Superficial retinal whitening/opacification of the posterior pole.
• Cherry-red spot at the fovea (transient; typically resolves over weeks).
• Narrowed retinal arterioles with boxcarring or segmentation of the blood column.
• Visible retinal arteriolar emboli.
• Cilioretinal artery sparing (15–30%): foveolar perfusion is maintained.
## Late signs (weeks later)
• Optic disc pallor and arteriolar attenuation.
• Inner-retinal atrophy.
• Vision of light perception or worse suggests Ophthalmic Artery Occlusion (OAO).
etiology: ## Embolic sources
• Cholesterol (Hollenhorst plaque): refractile, yellow crystals at bifurcations (carotid origin).
• Calcium: white plaques frequently causing distal infarction (cardiac valve origin).
• Platelet-fibrin: dull white plugs (carotid origin).
## Systemic vasculitis & inflammation
• Giant cell arteritis (GCA): mandates immediate exclusion in patients ≥50.
• Collagen vascular diseases: SLE, Polyarteritis nodosa.
## Hematologic disorders
• Hypercoagulable states: factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C/S deficiency.
• Hyperviscosity: polycythemia, multiple myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia.
• Sickle cell disease and profound anemia.
redFlags: ## Retinal stroke (code stroke)
• CRAO is a retinal stroke; transfer immediately to an Emergency Department/stroke center for emergent MRI/DWI and vascular workup.
## Giant cell arteritis (GCA)
• In patients ≥50 years, rule out GCA immediately via stat ESR, CRP, and platelets.
## Other concerns
• Concurrent TIA or stroke symptoms require urgent neurology/vascular intervention.
• Retinal whitening without a cherry-red spot and LP vision suggests OOA.
investigations: ## Emergency workup
• Immediate ED transfer for stroke protocol: MRI/DWI, carotid duplex, EKG, and echocardiogram.
• GCA panel: stat ESR, CRP, and platelets (if age ≥55 or no embolus seen).
## Systemic labs
• Blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, CBC, and PT/PTT.
• Younger patients (<50): hypercoagulable panel, syphilis testing, and protein electrophoresis.
## Ocular imaging
• OCT: shows inner retinal hyperreflectivity (acute) followed by thinning (late).
• IVFA: demonstrates delayed or absent arterial filling.
actionSteps: Arrange emergent ED transfer within the 4.5-hour stroke window.
Obtain stat GCA labs and start empiric steroids if GCA is suspected.
Coordinate carotid Doppler, ECG, and echocardiogram to identify embolic sources.
Consider ocular massage or AC paracentesis (low proven benefit).
treatment: ## Acute interventions (within 4–6 hours)
• Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis to lower IOP.
• Topical IOP-lowering drops (timolol, brimonidine).
• Inhaled carbogen (5% CO2 + 95% O2) or hyperbaric oxygen (if available within 24h).
## Systemic management
• Antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy as directed by neurology.
• Carotid endarterectomy for significant stenosis; anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation.
• Systemic steroids for confirmed GCA.
followUp: ## Vascular co-management
• Follow-up in 24–48 hours with neurology and vascular surgery.
## Ocular monitoring
• Re-examine at 1 week for neovascular complications.
• Monthly monitoring for 6 months to detect NVI or NVG.
• Refer for low-vision rehabilitation once vision is stable.
pearl: CRAO is a retinal stroke. The priority is preventing a secondary cerebral stroke, as 25% of patients have concurrent silent brain infarcts. The cherry-red spot is not permanent and resolves as infarction progresses.

name: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion
symptoms: Painless vision loss (typically unilateral).
findings: ## Acute fundus appearance
• "Blood and thunder" fundus: diffuse retinal hemorrhages in all four quadrants.
• Dilated and tortuous retinal veins.
• Optic disc edema and hemorrhages.
• Macular edema (ME).
## Late signs
• Optociliary collateral vessels on the disc (shunting blood from retinal to choroidal circulation).
• Neovascularization: NVI (iris), NVA (angle), NVD (disc), NVE (elsewhere).
## Subtypes
• Ischemic CRVO: VA <20/200, significant RAPD, and extensive capillary nonperfusion (>10 disc diameters on IVFA).
• Non-ischemic CRVO: VA often >20/200, mild/absent RAPD, and less severe fundus changes; 10% convert to ischemic.
etiology: ## Mechanism
• Central retinal artery (CRA) atherosclerosis compresses the adjacent vein at the lamina cribrosa, leading to thrombosis.
## Systemic risk factors
• Hypertension (HTN) is the most common association.
• Diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and glaucoma.
• Medications: oral contraceptives, diuretics.
## Hypercoagulable & inflammatory
• Young patients (<50): Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S deficiency, Antiphospholipid syndrome.
• Hyperviscosity: multiple myeloma, polycythemia, Waldenström macroglobulinemia.
• Vasculitis: Sarcoidosis, syphilis, SLE.
## Orbital compression
• Thyroid eye disease, orbital tumors, or AV fistulas.
redFlags: Ischemic CRVO → high risk of "90-day glaucoma" (neovascular glaucoma); requires monthly gonioscopy.
Anterior segment neovascularization (NVI/NVA) → mandates immediate PRP and/or anti-VEGF.
Bilateral or young patient (<50) → requires comprehensive hypercoagulable and hyperviscosity workup.
Vision <20/400 with cotton-wool spots → highly suspicious for the ischemic variant.
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• Gonioscopy BEFORE dilation: essential to rule out NVI and NVA.
• Dilated fundus examination and IOP measurement.
## Imaging
• OCT: baseline and serial monitoring for macular edema.
• IVFA: evaluate for capillary nonperfusion to risk-stratify neovascular potential.
## Systemic workup
• Blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, CBC, PT/PTT, and lipid profile.
• Target workup for young/bilateral cases: Hemoglobin electrophoresis, ANA, RPR/FTA-ABS, Protein C/S, Factor V Leiden, and Homocysteine.
actionSteps: Screen for systemic risk factors (HTN, DM, lipids) and glaucoma.
Obtain baseline OCT and widefield IVFA to assess ME and ischemia.
Initiate anti-VEGF therapy for macular edema.
Perform monthly follow-ups for 6 months with mandatory gonioscopy to detect NVI/NVA.
treatment: ## Macular edema (ME)
• Anti-VEGF (Standard of Care): ranibizumab, aflibercept, or bevacizumab.
• Intravitreal Steroids: Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) or triamcinolone (risks: cataract, high IOP).
## Neovascularization (NV)
• Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): indicated promptly if NVI or NVA is detected.
• Anti-VEGF: useful adjunct to PRP for rapid regression of neovascular vessels.
## Systemic optimization
• Manage underlying HTN, DM, and hyperlipidemia.
• Discontinue oral contraceptives; consider alternatives to diuretics.
• Aspirin 81–325 mg: commonly used but efficacy is unproven and may increase hemorrhage.
followUp: ## First 6 months
• Monthly visits to monitor for neovascular conversion and macular edema.
• Gonioscopy at every visit.
## Long-term
• Every 3 months after the first 6 months if stable.
• Annual systemic cardiovascular risk review with PCP.
pearl: In patients under 45, CRVO is a "hypercoagulable workup" until proven otherwise. For ischemic cases, remember the high risk of neovascular glaucoma within the first 90 days.

name: Crystalline Keratopathy
symptoms: Decreased vision (proportional to plaque density/location).
Photophobia.
Decreased corneal sensation (in certain etiologies).
Often asymptomatic; biofilm-sequestered organisms may not provoke typical pain or photophobia.
findings: ## Infectious crystalline keratopathy (ICK)
• Fine, white, branching, "snowflake" or "fern-like" stromal opacities.
• Key Diagnostic Clue: Significant disconnect between dense stromal infiltrate and a quiet, noninflamed eye.
• Organisms are sequestered within an exopolysaccharide biofilm, shielding them from host immunity and antibiotics.
## Clinical settings for ICK
• Post-Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Develops months to years later, usually on chronic topical steroids.
• Suture Tracks: Crystals propagate along sutures, which act as a biofilm scaffold and portal of entry.
• Other: Chronic contact lens wear, neurotrophic keratopathy, or post-refractive surgery interfaces.
## Causative organisms
• Streptococcus viridans (mitis group): Most common (>70%); produces glycocalyx biofilm.
• Others: Coagulase-negative Staph, Haemophilus, Pseudomonas, Atypical Mycobacteria (post-LASIK).
• Fungal: Candida, Alternaria.
## Non-infectious crystals
• Schnyder Dystrophy: Cholesterol/phospholipid deposits; associated with hyperlipidemia.
• Cystinosis: Polychromatic fine stromal crystals; associated with renal failure in children.
• Dysproteinemias: Multiple myeloma, MGUS, or Waldenström (diffuse fine stromal crystals).
• Bietti Dystrophy: Sparking yellow-white spots at the corneal limbus.
• Drug Deposition: Amiodarone, tamoxifen, or ciprofloxacin precipitates.
etiology: ## Infectious mechanism
• Biofilm formation on collagen or surgical hardware (sutures/flaps).
• Chronic topical steroid use is the primary permissive factor.
## Systemic & metabolic
• Schnyder: Autosomal dominant (AD) disorder of local corneal lipid metabolism.
• Cystinosis: Autosomal recessive (AR) systemic metabolic defect.
• Lymphoproliferative: Paraprotein deposition (Multiple Myeloma, cryoglobulinemia).
• Bietti: AR retinal and corneal crystalline dystrophy.
redFlags: Crystalline deposits post-PKP → suspect Strep viridans ICK; mandates prolonged fortified antibiotics.
Bilateral crystals in an adult → perform SPEP/UPEP to rule out Multiple Myeloma.
Crystals in a child → rule out Systemic Cystinosis (potentially fatal without renal management).
Progression despite antibiotics → consider atypical mycobacteria or surgical debulking.
investigations: ## Infectious workup
• Corneal cultures (bacterial and fungal).
• Mycobacterial cultures and acid-fast stains (especially for post-refractive surgery patients).
• Confocal microscopy: May visualize branching crystalline patterns.
## Systemic workup (non-infectious)
• Schnyder: Fasting lipid profile.
• Bietti: Electroretinogram (ERG).
• Cystinosis: Conjunctival biopsy, blood/bone marrow smear, and pediatric nephrology consult.
## Dysproteinemia workup
• Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) and Urine Protein Electrophoresis (UPEP).
• Free light chains, CBC with differential, serum calcium, and creatinine.
actionSteps: Differentiate between infectious (unilateral, post-surgical) and systemic (bilateral) causes.
For ICK: Initiate fortified topical antibiotics and reduce steroid frequency.
For suspected systemic cause: Coordinate with hematology or nephrology for metabolic/paraprotein screening.
Plan surgical debulking or repeat PKP for medically refractory ICK cases.
treatment: ## Infectious crystalline keratopathy
• Fortified Antibiotics: Topical Vancomycin (25–50 mg/mL) + Cefazolin (50 mg/mL) or Moxifloxacin.
• Frequency: Hourly initially; taper very slowly over weeks to months.
• Steroids: Reduce frequency or strength slowly (do not stop abruptly).
• Surgical: Suture removal, plaque debulking, or intrastromal antibiotic injections for resistant biofilm.
## Systemic & dystrophic causes
• Cystinosis: Topical cysteamine drops (dissolves crystals) and systemic cysteamine.
• Schnyder: Manage hyperlipidemia; consider lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty.
• Paraproteinemia: Treat the underlying hematologic malignancy.
followUp: ## ICK monitoring
• Frequent early follow-up (every few days) until clinical improvement is noted.
• Expect a slow response due to biofilm sequestration.
## Stable non-infectious cases
• Exams every 3–6 months once systemic management is established.
• Monitor visual acuity to determine the timing for corneal transplantation.
pearl: Branching corneal crystals are a major clinical "tell"—they can be the first sign of multiple myeloma or MGUS years before systemic symptoms appear. In post-graft patients, the "fern-like" infiltrate in a quiet eye is Strep viridans ICK until proven otherwise.

name: Crystalline Retinopathy
symptoms: Often asymptomatic; frequently an incidental finding on dilated exam.
Decreased central vision (if associated with macular edema or atrophy).
Key diagnostic indicator: specific drug exposure or systemic medical history.
findings: ## Hallmark
• Bright, refractile (sparkling) yellow-white intraretinal or intravascular deposits.
## Diagnostic triage
• Location: Perifoveal, diffuse posterior pole, intravascular, or mid-peripheral?
• Depth: Inner retina (superficial), outer retina/RPE, or intravascular?
• Systemic Clues: Drug history (Tamoxifen), renal status (Oxalosis), or IV drug use (Talc)?
## Specific drug patterns
• Tamoxifen: Bilateral perifoveal inner-retinal crystals (doughnut pattern); often associated with Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) and whorl-like corneal verticillata.
• Talc: Yellow-red intravascular refractile particles at arteriolar bifurcations; causes capillary nonperfusion and potentially disc/peripheral neovascularization.
• Canthaxanthin (Tanning Pills): Symmetric ring of superficial golden crystals in the inner retina; regresses slowly after cessation.
## Inherited & systemic patterns
• Bietti Crystalline Dystrophy: Yellow-white crystals at all retinal layers and the limbal corneal stroma; progressive RPE/choriocapillaris atrophy.
• Oxalosis (Primary or Methoxyflurane): Calcium-oxalate crystals at the RPE level; associated with systemic oxalosis and renal failure.
• MacTel 2: Tiny glistening crystals on the temporal parafoveal ILM; associated with right-angle venules and foveal thinning.
• Sjögren-Larsson Syndrome: Foveal crystals associated with ichthyosis and spasticity.
• Others: Nitrofurantoin, ethylene glycol, and chronic long-standing retinal detachment (cholesterol/oxalate crystals).
## Imaging characteristics
• OCT: Localizes crystals by depth (Inner retina: Tamoxifen/MacTel 2; RPE: Oxalosis/Bietti).
• IVFA: Identifies capillary nonperfusion (Talc) or macular edema (Tamoxifen).
• FAF: Highly sensitive for detecting RPE atrophy in Bietti dystrophy.
etiology: ## Drug toxicity
• Tamoxifen: Most common drug cause; risk increases with doses >20 mg/day or cumulative doses >7.7 g.
• Talc: IV drug abuse involving crushed oral tablets; talc filler lodges at vessel bifurcations.
• Methoxyflurane: Inhalational anesthetic metabolized to oxalic acid, causing retinal and systemic deposits.
• Canthaxanthin: Oral tanning agent requiring high cumulative doses (~19 g).
## Genetic & metabolic
• Bietti Dystrophy: Autosomal recessive CYP4V2 mutation affecting lipid metabolism; more common in East Asians.
• Primary Hyperoxaluria: Inherited oxalate overproduction leading to renal, cardiac, and retinal oxalosis.
## Other etiologies
• MacTel 2: Neurodegenerative condition frequently unmasking occult insulin resistance.
• West African Crystalline Maculopathy: Benign, stable yellow-white maculopathy in young patients.
• Ocular Siderosis: Retained intraocular metallic foreign body causing crystalline-like deposits.
redFlags: Bilateral progressive nyctalopia without drug history → suspect Bietti Crystalline Dystrophy; perform CYP4V2 testing.
Tamoxifen use with new visual symptoms → urgent evaluation for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).
Retinal crystals in the setting of renal failure → suspect systemic oxalosis; requires urgent nephrology referral.
Talc particles with neovascularization → high risk of vitreous hemorrhage; warrants PRP/Anti-VEGF.
Crystals following trauma → rule out a retained intraocular metallic foreign body.
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to determine crystal depth, location, and morphology.
• Corneal exam: Look for limbal crystals (Bietti) and whorl keratopathy (Tamoxifen).
• Skin exam: Check for IV drug track marks (Talc).
## Diagnostics & imaging
• OCT: Mandatory to detect CME and determine deposit depth.
• IVFA: Assess for capillary nonperfusion distal to emboli and confirm CME.
## Systemic & genetic
• Renal workup: 24-hour urine oxalate and creatinine if oxalosis is suspected.
• Lab tests: HbA1c (MacTel 2) and fasting lipids.
• Genetic testing: CYP4V2 for Bietti dystrophy confirmation.
actionSteps: Identify the crystalline pattern on fundus exam and localize depth via OCT.
Perform thorough medication reconciliation (Tamoxifen, tanning agents, anesthetics).
Coordinate with oncology or primary care to stop offending drugs.
Obtain urgent metabolic workup for suspected oxalosis (Renal/Hepatic).
treatment: ## Agent removal
• Coordinate drug cessation (Tamoxifen, Canthaxanthin, Nitrofurantoin) with the prescribing physician.
• Tamoxifen: An aromatase inhibitor may be a suitable alternative for postmenopausal patients.
## Complication management
• CME: Topical CAIs or intravitreal steroids.
• Neovascularization (Talc): Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) and Anti-VEGF injections.
## Systemic support
• Oxalosis: Urgent nephrology referral for primary hyperoxaluria management.
• Talc: Addiction-medicine/social-work referral.
• Progressive Dystrophies: Low-vision rehabilitation.
followUp: Obtain baseline OCT and autofluorescence to monitor stability or regression.
Perform annual exams for drug-induced cases after agent cessation.
Coordinate multidisciplinary care for patients with systemic metabolic or hematologic triggers.
differentials: Hard exudates (yellow, waxy, non-refractile; associated with edema)
pearl: Tamoxifen, canthaxanthin, and methoxyflurane all deposit intraretinal crystals—always perform a thorough drug history before pursuing expensive genetic or metabolic workups.

name: Cystoid Macular Edema
symptoms: Decreased central vision (often gradual over weeks).
Metamorphopsia (distorted vision) and central blur.
Typical onset 4–10 weeks following cataract surgery.
findings: ## Pathophysiology
• Fluid accumulation in the outer plexiform (Henle) and inner nuclear layers (INL).
• Radial geometry of Henle fibers creates a characteristic "petaloid" pattern.
## Irvine-Gass syndrome
• CME occurring specifically after cataract surgery; peak incidence at 6–10 weeks.
• Risk factors: vitreous loss, posterior capsule rupture, iris trauma, or prolonged surgery.
• Pre-existing risks: diabetes, uveitis, ERM, or retinitis pigmentosa.
## Fluorescein angiography (FA)
• Early phase: perifoveal dot-leakage from parafoveal capillaries.
• Late phase: classic "petaloid" or "spoke-wheel" pattern of hyperfluorescence.
• Optic disc leakage: frequent in Irvine-Gass (distinguishes it from diabetic or vein-occlusion CME).
## Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
• Hypo-reflective cystoid spaces in the INL and OPL.
• Loss of foveal depression and increased central foveal thickness (350–600 μm).
• Possible subfoveal neurosensory detachment.
## Differential by FA pattern
• Petaloid leak (True CME): Irvine-Gass, vein occlusion, uveitis, RP.
• Diffuse leak: Diabetic macular edema.
• No leak (Pseudo-CME): MacTel 2, tamoxifen, niacin, taxanes, X-linked retinoschisis.
## Red-flag mimic
• CME + new vitreous cells after cataract surgery → suspect chronic postoperative endophthalmitis (P. acnes or Staph epi).
etiology: ## Surgical / traumatic
• Postoperative: cataract (Irvine-Gass), laser photocoagulation, or cryotherapy.
• Complications: vitreous-to-wound, iris prolapse, or uveal incarceration.
## Vascular & inflammatory
• Retinal vascular disease: diabetes, CRVO, BRVO, or Coats disease.
• Uveitis: especially pars planitis (intermediate uveitis) and sarcoidosis.
• Vasculitis: Eales, Behçet, or MS-associated uveitis.
## Degenerative & dystrophic
• Retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
• Neovascular AMD and epiretinal membrane (ERM).
## Drug-induced
• Topical: prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost), epinephrine, and dipivefrin.
• Systemic (Pseudo-CME): nicotinic acid (niacin), taxanes (docetaxel), and fingolimod.
redFlags: Post-cataract vision loss with cystic changes → Irvine-Gass CME; requires NSAID/steroid combo.
CME in a non-operated eye → search for underlying uveitis, diabetes, or vascular occlusion.
Atypical CME unresponsive to anti-inflammatories → rule out drug toxicity or "Pseudo-CME" (no leak on FA).
CME + vitreous cells → rule out smoldering endophthalmitis.
investigations: ## Ocular examination
• Dilated fundus exam with 60/90D lens to evaluate foveal contour.
• Gonioscopy to rule out retained lens fragments or haptic malposition.
• Scleral depression to check for pars planitis (vitreous "snowbanks").
## Imaging
• OCT (Primary tool): documents foveal thickness and cystic spaces; used for serial monitoring.
• IVFA: confirms breakdown of blood-retinal barrier; distinguishes true CME from pseudo-CME.
## Systemic & supplemental
• HbA1c/Fasting glucose if diabetes is suspected.
• ERG if retinitis pigmentosa is suspected.
• Targeted serologies (ACE, syphilis, TB) if uveitis/vasculitis is suspected.
actionSteps: Obtain OCT to document fluid and FA to confirm petaloid leakage.
Start topical NSAID and steroid QID for 4–6 weeks.
Discontinue offending agents (prostaglandins, niacin).
Consider intravitreal steroids or anti-VEGF for refractory cases.
treatment: ## First-line (Irvine-Gass)
• Topical NSAID: Ketorolac 0.5%, Bromfenac 0.09%, or Nepafenac 0.3%.
• Topical Steroid: Prednisolone acetate 1% QID.
• Duration: 4–6 weeks, then slow taper.
## Second-line / refractory
• Intravitreal: triamcinolone (1–4 mg) or dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex).
• Anti-VEGF: Bevacizumab for persistent edema.
• Sub-Tenon triamcinolone injection.
## Systemic & surgical adjuncts
• Acetazolamide: useful specifically for RP-associated CME.
• Pars plana vitrectomy: for vitreomacular traction or vitreous-to-wound.
## Discontinue offending agents
• Topical: Prostaglandin analogs, epinephrine, dipivefrin.
• Systemic: Nicotinic acid (niacin).
followUp: Expect resolution over 3–6 months with appropriate treatment.
Monitor OCT every 4–6 weeks until fluid is resolved.
Counsel patient on visual prognosis; chronic CME may lead to permanent photoreceptor damage.
Monitor for IOP spikes if using long-term steroids.
pearl: Post-cataract CME (Irvine-Gass) peaks 4–6 weeks after surgery — an NSAID-steroid combo usually clears it, but suspect vitreous traction or epiretinal membrane if it refuses to resolve.

name: Dacryocystitis
symptoms: Painful, red swelling at the medial canthus.
Excessive tearing (epiphora).
Mucopurulent discharge expressible from the puncta.
Fever or malaise in severe cases.
findings: ## Acute signs
• Tender, erythematous, fluctuant swelling over the lacrimal sac.
• Swelling is located below the medial canthal tendon.
• Reflux of purulent material from the puncta upon sac compression.
• Potential progression to preseptal or orbital cellulitis.
## Chronic signs
• Recurrent mucoid or mucopurulent discharge without acute inflammation.
• Epiphora with expressible mucoid material.
• Possible cutaneous fistula in neglected cases.
## Pediatric considerations
• Congenital dacryocele (amniocele) appearing in the first weeks of life.
• Potential airway compromise in infants due to associated intranasal cysts.
etiology: ## Adult predisposition
• Acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO) is the primary cause.
• Pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae.
• Gram-negative organisms (Pseudomonas) more common in hospitalized/immunocompromised patients.
## Congenital & other
• Persistent imperforate valve of Hasner.
• Lacrimal sac dacryoliths or tumors (suspect if mass is chronic or unilateral).
redFlags: Signs of orbital cellulitis (proptosis, restricted motility, decreased vision).
Mass above the medial canthal tendon or bloody discharge → rule out lacrimal sac tumor.
Congenital dacryocele + respiratory distress → urgent airway evaluation for intranasal cyst.
Black nasal eschar in immunocompromised/diabetic patients → consider mucormycosis.
investigations: ## Acute workup
• Gram stain and culture of expressed purulent material.
• CT orbits and sinuses with contrast if orbital extension or atypical features are suspected.
## Chronic/atypical workup
• Lacrimal sac biopsy for chronic masses or suspected malignancy.
• Dacryocystography (DCG) or dye disappearance test after acute inflammation resolves.
actionSteps: Apply warm compresses and gentle lacrimal sac massage 4 times daily.
Initiate systemic antibiotics (oral or IV based on severity).
Perform incision and drainage (I&D) if a fluctuant abscess is present.
Schedule definitive dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) once the acute infection has settled.
treatment: ## Pharmacotherapy
• Mild: Oral Cephalexin (500 mg QID) or Amoxicillin-clavulanate (875 mg BID) x 7–10 days.
• Severe/Febrile: IV Cefazolin or Vancomycin/Ceftriaxone (if orbital/MRSA concern).
• Note: Topical antibiotics provide minimal benefit alone.
## Mechanical & surgical
• Warm compresses and sac massage.
• Transcutaneous I&D below the medial canthal tendon for fluctuant abscesses.
• Definitive DCR (external or endoscopic) is curative for underlying NLDO.
• Congenital Dacryocele: Probing under anesthesia ± intranasal cyst marsupialization.
followUp: Re-evaluate within 48–72 hours; escalate therapy/imaging if worsening.
Post-DCR: follow-up at 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months to ensure patency.
Biopsy any persistent mass or atypical chronic swelling.
differentials: Lacrimal sac tumor (mass often extends above medial canthal tendon)
Canaliculitis (Actinomyces; pouting punctum and sulfur granules)
pearl: Acute dacryocystitis occurs below the medial canthal tendon. A mass above the tendon is a tumor until proven otherwise. In newborns, medial canthal swelling (dacryocele) is an airway emergency until the nose is cleared of cysts.

name: Developmental Anterior Segment and Lens Anomalies/Dysgenesis
symptoms: infancy/childhood observation of corneal cloudiness or iris abnormalities
asymmetric red reflex
neonatal glaucoma triad: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm
asymptomatic iop elevation in older children
vision loss from amblyopia, anisometropia, or corneal opacity
positive family history (often autosomal dominant)
findings: ## Axenfeld–rieger spectrum
• posterior embryotoxon: anteriorly displaced, prominent schwalbe line
• iris changes: peripheral iris strands to schwalbe line, atrophy, corectopia, and pseudopolycoria
• axenfeld anomaly: isolated angle findings
• rieger anomaly: angle findings plus iris abnormalities
• rieger syndrome: ocular findings plus systemic features (dental, craniofacial, periumbilical)
• glaucoma: develops in ~50% of cases
## Peters anomaly
• central corneal opacity with underlying posterior corneal/descemet defect
• type i: iridocorneal adhesions only
• type ii: keratolenticular contact or cataract
• glaucoma: develops in ~50% of cases
• peters-plus syndrome: includes short stature, developmental delay, and cleft lip/palate
## Aniridia
• panocular disorder with variable iris hypoplasia
• foveal hypoplasia (presents with infancy-onset nystagmus and low vision)
• progressive keratopathy (limbal stem cell deficiency), cataract, and optic nerve hypoplasia
• glaucoma: develops in 50–75% of cases
• wagr syndrome: wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, mental retardation
## General signs
• congenital glaucoma: buphthalmos and haab striae (descemet breaks)
• posterior embryotoxon alone: normal variant in 15% of the population
etiology: ## Embryology
• developmental arrest of neural-crest cells during anterior segment formation
## Genetics
• pitx2 and foxc1: associated with axenfeld–rieger spectrum
• pax6: associated with aniridia and peters anomaly
• cyp1b1: associated with primary congenital glaucoma
• inheritance: typically autosomal dominant with variable expressivity; some sporadic cases
redFlags: buphthalmos or elevated iop in infancy
corneal clouding or haab striae in newborns
foveal hypoplasia or nystagmus (red flag for aniridia)
missed wilms tumor screening in aniridia patients
iris atrophy with corectopia and systemic anomalies
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• complete ophthalmic exam: corneal diameter, gonioscopy, iop, and disc evaluation
• exam under anesthesia (eua) often required for accurate measurements in infants
• cycloplegic refraction and visual acuity assessment
## Imaging and monitoring
• a-scan ultrasound: serial axial length monitoring for buphthalmos
• fundus photography for serial disc documentation
## Systemic screening
• genetic testing: pitx2, foxc1, pax6, cyp1b1, or microarray for 11p13 (aniridia)
• renal ultrasound (aniridia/wagr): every 3 months until age 5, then every 6–12 months until age 8
• multidisciplinary referral: dental, cardiac, craniofacial, and endocrine evaluations
actionSteps: measure corneal diameter, iop, and axial length (eua if necessary)
initiate genetic testing and family counseling
coordinate systemic screening (renal ultrasound for aniridia is critical)
aggressive management of glaucoma and amblyopia
treatment: ## Medical and refractive
• refractive correction and aggressive amblyopia therapy
• glaucoma meds: beta-blockers, pgans, or cais (avoid pilocarpine as it is ineffective)
## Surgical intervention
• glaucoma surgery: goniotomy or trabeculotomy (first-line); tube shunts for refractory cases
• structural surgery: cataract extraction or corneal transplant (staged with glaucoma control)
## Systemic management
• co-management with pediatric specialists for wilms tumor and systemic defects
followUp: ## Lifelong monitoring
• ophthalmic exam every 6 months to monitor iop and glaucoma progression
• frequent visits for amblyopia therapy and visual acuity testing
## Wagr screening
• serial renal ultrasound every 3 months until age 7–8 if wt1 deletion is confirmed
review: any infant with epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm requires iop and corneal diameter measurement to rule out congenital glaucoma

name: Diabetic Retinopathy
symptoms: often asymptomatic in early stages
blurred or fluctuating vision from macular edema
sudden vision loss or floaters from vitreous hemorrhage
progressive vision loss from tractional retinal detachment
findings: ## NPDR
• microaneurysms and dot-blot hemorrhages
• hard exudates and cotton-wool spots
• venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (irma)
## PDR
• neovascularization of the disc (nvd) or elsewhere (nve)
• preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage
• fibrovascular proliferation and tractional retinal detachment
## Diabetic macular edema (DME)
• retinal thickening or hard exudates within 1 disc diameter of the fovea
• center-involving if fovea is thickened on oct
## Staging (4-2-1 rule for severe NPDR)
• >20 intraretinal hemorrhages in 4 quadrants
• venous beading in 2 quadrants
• irma in 1 quadrant
etiology: ## Mechanism
• chronic hyperglycemia damages retinal capillary pericytes
• capillary non-perfusion and ischemia drive vegf release
## Risk factors
• duration of diabetes (strongest risk factor)
• poor glycemic control (hba1c), hypertension, and dyslipidemia
• pregnancy, nephropathy, and smoking
• early worsening: transient progression risk during rapid tightening of glycemic control
redFlags: vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment
neovascular glaucoma (nvi with elevated iop and pain)
center-involving dme with acute vision drop
pregnancy with pre-existing dr (high risk of rapid progression)
investigations: ## Ocular examination
• gonioscopy: perform before dilation to assess for nvi and nva
• slit lamp (90d/60d): rule out neovascularization and macular edema
• indirect ophthalmoscopy: examine the retinal periphery
## Imaging
• oct: assess presence and extent of dme
• ivfa: identify perfusion abnormalities, foveal ischemia, and subclinical neovascularization
• octa: assess central macular ischemia
## Systemic
• fasting blood sugar, hba1c, and lipid panel
• blood pressure monitoring
actionSteps: document dr stage with widefield imaging and oct macula
coordinate "abc" optimization: a1c <7%, bp <130/80, cholesterol control
refer to retina for center-involving dme or pdr
monitor pregnant patients monthly if severe npdr or pdr is present
initiate urgent iop control and pdr treatment if neovascular glaucoma occurs
treatment: ## Systemic optimization
• hba1c <7%: ~35% microvascular risk reduction per 1% drop
• blood pressure <130/80 mmhg: reduces dr progression by ~34%
• lipid control: statins and fenofibrate (reduces progression independently of lipids)
## Diabetic macular edema
• anti-vegf: first-line for center-involving dme (aflibercept, ranibizumab, bevacizumab)
• steroids: dexamethasone or fluocinolone implants (second-line; watch for cataract/iop)
• focal macular laser: for extrafoveal microaneurysms causing edema
## Proliferative DR
• panretinal photocoagulation (prp): durable, single-session for non-adherent patients
• anti-vegf: non-inferior to prp with better peripheral field preservation
• combination: anti-vegf plus prp for concurrent dme or dense vitreous hemorrhage
## Vitrectomy indications
• dense, non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage
• tractional rd involving or threatening the macula
• dense premacular hemorrhage or chronic refractory dme
followUp: ## Routine screening
• no retinopathy: annual dilated exam
• mild npdr: every 6–9 months
• moderate to severe npdr: every 3–6 months
• pdr: every 1–4 months depending on high-risk criteria
## Pregnancy
• pre-existing dm (no dr): exam first and third trimester
• mild to moderate npdr: every trimester
• high-risk npdr or pdr: monthly exams
• gestational diabetes: no retinopathy risk; no exam required
review: macular edema (not pdr) is the leading cause of visual loss in diabetic retinopathy
4-2-1 rule for severe npdr: 50% risk of developing pdr within 1 year
avoid anti-vegf in pregnancy when possible; observe dme as it often regresses postpartum

name: Dry Eye Syndrome
symptoms: burning, dryness, and foreign body sensation
mildly to moderately decreased vision
paradoxical excess tearing (reflex tearing)
exacerbation by smoke, wind, heat, low humidity, or prolonged visual tasks
findings: ## Ocular surface staining
• punctate corneal or conjunctival staining (fluorescein, rose bengal, or lissamine green)
• distribution usually inferior or in the interpalpebral zone
## Tear film
• excess mucus or debris in the tear film
• corneal filaments in severe cases
etiology: ## Classification (dews II)
• aqueous-deficient and evaporative subtypes; pure forms are rare and usually coexist
## Aqueous-deficient
• sjögren-associated: primary or secondary (ra, sle, systemic sclerosis)
• non-sjögren: age-related (most common), lacrimal gland obstruction, or infiltration (sarcoidosis, igg4)
• reflex block: post-refractive surgery (lasik/prk/smile) or cataract surgery
• systemic drugs: antihistamines, anticholinergics, tcas, ssris, isotretinoin, beta-blockers, diuretics
## Evaporative
• meibomian gland dysfunction (mgd): major cause due to lipid-layer deficiency
• blink abnormalities: reduced rate (screens) or parkinson disease
• lid malposition: ectropion, lagophthalmos, proptosis, or cn vii palsy
• vitamin a deficiency: mucin deficiency due to goblet cell loss
## Temporal patterns
• aqueous-deficient: worse as the day progresses
• evaporative/mgd: worse on awakening; clears with blinking
redFlags: filamentary keratitis or persistent epithelial defects
systemic features (dry mouth, parotid swelling, arthritis) suggesting sjögren syndrome
severe dry eye with lagophthalmos or cn vii palsy
severe neurotrophic dry eye post-lasik
investigations: ## Slit lamp
• assess tear meniscus height before instilling drops
• fluorescein staining for punctate erosions and tear break-up time (tbut <10 s abnormal)
• rose bengal or lissamine green for conjunctival staining
## Diagnostic battery
• schirmer i (unanesthetized): normal ≥15 mm; borderline 10–15 mm; abnormal ≤10 mm
• schirmer (anesthetized): measures basal tearing; abnormal ≤5 mm
• tear osmolarity: abnormal >308 mosm/l or asymmetry >8 mosm/l
• mmp-9 (inflammadry): indicates ocular surface inflammation (≥40 ng/ml)
## Systemic screening
• screen for sjögren syndrome (ss-a/ro, ss-b/la, ana, rf) if systemic symptoms are present
actionSteps: categorize subtype as aqueous-deficient vs evaporative (schirmer, tbut, meibography)
initiate lifestyle modifications and preservative-free artificial tears (4–6×/day)
add topical anti-inflammatories (cyclosporine/lifitegrast) if moderate or refractory
perform sjögren workup for severe bilateral disease or systemic symptoms
treatment: ## Mild to moderate
• artificial tears (preferably preservative-free) up to q1–2h
• lubricating gel or ointment at bedtime
• lifestyle: humidifiers and smoking cessation
## Anti-inflammatory
• cyclosporine (0.05% or 0.09%): for chronic inflammation; takes 1–3 months for effect
• lifitegrast (5%): improvement often within 2 weeks
• mild topical steroids: short-term bridge to reduce initial burning and inflammation
## Procedural
• punctal occlusion: collagen (temporary) or silicone (permanent) plugs
• thermal cautery: for permanent occlusion if plugs repeatedly fail
## Severe or adjunctive
• autologous serum tears and oral omega-3 fatty acids
• filament management: manual removal and 10% acetylcysteine q.i.d.
• bandage lenses or scleral lenses; moisture chamber goggles at night
• lateral tarsorrhaphy for refractory exposure-related dry eye
followUp: ## Clinical review
• follow up in 4–6 weeks to assess treatment response
• assess lid margin, meibomian glands, and tbut at each visit
## Escalation
• step up to topical cyclosporine/lifitegrast if refractory
• refer to rheumatology for confirmed sjögren or systemic autoimmune disease
review: symptom-exam correlation is poor; severe symptoms may exist with minimal signs
address lid malposition (exposure) before labeling as idiopathic dry eye
treat blepharitis and surface inflammation before performing punctal occlusion

name: Endogenous Bacterial Endophthalmitis
symptoms: decreased vision in an acutely ill or septic patient
ocular pain and redness
floaters and photophobia
recent hospitalization, indwelling catheter, or systemic procedure (e.g., heart valve, gi/gu surgery)
history of iv drug use
note: no history of recent intraocular surgery (distinguishes from exogenous)
findings: ## Signature findings
• chorioretinal abscesses: cream-yellow round elevations at the choroid/retina level
• severe vitritis, dense debris, and absent red reflex
• anterior chamber cell, flare, and hypopyon
• iris microabscesses
• roth spots: white-centered flame hemorrhages (septic emboli)
• advanced signs: corneal edema, chemosis, proptosis, and restricted motility (panophthalmitis)
• bilateral involvement in ~25% of cases
## Organism-source patterns
• klebsiella pneumoniae: associated with pyogenic liver abscess in asian diabetic patients; extremely poor prognosis
• staphylococcus aureus / streptococcus: associated with endocarditis, skin/soft-tissue infection, or orthopedic hardware
• bacillus cereus: associated with iv drug use; causes fulminant globe destruction within 24–48 hours
• gram-negative rods (e. coli, pseudomonas): associated with urinary or biliary sources
• neisseria meningitidis: associated with meningococcal sepsis and purpura
## Greenwald severity classification
• anterior focal: localized to iris/ac; best prognosis
• posterior focal: single chorioretinal abscess; intermediate prognosis
• anterior diffuse: severe anterior uveitis with hypopyon; guarded prognosis
• posterior diffuse: widespread retinitis/vitritis; poor prognosis
• panophthalmitis: entire globe and orbit involvement; often requires enucleation
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• hematogenous spread of infection from a distant systemic source to the eye
## Risk factors
• diabetes mellitus and immunocompromise
• iv drug use and endocarditis
• indwelling catheters, central lines, and recent gi/gu or cardiac surgery
redFlags: ocular inflammation in a septic or acutely ill patient
asian diabetic patients with suspected liver abscess (klebsiella)
fulminant progression in iv drug users (bacillus cereus)
right-sided endocarditis with embolic ocular findings
investigations: ## Ocular diagnostics
• b-scan ultrasound: mandatory if no fundus view to assess vitritis and abscesses
• vitreous biopsy: highest yield (~60%) for culture
• anterior chamber tap: lower yield (~20%)
## Systemic workup
• blood cultures (two sets) and urine culture
• echocardiography (tse or tte) to rule out endocarditis
• abdominal imaging (ct/mri) to identify occult abscess (especially liver)
• chest x-ray, cbc with differential, hba1c, and hiv testing
• lumbar puncture if meningeal signs are present
actionSteps: obtain immediate blood and urine cultures
perform urgent vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotic injection
