request infectious disease (id) consult for systemic co-management
order echocardiogram and abdominal imaging to identify the primary source
initiate broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics with good ocular penetration
treatment: ## Intravitreal therapy
• empiric vancomycin and ceftazidime
• add ampicillin or amphotericin-b if listeria or fungal infection is suspected
• avoid amikacin due to risk of macular infarction
## Systemic therapy
• iv antibiotics with vitreous penetration (e.g., fluoroquinolones, linezolid, meropenem)
• tailor antibiotics to the identified systemic source and culture results
## Surgical intervention
• urgent pars plana vitrectomy (ppv) for severe vitritis (va <20/400) or non-response to tap-and-inject
• evisceration or enucleation for blind, painful, uncontrolled infection
followUp: ## Inpatient monitoring
• daily ophthalmology examination until stabilized
• coordinate systemic surveillance (serial blood cultures/imaging) with medicine/id
## Outpatient monitoring
• weekly exams for one month following discharge
• serial echocardiograms to monitor for metastatic infection
review: endogenous endophthalmitis in an asian patient with liver abscess is klebsiella until proven otherwise
the eye exam serves as a window to occult sepsis; ocular findings may precede systemic criteria

name: Endophthalmitis
symptoms: sudden onset of decreased vision
increasing eye pain after surgical procedure or trauma
insidious vision loss, redness, and pain (subacute form)
findings: ## Anterior segment
• hypopyon and fibrin with severe anterior chamber reaction
• eyelid and corneal edema
• intense conjunctival injection and chemosis
## Posterior segment
• vitreous cells, haze, and vitreous abscesses
• decreased red reflex
## Subacute presentation
• white plaque or opacities on the lens capsule (c. acnes)
• clumps of fibrinous exudate in the ac, on the iris, or pupillary border
• transient response to steroids followed by recurrence
etiology: ## Postoperative
• acute (<6 weeks): s. epidermidis (most common), s. aureus, or streptococcus
• acute gram-negative: pseudomonas, proteus, klebsiella, e. coli
• chronic (>6 weeks): cutibacterium acnes or fungi (aspergillus, candida)
## Other causes
• post-injection: streptococcus (oral flora) or s. epidermidis
• post-traumatic: bacillus cereus (fulminant; associated with organic/soil matter)
• bleb-associated: streptococcus or gram-negative species from leaking blebs
• endogenous: hematogenous spread from endocarditis, ivdu, or catheters
redFlags: pain and vision loss post-surgery (endophthalmitis until proven otherwise)
hypopyon and severe vitritis within days of surgery
endogenous presentation signaling systemic sepsis
bleb-associated or bacillus cereus cases (highly fulminant)
investigations: ## Examination
• evaluate for wound/bleb leaks, exposed sutures, or vitreous to the wound
• b-scan ultrasound to assess vitritis and membranes if fundus view is limited
## Sampling (vision-based)
• vision lp or worse: diagnostic and therapeutic pars plana vitrectomy (ppv)
• vision hm or better: vitreous tap (aspiration) or ac paracentesis
## Laboratory
• smears: gram, giemsa, and methenamine-silver
• cultures: blood, chocolate, sabouraud, and thioglycolate media
actionSteps: perform vitreous tap for gram stain, culture, and pcr
inject intravitreal vancomycin (1mg) and ceftazidime (2.25mg) immediately
arrange immediate ppv if vision is light perception or worse (evs criteria)
initiate systemic workup if endogenous source is suspected
treatment: ## Intravitreal therapy
• vancomycin (1mg/0.1ml) and ceftazidime (2.25mg/0.1ml) cornerstone
• amikacin (0.4mg/0.1ml) if penicillin allergic
• consider dexamethasone (0.4mg/0.1ml) for severe vitritis
## Medical therapy
• prednisolone acetate 1% q1h for ac inflammation
• fortified antibiotics (vancomycin/tobramycin) if bleb/wound leak present
• atropine 1% bid–tid
## Prevention
• 5% povidone-iodine prep of conjunctiva/eyelids (proven risk reduction)
• intraoperative intracameral antibiotics
followUp: ## Early monitoring
• evaluate q12–24h initially; relief of pain is a key early sign of response
• clinical improvement (reduced hypopyon/inflammation) expected within 48h
## Long-term management
• oral prednisone 60mg daily x 5 days (per evs) once infection is sterilized
• reinject antibiotics or consider ppv if clinical status deteriorates
• slowly taper topical medications as the eye responds
review: any patient with pain and vision loss 1–7 days post-cataract surgery has endophthalmitis until proven otherwise
the endophthalmitis vitrectomy study (evs) provides the primary management framework

name: Epiretinal Membrane (Macular Pucker, Surface-Wrinkling Retinopathy, Cellophane Maculopathy)
symptoms: metamorphopsia (distorted vision) is the most common volunteered symptom
often asymptomatic; detected on routine examination
decreased central visual acuity
incidence increases with age; ~20% bilateral (often asymmetric)
findings: ## Clinical spectrum
• cellophane maculopathy: fine glistening membrane on the retinal surface
• macular pucker: thick gray-white membrane with prominent contraction
• retinal folds radiating from the membrane
• macular vessel displacement, straightening, or tortuosity drawn toward the membrane
• advanced: macular edema, intraretinal cystoid spaces, or macular detachment
## OCT diagnostics
• thin hyperreflective line along the ilm with focal "saw-tooth" adhesions
• retinal thickening and loss of foveal contour
• ectopic inner foveal layers (eifl) in advanced disease
## Govetto OCT staging
• stage 1: foveal pit preserved
• stage 2: pit lost; no eifl
• stage 3: eifl present
• stage 4: disorganized inner retina (worst prognosis)
## Pseudohole VS ftmh
• ring-shaped erm condensation may simulate a full-thickness hole (ftmh)
• watzke-allen sign: slit beam is distorted but not broken (true ftmh is broken)
etiology: ## Idiopathic
• ~95% of cases; typically associated with age-related pvd
## Secondary causes
• post-injury: retinal cryotherapy, photocoagulation, or prior retinal breaks/detachment
• surgical/traumatic: prior intraocular surgery or vitreous hemorrhage
• vascular: diabetic retinopathy or retinal vein occlusion
• inflammatory: uveitis
## Pediatric
• rare; occurs in young children without obvious underlying cause
redFlags: rapid decline in visual acuity or progressive metamorphopsia
erm associated with a lamellar macular hole
bilateral erm in a young patient (requires exclusion of inflammation)
recurrent erm after previous retinal surgery
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• dilated fundus exam with slit lamp biomicroscopy (60/90-d or contact lens)
• thorough peripheral retinal exam to rule out breaks
## Imaging
• oct: gold standard for staging, measuring eifl, and monitoring thickening
• octa: optional to rule out concurrent vascular pathology
actionSteps: perform oct to document stage, eifl, and foveal contour
observe asymptomatic cases with good visual acuity
vitrectomy with membrane peel for metamorphopsia or vision ≤20/40
prioritize cataract surgery if visually significant before membrane peel
treatment: ## Observation
• first-line for asymptomatic patients with good vision
• serial oct monitoring every 6 months
## Surgical intervention
• pars plana vitrectomy (ppv) with membrane and ilm peel
• indicated for significant metamorphopsia or progressive vision loss
• ilm peel is performed to reduce recurrence risk to ~1%
• manage underlying causes (e.g., uveitis) before surgical intervention
followUp: ## Monitoring
• examination and oct every 6 months for stable, asymptomatic cases
## Postoperative care
• gradual visual improvement expected over 3–6 months (up to 2 years)
• monitor for cataract progression (nearly universal in phakic patients)
review: 95% of cases are idiopathic and associated with age-related pvd
metamorphopsia is the hallmark symptom, though most patients remain asymptomatic initially
surgical success often sees vision improve from 20/110 preoperatively to 20/55 postoperatively

name: Episcleritis
symptoms: acute or rapid onset of redness (one or both eyes)
mild discomfort or foreign body sensation
no discharge and no photophobia
typically affects young-to-middle-aged adults; more common in women
frequent history of recurrent episodes
findings: ## Clinical types
• simple (sectoral or diffuse): salmon-pink redness of the superficial episcleral plexus
• nodular: discrete, mobile, elevated pink nodule; more symptomatic and tender
## Differentiation (phenylephrine test)
• episcleritis: superficial vessels blanch (redness fades) within 10–15 minutes
• scleritis: deep vessels do not blanch; violaceous hue and engorgement persist
## Mechanical signs
• cotton-swab test: superficial vessels move freely over the underlying sclera
• pain: mild discomfort only (unlike the severe boring pain of scleritis)
• vision, pupils, and anterior chamber are typically normal
etiology: ## Idiopathic
• ~70% of cases; most patients have no underlying systemic disease
## Systemic associations
• autoimmune: rheumatoid arthritis, sle, inflammatory bowel disease, ankylosing spondylitis, vasculitis
• skin/metabolic: rosacea, atopy, gout
• infectious: herpes zoster, syphilis
## Medications
• topiramate
• pamidronate
redFlags: progression to scleritis: severe pain that radiates or wakes the patient at night
deep scleral vessels that fail to blanch with phenylephrine 2.5%
recurrent bilateral episodes suggesting underlying systemic disease
failure to improve with standard topical therapy
investigations: ## Slit lamp evaluation
• phenylephrine 2.5% test: assess for blanching of superficial vs deep vessels
• cotton-swab test: check for vessel mobility over the sclera
• comprehensive exam: rule out corneal or anterior chamber involvement
## Systemic screening (for recurrent or nodular cases)
• labs: cbc, cmp, esr, crp, ana, rf, anti-ccp, and uric acid
• infectious: rpr, vdrl, and treponemal-specific assays
• specific markers: anca (vasculitis) or hla-b27 (if joint symptoms present)
actionSteps: perform phenylephrine 2.5% test to rule out scleritis
initiate chilled artificial tears and observation for mild cases
prescribe oral nsaids for symptomatic or nodular forms
order systemic workup only for recurrent, bilateral, or nodular episodes
treatment: ## Initial management
• chilled artificial tears 4x daily and cold compresses
• reassurance: most simple cases resolve spontaneously in 1–2 weeks
## Pharmacology
• oral nsaids: ibuprofen 400–600 mg 3x daily with food
• topical nsaids as an adjunct for persistent symptoms
• topical steroids: short course of weak steroids (e.g., loteprednol or fluorometholone) for refractory cases
## Systemic coordination
• treat underlying rosacea or gout; refer to rheumatology if autoimmune workup is positive
followUp: ## Monitoring
• re-examine in 1–2 weeks if symptomatic
• monitor iop closely if topical steroids are initiated
## Recurrence
• initiate systemic workup after >3 episodes
• refer to rheumatology for co-management if systemic disease is identified
review: ## Clinical pearl
• episcleritis is usually benign and self-limiting, whereas scleritis carries significant mortality risk if untreated
• phenylephrine 2.5% is the most important discriminator: superficial vessels blanch in episcleritis; deep vessels do not in scleritis
• nodular episcleritis lasts longer and has a higher rate of systemic association than the simple form

name: Erythema Multiforme, Stevens–Johnson Syndrome, and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis
symptoms: flu-like prodrome: fever, malaise, arthralgia, dysphagia
ocular: red eyes, pain, burning
cutaneous: skin rash with target lesions, dusky macules, or blisters
findings: ## Disease spectrum
• erythema multiforme (em) minor and major
• stevens–johnson syndrome (sjs): <10% body surface area (bsa) detached
• sjs/ten overlap: 10–30% bsa detached
• toxic epidermal necrolysis (ten): >30% bsa detached
• eye findings present in 50–80% of patients
## Mucocutaneous hallmarks
• target lesions: three concentric zones (central dusky, pale edema, erythematous rim)
• nikolsky sign: positive (epidermal sliding on lateral pressure)
• oral stomatitis with pathognomonic hemorrhagic lip crusting
## Acute ocular phase (<2 weeks)
• bilateral severe mucopurulent conjunctivitis and thick tarsal pseudomembranes
• conjunctival sloughing and large corneal epithelial defects
• eyelid margin ulceration and eyelash shedding
• high risk of corneal melt or perforation
## Chronic cicatricial phase
• severe dry eye (schirmer near zero) due to loss of goblet cells and lacrimal ductules
• symblepharon, ankyloblepharon, and keratinized lid margins
• limbal stem cell deficiency (lscd): causes conjunctivalization and neovascularization
• lid malposition: cicatricial entropion and trichiasis
## Prognostic tools
• scorten: predicts mortality based on age, hr, bsa, and bun
• sotozono grading: grade 3 (pseudomembrane + epithelial defect) mandates immediate amt
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• t-cell–mediated hypersensitivity activating cd8+ cytotoxic t cells
• granulysin drives widespread keratinocyte apoptosis
## Triggers
• em: infection-triggered (hsv most common, mycoplasma, adenovirus)
• sjs/ten: drug-triggered (satan mnemonic: sulfa, allopurinol, tetracyclines/anticonvulsants, nsaids, nevirapine)
## Pharmacogenomics
• hla-b*15:02 (carbamazepine), hla-b*58:01 (allopurinol), hla-b*57:01 (abacavir)
redFlags: acute ocular surface involvement in sjs
fever with mucosal ulcers and skin rash
suspected drug trigger (stop immediately)
late-stage limbal stem cell deficiency
investigations: ## Ocular evaluation
• slit-lamp exam with eyelid eversion for fornix inspection
• document epithelial defects and assign sotozono grade
## Systemic evaluation
• calculate scorten score and obtain skin biopsy
• dermatology and internal medicine consults
• cultures if secondary infection is suspected
actionSteps: stop the suspected drug immediately and document the allergy
admit to a specialized burn unit for systemic support
obtain ophthalmology consult within 24 hours of rash onset
perform amniotic membrane transplantation (amt) within 72 hours to 1 week
peel pseudomembranes daily with a moistened cotton swab
treatment: ## Acute systemic
• supportive care (hydration, wound care, nutrition) in burn unit
• adjuncts: consider ivig or cyclosporine
## Acute ocular
• topical steroids: prednisolone acetate 1% or difluprednate 4–8x daily
• aggressive preservative-free lubrication (tears, gels, and ointments)
• prophylactic topical antibiotics for epithelial defects
## Surgical intervention
• amniotic membrane transplant (amt) over lid margins, conjunctiva, and fornix (<72 hours)
• daily manual pseudomembrane peeling
followUp: ## Inpatient
• daily ophthalmic monitoring for defects, iop, and infection
## Chronic
• management of dry eye, symblepharon, and trichiasis
• lscd management: scleral lenses (prose), serum tears, or stem cell transplant
review: sjs is a day-one ophthalmic emergency; early amt is critical for preventing blindness
the 72-hour window for amniotic membrane placement is the gold standard for reducing cicatricial sequelae
stoppage of the offending drug is the single most important systemic intervention
pearl: sjs is an ophthalmic emergency on day one — amniotic membrane transplant within the first week dramatically reduces long-term cicatricial complications, so involve ophthalmology at the first mucocutaneous sign.
willsRef: Wills Eye §13.7 (Erythema Multiforme, Stevens–Johnson Syndrome, and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis)

name: Esodeviations
symptoms: diplopia (mainly in acquired or incomitant cases)
eye strain, headache, and asthenopia with near work
signs of amblyopia (fixation preference or reduced reading performance)
children with congenital esotropia often suppress and report no diplopia
findings: ## Pseudoesotropia
• appearance of inward deviation due to wide nasal bridge or epicanthal folds
• hirschberg light reflex and cover test are normal
• requires reassurance and observation, not surgery
## Cycloplegic refraction
• mandatory in every child with esotropia to reveal latent hyperopia
• use cyclopentolate 1% or atropine 1%
## Infantile (congenital) esotropia
• onset ≤6 months; large-angle (>30 pd) constant deviation
• cross-fixation behavior and minimal hyperopia
• associated with inferior oblique overaction, dvd, and latent nystagmus
## Accommodative esotropia
• onset 1–6 years with hyperopia ≥+2.00 d
• refractive: glasses alone eliminate the deviation
• non-refractive (high ac/a): greater esotropia at near; requires bifocals
• partially accommodative: residual deviation remains after full correction
## Sensory esotropia
• results from severe monocular vision loss (cataract, optic nerve hypoplasia, rb)
• disruption of fusion causes the eye to turn inward
## Motility signs
• cover test shows outward movement of nonfixating eye to take up fixation
• check for incomitance (deviation increasing in side gaze)
etiology: ## Primary types
• congenital/infantile: developmental large-angle deviation
• accommodative: hyperopia-driven convergence excess
## Secondary/acquired
• sensory: monocular vision loss (e.g., retinal disease, dense cataract)
• paralytic/incomitant: cn vi palsy (trauma, icp, tumor) or duane syndrome type i
• restrictive: thyroid myopathy of the medial rectus
redFlags: acute-onset esotropia with diplopia in an adult (rule out cn vi palsy/raised icp)
new esotropia in a child with associated neurological signs
high-ac/a esotropia failing bifocal management
unilateral vision loss presenting as sensory esotropia
investigations: ## Clinical examination
• visual acuity with best correction; stereopsis and color vision testing
• manifest and cycloplegic refractions (essential for all pediatric cases)
• ocular motility and incomitance evaluation
## Neurological and systemic
• cranial nerve assessment
• thyroid function tests if restrictive disease is suspected
• myasthenia workup (ice test, achr antibodies) if deviation is variable
## Imaging
• mri brain/orbits if acute non-accommodative, incomitant, or paretic deviation
actionSteps: perform cycloplegic refraction to identify accommodative components
prescribe full hyperopic correction for accommodative esotropia
initiate amblyopia therapy (patching/atropine) if fixation preference is noted
schedule surgical intervention for infantile or residual esodeviations
treatment: ## Refractive management
• correct hyperopia ≥+2.00 d; prescribe full cycloplegic refraction for patients <6 years
• push plus in manifest refraction for patients >6 years until distance vision blurs
• glasses must be worn full-time
## High AC/a ratio
• prescribe bifocals (executive or flat-top +2.50 to +3.00 add)
• bifocal line should be at the lower pupillary border
## Surgical management
• congenital esotropia almost always requires surgery (typically at 6–24 months)
• muscle surgery for residual or non-accommodative deviations
## Secondary/sensory
• treat underlying cause of vision loss and provide polycarbonate protective lenses
followUp: ## Monitoring
• evaluate for amblyopia and measure deviation with prisms at every visit
• re-evaluate 3–6 weeks after a new prescription is given
## Stability
• straight/stable eyes: follow several times a year in young children
• residual deviation: repeat cycloplegic refraction periodically to attempt more plus
review: every cross-eyed child needs a cycloplegic refraction before surgery
full hyperopic correction often eliminates accommodative esotropia entirely, sparing unnecessary operations
early surgery in infantile esotropia optimizes the chance of gross peripheral fusion

name: Exodeviations
symptoms: intermittent or constant outward drift of one eye
symptoms often worse with fatigue, illness, or distance fixation
diplopia (in acquired cases; children commonly suppress)
squinting or eye-closing in bright light (classic for intermittent exotropia)
findings: ## Intermittent exotropia (IXT)
• most common childhood exodeviation
• pathognomonic sign: child closes one eye in bright sunlight to suppress second image
• control grading (newcastle or mayo) is more critical than angle magnitude for management
• good control: phoria-only on cover test; fair control: intermittent tropia
• poor control: constant tropia >50% of waking hours
## IXT subtypes (distance–near relationship)
• basic: distance deviation equals near deviation
• true divergence excess: distance deviation significantly greater than near
• simulated divergence excess: distance equals near only after patch test
• convergence insufficiency type: near deviation greater than distance
## Constant & sensory types
• infantile exotropia: onset <6 months; large-angle; often linked to neurologic or craniofacial syndromes
• sensory exotropia: results from chronic monocular vision loss; more common than sensory esotropia in adults
## Motility patterns
• "v" pattern: greater exodeviation in upgaze (associated with io overaction)
• "a" pattern: greater exodeviation in downgaze (associated with so overaction)
• dissociated vertical deviation (dvd) and amblyopia may be present
etiology: ## Primary types
• intermittent exotropia: most common form; triggered by fatigue or distance fixation
• congenital (infantile): rare, large-angle, early onset; associated with neurologic disease
## Secondary & acquired
• sensory: chronic monocular vision loss (cataract, retinal disease) disrupting fusion
• cn iii palsy: "down-and-out" eye with ptosis and possible pupil involvement
• consecutive: overcorrection following prior esotropia surgery
• incomitant: duane syndrome type 2 or orbital disease
redFlags: new-onset exotropia with ptosis or mydriasis (rule out cn iii palsy/aneurysm)
intermittent exotropia progressing to constant tropia (risk of fusion loss)
sensory exotropia secondary to unidentified unilateral vision loss
bilateral exotropia with upgaze limitation (parinaud syndrome; image dorsal midbrain)
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• visual acuity with best correction to assess for amblyopia
• ocular motility: check for oblique overactions, a/v patterns, or duane syndrome
• prism and cover test: measure in cardinal fields and at distance/near
• stereopsis and color vision testing
## Diagnostic tests
• patch test: monocular occlusion for 30–60 min to reveal full fusion-free angle
• cycloplegic refraction: essential to identify refractive components
• myasthenia workup: ice test or antibodies if deviation is variable/fatigable
## Imaging
• mri brain/orbits: if neurologic disease, parinaud syndrome, or new cn iii palsy is suspected
actionSteps: measure deviation at distance/near and assign a control grade
perform patch test to differentiate true vs. simulated divergence excess
prescribe alternate daily patching or over-minus lenses for fair control
refer for surgery if control is poor or fusion is deteriorating
treatment: ## Conservative measures
• correct significant refractive errors and treat underlying amblyopia
• alternate daily patching to reduce suppression and improve fusion control
• over-minus lenses to stimulate accommodative convergence
• orthoptic exercises for convergence insufficiency
## Surgical intervention
• infantile exotropia: surgery typically performed within 1 year of onset
• intermittent exotropia: indicated for poor control or frequent manifest tropia
• sensory exotropia: surgery for alignment/cosmesis
## Special considerations
• sensory cases: mandatory polycarbonate protective lenses for the better-seeing eye
• incomitant types: treat underlying cause (e.g., third nerve palsy)
followUp: ## Monitoring
• orthoptic assessment every 6 months for stable intermittent cases
• follow every 3–6 weeks after changing refractive/minus lens prescriptions
• evaluate for amblyopia at every pediatric visit
## Post-surgical
• longer intervals once successful surgical alignment is achieved
review: control of intermittent exotropia (how often it is manifest) drives surgical timing more than the angle magnitude
closing one eye in bright sunlight is a pathognomonic behavior for intermittent exotropia
adults with monocular blindness more commonly develop exotropia than esotropia

name: Exposure Keratopathy
symptoms: irritation, burning, and foreign body sensation
excessive tearing and redness
symptoms typically worse in the morning
findings: ## Eyelid dysfunction
• inadequate blink or incomplete closure (lagophthalmos)
• eyelid deformity, malposition (ectropion), or retraction
## Corneal and surface signs
• hallmark: inferior punctate epithelial erosions (spk)
• conjunctival injection and chemosis
• advanced: corneal erosion, stromal infiltrate, ulceration, or thinning
etiology: ## Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy
• bell’s palsy (idiopathic/viral) and ramsay-hunt syndrome (vzv)
• iatrogenic: post-acoustic neuroma surgery or parotid malignancy infiltration
• central stroke: typically spares the upper face and is less severe
## High-risk "blind-and-numb" cornea
• combined cn vii palsy and cn v involvement (reduced sensation)
• poor bell phenomenon (globe fails to rotate upward on closure)
• high risk of rapid progression to perforation
## Orbital and lid causes
• proptosis: thyroid eye disease (ted) or orbital tumors
• structural: post-blepharoplasty retraction or floppy eyelid syndrome (osa)
## Reduced blink
• parkinson disease or neurotrophic state
• icu/sedated patients: loss of blink reflex and lid closure
redFlags: inferior corneal thinning or ulceration (perforation risk)
combined cn vii palsy, anesthesia (cn v), and poor bell phenomenon
proptotic thyroid eye disease with central exposure
unconscious or ventilated icu patients without lid protection
investigations: ## Lid and blink function
• evaluate gentle closure (simulating sleep) to find nocturnal lagophthalmos
• assess bell phenomenon (upward rotation on forced closure)
• check lid laxity (snap-back/distraction tests for floppy eyelid)
## Corneal integrity
• fluorescein staining: check for hallmark inferior spk or epithelial defects
• corneal sensation: test before anesthesia to assess cn v status
## Systemic workup
• investigate cn vii palsy source (mri for cpa tumor or parotid exam)
• thyroid function tests and orbital imaging if proptosis is present
• sleep study if floppy eyelid/osa suspected
actionSteps: initiate aggressive lubrication: pf tears q1h and ointment qhs
utilize moisture chambers or lid taping overnight
address the underlying cause (e.g., bell’s palsy, ted, ectropion)
perform surgical intervention (tarsorrhaphy/lid weight) if refractory
treatment: ## Medical management
• intensive pf artificial tears (q1–2h) and lubricating ointment (qhs to q2h)
• nocturnal protection: eyelid taping, moisture-chamber goggles, or patching
• in-office amniotic membrane (prokera) for non-healing defects
## Surgical intervention
• tarsorrhaphy: partial or temporary sewing/gluing of lids
• gold or platinum weight implants: for permanent cn vii palsy
• lid reconstruction: for ectropion or cicatricial retraction
• orbital decompression: for severe thyroid-related proptosis
## Infection control
• broad-spectrum topical antibiotics if an infiltrate or ulcer develops
followUp: ## Monitoring
• corneal ulcer present: re-evaluate every 1–2 days until stable
• mild/moderate spk: follow every few weeks to months
• every visit: reassess staining pattern, bcva, and eyelid closure effectiveness
review: if the eyelids do not meet during a blink, the cornea will dry regardless of lubricant frequency
lateral tarsorrhaphy or lid weight is the definitive fix for chronic exposure
pearl: if the eyelids do not meet during a forced blink, the cornea will dry out regardless of how many drops you prescribe — lateral tarsorrhaphy or lid weight is the definitive fix for chronic exposure.

name: Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy
symptoms: often asymptomatic (discovered on screening)
decreased vision from macular dragging or detachment
strabismus or leukocoria in childhood
findings: ## Vascular & peripheral
• peripheral retinal nonperfusion (typically temporal)
• fimbriated border of peripheral vessels
• supernumerary vessels and anomalous branching
## Tractional & exudative
• fibrovascular proliferation at the vascular–avascular border
• temporal dragging of the macula
• radial retinal folds
• subretinal lipid exudation
## Advanced complications
• tractional, rhegmatogenous, or exudative retinal detachment
• vitreous hemorrhage
• neovascular glaucoma, band keratopathy, or phthisis bulbi
etiology: ## Genetics & mechanism
• defects in wnt signaling (fzd4, lrp5, tspan12, ndp genes)
• inheritance: autosomal dominant (most common), recessive, or x-linked
• incomplete peripheral retinal vascularization in a full-term infant
## Clinical associations
• osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome: associated with lrp5 mutations (check bone density)
• key distinction: occurs without a history of prematurity or supplemental oxygen
redFlags: peripheral avascular retina with neovascularization
progressive macular dragging or tractional retinal detachment
positive family history with asymmetric clinical signs
unexplained vitreous hemorrhage in a young adult
investigations: ## Imaging
• widefield fluorescein angiography (fa): essential to identify nonperfusion and leakage
• fa is the most sensitive test for identifying asymptomatic carriers
## Clinical screening
• mandatory dilated fundus exam for all first-degree relatives
• genetic testing: fzd4, lrp5, tspan12, and ndp
• systemic workup: inquire about fractures and consider dxa scan if lrp5 mutation suspected
actionSteps: perform widefield fa to map avascular zones and identify neovascularization
screen all first-degree family members with dilated exams and fa
apply prophylactic laser to avascular peripheral retina
refer for vitrectomy if tractional detachment or macular dragging is present
treatment: ## Medical & laser
• laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy of avascular zones to prevent proliferation
• anti-vegf injections for neovascular leakage or macular edema
## Surgical intervention
• pars plana vitrectomy or scleral buckle for retinal detachment
## Vision support
• refractive correction and aggressive amblyopia therapy
• genetic counseling for the family
followUp: ## Monitoring
• follow every 3–6 months for pediatric patients depending on disease stage
• lifelong annual surveillance: late progression and detachment can occur in adulthood
## Family management
• serial screening of siblings and relatives until status is confirmed by fa or genetics
differentials: retinopathy of prematurity (rop): distinguished by full-term birth and family history
review: fevr in a full-term child is distinguished from rop by the absence of prematurity and presence of autosomal dominant inheritance
widefield fa is indispensable for identifying asymptomatic carriers among family members

name: Fuchs Endothelial Dystrophy
symptoms: glare and blurred vision, typically worse on awakening
vision improves throughout the day as the cornea dehydrates
severe pain if epithelial bullae rupture
onset typically in the 5th–6th decades
findings: ## Corneal guttae
• pathognomonic central refractile "dewdrop" excrescences of descemet membrane
• "beaten metal" or "orange peel" appearance on specular reflection
• best visualized via retroillumination or non-contact specular microscopy
## Endothelial & stromal signs
• fine brown pigment dusting on the endothelial surface
• descemet membrane folds and progressive central-to-peripheral stromal edema
• hallmark pattern: morning worsening with afternoon improvement
## Late-stage complications
• epithelial microcystic edema and bullae
• ruptured bullae causing severe pain, foreign body sensation, and recurrent erosions
• subepithelial fibrosis and pannus in chronic cases (may limit visual potential post-ek)
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• primary endothelial dystrophy with accelerated apoptotic cell loss
• endothelial pump failure and stromal edema occur when density drops below ~500 cells/mm²
• phacoemulsification significantly accelerates endothelial cell loss
## Genetics & risk
• female predominance (~3:1); typically autosomal dominant
• tcf4 gene (ctg18.1 trinucleotide repeat) is the most common variant
• col8a2 gene associated with rare early-onset disease
redFlags: central corneal edema with bullae and acute pain
rapid progression in middle-aged patients (reconsider ice or ppmd)
concurrent cataract with borderline low endothelial cell counts
pseudophakic bullous keratopathy from marginal endothelium
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• retroillumination to highlight guttae; fluorescein to identify ruptured bullae
• iop measurement (address elevations to reduce edema)
## Imaging & measurements
• pachymetry: rising central corneal thickness signals impending pump failure
• specular microscopy: quantifies endothelial cell density (limited in advanced edema)
• corneal tomography: useful for monitoring progression
actionSteps: monitor progression with serial specular microscopy and pachymetry
initiate topical sodium chloride 5% for early morning edema
refer for endothelial keratoplasty (dmek preferred) if vision-limiting blur persists
perform combined phaco-dmek if visually significant cataract coexists
treatment: ## Medical management
• topical sodium chloride 5% drops (4x daily) and ointment (bedtime)
• hairdryer method: gentle warm air at arm’s length each morning to assist dehydration
• bandage contact lens and antibiotic prophylaxis for ruptured bullae
## Surgical options
• endothelial keratoplasty: dmek (preferred) or dsaek
• descemet stripping only (dso): for milder forms of central disease
• penetrating keratoplasty (pk): reserved for cases with deep stromal scarring
## Surgical precautions
• baseline specular microscopy is mandatory before any intraocular surgery
• combined phaco-dmek indicated if cell count is <1000–1500 cells/mm²
followUp: ## Monitoring
• follow every 3–12 months to monitor iop and corneal thickness
• visual acuity often remains stable for years due to slow progression
review: morning blur that clears by afternoon is pathognomonic; it reflects overnight edema that evaporates once the lids open
once blur persists all day, the endothelium is decompensating and dmek is indicated

name: Fungal Keratitis
symptoms: pain, photophobia, and redness
tearing and mucopurulent discharge
indolent clinical course compared to bacterial keratitis
history of minor trauma with vegetable matter (e.g., branch, plant material)
contact lens wear or chronic ocular surface disease
poor response to conventional antibacterial therapy
findings: ## Corneal signs
• stromal infiltrate with characteristic feathery edges
• satellite lesions surrounding the primary infiltrate
• infiltrate may extend beyond the borders of the epithelial defect
## Other signs
• conjunctival injection and chemosis
• mucopurulent discharge
• anterior chamber reaction or hypopyon
etiology: ## Filamentous fungi
• fusarium species: most common (especially post-vegetative trauma or contact lens wear)
• aspergillus species
## Yeasts
• candida species: common in chronic surface disease or topical steroid use
## Risk factors
• warm, humid climates
• poor contact lens hygiene
• immunocompromise or chronic steroid use
redFlags: history of vegetative trauma (plant, branch, or soil)
feathery infiltrate margins and satellite lesions
clinical worsening while on broad-spectrum antibacterials
deep stromal involvement or endothelial plaques
investigations: ## Corneal scraping
• scrape deep into the edge of the ulcer
• gram and giemsa stains
• koh prep or calcofluor white for fungal elements
• specialized histology: pas, gomori methenamine silver (gms), and h&e
## Cultures
• sabouraud agar (incubated at 25°c and 37°c)
• concurrent bacterial cultures
• culture of contact lens case and solution
## Adjunctive
• confocal microscopy: may visualize hyphae in vivo
• corneal biopsy if cultures are persistently negative
actionSteps: perform deep corneal scraping for smears and fungal culture (sabouraud)
initiate hourly topical natamycin 5% or voriconazole 1%
avoid topical steroids until the organism is definitively cleared
consider oral voriconazole for deep or refractory disease
treatment: ## Topical therapy
• natamycin 5% suspension q1h: first-line for filamentous fungi (fusarium)
• voriconazole 1% or amphotericin b 0.15% q1h: for yeasts or aspergillus
• epithelial debridement to improve drug penetration
## Systemic & adjunctive
• oral voriconazole: 200 mg b.i.d. (load 400 mg b.i.d.) for deep disease
• intracameral or intrastromal voriconazole (50 mcg/0.1 ml) for refractory cases
• cyclopentolate 1% or atropine 1% for pain and synechiae prevention
## Surgical
• therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty (pk) for perforation or medical failure
followUp: ## Monitoring
• daily examination during the acute phase
• initial clinical response is significantly slower than bacterial keratitis
## Interpretation
• stability is a favorable sign; epithelial healing is not a reliable success metric
• treatment typically lasts weeks to months
review: high clinical suspicion is required; feathery margins and satellite lesions are hallmarks
prognosis is often poor, with significant risk of severe visual loss or evisceration
epithelialization can inhibit drug penetration; repeated debridement may be necessary
pearl: High clinical suspicion is critical — delayed diagnosis is common. Key distinguishing features: feathery margins + satellite lesions + hypopyon + scanty secretions + history of plant/vegetative trauma or contact lens use in warm climates. Prognosis is poor: 26-63% experience severe visual loss; 15-20% require evisceration. Epithelialization may inhibit drug penetration — debridement helps.

name: Arteritic AION (Giant Cell Arteritis)
symptoms: sudden, painless, and severe vision loss
initially unilateral; high risk for rapid bilateral involvement
new-onset headache or scalp tenderness (e.g., pain with hair combing)
jaw claudication (pain while chewing)
polymyalgia rheumatica (proximal muscle/joint aches)
anorexia, weight loss, and low-grade fever
findings: ## Ocular signs
• visual acuity often counting fingers or worse
• rapd and dyschromatopsia
• pale, chalky-white disc edema (differs from sectoral edema of naion)
• altitudinal or central visual field defects
• possible concurrent central retinal artery occlusion (crao) or cn vi palsy
## Systemic signs
• palpable, tender, and non-pulsatile temporal artery
## Stat labs
• markedly elevated esr (men: >age/2; women: >[age+10]/2)
• elevated crp (does not rise with age; highly sensitive)
• thrombocytosis (elevated platelet count)
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries
• involves posterior ciliary arteries causing ischemic optic neuropathy
• characterized by "skip lesions" (discontinuous inflammation)
## Risk factors
• age ≥55 (typically >70)
• female predominance; caucasian/northern european ancestry
• 50% associated with polymyalgia rheumatica
redFlags: any new vision loss in patients ≥55 years (requires stat labs)
jaw claudication or scalp tenderness (highly specific for gca)
fellow-eye involvement within days to weeks if untreated
chalky-white disc edema (aaion) vs sectoral edema (naion)
investigations: ## Ocular evaluation
• pupillary assessment for rapd and color plate testing
• dilated fundus exam to rule out retinal etiologies
## Stat laboratory
• stat esr, crp, and platelet count (thrombocytosis)
• esr may be normal in 10–20% of cases
## Temporal artery biopsy
• adequate specimen length (2–3 cm) to account for skip lesions
• histology remains positive for up to 2 weeks after initiating steroids
• do not delay steroid treatment while awaiting biopsy
actionSteps: start high-dose steroids immediately based on clinical suspicion
obtain stat esr, crp, and platelet count
arrange temporal artery biopsy within 1 week
consult rheumatology for long-term co-management
treatment: ## Acute steroids
• iv methylprednisolone (1g daily for 3 days or 250mg q6h)
• transition to oral prednisone (1mg/kg/day, usually 80–100mg)
• transition to a very slow oral taper over 12–18 months
## Adjuncts
• steroid-sparing agents (e.g., tocilizumab or methotrexate) for refractory cases
• ppi for gi protection and bisphosphonates/calcium for bone health
• monitor blood glucose and symptoms during taper
followUp: ## Acute monitoring
• inpatient hospitalization for iv steroids and systemic evaluation
• assess fellow-eye status daily in the acute phase
## Long-term
• manage with rheumatology; adjust taper based on esr, crp, and symptoms
• lifelong vigilance for relapse or fellow-eye involvement
differentials: optic neuritis (presents with pain on eye movement)
pearl: gca is the most common systemic vasculitis in adults >50. esr typically >50 (often >100), crp elevated — both together increase sensitivity. temporal artery biopsy: 15-20% false negative rate (skip lesions) — do not delay steroids for biopsy. fellow eye risk without treatment: 25-50% within days. steroids should be started immediately when gca is suspected — they do not significantly affect biopsy for up to 2 weeks.

name: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Keratitis
symptoms: red eye, pain, and foreign body sensation
photophobia and tearing
decreased vision
vesicular skin rash (e.g., eyelids)
usually unilateral; history of previous episodes
findings: ## Epithelial keratitis (active viral replication)
• dendritic keratitis: thin, linear, branching ulcer with pathognomonic club-shaped terminal bulbs
• geographic ulcer: large, amoeba-shaped ulcer with dendritic edges (often driven by topical steroids)
• staining: central ulceration stains with fluorescein; swollen borders stain with rose bengal/lissamine green
• hallmark: significantly decreased corneal sensation
## Eyelid & conjunctival involvement
• clear vesicles on an erythematous base progressing to crusting
• acute unilateral follicular conjunctivitis ± conjunctival dendrites
## Stromal & endothelial disease (immune-mediated)
• disciform endotheliitis: central disc of stromal/epithelial edema with underlying kps
• necrotizing stromal keratitis: opaque, necrotic infiltrate with high risk of thinning/perforation
• "ghost dendrites": subepithelial scars remaining after epithelial resolution
## Neonatal/pediatric HSV
• rare but devastating; often bilateral with severe cns or multiorgan involvement
• increased risk of extensive scarring and astigmatism
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• primary hsv-1 infection typically occurs in childhood; virus establishes latency in trigeminal ganglion
• reactivation triggers: uv light, fever, stress, immunosuppression, menstruation, or trauma
## Mechanism
• epithelial disease reflects live viral replication
• stromal and endothelial disease are largely immune-mediated responses to viral antigens
redFlags: central stromal thinning or impending perforation
hsv endotheliitis with corneal edema and significant iop elevation
concurrent iritis with hypopyon
atypical dendrites in a contact lens wearer (rule out acanthamoeba)
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• test corneal sensation with a cotton wisp before instilling anesthetic
• slit-lamp evaluation with fluorescein and rose bengal/lissamine green
• dilated fundus exam to rule out viral retinitis
## Laboratory (if diagnosis is unclear)
• viral pcr or culture: swab cornea, conjunctiva, or unroofed skin vesicles
• giemsa stain: shows multinucleated giant cells
• hsv antibody titers: absence of hsv-1 antibodies helps rule out hsv stromal disease
actionSteps: document corneal sensation and staining pattern at the slit lamp
initiate oral or topical antiviral therapy for epithelial disease
avoid topical steroids for pure epithelial keratitis
coordinate steroid use with antiviral cover for immune-mediated stromal disease
treatment: ## Epithelial disease
• oral: acyclovir 400 mg 5x/day or valacyclovir 500 mg t.i.d. for 7–10 days (preferred by many)
• topical: ganciclovir 0.15% gel 5x/day until healed, then t.i.d. for 7 days
• adjunct: limited debridement of infected epithelial cells
## Stromal/endothelial disease
• topical steroids (e.g., prednisolone acetate 1%) with prophylactic antiviral cover
## Adjunctive therapy
• cycloplegic (cyclopentolate 1% t.i.d.) for photophobia/ac reaction
• prophylactic topical antibiotic to prevent secondary infection
• long-term oral prophylaxis (acyclovir 400 mg b.i.d.) to reduce recurrence risk
followUp: ## Monitoring schedule
• re-examine in 2–7 days to evaluate response; then every 1–2 weeks
• monitor ulcer size, corneal thickness, iop, and ac reaction at each visit
## Steroid management
• taper stromal steroids very slowly over months to years
• continue systemic antiviral prophylaxis until steroids are once daily or less
## Surgical intervention
• corneal transplantation for visually significant postherpetic scarring
differentials: herpes zoster ophthalmicus (pseudodendrites lack terminal bulbs)
review: hsv keratitis is a leading cause of corneal blindness in developed countries
reduced corneal sensation is a critical diagnostic clue; test this first
topical steroids are contraindicated in active epithelial disease as they promote geographic ulcers
pearl: HSV keratitis is the most common cause of corneal blindness in developed countries. Reduced corneal sensation is a key clinical clue — test with a wisp of cotton before touching the cornea. Dendritic ulcers have pathognomonic terminal bulbs; pseudodendrites (e.g., healing abrasion, acanthamoeba) lack these bulbs.

name: Horner Syndrome
symptoms: ptosis and anisocoria (often asymptomatic)
anhidrosis (lack of sweating) on affected side
acute painful horner: neck or face pain suggests carotid dissection
findings: ## Pupil
• anisocoria greater in dim illumination (dilation lag)
• affected pupil is smaller (miosis) and dilates slower than the normal eye
• light and near reactions are intact
## Eyelid
• mild ptosis (~2 mm) from müller muscle weakness
• "upside-down ptosis" (elevation of the lower lid)
## Other signs
• iris heterochromia (lighter iris on affected side) if congenital
• conjunctival hyperemia and slightly lower iop on affected side
• transiently increased accommodative amplitude
etiology: ## First-order (central)
• stroke (e.g., wallenberg syndrome), tumor, or multiple sclerosis
## Second-order (preganglionic)
• pancoast tumor (lung apex), thyroid adenoma, or aortic aneurysm
• pediatric: neuroblastoma or birth trauma
## Third-order (postganglionic)
• internal carotid artery dissection
• cavernous sinus pathology or tollosa-hunt syndrome
• cluster headache or migrainous syndromes
• neck trauma or otitis media
redFlags: acute painful horner (neck/face pain): emergent carotid artery dissection risk
horner with arm pain/wasting: suggests pancoast tumor
pediatric horner without surgery history: requires neuroblastoma workup
horner with cranial nerve palsies: suggests brainstem or cavernous sinus lesion
investigations: ## Pharmacologic testing
• apraclonidine 0.5%: reversal of anisocoria confirms horner (affected pupil dilates)
• hydroxyamphetamine: failure to dilate suggests third-order (postganglionic) lesion
• cocaine 10%: failure of horner pupil to dilate confirms the diagnosis
## Imaging
• cta or mra of head and neck: mandatory for acute painful horner (dissection)
• mri brain/neck/chest: to evaluate the full oculosympathetic pathway
## Pediatric specialty
• urinary catecholamines (vma/hva) and chest/abdominal imaging for neuroblastoma
actionSteps: confirm diagnosis with apraclonidine or cocaine drops
order emergent cta/mra head and neck if pain is present (rule out dissection)
image the full sympathetic pathway (brain to t2) if the cause is unknown
initiate systemic workup for children to exclude neuroblastoma
treatment: ## Primary
• directed at the underlying systemic cause (e.g., tumor, stroke, or dissection)
## Vascular
• anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy for carotid dissection
## Surgical
• müller muscle resection for stable, symptomatic ptosis after clear diagnosis
followUp: ## Acute
• immediate neurology or vascular surgery referral for carotid dissection
## Long-term
• monitoring for stability once underlying life-threatening causes are excluded
• annual pediatric follow-up for congenital cases after negative initial screen
differentials: physiologic anisocoria (equal in light and dark)
adie tonic pupil (anisocoria greater in light)
third nerve palsy (ptosis with a large pupil)
review: acute painful horner syndrome is a carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise
the dilation lag in dim light is a key clinical discriminator for horner syndrome
anhidrosis distribution helps localize the lesion: central/preganglionic involves the face; postganglionic often spares it
pearl: Horner localization matters: Central (first-order — brain/brainstem): MRI brain. Preganglionic (second-order — from C8-T2 via lung apex): MRI/CT chest, look for Pancoast tumor. Postganglionic (third-order — carotid/cavernous): MRA carotid, look for carotid dissection. In acute painful Horner: carotid dissection until proven otherwise.

name: Hypertensive Retinopathy
symptoms: usually asymptomatic (detected on routine fundus exam)
decreased vision possible in grade 3–4
acute headache, visual obscurations, or neurologic deficits suggest hypertensive emergency
findings: ## Keith-wagener-barker (kwb) classification
• grade 1: generalized retinal arteriolar narrowing; a:v ratio drops from 2:3 toward 1:2
• grade 2: a/v nicking (gunn sign), venous banking, and copper/silver-wiring sclerosis
• grade 3: hemorrhages (flame-shaped), cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and macular star
• grade 4: grade 3 changes plus optic disc edema (papilledema); defines hypertensive emergency
## Hypertensive choroidopathy
• elschnig spots: hyperpigmented scars with depigmented rings (focal infarction)
• siegrist streaks: linear hyperpigmentation along sclerotic choroidal vessels
• common in acute htn (preeclampsia, pheochromocytoma)
## Other signs
• hypertensive optic neuropathy: bilateral disc edema with macular star
• serous retinal detachment: bilateral exudative detachments (common in eclampsia)
• grade 3–4 correlates with nephropathy, lvh, and high stroke mortality
etiology: ## Primary
• essential hypertension (~90% of cases)
## Secondary
• renal: parenchymal disease or renal artery stenosis
• endocrine: pheochromocytoma, cushing syndrome, or conn syndrome
• pregnancy: pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
• drug-induced: cocaine, amphetamines, nsaids, or oral contraceptives
redFlags: grade 4 retinopathy (disc edema): represents a hypertensive emergency
pregnancy with retinopathy signs (emergent ob referral for eclampsia)
acute severe htn with neurologic signs (rule out hemorrhage or pres)
accelerated htn in a young patient (secondary causes)
investigations: ## Bedside and ocular
• blood pressure measurement in both arms
• dilated fundus exam to grade kwb stage
## Systemic (grade 3–4)
• bmp (cr/bun), urinalysis (proteinuria), and ecg/echo (lvh)
## Secondary screening
• renal mra/cta, plasma metanephrines, or 24-hour aldosterone:renin ratio
• polysomnography for obstructive sleep apnea
actionSteps: grade 4 (disc edema) → emergent inpatient admission for controlled bp reduction
identify end-organ damage (renal, cardiac, neurologic)
refer pregnant patients immediately to obstetrics
evaluate young or resistant hypertensive patients for secondary causes
treatment: ## Hypertensive emergency
• inpatient admission for urgent bp control
• target: reduce mean arterial pressure (map) by ~25% over several hours
• warning: avoid rapid normalization to prevent watershed stroke or naion
## Long-term management
• treat underlying secondary causes (e.g., pheochromocytoma)
• coordinate chronic control with pcp to prevent vein occlusions and naion
followUp: ## Monitoring
• malignant hypertension: urgent/daily until stable, then 1 month
• chronic htn: every 3–6 months based on stage
## Resolution
• hemorrhages and edema resolve over weeks/months with bp control
• arteriolar narrowing and nicking often persist permanently
review: grade 4 kwb is a hypertensive emergency and requires systemic organ damage screening
the "macular star" consists of lipid exudates in henle’s fiber layer
choroidal signs (elschnig spots) are highly indicative of acute, severe hypertensive episodes
pearl: Malignant hypertension (BP >180/120 with organ damage) requires emergency BP reduction — but not to normal (cerebral autoregulation requires staged reduction). Keith-Wagener-Barker (KWB) grading: Grade 3 = hemorrhages/cotton wool spots; Grade 4 = papilledema. Choroidal disease (Elschnig spots, Siegrist streaks) in malignant hypertension indicates choroidal ischemia.

name: Hyphema and Microhyphema
symptoms: • Blurred vision, eye pain, photophobia, and tearing following trauma
• History of high-velocity injury (e.g., ball, fist, airbag, BB pellet)
• History of sickle cell disease/trait, anticoagulant use, or bleeding diathesis
• Microhyphema: subtle drop in vision or dull ache (often an incidental finding)
• Spontaneous hyphema: transient visual loss or presentation without a history of trauma
findings: ## Hyphema Grading (Wills Eye)
• Microhyphema: RBCs suspended in the AC; no macroscopic layering (visible via slit lamp only)
• Grade I: Layered blood filling <1/3 of the anterior chamber volume
• Grade II: Layered blood filling 1/3 to 1/2 of the anterior chamber volume
• Grade III: Layered blood filling 1/2 to near-total of the anterior chamber volume
• Grade IV (8-ball hyphema): Total dark, deoxygenated clot completely filling the anterior chamber
## Associated Clinical Signs
• Layered red blood in the AC that gravitates inferiorly with head position
• Elevated IOP and secondary rust-colored corneal blood staining
• Iris/angle trauma: iridodialysis, angle recession, and pupillary irregularities/sphincter tears
• Posterior segment trauma: commotio retinae, vitreous hemorrhage, lens subluxation, or retinal dialysis
etiology: ## Traumatic Causes
• Blunt ocular trauma (most common): mechanical disruption of iris or ciliary body vasculature
• Penetrating ocular trauma: requires immediate exclusion of an open or ruptured globe
## Spontaneous & Non-Traumatic Causes
• Post-surgical/Device-related: Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema (UGH) syndrome caused by iris-IOL chafing
• Anterior segment neovascularization: rubeosis iridis secondary to diabetic retinopathy, old CRVO, or OIS
• Inflammatory/Uveitic: herpetic keratouveitis or Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis
• Intraocular tumors: juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG), iris melanoma, or retinoblastoma
• Systemic & Pharmacological: systemic anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or underlying bleeding diatheses
redFlags: • Sickle cell trait or disease: rigid RBCs cannot clear the trabecular meshwork; an IOP ≥24 mmHg risks rapid optic nerve infarction
• Rebleed window (days 2–5): highest risk occurs as the initial clot retracts and lyses; rebleeds are often more severe than the primary event
• Systemic CAI contraindication: strictly avoid acetazolamide and hyperosmotics (mannitol) in sickle cell patients as it induces hypoxia/acidosis and worsens sickling
• Early corneal blood staining: a critical red flag indicating the immediate necessity for surgical AC washout
• Delayed presentation: must rule out an occult or posterior globe rupture hidden by periocular swelling
investigations: ## Clinical Diagnostics
• Baseline visual acuity, daily applanation IOP measurements, and detailed slit-lamp grading
• Dilated fundus examination (avoiding scleral depression acutely) once globe integrity is fully confirmed
## Laboratory & Imaging Workup
• Sickle cell screen (Sickledex / Hb electrophoresis): mandatory for all at-risk ethnicities or patients with unknown status
• CT scan of the orbits: indicated if orbital fractures or an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) are suspected
• B-scan ultrasonography: indicated if a dense hyphema or vitreous hemorrhage completely obscures the posterior segment view
• Coagulation panel (CBC, PT/INR, and PTT) for all spontaneous, non-traumatic cases
• Delayed Gonioscopy: safely perform at 4 weeks post-injury to document the presence and extent of angle recession
actionSteps: • Enforce strict bed rest with head elevation ≥30° and a rigid eye shield worn at all times (avoid patching)
• Discontinue aspirin, NSAIDs, and systemic anticoagulants immediately; utilize acetaminophen for analgesia
• Initiate topical cycloplegics (atropine 1%) and potent topical corticosteroids (prednisolone acetate 1%)
• Perform a mandatory sickle cell screen on at-risk patients within 24 hours and avoid systemic CAIs if positive
• Arrange an urgent surgical AC washout if the patient meets criteria for refractory IOP, corneal staining, or a persistent 8-ball clot
treatment: ## Medical Management
• Topical prednisolone acetate 1% (ranging from QID to Q1h depending on inflammation levels)
• Topical cycloplegia: atropine 1% drops (daily to BID) to stabilize the blood-aqueous barrier and prevent synechiae
• IOP control (Non-Sickle): topical beta-blockers, alpha2-agonists, or topical CAIs (strictly avoid miotics like pilocarpine)
• IOP control (Sickle Cell): treat aggressively; use topical agents and consider oral methazolamide if a systemic CAI is absolutely required
## Surgical Intervention (AC Washout)
• Indications: IOP >60 mmHg for 48 hours, IOP >50 mmHg for 5 days, or a total (8-ball) hyphema persisting >5 days with IOP ≥25 mmHg
• Any initial manifestation of impending corneal blood staining requires immediate washout
• Sickle cell patients carry a significantly lower threshold for surgical intervention due to low pressure tolerance
followUp: ## Acute Phase Monitoring
• Perform daily slit-lamp examinations and IOP checks for the first 5 days to monitor the peak rebleed window
• Instruct the patient to continue utilizing the rigid eye shield during sleep for at least 1 week
• Follow weekly after the acute window until the hyphema has completely resolved and pressures are stable
## Long-Term Surveillance
• Taper topical medications gradually as cellular activity quietens; watch closely for secondary steroid IOP spikes
• Schedule a comprehensive check at 4 weeks for gonioscopy (to map angle recession) and a depressed fundus exam (to rule out peripheral retinal breaks)
• Mandate lifelong annual follow-up appointments due to the persistent risk of delayed angle-recession glaucoma
differentials: • Neovascular hyphema (associated with rubeosis iridis and neovascular glaucoma)
• Primary anterior uveitis with a dense fibrinous or hypopyon reaction
• Iris or ciliary body tumors (e.g., juvenile xanthogranuloma, iris melanoma, retinoblastoma)
review: • A hyphema presenting in a patient with sickle cell disease or trait constitutes a true ophthalmic emergency due to rapid trabecular clog
• Strict bed rest with head elevation allows blood to layer inferiorly, clearing the visual axis and safeguarding the superior outflow angle
• Avoid standard pressure patches; a rigid shield prevents accidental external digital pressure without masking early rebleed signs
• Rebleed incidents peak as the initial fibrin clot naturally degrades and retracts between days 2 and 5
pearl: Sickle cell + hyphema is a true ophthalmic emergency: sickled RBCs clog the trabecular meshwork and can infarct the optic nerve at IOP levels that normal eyes tolerate (~24 mmHg). Screen every at-risk patient, avoid systemic acetazolamide or hyperosmotics, and lower your threshold to wash out the AC. Rebleed risk peaks at days 2–5 as the clot naturally retracts; enforce activity restrictions and avoid all NSAIDs/aspirin.
draw: layered red blood in the anterior chamber settling inferiorly or suspended RBCs

name: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus
symptoms: prodrome: dermatomal pain, paresthesias, headache, fever, and malaise
acute: painful vesicular skin rash, blurred vision, and red eye
chronic: postherpetic neuralgia (persistent pain after rash resolution)
findings: ## Cutaneous signs
• acute vesicular rash respecting the midline in the v1 (trigeminal) distribution
• unilateral involvement; typically spares the lower eyelid (v2)
• hutchinson sign: vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (nasociliary branch involvement)
## Ocular signs
• pseudodendritic keratitis: elevated mucous plaques without terminal bulbs
• stromal keratitis, endotheliitis, and neurotrophic keratopathy
• anterior uveitis (often with sector iris atrophy) and secondary glaucoma
• episcleritis or scleritis
## Severe/neurological
• retinitis: acute retinal necrosis (arn) or progressive outer retinal necrosis (porn)
• optic neuritis and cranial nerve palsies (iii, iv, vi)
• vzv vasculitis (stroke risk weeks after hzo)
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (vzv) from the trigeminal (v1) ganglion
## Risk factors
• age >50 years
• immunocompromise: hiv, malignancy, chemotherapy, or organ transplant
## Mechanism
• direct viral invasion (epithelium/retina) and immune-mediated inflammation (stroma/uvea)
redFlags: hutchinson sign: high risk for ocular involvement; mandates slit-lamp exam
acute retinal necrosis: peripheral necrotizing retinitis with vitritis
corneal perforation or severe necrotizing stromal thinning
contralateral hemiparesis weeks post-hzo: suggests vzv-related stroke
investigations: ## Ocular diagnostics
• slit-lamp exam with iop measurement and corneal staining (fluorescein/rose bengal)
• dilated fundus exam: mandatory to rule out peripheral retinitis (arn/porn)
## Systemic screening
• consider hiv testing or malignancy screen in young/healthy patients with hzo
• neuroimaging (mra/mri) if neurological deficits or vzv vasculitis suspected
actionSteps: initiate systemic antiviral therapy within 72 hours of rash onset
perform comprehensive slit-lamp exam to assess corneal and uveal involvement
add topical steroids for stromal disease or uveitis only with antiviral cover
coordinate with pain management for postherpetic neuralgia
treatment: ## Systemic antivirals (7–10 days)
• valacyclovir 1 g t.i.d. (preferred)
• famciclovir 500 mg t.i.d.
• acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day
• iv acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for retinitis, cns, or immunocompromised patients
## Ocular therapy
• uveitis/stromal keratitis: topical prednisolone acetate 1% (4–8x/day) + cycloplegic
• epithelial plaques: topical ganciclovir gel or lubricants
• secondary glaucoma: aqueous suppressants (avoid prostaglandins)
## Supportive & chronic
• skin: bacitracin or erythromycin ointment to lesions to prevent superinfection
• neurotrophic: aggressive lubrication, serum tears, or tarsorrhaphy
• pain: gabapentin, pregabalin, or tcas for neuralgia
followUp: ## Acute phase
• every 1–7 days if ocular involvement is present
• every 1–4 weeks if no ocular signs during the initial rash
## Maintenance
• every 3–6 months following resolution
• very slow steroid taper over months/years; watch for relapses during dose reduction
differentials: herpes simplex virus (hsv) keratitis (true dendrites with terminal bulbs)
review: hutchinson sign is predictive because the nasociliary nerve supplies both the nose tip and the eye
pseudodendrites in hzo are mucous plaques that stain better with rose bengal than fluorescein
vzv vasculitis is a late and life-threatening complication that can cause ischemic stroke
pearl: Hutchinson sign (rash on tip of nose) predicts ocular involvement because the nasociliary nerve supplies both the nose tip and the eye. Start antivirals within 72 hours to reduce post-herpetic neuralgia and eye complications.

name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)
symptoms: daily headache (often worst on waking or with valsalva)
transient visual obscurations (seconds of graying-out with posture changes)
pulsatile tinnitus (unilateral/bilateral "whooshing" sound)
horizontal binocular diplopia (from cn vi palsy)
nausea or vomiting accompanying headaches
typically occurs in obese women of reproductive age (bmi >30)
findings: ## Papilledema (bilateral optic disc edema)
• blurred disc margins and obscuration of vessels crossing the disc
• peripapillary flame hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots
• paton lines: retinal or choroidal folds
• frisén scale (grade 0–5) used for clinical staging
## Visual field defects
• earliest sign: enlarged blind spot
• inferonasal step or arcuate defects
• progressive peripheral constriction; generalized depression in advanced disease
• acuity and color vision loss are late, severe findings
## MRI/MRV features
• empty sella and posterior flattening of the globes
• distended perioptic subarachnoid space and optic nerve tortuosity
• transverse venous sinus stenosis
## Neurologic status
• normal neuro exam except for possible unilateral or bilateral cn vi palsy
• any other focal deficit excludes iih and mandates re-imaging
etiology: ## Mechanism
• increased csf pressure without mass, hydrocephalus, or venous thrombosis
• likely impaired csf absorption at arachnoid granulations
## Triggers & associations
• strong link to obesity and rapid weight gain
• medication-induced: tetracyclines (doxycycline/minocycline), vitamin a/retinoids, corticosteroid withdrawal, and lithium
redFlags: progressive vision loss despite maximal medical therapy
fulminant iih: rapid, aggressive vision decline over days
atypical demographic (male, non-obese, or elderly) suggesting secondary cause
bilateral cn vi palsy with altered consciousness
investigations: ## Mandatory imaging
• mri brain + mrv with contrast: rules out mass, hydrocephalus, and venous sinus thrombosis
## Lumbar puncture (post-imaging)
• opening pressure >25 cm h2o (lateral decubitus, legs extended)
• normal csf composition (cytology/chemistry)
## Ocular monitoring
• automated perimetry (humphrey 24-2): most sensitive for progression
• oct rnfl to quantify edema and monitor for atrophy
• fundus photography for serial disc documentation
actionSteps: obtain stat mri/mrv to exclude secondary causes of raised icp
perform lp to confirm opening pressure >25 cm h2o
initiate intensive weight loss counseling (sustained 6–10% reduction is curative)
start acetazolamide and titrate based on symptoms and visual field
treatment: ## Medical management
• weight loss: first-line and potentially curative
• acetazolamide (titrated up to 4g/day): reduces csf production (iihtt protocol)
• topiramate: second-line; useful for concurrent weight loss and headache
## Surgical (medical failure or threatened vision)
• optic nerve sheath fenestration (onsf): protects the nerve directly
• csf diversion (vp or lp shunt): for intractable headache or vision loss
• venous sinus stenting: if significant pressure gradient across stenosis exists
## Pregnancy
• acetazolamide generally used after 20 weeks; vaginal delivery usually safe
followUp: ## Clinical review
• follow every 4–6 weeks initially with va, color vision, and humphrey vf
• vision, not headache, drives treatment escalation
• repeat oct rnfl to monitor for thinning (fiber loss is irreversible)
## Long-term
• annual monitoring once stable and papilledema has resolved
review: the modified dandy criteria require normal imaging and normal csf chemistry to diagnose iih
transient visual obscurations (graying out) are common and related to postural icp changes
papilledema can be asymmetric; this does not rule out the diagnosis
pearl: In IIH, the field defect drives treatment, not the headache — losing nerve fibers is irreversible, so escalate (ONSF or shunt) when the field worsens even if the patient feels better.

name: Idiopathic Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy (PCV)
symptoms: decreased central vision (sudden or gradual)
sudden vision loss often from massive submacular hemorrhage
metamorphopsia and central scotoma
recurrent serous or hemorrhagic pigment epithelial detachments (ped)
findings: ## Clinical hallmarks
• multiple large orange-red subretinal nodules (polyps)
• branching inner-choroidal vascular network (bvn)
• massive sub-rpe or subretinal hemorrhage (cardinal differentiator from typical wet amd)
• absence of large soft drusen or geographic atrophy
• common in asian and african-american populations; occurs at a younger age than typical amd
## Icg angiography (gold standard)
• punctate, focal hyperfluorescent nodules ("salmon-pink popcorn")
• bvn visible in early phases; polyps may show dynamic pulsation
## OCT signs
• "thumb-like" ped: sharp, dome-shaped sub-rpe elevation representing a polyp
• double-layer sign: shallow irregular separation of rpe from bruch membrane (the bvn)
• peaked or notched peds
## Pachychoroid spectrum
• thickened choroid with dilated haller vessels (pachyvessels)
• related to cscr and pachychoroid neovasculopathy
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• abnormal dilated choroidal vascular network with aneurysmal terminal dilations (polyps)
• part of the pachychoroid disease spectrum
• high association with systemic hypertension
redFlags: massive subretinal or suprachoroidal hemorrhage
recurrent exudation despite anti-vegf therapy
sudden metamorphopsia in a patient with a history of hypertension and pigmented skin
unresponsive "wet amd" in asian or african-american patients
investigations: ## Imaging
• icg angiography (icga): mandatory gold standard to visualize polyps and bvn
• ivfa: often misleadingly suggests "occult cnv"
• oct: monitor for subretinal fluid, thumb-like peds, and double-layer sign
• octa: non-invasive detection of bvn flow signal
## Clinical exam
• biomicroscopy for orange-red nodules and subretinal lipid/hemorrhage
actionSteps: confirm diagnosis with icg angiography to distinguish from neovascular amd
initiate anti-vegf therapy (monotherapy or combined with pdt)
coordinate urgent surgical displacement (tpa + gas) for massive foveal-threatening hemorrhage
monitor the fellow eye (25% bilateral rate)
treatment: ## First-line therapy
• anti-vegf monotherapy (aflibercept, faricimab, brolucizumab): effective for exudation
• combination therapy (everest-ii/planet trials): pdt with verteporfin + anti-vegf for superior polyp closure
## Hemorrhage management
• pneumatic displacement: intravitreal tpa + gas (sf6/c3f8)
• pars plana vitrectomy with subretinal tpa for severe bleeds
## Local destruction
• thermal laser photocoagulation for extrafoveal polyps
followUp: ## Monitoring
• follow every 1–2 months with oct initially
• icga and fa periodically based on disease activity
## Long-term prognosis
• vision generally better than neovascular amd if polyps are successfully closed
• high recurrence rate requires lifelong monitoring
review: pcv is a pachychoroid-related disease characterized by aneurysmal dilations of the inner choroidal vessels
icg angiography is indispensable for the diagnosis of pcv and identifies lesions missed by standard ivfa
massive submacular hemorrhage is more common in pcv than in typical wet amd
pearl: In pigmented patients, "wet AMD" that does not respond to anti-VEGF is usually polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy — ICG angiography makes the diagnosis and combined PDT plus anti-VEGF is often the answer.

name: Inflammatory Orbital Disease
symptoms: early: morning eyelid puffiness, redness, and upper lid retraction (ted hallmark)
late: proptosis (prominent eyes), lateral flare, and persistent chemosis
diplopia and a sensation of "pressure" behind the eyes
decreased vision (concerning for dysthyroid optic neuropathy)
idiopathic orbital inflammation (ioi): acute, painful, "explosive" onset
pediatric ioi: may include fever, headache, and lethargy
findings: ## Idiopathic orbital inflammation (ioi)
• "orbit in a hurry": acute painful unilateral proptosis and diplopia
• imaging hallmark: extraocular muscle (eom) enlargement that includes tendon insertions
• diagnostic test: dramatic response to systemic steroids within 24–48 hours
• subtypes: myositic, dacryoadenitic (s-shaped lid), scleroposterior, diffuse, and apical
## Thyroid eye disease (ted)
• most common cause of orbital inflammation in adults; usually painless
• eyelid signs: upper lid retraction with lateral flare and lid lag (von graefe sign)
• imaging hallmark: eom enlargement sparing the tendon insertions (muscle belly only)
• muscle frequency: inferior > medial > superior > lateral (imsl)
• associated signs: elevated iop in upgaze and superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis
## Systemic correlates
• ted: 80% are hyperthyroid; symptoms include goiter, weight loss, and hand tremor
• concomitants: myasthenia gravis (fluctuating ptosis/diplopia) occurs in a minority
etiology: ## Non-specific & autoimmune
• idiopathic orbital inflammation (ioi): nonspecific lymphoplasmacytic inflammation
• thyroid eye disease (ted): autoimmune targeting of orbital fibroblasts
• igg4-related disease: characterized by storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis
## Granulomatous & infectious
• sarcoidosis, gpa (wegener), tuberculosis, and syphilis
• infectious mimics: orbital cellulitis, mucormycosis, and aspergillosis
redFlags: rapid vision loss or apd (optic nerve compression)
bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement (suspect lymphoma, sarcoid, or igg4)
lack of response to steroids within 72 hours (mandates biopsy)
sinus destruction on imaging (suggests gpa or malignancy)
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• hertel exophthalmometry to quantify proptosis
• iop in primary and upgaze (correlation with inferior rectus thickening)
• assessment for exposure keratopathy and optic neuropathy (color vision, perimetry)
## Imaging (CT/MRI)
• ted: myogenic vs. lipogenic variants; check for apical crowding
• ioi: check for tendon involvement and "ring sign" (scleral thickening)
## Systemic & labs
• thyroid panel: tsh, t3, t4, tsi, and tpo antibodies
• inflammatory markers: esr, crp, ana, ace, anca, and serum igg4
## Biopsy
• strongly considered for atypical, bilateral, or steroid-refractory cases
actionSteps: obtain orbital ct or mri to differentiate eom belly vs. tendon involvement
rule out infectious mimics (fever, sinus disease) before starting steroids
initiate oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) for suspected ioi or active ted
refer to endocrinology for systemic thyroid management
treatment: ## Thyroid eye disease
• mandatory smoking cessation (smoking significantly worsens ted progression)
• active phase: pulsed iv methylprednisolone or teprotumumab (igf-1r inhibitor)
• mild/stable: lubricants, selenium (100 µg b.i.d.), and head elevation at night
• surgical sequence: decompression → strabismus surgery → eyelid repair
## Idiopathic orbital inflammation
• systemic steroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) with slow taper
• steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, rituximab) for recurrent disease
• low-dose orbital radiation (20 gy) for refractory cases post-biopsy
## Igg4-related disease
• systemic steroids followed by steroid-sparing immunosuppression
followUp: ## Urgent
• daily or immediate follow-up for dysthyroid optic neuropathy or severe exposure
## Routine
• ted: follow every 3–6 months if stable; monitor tfts every 6–12 months
• ioi: re-evaluate 1–2 days after steroid initiation; use slow taper to prevent bounce-back
• maintain high vigilance for systemic igg4 or lymphoma in bilateral cases
review: ioi is a diagnosis of exclusion; tendon involvement on imaging distinguishes it from ted
dramatic response to steroids within 48 hours is a diagnostic hallmark of ioi
smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor in thyroid eye disease
pearl: Idiopathic orbital inflammation is a diagnosis of exclusion — IgG4-related disease, GPA, sarcoid, thyroid eye disease, and lymphoma all mimic it, so biopsy atypical cases before long-term immunosuppression.

name: Intermediate Uveitis
symptoms: painless floaters and blurred vision
minimal photophobia or redness (characteristically a "quiet" eye)
usually bilateral but often asymmetric
typically affects patients aged 15–40 years
findings: ## Signature signs
• snowballs: discrete, spherical, white-yellow vitreous cellular aggregates
• snowbanking: confluent white fibroglial exudates over the inferior pars plana
• vitritis: significant vitreous haze and cells out of proportion to anterior segment reaction
## Clinical complications
• cystoid macular edema (cme): most common cause of vision loss
• peripheral retinal periphlebitis and vascular sheathing
• peripheral neovascularization (may lead to vitreous hemorrhage)
• secondary signs: posterior subcapsular cataract, band keratopathy, and glaucoma
etiology: ## Idiopathic
• pars planitis: subtype accounting for >70% of cases (idiopathic snowbanking/snowballs)
## Systemic associations
• multiple sclerosis (ms): associated with 10–20% of cases; uveitis may precede demyelination
• sarcoidosis: often presents with prominent vitritis and snowballs
• infectious: lyme disease, syphilis, and tuberculosis
## Masquerades
• primary intraocular lymphoma (suspect in patients >50 years)
• toxocariasis or retinoblastoma (suspect in children)
redFlags: unexplained vitritis in a young woman (requires ms screening/mri)
new-onset intermediate uveitis in patients >50 years (rule out lymphoma)
use of anti-tnf-α agents if ms is suspected (can worsen demyelination)
vitreous hemorrhage in a young patient (check for neovascular snowbanks)
investigations: ## Ocular diagnostics
• indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression: mandatory to view inferior pars plana
• oct and fa: to identify cme, retinal vasculitis, or neovascularization
• diagnostic vitrectomy: indicated in older patients to rule out lymphoma
## Systemic workup
• labs: rpr/fta-abs (syphilis), ace (sarcoid), quantiferon-tb gold, and lyme titers
• imaging: chest x-ray or ct (sarcoid/tb)
• mri brain with gadolinium: if neurological symptoms or high ms suspicion
actionSteps: exclude infectious and masquerade causes before starting steroids
screen for ms in adults and sarcoid/lyme in younger patients
treat vision-threatening cme aggressively
monitor iop closely for steroid-induced spikes
treatment: ## Local therapy (unilateral/CME)
• periocular (sub-tenon) or intravitreal triamcinolone injections
• long-acting steroid implants (ozurdex/yutiq) for chronic non-infectious cases
## Systemic therapy (bilateral/severe)
• oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) with a slow taper
• steroid-sparing agents: methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, or azathioprine
• biologic therapy: adalimumab (only if ms is excluded)
## Surgical/procedural
• pars plana vitrectomy: for non-resolving haze, erm, or traction
• laser or cryotherapy: for peripheral neovascularization
followUp: ## Monitoring
• acute: every 1–4 weeks depending on cme presence
• stable: every 3–6 months to monitor for quiet inflammation
• co-manage with rheumatology or neurology for systemic associations
review: cme is the primary cause of vision loss in intermediate uveitis
scleral depression is essential to visualize the snowbanks of pars planitis
always rule out intraocular lymphoma in any patient over 50 presenting with vitritis
pearl: Snowbanking at the pars plana with vitreous snowballs is pars planitis — screen for MS in adults and for sarcoidosis and Lyme in the young; most need chronic steroid-spancy immunosuppression.

name: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO)
symptoms: horizontal binocular diplopia (worse on lateral gaze)
blurry vision or vague visual complaints
oscillopsia (world moving) due to abducting nystagmus
may be asymptomatic and detected only on examination
findings: ## Hallmark exam
• ipsilateral adduction deficit: the eye on the side of the mlf lesion cannot move inward
• contralateral abducting nystagmus: the other eye shakes when looking away from the lesion
• convergence is preserved: adduction works at near (uses a different pathway)
• adduction lag: the weak eye moves slower than the abducting eye during saccades
## Neuro-localization
• lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (mlf)
• ipsilateral to the eye with the adduction deficit
