• one-and-a-half syndrome: ino plus ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy
## Associated findings
• skew deviation: vertical misalignment of the eyes
• upbeat nystagmus on upgaze (especially in bilateral cases)
• webino: wall-eyed bilateral ino (exotropia in primary position)
etiology: ## Multiple sclerosis (MS)
• most common cause in young patients; frequently bilateral
• bilateral ino in a young adult is ms until proven otherwise
## Brainstem stroke
• most common cause in elderly patients; usually unilateral
• lacunar infarct of the paramedian pontine or midbrain perforators
## Other causes
• brainstem tumors, aums, or trauma
• infectious/inflammatory: sarcoidosis, behçet, cryptococcosis, or syphilis
redFlags: bilateral ino in a young patient (multiple sclerosis)
unilateral ino in an older patient with vascular risks (stroke)
one-and-a-half syndrome (indicates a larger pontine lesion)
ino with other brainstem signs (ataxia, facial weakness, altered consciousness)
investigations: ## Clinical diagnostics
• horizontal saccade testing: look for slow adduction (most sensitive)
• near-point convergence: confirms adduction works for non-lateral gaze
• optokinetic drum: unmasks subtle adduction lag
• exclude myasthenia gravis ("pseudo-ino"): check lid twitch and fatigability
## Imaging (mandatory)
• mri brain with gadolinium: look for t2/flair signal in the paramedian brainstem
• dwi sequence: to identify acute ischemic infarcts
## Systemic workup
• young patients: mri spine, lp for oligoclonal bands, and visual evoked potentials
• older patients: mra/cta head and neck, echocardiogram, and lipid/a1c labs
actionSteps: order mri brain with contrast focused on the brainstem
screen young patients for demyelinating disease (ms)
initiate stroke workup for elderly patients with acute symptoms
evaluate for myasthenia gravis if the presentation is variable or atypical
treatment: ## Primary
• treat the underlying etiology (ms therapies, stroke prevention, or tumor resection)
## Symptomatic
• prism glasses or monocular occlusion for persistent diplopia
• strabismus surgery: reserved for stable, chronic, non-resolving cases
## Prognosis
• many lesions resolve over weeks to months as inflammation or ischemia settles
followUp: ## Monitoring
• neurology referral for long-term management of ms or stroke risk
• evaluate for development of new neurologic deficits
• follow-up mri based on initial diagnosis and therapy response
differentials: third nerve palsy (medial rectus weakness + ptosis/pupil signs)
thyroid eye disease (ted) or orbital myositis
review: ino is defined by weak adduction in one eye and nystagmus in the abducting eye
the mlf lesion is always on the side of the eye that cannot adduct
convergence is the clinical key: if the eye adducts at near but not on side-gaze, the lesion is in the mlf, not the muscle
pearl: INO in a young adult is MS; in an older adult, it's a lacunar stroke — the adducting eye fails, the abducting eye has nystagmus, and the MLF is ipsilateral to the weak adduction.

name: Interstitial Keratitis (IK)
symptoms: gradual vision decrease, photophobia, and ocular pain (active)
tearing and redness; often bilateral (e.g., congenital syphilis)
symptoms typically manifest between ages 5 and 20 in congenital syphilis
systemic cues: hearing loss/vertigo (cogan) or skin anesthesia (leprosy)
findings: ## Active phase
• deep stromal edema with dense limbus-to-limbus haze
• "salmon patch": pink sector of confluent deep stromal vessels (classic syphilis)
• anterior chamber reaction (cells/flare) and mutton-fat keratic precipitates
## Chronic / inactive phase
• ghost vessels: pathognomonic empty, non-perfused stromal vessel channels
• stromal clearing with persistent scarring or "ghost" lines
## Hutchinson triad (congenital syphilis)
• interstitial keratitis
• sensorineural hearing loss (cn viii deafness)
• hutchinson teeth: notched, peg-shaped permanent upper incisors
## Cogan syndrome
• autoimmune ik plus acute vestibuloauditory dysfunction (vertigo, tinnitus)
• medical emergency: hearing loss can become permanent within weeks
## Other etiology clues
• hsv: most common adult cause; usually unilateral and sectoral
• tuberculosis: unilateral, sectoral, often with peripheral phlyctenules
• leprosy: "beads on a string" segmental thickening of corneal nerves
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• non-ulcerative inflammation of the corneal stroma
• typically a delayed immune-mediated reaction rather than active infection
## Primary causes
• syphilis: congenital (bilateral, 80%) or acquired (unilateral)
• hsv/vzv: common adult triggers
• tuberculosis, lyme disease, and ebv
• autoimmune: cogan syndrome (associated with systemic vasculitis)
redFlags: cogan syndrome: rapid hearing loss risk; requires high-dose systemic steroids
congenital syphilis stigmata (saddle nose, hutchinson teeth)
active stromal inflammation with neovascularization
corneal thinning or descemetocele formation
investigations: ## Clinical diagnostics
• check corneal sensation and look for madarosis (leprosy)
• dilated fundus exam: salt-and-pepper chorioretinitis (syphilis)
• audiology consult if cogan syndrome is suspected
## Laboratory workup
• syphilis serology: fta-abs (treponemal) and rpr/vdrl (activity)
• tb screen: quantiferon-tb gold or ppd
• lyme serology in endemic areas
## Imaging
• chest x-ray if tb is suspected; mri/mrv if neurosyphilis is a concern
actionSteps: perform comprehensive serologic workup (syphilis, lyme, tb)
initiate topical steroids for active inflammation; taper very slowly
coordinate systemic antimicrobial therapy with infectious disease (id)
refer for systemic steroids/immunosuppression if cogan syndrome suspected
treatment: ## Ocular (active)
• topical prednisolone acetate 1% (q2–6h) with a slow taper over months
• topical cycloplegic (atropine 1%) for comfort and synechiae prevention
## Systemic (etiology-specific)
• syphilis: penicillin g iv (id consult for neurosyphilis staging)
• cogan syndrome: high-dose systemic corticosteroids (urgent hearing rescue)
• tuberculosis: ripe regimen; lyme: doxycycline or ceftriaxone
## Refractive (chronic)
• rgp or scleral contact lenses for irregular astigmatism from scarring
• keratoplasty (corneal transplant) for visually significant central scars
followUp: ## Monitoring
• follow weekly in the active phase until inflammation settles
• monitor iop closely during long-term steroid use
• inactive ghost vessels require no treatment but document prior infection risk
review: ghost vessels represent a permanent "biologic record" of prior stromal inflammation
cogan syndrome is an eye finding that signals an ear emergency
salt-and-pepper fundus changes are a hallmark of congenital syphilis
pearl: Ghost vessels in a non-inflamed deep stroma are a permanent record of old syphilitic or Cogan interstitial keratitis — they need no treatment but always prompt a history of untreated prior infection.

name: Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB)
symptoms: eye pain and decreased vision
may be asymptomatic if the entry wound is small (e.g., metal-on-metal hammering)
history of grinding, hammering, or high-velocity projectiles striking the eye
findings: ## Strict MRI contraindication
• do NOT perform mri if a ferrous (iron/steel) iofb is possible
• the magnetic field can rotate or eject metal, causing catastrophic hemorrhage or nerve transection
## Clinical signs
• peaked pupil or iris transillumination defect (tid) pointing to entry site
• seidel-positive corneal/scleral perforation wound
• focal lens opacity along the entry tract or visible iofb in the vitreous/ac
• asymmetrically low iop compared to the fellow eye
## Chronic toxicity (retained IOFB)
• siderosis bulbi (iron): iris heterochromia (rust color), mydriasis, and pigmentary retinopathy
• chalcosis bulbi (copper): "sunflower" cataract and peripheral k-f-like rings
• organic matter (wood): extremely high risk for fulminant b. cereus endophthalmitis
etiology: ## Mechanism
• high-velocity projectiles from metal-on-metal hammering, grinding, or firearms
• explosions or agricultural machinery accidents
## Material reactivity
• high: iron, steel, copper (>85%), and vegetable/organic matter
• mild: nickel, aluminum, and zinc
• inert: gold, silver, glass, plastic, and stone
redFlags: any history of high-velocity injury necessitates a ct scan of the orbits
wooden/organic foreign bodies are often occult on ct; suspect if mechanism fits
organic iofbs require immediate removal to prevent rapidly blinding endophthalmitis
retained iron iofbs cause irreversible retinal b-wave attenuation on erg
investigations: ## Imaging (mandatory)
• non-contrast ct orbits (1-mm thin cuts) is the gold standard for localization
• ubm or b-scan (performed gently) if the view is obscured and globe is stable
## Clinical exam
• search the angle and iris for hidden fbs; check for iris tids and lens integrity
• dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy (if globe is sufficiently stable)
• serial erg for suspected retained iron to monitor for siderosis
actionSteps: place a rigid fox shield over the eye immediately (do not patch or apply pressure)
keep the patient npo for urgent surgical intervention
start iv broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin and ceftazidime)
obtain an urgent non-contrast ct orbit to rule out a metallic iofb
treatment: ## Medical
• iv antibiotics: vancomycin 1 g and ceftazidime 1 g every 12 hours
• update tetanus prophylaxis status
## Surgical
• urgent pars plana vitrectomy for iofb removal (ideally within 24 hours)
• primary closure of the entry wound
• intravitreal antibiotics are often administered at the time of surgery
followUp: ## Monitoring
• daily exams for the first week post-op to monitor for endophthalmitis
• evaluate for sympathetic ophthalmia in the fellow eye (rare but serious)
• monthly exams until 6 months post-injury
differentials: corneal or conjunctival foreign body without penetration
ruptured globe without a retained foreign body
review: ct is mandatory for any metal-on-metal history, regardless of how small the wound appears
never use mri to screen for intraocular foreign bodies in trauma cases
organic foreign bodies carry the highest risk of acute infectious complications
pearl: Every eye injury from metal-on-metal work needs a CT orbit before MRI — a ferrous IOFB pulled by MRI has blinded patients who said "just a little piece went in my eye."

name: Iridocorneal Endothelial Syndrome (ICE)
symptoms: usually asymptomatic in early stages
later: irregular pupil shape, blurred vision, or monocular diplopia
pain and photophobia if iop rises or corneal edema develops
strictly unilateral; typically affects women aged 20–50
sporadic presentation (not inherited)
findings: ## Signature endothelial signs
• "beaten-bronze" or hammered-silver appearance of the posterior cornea
• specular microscopy (diagnostic): large, pleomorphic, dark "ice cells" with reversed polarity
• corneal edema can occur even at normal or only mildly elevated iop
## Iris & angle changes
• progressive corectopia (displaced pupil) and polycoria (multiple iris holes)
• gonioscopy: high PAS extending anterior to schwalbe line (nearly pathognomonic)
• secondary angle-closure glaucoma from contracting endothelial membranes over the trabecular meshwork
## Clinical subtypes
• chandler syndrome: corneal edema and "beaten-bronze" signs dominate; minimal iris changes
• progressive iris atrophy: marked full-thickness iris holes and corectopia
• cogan–reese syndrome: pedunculated nodules (islands of iris) on the anterior iris surface
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• abnormal corneal endothelium acquires epithelial-like properties and migrates across the angle and iris
• a contracting basement-membrane-like sheet pulls the iris forward, creating holes and closing the angle
• etiology is unknown; a viral trigger (hsv or ebv) has been postulated
redFlags: unilateral corneal edema with pupillary distortion in a middle-aged woman
progressive secondary glaucoma that is refractory to medical therapy
bilateral findings: reconsider axenfeld-rieger or posterior polymorphous dystrophy
rapid endothelial graft failure due to recipient cell migration
investigations: ## Diagnostics
• specular microscopy: essential to identify characteristic ice cells
• gonioscopy: to identify anteriorly displaced pas and angle closure
• slit-lamp exam: document corectopia, iris nodules, and "beaten-bronze" reflex
## Monitoring
• baseline glaucoma workup: iop, optic nerve assessment, and visual fields
• ultrasound biomicroscopy (ubm): if corneal edema obscures angle visualization
actionSteps: perform specular microscopy of both eyes to confirm unilateral "ice cells"
initiate aqueous suppressants for iop control; avoid miotics
refer for glaucoma surgery (tube shunt or mmc-trabeculectomy) if medically uncontrolled
coordinate endothelial keratoplasty (dmek/dsaek) for visually significant edema
treatment: ## IOP management
• medical: aqueous suppressants are first-line
• surgical: tube shunts are generally preferred over trabeculectomy (which often fails due to membrane overgrowth)
## Corneal management
• dmek or dsaek for corneal decompensation
• note: recipient endothelium may continue to migrate, leading to graft failure
## Iris management
• surgical reconstruction or prosthetic iris for cosmetic or functional (glare) concerns
followUp: ## Schedule
• every 3–6 months to monitor iop, corneal clarity, and angle status
• evaluate for surgical failure (membrane overgrowth of tube or ostium)
• unilateral surveillance: fellow eye involvement is extremely rare
review: ice syndrome is a unilateral disease of a migrating endothelial membrane
the "membrane theory" explains the unique pas that extend past schwalbe line
chandler syndrome is the most common variant and often presents with blurred vision from edema
pearl: A middle-aged woman with unilateral iris atrophy, corectopia, and secondary glaucoma has ICE syndrome — the abnormal endothelium crawls across the angle and iris, and tube shunts outperform trabeculectomy here.

name: Iridodialysis and Cyclodialysis
symptoms: usually asymptomatic early (unless hyphema present)
large iridodialysis: monocular diplopia, debilitating glare, and photophobia
blurred vision if hypotony maculopathy develops from a cleft
history of blunt or penetrating ocular trauma
findings: ## Iridodialysis (iris disinsertion)
• tearing of the iris root from the ciliary body
• d-shaped or crescentic pupil with a dark peripheral gap
• posterior lens surface or zonules may be visible through the gap
## Cyclodialysis (ciliary body disinsertion)
• tearing of the ciliary body from the scleral spur
• creates a direct communication between the anterior chamber and suprachoroidal space
• hallmark: profound ocular hypotony (iop often <5 mmhg)
• clefts are often subtle; detected via gonioscopy or ubm/as-oct
## Associated traumatic signs
• hyphema and angle recession
• iridodonesis or phacodonesis (from lens subluxation)
• hypotony maculopathy: chorioretinal folds and optic disc edema
etiology: ## Mechanism
• blunt trauma: anteroposterior compression leads to equatorial expansion, shearing tissues at their thinnest points (iris root/scleral spur)
• iatrogenic: complications during phacoemulsification or vitreoretinal surgery
## Physiology
• cleft leads to massive uveoscleral outflow (hypotony)
• dialysis creates a functional "second pupil" (polycoria)
redFlags: persistent hypotony (iop <5) following trauma: suspect a hidden cyclodialysis cleft
monocular diplopia: occurs when the iris gap allows a second image to reach the retina
sudden iop spike following cleft closure (pressure "rebound")
angle recession >180°: significant long-term risk for traumatic glaucoma
investigations: ## Clinical diagnostics
• slit-lamp exam: document pupil shape and peripheral gaps
• gonioscopy (mandatory): identify the cleft and quantify angle recession
• tonometry: monitor for profound hypotony or delayed hypertension
## Imaging & posterior segment
• ubm or as-oct: if gonioscopy is inconclusive or corneal edema is present
• dilated fundus exam: rule out retinal dialysis, commotio retinae, and choroidal rupture
actionSteps: perform gonioscopy to map the disinsertion and locate any potential clefts
initiate cycloplegia (atropine 1%) to help stabilize the ciliary body/iris position
obtain as-oct or ubm if the iop is low but no cleft is visible on gonioscopy
refer for surgical repair if the dialysis is symptomatic or hypotony is persistent
treatment: ## Iridodialysis
• conservative: tinted contact lenses or sunglasses for glare/diplopia
• surgical: iris suturing (mccannel or siepser technique) for large, symptomatic defects
## Cyclodialysis cleft
• medical: atropine 1% and topical steroids to encourage cleft closure
• procedural: argon laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, or surgical pucker/cleft closure
## Associated glaucoma
• aqueous suppressants for iop elevation due to angle recession
followUp: ## Short-term
• weekly iop checks initially to monitor for hypotony resolution or pressure spikes
• follow-up fundus exam to monitor for maculopathy if hypotony persists
## Long-term
• lifetime annual glaucoma screening (vf and oct) for patients with angle recession
review: an iridodialysis is a cosmetic and optical problem; a cyclodialysis is a physiological problem (hypotony)
hypotony maculopathy is a serious threat to vision that requires anatomical closure of the cleft
gonioscopy is the "gold standard" for identifying these traumatic angle injuries
pearl: Unexplained hypotony after blunt trauma is a cyclodialysis cleft until proven otherwise — gonioscopy is the test that finds it, and closure restores IOP and vision.

name: Isolated Fourth Cranial Nerve Palsy
symptoms: binocular vertical or oblique diplopia
difficulty with downgaze tasks (reading, walking down stairs)
sensation of tilted objects (excyclotorsion)
compensatory head tilt to the side opposite the affected eye
may be asymptomatic if it is a long-standing congenital palsy
findings: ## Cardinal deficit
• deficient depression of the eye when adducted (nasal gaze)
• affected eye is higher (hypertropic) in primary gaze
## Parks–bielschowsky three-step test
• step 1: identify which eye is hyper in primary gaze
• step 2: hypertropia worsens on horizontal gaze toward the contralateral side
• step 3: hypertropia worsens on ipsilateral head tilt (bielschowsky sign)
## Clinical clues
• compensatory head tilt toward the contralateral shoulder
• large vertical fusional amplitudes (>6 Δ) suggest a decompensated congenital palsy
• bilateral signs: alternating hyperdeviation and excyclotorsion >10° (double maddox rod)
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• congenital (most common): often decompensates in adulthood due to loss of fusion
• trauma: most common acquired cause (cn iv is thin and has a long intracranial course)
• microvascular: ischemia from diabetes or hypertension
## Rare causes
• demyelinating disease (ms), brainstem tumors, or raised icp
• giant cell arteritis (gca) in patients ≥55 years
redFlags: bilateral cn iv palsy (strongly associated with high-velocity head trauma)
associated sensory loss or other cn palsies (rule out cavernous sinus/brainstem lesion)
new palsy in a young patient without trauma (suspect ms or decompensated congenital)
progressive or non-resolving palsy (mandates imaging to rule out tumor)
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• old photographs: check for a chronic head tilt to confirm congenital origin
• measure vertical fusional amplitudes with a prism bar
• parks–bielschowsky three-step test
• double maddox rod test if bilateral involvement is suspected
## Imaging & labs
• mri brain with 3t thin-section protocol (ciss/fiesta) to visualize the trochlear nerve
• blood pressure, hba1c, and fasting glucose
• esr, crp, and platelets if gca is suspected (age ≥55)
actionSteps: perform the three-step test and check old photos for chronic head tilt
measure vertical fusional amplitudes to differentiate congenital vs. acquired
order mri with cranial-nerve-targeted protocol if the palsy is atypical or progressive
manage diplopia with prisms, occlusion, or strabismus surgery
treatment: ## Medical & supportive
• manage systemic risk factors (bp, glucose)
• symptomatic diplopia: patch one eye (avoid in children <11) or use prism spectacles
• observation: microvascular palsies often resolve spontaneously within 3 months
## Surgical
• strabismus surgery (e.g., harada-ito or inferior oblique weakening)
• indicated for stable (>6 months) and bothersome diplopia or severe head tilt
followUp: ## Monitoring
• neurology or neuro-ophthalmology referral for atypical or progressive cases
• follow every 4–6 weeks initially for acquired microvascular cases
• surgical evaluation once measurements are stable for at least 6 months
differentials: skew deviation (vertical tropia that improves when supine)
review: the superior oblique muscle normally depresses, intorts, and abducts the eye
bielschowsky’s head tilt test is the definitive bedside clinical maneuver for cn iv palsy
congenital cases often only need surgery when the patient can no longer compensate for the deviation
pearl: Head tilt in old family photographs is the giveaway for congenital CN IV palsy — three-step test plus photo review saves the neuroimaging in a classic presentation.
willsRef: Wills Eye §10.7 (Isolated Fourth Cranial Nerve Palsy)

name: Isolated Seventh Cranial Nerve Palsy
symptoms: sudden onset of unilateral facial weakness or total paralysis
inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos) with secondary irritation
drooling, slurred speech, and food collecting in the cheek
altered taste (anterior 2/3 of tongue) or hyperacusis
retro-auricular pain (behind the ear) often precedes the weakness
blurred vision or foreign body sensation from corneal exposure
findings: ## Central VS. peripheral
• central (umn/stroke): spares the forehead due to bilateral innervation
• peripheral (lmn/bell): involves the forehead (unable to wrinkle brow)
## Ocular signs
• lagophthalmos: incomplete eyelid closure on the affected side
• positive bell phenomenon: the eye rotates upward during attempted closure
• exposure keratopathy: ranges from punctate staining to stromal melting
• lower lid ectropion and epiphora (tearing) due to lacrimal pump failure
## Systemic & chronic signs
• ramsay hunt (vzv): vesicles on the pinna, ear canal, or soft palate
• synkinesis: aberrant regeneration (e.g., eye closes when smiling)
• crocodile tears: tearing while eating (gustolacrimal reflex)
etiology: ## Idiopathic & viral
• bell palsy: most common; idiopathic (likely hsv-1 reactivation)
• ramsay hunt syndrome: varicella-zoster virus (vzv) of the geniculate ganglion
## Other causes
• infectious: lyme disease (suspect if bilateral), hiv, or syphilis
• trauma: temporal bone fractures or parotid/mastoid surgery
• neoplasm: acoustic neuroma (cpa mass) or parotid gland tumors
• inflammatory: sarcoidosis
redFlags: forehead sparing (suggests a central umn lesion like stroke or tumor)
bilateral simultaneous palsy (suspect lyme, sarcoidosis, or guillain-barré)
multiple cranial nerve deficits (v, vi, viii) (localizes to cpa or brainstem)
vesicles in the ear or mouth (requires immediate antiviral for ramsay hunt)
progressive worsening >3 weeks or no recovery by 3 months (rule out cancer)
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• bedside: test forehead movement and orbicularis strength
• slit-lamp: evaluation for exposure-related corneal thinning
• ear/oropharynx: check for vesicles or parotid masses
## Laboratory & imaging
• bilateral workup: lyme titers, ace level, and rpr/fta-abs
• mri brain/cpa with contrast: if other cn involved or no recovery at 3 months
• ct temporal bone: if history of head trauma
actionSteps: start oral prednisone within 72 hours of bell palsy onset (e.g., 60mg for 5 days)
add valacyclovir (1g t.i.d.) if ramsay hunt or severe viral palsy suspected
aggressive corneal protection: pf tears q1h and thick ointment at bedtime
teach eyelid taping or moisture chamber techniques for overnight protection
treatment: ## Medical
• corticosteroids (prednisone) and antivirals (valacyclovir) for acute phase
## Corneal protection
• preservative-free artificial tears, lubricating ointments, and moisture goggles
• bandage contact lens for persistent epithelial defects
## Surgical & procedural
• upper lid weight (gold/platinum) or tarsorrhaphy for severe lagophthalmos
• botulinum toxin to manage synkinesis or induce protective ptosis
followUp: ## Monitoring
• high-risk (poor bell phenomenon): every 1–3 days until stable
• routine bell palsy: re-evaluate at 1 week and 1 month
• refer to ophthalmology immediately if redness, pain, or vision loss occurs
review: the forehead is the anatomical key to differentiating central from peripheral palsy
corneal protection is the primary ophthalmic goal to prevent permanent scarring
most bell palsy cases show signs of recovery within 3 to 6 weeks
pearl: Facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal is Ramsay-Hunt — start antivirals and steroids within 72 hours to maximize recovery; the ENT consult is for the hearing, not the nerve.
willsRef: Wills Eye §10.9 (Isolated Seventh Cranial Nerve Palsy)

name: Keratoconus
symptoms: progressive decrease in vision (irregular astigmatism)
starbursts, ghosting, and halos around lights
onset typically during puberty; stabilizes in middle age
acute hydrops: sudden vision drop, pain, and profuse tearing
findings: ## Classic slit-lamp tetrad
• fleischer ring: brown-yellow epithelial iron deposit at the base of the cone
• vogt striae: fine vertical deep-stromal stress lines (disappear with globe compression)
• munson sign: v-shaped lower-lid indentation on downgaze due to cone protrusion
• apical thinning: central or paracentral stromal thinning ± scarring
## Early & optical signs
• charleux "oil-droplet" red reflex on direct ophthalmoscopy
• scissoring reflex on retinoscopy
## Topography & tomography
• topography: asymmetric inferior or inferotemporal steepening (i-s ratio > 1.4)
• tomography (pentacam): posterior corneal elevation and thinning are earlier indicators than topography
## Acute hydrops
• dense central/inferior stromal edema from a rupture in descemet membrane
• allows aqueous humor to flood the stroma; usually resolves over 2–4 months
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• non-inflammatory progressive ectasia causing corneal thinning and protrusion
• associated with chronic eye rubbing (strongest modifiable risk factor)
• multifactorial: atopy, down syndrome, marfan syndrome, and ehlers-danlos
• enzymatic imbalance leads to weakened stromal cross-linking
redFlags: sudden pain and opacity (acute hydrops)
documented rapid topographic progression in a teenager/young adult
history of aggressive eye rubbing (requires immediate behavioral counseling)
severe thinning approaching the limbus (suspect pellucid marginal degeneration)
investigations: ## Diagnostics
• scheimpflug tomography (e.g., pentacam): mandatory for staging and CXL planning
• computer-assisted topography: to map anterior curvature
• pachymetry: to measure the thinnest point of the cornea
• slit-lamp exam under cobalt blue light to highlight fleischer rings
actionSteps: enforce strict "no rubbing" policy and treat underlying atopic disease
perform serial tomography every 3–6 months to monitor for progression
initiate corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) if progression is documented
rehabilitate vision with rigid gas permeable (RGP) or scleral contact lenses
treatment: ## Non-surgical
• behavioral: strict avoidance of eye rubbing
• optical: glasses (mild), RGP lenses, or scleral lenses (moderate-to-severe)
## Surgical & procedural
• corneal cross-linking (CXL): uses riboflavin and UV-A to stabilize the stroma
• intracorneal ring segments (icrs): to flatten the cone and improve lens tolerance
• keratoplasty (dalk or pkp): for advanced scarring or contact lens intolerance
## Hydrops management
• conservative: cycloplegics, hypertonic saline (muro 128), and aqueous suppressants
followUp: ## Schedule
• every 6 months during the progressive years (teens to 30s)
• annual follow-up once stable (typically after age 40)
• post-CXL monitoring to ensure ectasia stabilization
differentials: keratoglobus (global thinning from limbus to limbus)
review: keratoconus is often markedly asymmetric; always check the "normal" fellow eye with tomography
eye rubbing is a mechanical catalyst for progression and must be addressed
hydrops usually leaves a scar that can flatten the cornea but often necessitates a transplant
pearl: Keratoconus is a bilateral (though often asymmetric) progressive corneal ectasia. Onset typically puberty to 30s. Associated with eye rubbing, atopy, Down syndrome. Hydrops (acute stromal edema from Descemet rupture) presents with sudden vision loss and opacity — paradoxically reduces progression. CXL is the only treatment proven to halt progression.

name: Lacrimal Gland Mass/Chronic Dacryoadenitis
symptoms: progressive swelling of the outer one-third of the upper eyelid
pain (highly suggestive of malignancy or acute infection)
double vision due to mass effect on extraocular muscles
inferomedial globe displacement ("down and in")
v1/v2 numbness (forehead/temple) suggests perineural invasion by carcinoma
findings: ## Clinical signs
• s-shaped upper eyelid deformity: classic for lacrimal gland enlargement
• "down and in" proptosis (inferomedial displacement)
• "salmon patch" subconjunctival extension suggests lymphoma (malt)
## Imaging discriminators (CT/MRI)
• pleomorphic adenoma: painless, >1 year history, fossa remodeling without erosion
• adenoid cystic carcinoma (acc): painful, subacute growth, frank bony erosion
• bilateral enlargement: suspect igg4-rd, sarcoidosis, or sjögren syndrome
• lymphoma: lesion typically "molds" to the globe and conforms to orbital anatomy
etiology: ## Epithelial tumors
• pleomorphic adenoma: benign mixed tumor; most common epithelial tumor
• adenoid cystic carcinoma (acc): most common malignant epithelial histology
## Inflammatory / systemic
• sarcoidosis: often bilateral and painless; may have lung or skin signs
• igg4-related dacryoadenitis: increasingly recognized systemic inflammatory cause
• idiopathic orbital inflammation (ioi): usually more acute and painful
## Other
• lymphoma: often indolent; malt is the most common subtype
• dacryops: simple lacrimal gland ductal cyst
redFlags: pain or rapid growth (strongly suggests adenoid cystic carcinoma)
bony erosion on ct (indicator of malignancy)
v1/v2 numbness (sign of perineural invasion into the forehead or temple)
bilateral involvement (mandates systemic workup for igg4, sarcoid, or lymphoma)
investigations: ## Imaging
• orbital ct (thin-cut): best to evaluate for bony remodeling vs. frank erosion
• chest ct: to screen for sarcoidosis or primary systemic malignancy
## Laboratory
• ace, lysozyme, and chest imaging for sarcoidosis
• serum igg4 levels, c-anca/p-anca, and cbc with differential
## Biopsy protocol
• STRICT RULE: do NOT perform incisional biopsy on suspected pleomorphic adenoma (seeds tumor and risks malignancy); excise en bloc
• biopsy with flow cytometry is indicated for suspected lymphoma or inflammatory disease
actionSteps: order orbital ct to differentiate between bony remodeling and frank erosion
perform systemic workup (ace, igg4, chest ct) for bilateral cases
arrange for en bloc excision of circumscribed, painless, long-standing masses
consult oncology and neuro-ophthalmology for painful masses with bony erosion
treatment: ## Benign epithelial
• pleomorphic adenoma: complete surgical en bloc excision (capsule must remain intact)
## Malignant epithelial
• acc: radical surgical resection often with involved bone + adjunctive radiation
## Inflammatory / systemic
• sarcoidosis and igg4-rd: systemic corticosteroids or steroid-sparing agents
• lymphoma: localized radiation or systemic chemotherapy depending on subtype
followUp: ## Monitoring
• chronic inflammatory: follow response to steroids; screen for systemic relapse
• post-excision: serial imaging to monitor for recurrence (especially foracc and pleomorphic adenoma)
• oncology co-management for all malignant histologies
review: approximately 50% of lacrimal gland epithelial tumors are malignant
adenoid cystic carcinoma is notorious for perineural spread and late recurrence
bilateral lacrimal gland swelling is a hallmark of systemic granulomatous or lymphoproliferative disease
pearl: A pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland must be excised en bloc — incisional biopsy seeds tumor into orbit and virtually guarantees recurrence with malignant transformation risk.

name: Leukocoria
symptoms: abnormal white reflex noticed in flash photos ("the glow"), direct sunlight, or exam
poor visual tracking, strabismus (eye turn), or nystagmus
parents often report the reflex before clinical symptoms appear
eye pain or redness may occur in advanced cases of retinoblastoma
findings: ## Clinical signs
• abnormal white, yellow, or gray pupillary reflex on red reflex testing
• absent or dulled red reflex on direct ophthalmoscopy
• underlying cause: retinoblastoma, cataract, coats disease, pfv, or rop
• intraocular calcifications on b-scan suggest retinoblastoma
• microphthalmos (small eye) suggests persistent fetal vasculature (pfv)
etiology: ## Retinoblastoma (RB)
• malignant retinal tumor; mean age 18 months
• hereditary (germline rb1) in 40%; bilateral in ~30%
• classic: chalky white mass with calcifications
## Coats disease
• idiopathic retinal telangiectasia with massive subretinal exudation ("xanthocoria")
• predominantly unilateral in young boys
## Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV)
• congenital failure of hyaloid regression; fibrovascular stalk from nerve to lens
• associated with a small eye (microphthalmos) and retrolental membrane
## Toxocariasis
• nematode infection causing a localized white granuloma or diffuse vitritis
• history of contact with puppies or geophagia (eating dirt)
## Other
• retinopathy of prematurity (rop), pediatric cataract, or retinal astrocytic hamartoma
redFlags: leukocoria is a life-threatening emergency until retinoblastoma is ruled out
any child with an abnormal red reflex requires a dilated exam within 48–72 hours
bilateral retinoblastoma indicates germline mutation and risk of trilateral rb (pineoblastoma)
delayed diagnosis risks extraocular extension, metastasis, and death
investigations: ## Imaging (mandatory)
• b-scan ultrasonography: demonstrates calcification (>90% sensitive for rb)
• mri orbits/brain: evaluates tumor extent and screens for pineoblastoma (avoids radiation)
• ct: confirms calcification but increases radiation risk in potentially mutated children
## Clinical exam
• comprehensive dilated exam (usually eua: examination under anesthesia)
• corneal diameter measurement: helps identify microphthalmos (pfv)
## Laboratory & genetic
• rb1 genetic testing for patient and first-degree relatives
• toxocara elisa if granulomatous inflammation is suspected
actionSteps: refer urgently to pediatric ophthalmology/ocular oncology for exam under anesthesia (eua)
obtain stat b-scan ultrasound to check for intraocular calcification
order mri orbits and brain to rule out intracranial involvement (trilateral rb)
initiate genetic counseling if retinoblastoma is confirmed
treatment: ## Retinoblastoma
• chemoreduction: systemic or selective intra-arterial chemotherapy (iac)
• focal therapy: cryotherapy, laser, or plaque radiotherapy
• enucleation for advanced unilateral disease or unsalvageable globes
## Coats disease
• laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy of telangiectatic vessels; anti-vegf
## PFV / pediatric cataract
• lensectomy and vitrectomy for visual rehabilitation
## Toxocariasis
• topical or systemic steroids for inflammation; vitrectomy for traction bands
followUp: ## Schedule
• emergent oncology workup followed by close intervals (weeks) during treatment
• lifelong surveillance for second primary malignancies in germline rb patients
• regular family screening for those at risk of hereditary rb
review: retinoblastoma often presents as a white mass filling the vitreous (endophytic) or subretinal space (exophytic)
the presence of a cataract in a small eye often points to pfv rather than rb
calcification seen on imaging in a child with a white pupil is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise
pearl: White pupil in a child is RETINOBLASTOMA until proven otherwise — an ocular oncology EMERGENCY. First test is an exam under anesthesia with indirect ophthalmoscopy (not outpatient slit lamp), plus urgent B-scan (intraocular calcification >90%) and MRI brain/orbits (extent + TRILATERAL retinoblastoma screening for pineoblastoma). Germline RB1 mutation (bilateral or familial cases) carries lifelong risk of second primary malignancies — osteosarcoma, soft-tissue sarcomas, melanoma — requiring lifelong surveillance.

name: Normal Pressure Glaucoma (NPG)
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Asymptomatic until advanced; often discovered during routine examination.
• Gradual loss of paracentral and peripheral vision.
• History of migraines, Raynaud phenomenon, or obstructive sleep apnea.
• Vision loss continues despite intraocular pressures (IOP) within normal limits.
findings: ## Diagnostic criteria
• Glaucomatous neuropathy with IOP consistently ≤21 mm Hg.
• Requires diurnal IOP documentation to ensure peaks are not missed.
## Characteristic optic disc signs
• Drance (splinter) hemorrhages: 2–4× more common than in high-tension glaucoma.
• Focal notching of the neuroretinal rim (especially inferior/inferotemporal).
• Acquired optic disc pits and peripapillary atrophy.
## Visual field pattern
• Dense paracentral defects closer to fixation than typical POAG.
• Central vision threatened earlier in the disease course.
## Systemic clues
• Thin central corneal thickness (CCT).
• Nocturnal systemic hypotension (often from over-treated high blood pressure).
• Obstructive sleep apnea (nocturnal hypoxia).
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• IOP-dependent damage: Damage occurs even at "normal" pressures.
• IOP-independent damage: Vascular dysregulation, nocturnal hypotension, and vasospasm.
• Accelerated retinal ganglion cell apoptosis.
redFlags: • Pallor out of proportion to cupping (rule out non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy).
• Visual field defects respecting the vertical midline (suspect chiasmal compression).
• Progression despite IOP in the low teens (target <10 mm Hg).
• Splinter hemorrhages (sentinel sign of active progression).
investigations: ## Clinical workup
• Baseline glaucoma evaluation: IOP, gonioscopy, and automated perimetry.
• Diurnal IOP curve: To rule out intermittent pressure spikes.
• Color plate testing and VA: To screen for optic nerve pallor/compression.
## Systemic & imaging
• 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring: Check for "nocturnal dipping".
• Sleep apnea screen (STOP-Bang) and polysomnography.
• MRI brain/orbits with gadolinium: If neurological signs or atypical field loss present.
actionSteps: • Perform diurnal IOP monitoring to confirm the normal pressure diagnosis.
• Rule out compressive lesions with MRI if disc pallor or atypical field loss is present.
• Evaluate systemic factors: Nocturnal hypotension and obstructive sleep apnea.
• Target a 30% IOP reduction from baseline using medical or laser therapy.
treatment: ## Medical & laser
• Target: Lower IOP by ≥30% (reduces progression risk from 35% to 12% per CNTGS).
• Prostaglandin analogs (first-line) and SLT (effective primary option).
• Brimonidine: Preferred over timolol due to potential neuroprotection (LoGTS trial).
## Systemic adjustments
• Coordinate with PCP to avoid evening/bedtime antihypertensive dosing.
• Treat obstructive sleep apnea if identified.
## Surgical
• Trabeculectomy with MMC or tube shunt for very low IOP targets (often ≤10 mm Hg).
followUp: ## Monitoring
• Every 3–6 months with IOP, visual fields (10-2 often needed), and OCT RNFL.
• Aggressive IOP lowering even if pressures appear "normal".
• Co-manage with PCP for systemic vascular risk factors.
differentials: • Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) with missed pressure peaks.
review: • NPG is more common in East Asian populations and in females with vasospastic disorders.
• Diurnal pressure monitoring is the only way to be sure IOP doesn't spike during off-hours.
• Disc hemorrhages are a critical sign that current treatment is insufficient.
pearl: A glaucomatous disc with "normal" IOPs still needs aggressive pressure lowering — and if the cup doesn't match the field (pallor > cupping, young patient), image the chiasm with an MRI before labeling it NTG.
willsRef: Wills Eye §9.2 (Low-Tension Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (Normal Pressure Glaucoma))

name: Lyme Optic Neuropathy
symptoms: Endemic regions: Northeast (Virginia → Maine) and upper Midwest (Wisconsin/Minnesota) United States account for the vast majority of US cases; also Pacific Northwest and most of Europe.
Bimodal age distribution: children 5–15y often present with neurologic manifestations (CN VII palsy, meningitis); adults 45–65y more often present with arthritis and late manifestations.

Tick exposure (Ixodes scapularis in US, I. ricinus in Europe) in spring/summer — most cases May–August. Consider Lyme higher on the optic neuritis differential in July/August than you would for an MS-pattern presentation.
Subacute monocular visual loss (days to weeks) — may mimic demyelinating optic neuritis.
Pain on eye movement when true optic neuritis form — not universal.
Blurred vision with central or cecocentral scotoma.
Early localized (days–weeks after bite): erythema migrans rash (bulls-eye), flu-like illness, arthralgia, headache.
Early disseminated (weeks–months): cranial neuritis (especially CN VII palsy, often bilateral), meningitis, carditis with AV block, migrating oligoarthritis.
Migratory arthralgia — joint pain that shifts from one large joint to another over days (classic Borrelia signature); high-yield on history.
Late disseminated (months–years): chronic arthritis, encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (Europe).
Recent tick exposure, outdoor activity in endemic region, or known tick bite in the last weeks to months?
Prior erythema migrans rash (even if transient)?
Cranial nerve palsies — facial droop, diplopia, hearing loss?
Headache, neck stiffness, or photophobia (meningitic features)?
findings: Reduced visual acuity, dyschromatopsia (especially for red), and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in unilateral disease.
Optic disc edema — most common ocular manifestation of Lyme optic nerve involvement (either true papillitis or papilledema from Lyme meningitis).
Retrobulbar optic neuritis with a normal disc acutely is possible (indistinguishable from MS-type optic neuritis without serology).
Central, cecocentral, or altitudinal visual field defect on perimetry.
Reduced RNFL thickness on OCT after the acute edema subsides.
Vitritis — mild-to-moderate vitreous cells favor Lyme over MS-type optic neuritis (where the vitreous is typically clean).
Peripheral anterior or intermediate uveitis may coexist.
Episcleritis, keratitis, or conjunctivitis in a minority.
Bilateral disc swelling if raised ICP from Lyme meningitis.
Unilateral or, classically, BILATERAL CN VII palsy — bilateral facial palsy in an endemic region is almost pathognomonic for Lyme.
Meningismus (nuchal rigidity, Kernig/Brudzinski) if Lyme meningitis present.
Erythema migrans if still within early stage.
etiology: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto — primary pathogen in North America.
B. afzelii and B. garinii — predominant in Europe; B. garinii especially associated with neurologic manifestations.
Proposed mechanisms: direct spirochetal invasion of the optic nerve, immune-mediated demyelination, or inflammation from contiguous Lyme meningitis causing raised ICP / papilledema.
Co-infection with Anaplasma, Babesia, or Ehrlichia (shared tick vector) should be considered when systemic illness is severe.
redFlags: Bilateral disc swelling + headache + meningismus → Lyme meningitis with papilledema; urgent LP and IV therapy.
Rapidly progressive vision loss despite serology workup → do not delay empiric IV ceftriaxone in endemic region.
Optic neuritis + unexplained cranial nerve palsy (especially CN VII) → strongly suggests Lyme over MS.
Positive Lyme serology should not substitute for MRI — exclude demyelinating lesions and other compressive causes.
investigations: Visual acuity, pupils (RAPD), color vision (Ishihara), automated perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2).
Dilated fundus exam + OCT RNFL to document disc edema and track resolution.

Two-tier Lyme serology (CDC criteria): ELISA screen, followed by Western blot (IgM and IgG) if reactive or equivocal. Modified two-tier assays (two ELISAs) are becoming more common in some labs; the two-tier principle is unchanged.
Antibody window: IgM takes 2–4 weeks to appear, IgG 4–6 weeks — a negative test within the first week does NOT exclude Lyme. Re-test at 2–4 weeks if suspicion remains high.
MRI brain + orbits with gadolinium — rule out MS plaques and characterize optic nerve enhancement.
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure — CSF pleocytosis, elevated protein, intrathecal Borrelia antibody (CSF:serum antibody index).
PCR for Borrelia DNA in CSF has modest sensitivity; use alongside serology.
Consider co-infection testing (Babesia smear/PCR, Anaplasma/Ehrlichia PCR) in endemic regions with systemic illness.
Rule out alternative causes: syphilis (RPR/FTA-ABS), TB (QuantiFERON), sarcoid (ACE, chest imaging), MS (MRI, OCB).
actionTitle: URGENT — empiric IV antibiotics + neurology/ID consult
actionSteps: Urgent neuro-ophthalmology and infectious-disease referral.
Start empiric IV ceftriaxone while serology pending if clinical suspicion is high in endemic region.
Lumbar puncture — ideally before or shortly after first antibiotic dose.
Admit for observation if vision deteriorating, raised ICP, or systemic compromise.
treatment: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily × 14–28 days — first-line for neuroborreliosis including optic nerve involvement.
IV cefotaxime or penicillin G are acceptable alternatives.

Oral doxycycline 100 mg BID × 14–21 days — reserved for isolated peripheral Lyme disease without CNS involvement. Recent European data suggest efficacy in some neuroborreliosis cases, but for optic nerve involvement (vision at risk) IV ceftriaxone remains the preferred choice in the US.
Do NOT give steroids alone — they can promote spirochetal proliferation. If needed for severe inflammatory edema, only after effective antibiotic coverage is established.
Treat raised ICP (acetazolamide) if Lyme meningitis with papilledema.
Address co-infections if identified (atovaquone + azithromycin for Babesia, doxycycline for Anaplasma/Ehrlichia).
followUp: Weekly clinical exam during IV therapy — VA, pupils, color vision, fundus, OCT.
Re-examine 1 month and 3 months post-treatment to confirm resolution of disc edema and improvement in visual fields.
Persistent "post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome" symptoms do NOT warrant prolonged or repeated antibiotics (IDSA and AAN guidance); manage symptomatically.
Monitor for MS-conversion over years if MRI shows demyelinating lesions — serology does not exclude dual diagnosis.
differentials: MS-related optic neuritis — the primary mimicker; MRI + OCB help distinguish
Neuromyelitis optica / MOG-IgG associated optic neuritis
Tuberculous optic neuritis or meningitis with papilledema
Toxic/nutritional optic neuropathy (especially in co-endemic regions)
pearl: Lyme disease is a great mimicker of multiple sclerosis. In endemic areas (Northeast US, upper Midwest, Pacific NW, Europe), always obtain Lyme two-tier serology before committing a patient to demyelinating-disease immunotherapy. Bilateral facial nerve palsy, erythema migrans, summer/spring presentation, or cranial neuropathy cluster should raise suspicion immediately. Treatment is IV ceftriaxone for any CNS involvement — oral doxycycline is inadequate for optic nerve or meningeal disease.

name: Malignant Melanoma of the Iris
symptoms: often asymptomatic; frequently detected during routine dilated examination
blurred vision or metamorphopsia if the tumor causes exudative detachment
floaters associated with vitreous hemorrhage or tumor-induced uveitis
acquired heterochromia (iris darkening) in diffuse variants
findings: ## Clinical hallmarks
• unilateral pigmented (rarely amelanotic) mass with prominent intrinsic feeder vessels
• predilection for the inferior iris and patients with light iris color
• ectropion uveae: outward rotation of the pupillary margin (classic tractional sign)
• corectopia: distorted pupil pulled toward the tumor site
• sector cataract: focal lens opacity at the point of tumor-lens contact
## Secondary complications
• spontaneous hyphema (bleeding into the anterior chamber)
• secondary glaucoma: tumor invasion of the angle or pigment seeding
## Imaging & diagnostics
• ultrasound biomicroscopy (ubm): mandatory to measure thickness and check ciliary body extension
• transillumination: solid melanoma blocks light (distinguishes it from a clear iris cyst)
• as-oct: high-resolution imaging for smaller, anterior lesions
etiology: ## Pathogenesis
• arises from uveal melanocytes; most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults
• risk factors: ocular melanocytosis (nevus of ota), bap1 mutation, and light skin/iris
## Cytogenetics
• monosomy 3 and gain of 8q are strong predictors of metastatic spread (liver)
redFlags: new or growing pigmented lesion with associated ectropion uveae
unilateral elevated iop with a darker iris (suspect diffuse iris melanoma)
bony erosion or extrascleral extension on imaging
systemic symptoms like weight loss or hepatomegaly
investigations: ## Ocular evaluation
• detailed slit-lamp exam with gonioscopy to evaluate angle invasion
• indirect ophthalmoscopy to rule out ciliary body or choroidal involvement
• ubm: to determine basal diameter and apical thickness
## Systemic staging
• lfts and ldh; liver mri or ultrasound to screen for metastasis
• fine-needle aspiration biopsy (fnab) for cytogenetics (monosomy 3)
actionSteps: document tumor dimensions with high-resolution photography and ubm
assess for high-risk features using the abcdef mnemonic
refer to ocular oncology for plaque brachytherapy or surgical resection
initiate systemic surveillance every 6 months if high-risk cytogenetics are present
treatment: ## Local control
• plaque brachytherapy (i-125 or ru-106) for most circumscribed tumors
• proton beam irradiation for tumors involving the angle
• surgical resection (iridocyclectomy) for localized iris/ciliary body lesions
• enucleation for diffuse melanoma or blind, painful eyes with glaucoma
## Systemic
• oncology co-management for high-risk patients
followUp: ## Monitoring
• every 3–12 months with photographs and ubm to monitor for growth
• monitor iop closely for development of secondary glaucoma
• lifelong liver imaging surveillance for high-risk cases
differentials: iris nevus (stable, no vessels, no ectropion uveae)
lisch nodules (bilateral, associated with neurofibromatosis type 1)
review: iris melanomas have a better prognosis than choroidal melanomas due to earlier detection
diffuse iris melanoma is the most dangerous variant because it is often missed
the presence of intrinsic feeder vessels is a key clinical differentiator from a benign nevus
pearl: A choroidal melanoma does not spare the life of the patient if it spares the eye — the #1 prognostic factor is tumor cytogenetics (class 2, monosomy 3), not size or globe-conservation status.
willsRef: Wills Eye §5.13 (Malignant Melanoma of the Iris)

name: Miscellaneous Optic Neuropathies
symptoms: painless, progressive, bilateral loss of vision over weeks to months
reduced central vision (typically 20/50 to 20/200)
early red-green dyschromatopsia (often disproportionate to acuity)
cecocentral or central scotomas on field testing
findings: ## Toxic / nutritional pattern
• bilateral, symmetric, and painless vision loss
• optic disc often appears normal early ("disc looks better than the vision")
• late finding: temporal pallor progressing to diffuse optic atrophy
• cecocentral scotoma: a field defect involving both the fixation and the blind spot
## Ethambutol optic neuropathy
• dose-dependent risk (threshold ~15 mg/kg/day); increased risk with renal impairment
• red-green color loss is the first detectable sign (screen monthly)
• mandatory baseline exam: va, color plates, and automated fields
## Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)
• young men (15–30); rapid, sequential bilateral central vision loss
• pathognomonic sign: peripapillary telangiectasias that do NOT leak on fluorescein
• maternal inheritance pattern (mitochondrial)
## Compressive optic neuropathy
• optociliary shunt vessels: retinochoroidal collaterals (classic for nerve sheath meningioma)
• "railroad-track" tubular enhancement on mri in optic nerve sheath meningioma
etiology: ## Toxic
• medications: ethambutol, linezolid, amiodarone, isoniazid, and digitalis
• substances: methanol (acute/severe), tobacco, and heavy metals (lead, mercury)
## Nutritional
• vitamin deficiencies: b12 (pernicious anemia/gastric bypass), b1 (thiamine), and folate
• copper deficiency (post-bariatric or excessive zinc intake)
## Inherited / compressive
• lhon: mitochondrial mutations (11778, 3460, 14484)
• tumors: optic nerve glioma (nf1-associated) and meningioma
redFlags: painless progressive vision loss (mandates mri to rule out compressive tumor)
maternally inherited vision loss (genetic testing for lhon)
visual field defects respecting the vertical midline (suspect chiasmal lesion)
rapid recovery after stopping a toxin (e.g., ethambutol or linezolid)
investigations: ## Imaging (mandatory)
• mri brain and orbits with contrast: focus on the chiasm and optic nerve sheaths
## Laboratory workup
• b12, folate, thiamine, methylmalonic acid, and homocysteine
• copper and ceruloplasmin; heavy metal screen
• lhon genetic testing (mtdna) if family history or disc swelling present
## Clinical tools
• automated perimetry (30-2 or 10-2 for central defects)
• color vision testing (ishihara/hrr) and oct rnfl
actionSteps: obtain mri with contrast to exclude compressive sellar or orbital masses
draw b12, folate, thiamine, and copper levels immediately
stop any suspected toxic medications (ethambutol, linezolid) in coordination with specialists
initiate empiric vitamin replacement (thiamine, folate, b12) while awaiting lab results
treatment: ## Toxic / nutritional
• remove causative agent (alcohol, tobacco, or medication)
• replace nutrients: thiamine 100 mg po bid, folate 1 mg daily, and b12 1000 mcg im
## LHON
• strictly avoid tobacco (even second-hand) and alcohol
• consider idebenone therapy (where available/licensed)
## Compressive
• fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy for meningioma; chemotherapy for glioma
followUp: ## Monitoring
• monthly initially to track acuity, color vision, and field resolution
• transition to every 6–12 months once stabilized
• coordination with pcp for long-term nutritional management
review: toxic neuropathies typically present with bilateral, symmetric cecocentral scotomas
red-green color loss often precedes acuity loss in ethambutol toxicity
optociliary shunt vessels are a classic sign of optic nerve sheath meningioma
pearl: When the optic neuropathy does not fit a box, work through the "ION, IT, IS, DDx Checklist": Infiltrative, Toxic-nutritional, Infectious, Inflammatory, Ischemic, Inherited, Compressive, Traumatic — then image.

name: Miscellaneous Orbital Diseases
symptoms: gradual, painless proptosis: the most common orbital presentation
positional proptosis: proptosis worsening with Valsalva or head-down (Trendelenburg) position, suggesting orbital varix
pulsatile proptosis: may be accompanied by a "whooshing" bruit (Carotid-Cavernous Fistula) or absent sphenoid wing (NF1)
acute proptosis in a child: often with bruising, suggests lymphangioma hemorrhage ("chocolate cyst") or rhabdomyosarcoma
superolateral orbital rim mass in a child: classic for orbital dermoid
bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement: consider IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, or lymphoma
findings: ## Proptosis characteristics
• axial or non-axial displacement: measured via Hertel exophthalmometry (significant if >22 mm or >2 mm asymmetry)
• globe displacement opposite the mass: e.g., superior mass pushes globe downward
• resistance to retropulsion: suggests a retro-orbital space-occupying lesion
## Vascular signs (CCF)
• classic triad: pulsatile proptosis, orbital bruit, and "corkscrew" arterialized episcleral vessels
• elevated IOP and chemosis are common in high-flow fistulas
## Neurologic signs
• optic neuropathy: reduced acuity, color desaturation, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)
• optociliary shunt vessels: retinochoroidal collaterals classic for optic nerve sheath meningioma
## Pediatric signs
• superolateral palpable mass at the frontozygomatic suture: orbital dermoid
• "S-shaped" upper lid ptosis: plexiform neurofibroma (NF1)
etiology: ## Vascular & cystic
• cavernous hemangioma: most common benign orbital tumor in adults; encapsulated and slow-growing
• orbital varix: direct venous communication causing intermittent proptosis
• orbital dermoid: congenital cyst located at bony sutures
## Neoplastic
• rhabdomyosarcoma: most common primary orbital malignancy in children; rapid onset (weeks)
• orbital lymphoma: most common adult orbital malignancy; often indolent molding to the globe
• metastatic disease: breast (scirrhous variant causes paradoxical enophthalmos), lung, and prostate
## Inflammatory & infectious
• thyroid eye disease (TED): the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults
• mucormycosis: life-threatening fungal infection in immunocompromised/diabetic patients
• IgG4-related disease: bilateral lacrimal gland and extraocular muscle enlargement
redFlags: ANY PROPTOSIS WITH A NEW RAPD: an orbital compartment emergency requiring immediate imaging and management
rapid proptosis in a child: rhabdomyosarcoma until proven otherwise (requires biopsy within days)
black eschar on palate or turbinates: pathognomonic for mucormycosis; a surgical and medical emergency
rock-hard globe with vision loss (orbital compartment syndrome): requires immediate bedside lateral canthotomy
pulsatile proptosis with a bruit: suggests a carotid-cavernous fistula
investigations: ## Imaging
• CT orbits: best for bone detail, calcification (meningioma "tram-tracks"), and dermoid fat density
• MRI orbits with fat suppression: best for soft-tissue detail and intracranial extension
## Clinical & labs
• Hertel exophthalmometry: for serial quantification of proptosis
• systemic workup: TSH (thyroid), ACE (sarcoid), ANCA (GPA), and IgG4 subclass levels
• incisional biopsy: for definitive diagnosis of suspected malignancies or inflammatory masses
actionSteps: perform comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic exam including pupils, color vision, and Hertel measurements
order urgent CT/MRI if optic neuropathy (RAPD) or rapid progression is noted
rule out thyroid eye disease (TSH/imaging) in any adult with new proptosis
coordinate emergency surgical debridement and IV antifungals for suspected mucormycosis
treatment: ## Surgical
• orbital dermoid: complete excision intact to avoid keratin-induced inflammation
• cavernous hemangioma: observation or surgical excision if symptomatic/compressive
• mucormycosis: emergent debridement + IV liposomal amphotericin B
## Medical & radiation
• rhabdomyosarcoma: chemotherapy and radiotherapy (not primary surgical resection)
• orbital lymphoma: radiation for localized disease; chemotherapy for systemic/high-grade disease
• optic nerve sheath meningioma: fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy to preserve vision
• IgG4-RD / Sarcoidosis: systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents
followUp: ## Monitoring
• stable vascular/cystic lesions: serial Hertel and imaging every 6–12 months
• inflammatory disease: co-manage with rheumatology; monitor for systemic recurrence
• malignancy: long-term oncology surveillance based on tumor grade and stage
review: TED must be excluded in every case of adult proptosis before other diagnoses are considered
orbital compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; do not wait for imaging to perform a canthotomy
cavernous hemangiomas are benign but can cause vision loss through direct optic nerve compression
pearl: Pattern-match orbital disease by demographics: adults with slow painless proptosis → cavernous hemangioma; child with superolateral mass → dermoid; child with rapid proptosis → rhabdomyosarcoma until proven otherwise; adult with pulsatile proptosis and bruit → carotid–cavernous fistula; bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement → IgG4 until proven otherwise; paradoxical enophthalmos → scirrhous breast metastasis. ANY proptosis with an RAPD or color desaturation is an emergency — image TODAY. The most common cause of proptosis in adults, by far, is thyroid eye disease — always check TSH first.

name: Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid (Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid)
symptoms: insidious onset of chronic dryness, redness, and burning sensation
foreign body sensation, tearing, and blepharospasm
progressive bilateral involvement typically in patients over 55
decreased vision and photophobia in advanced stages
findings: ## Progressive cicatrizing conjunctivitis
• chronic scarring that starting as a non-specific "red eye"
• symblepharon (hallmark): fibrous adhesions between bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva
• fornix foreshortening: measured depth <11 mm (serial measurement tracks progression)
• ankyloblepharon: fusion of the lids to the globe in end-stage disease
## Lid & corneal sequelae
• trichiasis and entropion (misdirected lashes and inward lid rotation)
• keratinization of the conjunctiva and severe goblet cell loss
• limbal stem cell deficiency and eventual corneal opacification
## Extraocular mucosa
• desquamative gingivitis (red, sloughing gums) is the most common finding
• bullae and ulcers of the oral, nasopharyngeal, or esophageal mucosa
etiology: ## Autoimmune
• type II hypersensitivity: autoantibodies against basement membrane proteins (BP180, laminin-332)
• drug-induced: long-term use of topical glaucoma drops (pilocarpine, epinephrine)
redFlags: progressive symblepharon formation (requires aggressive systemic immunosuppression)
esophageal or tracheal strictures (life-threatening systemic involvement)
corneal melting or epithelial breakdown
failure to respond to initial dapsone therapy
investigations: ## Clinical assessment
• forniceal measurement: pull lower lid down while patient looks up to expose symblepharon
• check oral and nasal mucosa for ulcers
## Diagnostics
• conjunctival biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (DIF): from PERILESIONAL (adjacent uninvolved) tissue
• DIF signature: linear deposition of IgG, IgA, or C3 along the basement membrane
• indirect immunofluorescence on serum if biopsy is inconclusive
actionSteps: perform conjunctival biopsy with DIF from perilesional tissue to confirm diagnosis
refer to dermatology/rheumatology for systemic immunosuppressive therapy
implement aggressive preservative-free lubrication and moisture chamber protection
screen for life-threatening esophageal or laryngeal mucosal involvement
treatment: ## Systemic (primary)
• dapsone: first-line for mild/moderate disease (monitor for hemolysis)
• steroid-sparing agents: methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide
• biologic therapy: rituximab or ivig for severe, progressive cases
## Ocular surface
• preservative-free artificial tears, autologous serum, and moisture goggles
• bandage or scleral lenses to protect the cornea
## Surgical
• entropion or trichiasis repair only when the disease is medically quieted
• note: surgery during active inflammation significantly accelerates scarring
followUp: ## Monitoring
• monthly during active phases; every 3 months once inflammation is quiet
• serial measurement of inferior fornix depth to document stability
• co-management with dermatology for immunosuppressant safety monitoring (CBC, LFTs)
differentials: stevens–johnson syndrome (acute onset, history of drug reaction)
review: ocp is a clinical diagnosis; a negative biopsy does not exclude the disease if scarring is progressive
shortening of the inferior fornix is often the very first sign of the disease
systemic therapy is required to stop the immunological process; drops alone are insufficient
pearl: Shortening of the inferior fornix is the earliest ocular sign of MMP — by the time you see symblepharon and cicatrization, the disease is advanced; systemic immunosuppression must start before surgical repair.
willsRef: Wills Eye §5.10 (Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid (Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid))

name: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
symptoms: painless, variable, and often asymmetric droopy eyelid (ptosis)
double vision (diplopia) that fluctuates or worsens with fatigue
symptoms typically worse later in the day or after sustained activity
facial weakness (flat smile), weak chewing, or difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
proximal limb weakness (difficulty with stairs or overhead reaching)
shortness of breath (medical emergency: myasthenic crisis)
findings: ## Hallmark features
• fatigability: muscle strength declines with repeated use or over time
• variable motility: can mimic any pupil-sparing cranial nerve palsy or gaze palsy
• normal pupils: pupils are never involved; their involvement excludes MG
## Bedside diagnostics
• cogan lid twitch: brief upward overshoot of the lid after looking from down to primary gaze
• curtain sign (enhanced ptosis): lifting the more-ptotic lid causes the other lid to drop
• ice pack test: 2 minutes of cooling improves ptosis by ≥2 mm (increases ACh half-life)
• orbicularis weakness: eyelids are easily pried open against the patient's resistance
## Systemic signs
• "MG sneer": mid-facial weakness on attempted smiling
• bulbar signs: dysarthria (slurred speech) and weak cough
etiology: ## Autoimmune mechanism
• post-synaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies block neuromuscular transmission
• subset cases involve anti-MuSK or anti-LRP4 antibodies
## Thymic involvement
• 10–15% of patients have a thymoma; thymic hyperplasia is common in younger patients
## Overlap
• associated with other autoimmune conditions like Graves disease (5%), SLE, and RA
redFlags: bulbar symptoms (slurred speech, difficulty swallowing) → impending crisis
shortness of breath or weak respiratory effort → admit for FVC/NIF monitoring
thymoma on chest CT → requires surgical thymectomy
use of contra-indicated meds (e.g., fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, magnesium)
investigations: ## Clinical tests
• ice pack test or rest test (30 minutes of dark rest) to observe improvement
• sustained upgaze for 60 seconds to document progressive ptosis
## Laboratory & imaging
• serology: acetylcholine receptor (AChR) binding, blocking, and modulating antibodies
• chest CT (mandatory): to rule out thymoma in all confirmed cases
• thyroid function tests (TSH, fT4): screen for concurrent Graves disease
## Electrophysiology
• single-fiber EMG (SFEMG): most sensitive test for ocular MG (increased jitter)
• repetitive nerve stimulation: look for decremental response
actionSteps: perform bedside ice pack and fatigability tests
order AChR, MuSK, and LRP4 antibody serology
obtain chest CT to screen for thymoma
refer to neurology for SFEMG and possible systemic therapy initiation
treatment: ## Pharmacologic
• pyridostigmine (Mestinon): first-line symptomatic relief (anticholinesterase)
• systemic steroids: used for persistent ocular symptoms; hospitalize for initiation if risk of crisis
• steroid-sparing agents: mycophenolate, azathioprine, or rituximab (especially for anti-MuSK)
## Acute intervention
• plasmapheresis or IVIG: for myasthenic crisis or pre-surgical optimization
## Surgical
• thymectomy: indicated for thymoma and often beneficial for generalized AChR+ disease
followUp: ## Monitoring
• monitor for progression to generalized disease (~50% generalize within 2 years)
• re-evaluate bulbar and limb strength at every visit
• provide a list of medications to avoid (fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers, statins)
review: MG is the "great imitator" because it can mimic almost any motility deficit except a pupil abnormality
the ice pack test is safer and often more convenient than the Tensilon test
thymectomy is a critical component of management for both oncologic and immunologic reasons
pearl: MG is the great imitator of other ocular motility disorders. Anti-AChR antibodies positive in 85% generalized, 50% ocular MG. Anti-MuSK positive in seronegative generalized MG. Tensilon (edrophonium) test largely replaced by ice pack test (safer, no cardiac risk). CT chest mandatory — 10-15% have thymoma. Ocular MG: 50% generalize within 2 years.

name: Neovascular Glaucoma
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Often asymptomatic in early stages.
• Severe ocular pain and frontal headache (in late stages).
• Diffuse ocular redness and photophobia.
• Profoundly decreased vision.
findings: ## Iris and angle
• Neovascularization of the iris (NVI): Earliest visible sign typically at the pupillary margin.
• Neovascularization of the angle (NVA) on gonioscopy.
• Ectropion uveae (eversion of the pupillary margin pigment).
• Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) and progressive, irreversible "zippering" angle closure (late).
## Anterior segment
• Mild anterior chamber cell and flare.
• Conjunctival injection.
• Microcystic corneal edema (with acute IOP rise).
• Spontaneous hyphema.
## Posterior segment
• Glaucomatous optic nerve cupping.
• Visual field loss characteristic of severe glaucoma.
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Retinal ischemia → VEGF release → Iris/angle neovascularization → Fibrovascular angle closure.
## Common causes
• Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR).
• Ischemic Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO; classic "90-day glaucoma").
• Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS; secondary to severe carotid occlusive disease).
• Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).
## Other causes
• BRVO/BRAO, chronic uveitis, chronic retinal detachment, intraocular tumors, trauma, or previous radiation.
redFlags: • Rubeosis iridis: Angle closure can develop aggressively within weeks of onset.
• Systemic etiology: Underlying causes like PDR, ischemic CRVO, and OIS require urgent systemic investigation.
• Pain + IOP >40 mmHg + corneal edema strongly suggests a poor long-term visual prognosis.
• Treating the IOP medically without treating the underlying ischemia (via PRP) is completely futile.
investigations: ## Ocular examination
• Applanation IOP measurement and meticulous gonioscopy (assess directly for NVA and PAS extent).
• Dilated fundus exam to identify the primary etiology and assess the optic nerve.
## Imaging
• Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to identify areas of profound retinal ischemia and guide targeted PRP.
• B-scan ultrasound if the ocular media is opaque (e.g., dense cataract or vitreous hemorrhage) to rule out an underlying tumor or retinal detachment.
## Systemic workup
• Carotid Doppler ultrasound if no direct retinal etiology is found (mandatory to rule out OIS).
actionSteps: • Stage via gonioscopy: Stage 1 (NVI, open angle), Stage 2 (NVA, open angle), Stage 3 (PAS closure).
• Recognize that Stage 1–2 is the critical reversible window before permanent PAS formation occurs.
• Administer intravitreal anti-VEGF immediately to rapidly regress vessels (typically clears in 24–72 hours).
• Schedule mandatory Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) within 1–2 weeks; anti-VEGF is only a temporary bridge, not a cure.
• Initiate maximal topical IOP therapy (strictly avoid pilocarpine and prostaglandins).
• Arrange for a surgical glaucoma drainage device (Ahmed/Baerveldt) once the neovascularization is fully quiescent.
treatment: ## Medical management
• IOP reduction: Topical beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, and CAIs (± systemic oral/IV acetazolamide).
• Inflammation and pain control: Topical prednisolone acetate 1% and cycloplegics (atropine 1%).
• Osmotics: IV mannitol for refractory emergent IOP spikes.
## Ischemia treatment
• Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): The definitive, permanent treatment to eliminate the hypoxic VEGF source.
• Intravitreal anti-VEGF (e.g., bevacizumab): Rapid temporary regression of NVI/NVA; acts strictly as a bridge to PRP or surgery.
## Surgical options
• Glaucoma Drainage Device (Ahmed/Baerveldt tube shunts): The overwhelmingly preferred surgical option.
• Cyclophotocoagulation (CPC): Reserved for pain control in blind, painful eyes or eyes with extremely poor visual potential.
• Trabeculectomy: Carries a high failure rate; considered only once the neovascularization is proven to be completely inactive.
followUp: • Daily ophthalmic review until the IOP is adequately controlled.
• Urgent application of PRP as soon as corneal media allows.
• Mandatory tight coordination between Retina and Glaucoma subspecialists.
• Manage underlying systemic disease: Aggressive diabetes optimization or immediate carotid surgical workup.
review: • NVG is a devastating end-stage manifestation of massive retinal ischemia.
• The "90-day rule": NVI develops in ~33% of ischemic CRVO cases approximately 3 months post-occlusion.
• The golden rule: Anti-VEGF merely buys time, PRP buys the cure.
• Stage 1–2 (open angle without synechiae) represents the critical, narrow window for reversible intervention.
pearl: Neovascular glaucoma is a devastating end-stage of retinal ischemia. NVI at the pupillary margin is the earliest visible sign. The "90-day rule" after ischemic CRVO: NVI develops in ~33% without treatment. Intravitreal anti-VEGF rapidly reverses rubeosis — but it is never a standalone treatment. The golden rule: Anti-VEGF buys you time, PRP buys you a cure. Always stage the angle: Stages 1–2 (open angle) are the reversible window where aggressive PRP can restore normal outflow; Stage 3 (PAS closure) is largely irreversible and strictly requires a tube shunt or CPC.
draw: Rubeosis at pupillary margin and angle neovascularization with fibrovascular membrane

name: Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION)
symptoms: • Sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss (often noticed upon awakening)
• Typical age 50–70 years (younger if strong vasculopathic risk factors are present)
• Altitudinal visual field defect (typically inferior)
• Absence of pain on eye movement
findings: ## Clinical Exam
• Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) — essentially always present in unilateral cases
• Variable visual acuity (ranging from 20/20 to count fingers; often >20/64)
• Dyschromatopsia proportional to the degree of visual acuity loss
## Funduscopy
• Segmental or diffuse pallid (pale) optic disc swelling
• Flame hemorrhages at or near the disc margin
• Fellow eye: small, crowded optic nerve head ("disc at risk" with a C/D ratio ≤0.2)
## Evolution
• Disc edema typically resolves to optic atrophy without cupping within 4–8 weeks
• Stable visual field/acuity after the initial event; spontaneous mild improvement occurs in ~30%
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Acute ischemia of the short posterior ciliary arteries (SPCAs) supplying the anterior optic nerve
• Anatomic compartment syndrome: axonal swelling inside a tight, crowded scleral canal ("disc at risk")
## Risk Factors
• Vasculopathic: hypertension (especially nocturnal dips), diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia
• Sleep apnea: strong correlation (routinely screen with the STOP-BANG questionnaire)
• Systemic: anemia, perioperative hypotension (e.g., prolonged prone spine or cardiac surgeries)
• Medications: PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil), amiodarone
redFlags: • ALWAYS exclude Arteritic AION / Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA): check for age ≥70, chalky-white edema, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or systemic symptoms
• Progression beyond 2–4 weeks: strongly consider a compressive or infiltrative optic neuropathy
• Fellow-eye involvement: occurs in roughly 15–25% of patients within 5 years
investigations: ## Urgent Labs (To Rule Out GCA)
• Same-day ESR, CRP, and complete blood count (for platelet count) for all patients aged ≥50
## Ophthalmic Testing
• Automated perimetry (Visual Field): documents an altitudinal defect or a horizontal step
• Fundus photography and OCT RNFL: used to baseline and document active edema vs. subsequent atrophy
## Systemic Workup
• Blood pressure monitoring (assess for nocturnal troughs), HbA1c, and lipid panel
• Polysomnography (sleep study) if Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is suspected
• MRI of the brains and orbits: indicated only if presentation is atypical (pain, progression, or young age)
actionSteps: • Order urgent, same-day ESR, CRP, and platelets to safely rule out GCA
• Examine the fellow eye's fundus for a "disc at risk" to help confirm the NAION clinical profile
• Screen for underlying sleep apnea and counsel on modifying systemic vasculopathic risks
• Counsel the patient: there is no proven acute treatment; management focuses entirely on protecting the fellow eye
treatment: ## Acute Management
• No proven effective treatment exists (systemic steroids and surgical optic nerve decompression are not standard of care)
• Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapies show no proven benefit for the acute event
## Risk Modification
• Avoid nocturnal hypotension: advise moving evening anti-hypertensive medications to the morning layout
• Treat obstructive sleep apnea aggressively with CPAP therapy if diagnosed
• Discontinue PDE-5 inhibitors immediately if a temporal association is suspected
• Optimize systemic factors: glycemic index, lipid profiles, and smoking cessation
followUp: • Follow up monthly for the first 3 months, then move to every 6 to 12 months
• Perform serial automated perimetry and structural fundus assessments
• Thoroughly counsel on the 15–25% 5-year risk to the fellow eye; advise immediate emergency review if new symptoms manifest
differentials: • Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AAION / Giant Cell Arteritis)
• Optic Neuritis (demyelinating or atypical atypical presentations)
• Papilledema (bilateral early on, but can present asymmetrically)
review: • NAION stands as the most common acute optic neuropathy in patients over 50 years old
• Key clinical signature: an inferior altitudinal field defect matched with a crowded fellow "disc at risk"
• Missing an atypical GCA presentation is the most dangerous diagnostic pitfall—always check baseline inflammatory markers
• Nocturnal hypotension is a highly preventable mechanical trigger—ensure antihypertensives aren't bottoming out their BP overnight
pearl: NAION: "Disc at risk" — a structurally small cup-to-disc ratio leaves no baseline geographic room for nerve fibers to swell without secondary mechanical compression. Nocturnal hypotension (trough blood pressure) acts as a classic trigger; taking anti-hypertensives right at bedtime can exacerbate this drop. The 5-year recurrence risk in the fellow eye hovers around 15–25%, whereas recurrence in the exact same eye is incredibly rare. PDE-5 inhibitors are strongly linked to incidents, particularly in patients holding the classic structural disc at risk.
draw: pallid segmental disc swelling with flame hemorrhages and inferior altitudinal defect

name: Nonexudative (Dry) Age-Related Macular Degeneration
symptoms: • gradual loss of central vision (months to years)
• metamorphopsia (distortion on amsler grid)
• paracentral scotoma
• reduced contrast sensitivity and difficulty with low-light tasks
• may be asymptomatic in early stages
findings: ## Drusen characteristics
• hard drusen: <63 μm, well-defined; low risk of progression
