• soft drusen: ≥63 μm, fuzzy edges; high risk for amd progression
• large drusen: ≥125 μm (areds high-risk marker)
• reticular pseudodrusen: subretinal deposits above the rpe; high risk for ga and wet amd
## RPE changes
• rpe mottling, hyperpigmentation, or focal pigment aggregates
• geographic atrophy (ga): sharply demarcated areas of rpe and photoreceptor loss
• increased visibility of deep choroidal vessels within atrophic patches
## AREDS severity score (5-year risk)
• 1 point per eye for large drusen; 1 point per eye for pigmentary changes
• score 0 (0.5% risk) to score 4 (50% risk of advanced amd)
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• age-related rpe and photoreceptor degeneration
• accumulation of lipoproteinaceous debris (drusen) in bruch’s membrane
## Risk factors
• age >55, caucasian ethnicity, and family history
• smoking (primary modifiable risk)
• genetics: cfh y402h and arms2/htra1 variants
redFlags: • conversion to wet amd: new metamorphopsia or sudden scotoma
• sudden drusen regression: can herald impending cnvm or geographic atrophy
• ga expansion: hyperautofluorescent borders on faf predict rapid growth
investigations: ## Imaging
• oct: quantify drusenoid ped, geographic atrophy, and hyperreflective foci
• fundus autofluorescence (faf): track ga expansion and assess border activity
• near-infrared imaging: best modality for detecting reticular pseudodrusen
## Monitoring
• amsler grid: daily home monitoring for metamorphopsia
• preferential hyperacuity perimetry (php): e.g., foreseehome for early cnvm detection
## Exudative workup (if suspected)
• urgent oct, ivfa, or octa to rule out choroidal neovascularization (cnv)
actionSteps: • initiate areds2 supplements for intermediate or advanced amd
• counsel on smoking cessation and mediterranean diet
• provide amsler grid and instruct on daily home monitoring
• discuss complement inhibitors if geographic atrophy is approaching fovea
treatment: ## AREDS2 supplements
• formula: vit c (500mg), vit e (400iu), zinc (80mg), copper (2mg), lutein (10mg), zeaxanthin (2mg)
• replaces beta-carotene with lutein/zeaxanthin to avoid lung cancer risk in smokers
• reduces progression to advanced amd by ~25% in high-risk patients
## Geographic atrophy (FDA-approved)
• pegcetacoplan (syfovre): c3 inhibitor; slows ga growth by 15-20%
• avacincaptad pegol (izervay): c5 inhibitor
• note: 2-7% risk of conversion to wet amd; does not improve vision
## Lifestyle & support
• smoking cessation, mediterranean diet, and uv protection
• low-vision rehabilitation: magnifiers and eccentric viewing training
followUp: • every 6–12 months for early/intermediate disease
• daily home amsler grid monitoring
• urgent retina referral if new exudative symptoms develop
review: • areds2 vitamins are only indicated for intermediate or advanced disease
• soft drusen and reticular pseudodrusen are the highest risk clinical markers
• geographic atrophy treatment slows progression but carries a risk of exudative conversion
pearl: areds2 vitamins are only for intermediate or advanced amd — prescribing them for small drusen offers no benefit and may give false reassurance.
draw: macula with soft yellow drusen, pigmentary mottling, and areas of sharply demarcated atrophy

name: Nonphysiologic Visual Loss
symptoms: • loss of vision without organic explanation
• malingering: intentional feigning for secondary gain (financial/legal)
• psychogenic (conversion): patient truly believes vision is lost due to psychological stress
findings: ## Clinical examination
• normal pupillary light reactions and normal dilated fundus exam
• no ocular or neuro-ophthalmic findings explain the deficit
• behavior: saccades to command, glancing at new people, or reaching accurately for objects
## Bedside testing
• stereopsis (titmus/randot): identifying the "fly" requires ≥20/70 acuity
• mirror test: involuntary tracking of reflection proves vision is present
• optokinetic (okn) drum: reflex nystagmus confirms vision better than counting fingers
• base-out 4pd prism: convergent refixation proves foveal vision
## Visual fields
• tubular ("tunnel") field: pathognomonic if area stays same size at 1m and 2m
• goldmann patterns: star-shaped, spiraling, or crossing isopters
## Objective testing
• normal pattern vep, multifocal erg, and full-field erg
• normal oct and fundus autofluorescence (faf)
etiology: ## Psychogenic (conversion)
• unconscious production of symptoms triggered by trauma, school failure, or abuse
## Malingering
• intentional feigning for disability claims, litigation, or military avoidance
## Factitious (Munchausen)
• intentional production to assume the sick role (primary gain)
redFlags: • organic mimics: occult maculopathy (azoor, mewds), cone dystrophy, or early compressive neuropathy
• pediatric triggers: bullying, parental conflict, or munchausen-by-proxy
• adult secondary gain: requires meticulous documentation for legal/insurance purposes
investigations: ## Total blindness claims (NLP/HM)
• pupillary testing: absence of rapd in unilateral nlp is impossible
• mirror and okn drum tests to elicit involuntary tracking
## Subnormal vision claims (20/40 to 20/400)
• fogging test: add +4.00 to "good" eye while testing binocularly in phoropter
• distance-near discrepancy: 20/100 at 20ft should be 20/50 at 10ft
• vertical prism dissociation: seeing two images with prism proves near-symmetric vision
## Imaging & electrophysiology
• oct macula and rnfl to exclude subtle organic disease
• full-field and multifocal erg to rule out outer retinal dystrophies
• pattern vep to objectively assess optic nerve pathways
actionSteps: • perform objective bedside discriminators (mirror, prism, okn)
• document normal structural (oct) and functional (erg/vep) testing
• use "face-saving" language: emphasize that eyes are healthy and recovery is expected
• refer for psychology/psychiatry if stressors are identified
treatment: ## Communication strategy
• do not confront the patient; avoids destroying the therapeutic relationship
• provide a "way out": e.g., "these drops will help your vision return to normal"
## Management
• reassurance once organic disease is excluded
• multidisciplinary care: coordinate with primary care, neurology, and psychiatry
• positive reinforcement of objective improvements
followUp: • follow-up visits to demonstrate documented improvement
• pediatric cases: usually resolve within weeks with reassurance
• adult cases: may require formal psychiatric evaluation and long-term support
differentials: • occult maculopathy (e.g., azoor, cone dystrophy, solar retinopathy)
• early compressive or infiltrative optic neuropathy
review: • diagnosis of exclusion: organic pathology must be completely ruled out by oct/erg/vep
• tubular visual fields are a classic hallmark of nonphysiologic loss
• face-saving reassurance is more effective than direct confrontation
pearl: in functional visual loss, never confront — offer "tests that will help us figure this out" and let the exam prove normal function while the patient saves face.
draw: tubular visual field diagram (same diameter at 1m and 2m) or okn drum test

name: Ocular Histoplasmosis
symptoms: • often asymptomatic (discovered on routine exam)
• metamorphopsia or central scotoma (if cnv develops)
• decreased or distorted central vision
• history: geographic exposure to ohio-mississippi river valley
findings: ## Hallmark triad
• histo spots: multiple small (<1 mm), yellow-white, punched-out chorioretinal scars
• peripapillary atrophy (ppa): ring of chorioretinal scarring around the optic disc
• absence of vitreous cells: quiet anterior chamber and vitreous (obligatory for diagnosis)
## Mechanisms of vision loss
• choroidal neovascularization (cnv): gray-green subretinal patch with srf, lipid, or hemorrhage
• peripapillary region: most common site of cnv origin
• disciform scar: end-stage result of untreated macular cnv
## Imaging
• oct: subretinal hyperreflective material with overlying srf
• ivfa: lacy early hyperfluorescence with late leakage confirming cnv
• oct-a: non-invasive detection of fibrovascular membranes
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• prior systemic infection with histoplasma capsulatum (fungal inhalation)
• hematogenous seeding of the choroid leaves residual "punched-out" scars
## Disease nature
• pohs is a late sequela of healed infection, not an active ocular infection
• vision loss is driven by neovascularization, not primary inflammation
redFlags: • macular cnv: urgent need for anti-vegf to prevent permanent disciform scarring
• vitritis/cells: presence of inflammation should prompt reconsideration of diagnosis (e.g., multifocal choroiditis)
• fellow-eye risk: ~20% lifetime risk of cnv in the second eye
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• slit-lamp: essential to confirm absence of ac/vitreous cells
• dilated fundus exam: screen for active cnv (blood, fluid, or gray membranes)
## Imaging & monitoring
• oct: primary tool for diagnosing and tracking cnv response
• ivfa: confirms leakage if oct is equivocal
• amsler grid: daily home self-monitoring for high-risk eyes
actionSteps: • confirm clinical triad: ppa, punched-out scars, and no vitritis
• baseline oct and amsler grid education for both eyes
• treat active macular cnv with urgent intravitreal anti-vegf
• emphasize importance of prompt return for new metamorphopsia
treatment: ## Active CNV
• intravitreal anti-vegf: first-line therapy; excellent visual outcomes if prompt
• photodynamic therapy (pdt) or focal laser: rarely used/historical options
## Inactive disease
• no treatment indicated for histo spots or ppa in the absence of cnv
## Note on antifungals
• systemic or topical antifungals are NOT indicated; pohs is not an active infection
followUp: • every 6 months for monitoring of stable/inactive scars
• daily home amsler grid for patients with macular/peripapillary histo spots
• coordinate treatment with a retina specialist for active cnv
differentials: • multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis (mcp): distinguished by presence of vitritis
• old toxoplasmosis: typically larger, more pigmented/atrophic scars
• angioid streaks: jagged lines radiating from the disc (different etiology)
• birdshot chorioretinopathy: different spot morphology and location
review: • pohs is characterized by its lack of active inflammation (vitritis)
• clinical management focuses entirely on the detection and treatment of cnv
• the fellow eye must be monitored aggressively after unilateral cnv occurs
pearl: histo spots, peripapillary atrophy, and a macular cnv make pohs — there is no active inflammation, so steroids are wrong and anti-vegf is right.
draw: punched-out yellow retinal spots with peripapillary scarring and a macular subretinal hemorrhage/gray membrane

name: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome/Carotid Occlusive Disease
symptoms: • subacute vision loss (weeks to months)
• "ocular angina": dull periorbital pain that worsens when lying flat (recumbency)
• light-induced amaurosis: vision loss when moving from dark to bright light
• prolonged visual recovery after bright light (e.g., camera flash)
• history of amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss)
findings: ## Posterior segment
• mid-peripheral "blotty" hemorrhages (watershed ischemia)
• dilated but straight (non-tortuous) retinal veins ("beaded" appearance)
• narrowed retinal arteries
## Anterior segment
• rubeosis iridis (nvi): occurs in ~66% of symptomatic cases
• paradoxically normal or low iop initially (ischemic ciliary body under-produces aqueous)
• mild "pseudo-iritis" (flare > cell)
• asymmetric cataract or iris atrophy
## Diagnostic imaging
• ivfa: prolonged arm-to-retina time (>15s), patchy choroidal filling, and late vessel staining
• orbital doppler: reversed flow in ophthalmic artery (eca filling ica via collaterals)
• carotid imaging: duplex ultrasound (first-line) or cta/mra of neck
etiology: ## Primary cause
• severe (≥90%) ipsilateral internal carotid artery (ica) stenosis or occlusion
## Other causes
• ophthalmic artery disease, giant cell arteritis (gca), or takayasu arteritis
• carotid dissection or fibromuscular dysplasia
redFlags: • iop spike after carotid surgery: revascularized ciliary body resumes aqueous production against a closed angle
• cardiovascular risk: 5-year mortality is ~40% (mostly cardiac events)
• ois vs crvo: ois has straight veins and pain on recumbency; crvo has tortuous veins and is usually painless
investigations: ## Ocular workup
• gonioscopy: screen for angle neovascularization (nva)
• fluorescein angiography (ivfa): look for delayed filling and peripheral non-perfusion
## Mandatory systemic workup
• carotid duplex ultrasound, followed by cta or mra of the neck
• cardiology referral: high association with coronary artery disease (cad)
• vasculopathic screen: bp, hba1c, lipids, and peripheral pulses
actionSteps: • order carotid duplex + cta/mra to quantify stenosis
• refer urgently to vascular surgery for stenosis ≥70%
• pre-treat eyes with rubeosis using prp/anti-vegf before carotid revascularization
• coordinate systemic management (antiplatelets, statins) with pcp and cardiology
treatment: ## Vascular intervention
• carotid endarterectomy (cea) or stenting for symptomatic stenosis ≥70%
## Ocular management
• panretinal photocoagulation (prp) for iris/angle/retinal neovascularization
• intravitreal anti-vegf for nvi/nvg or macular edema
• topical aqueous suppressants (avoid prostaglandins if inflamed)
## Systemic management
• antiplatelet therapy (aspirin/clopidogrel) and statins
• aggressive management of bp, glucose, and smoking cessation
followUp: ## Ocular monitoring
• every 2–4 weeks initially to screen for nvi/nvg
• gonioscopy at every visit until stable
## Systemic monitoring
• coordinate long-term care with vascular surgery and neurology
• educate patient on stroke/mi warning signs
differentials: • dilated AND tortuous veins; hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants; usually painless
• usually bilateral; typically includes microaneurysms and hard exudates
• large-vessel vasculitis; check for absent pulses in the neck/arms
review: ## Clinical pearl
• mid-peripheral hemorrhages with straight veins should always trigger a carotid workup
• visual prognosis is often poor (60% at hand motion within 5 years), but saving the patient’s life via cardiac/vascular referral is the priority
pearl: slow-to-dilate pupils with mid-peripheral hemorrhages and new iris neovascularization in an older patient is ocular ischemic syndrome — get a carotid doppler before treating it as a vein occlusion.
draw: dilated straight veins and mid-peripheral blot hemorrhages with rubeosis iridis
willsRef: Wills Eye §11.11 (Ocular Ischemic Syndrome/Carotid Occlusive Disease)

name: Ocular Tuberculosis
symptoms: • insidious decreased vision, floaters, or redness (weeks to months)
• often asymptomatic and found incidentally in high-prevalence populations
• systemic: chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, or fever (often absent)
• risk: travel to endemic areas (india, se asia, africa), hiv, or homelessness
findings: ## Anterior segment
• granulomatous uveitis: large "mutton-fat" kps and iris nodules (busacca/koeppe)
• extensive posterior synechiae ("sticky" uveitis)
## Posterior segment
• choroidal tubercles: pathognomonic yellowish, ill-defined lesions (miliary tb)
• serpiginous-like choroiditis: placoid lesions progressing centrifugally
• retinal vasculitis (eales-like): peripheral non-perfusion and neovascularization
## Optic nerve & other
• neuroretinitis, optic neuritis, or papilledema (if meningitis present)
• phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis (hypersensitivity response)
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• mycobacterium tuberculosis infection via hematogenous spread
• direct ocular infection or immune-mediated response to circulating antigens
## Disease nature
• can occur without active pulmonary disease (chest x-ray may be normal)
• reactivation of latent tb (hiv, tnf-α inhibitor use, or steroid use)
redFlags: • initiating tnf-α inhibitors (e.g., adalimumab) without tb screening can reactivate latent disease
• choroidal tubercles in a febrile patient suggests life-threatening miliary tb
• hiv coinfection dramatically increases risk; always test hiv in suspected cases
investigations: ## TB screening
• interferongamma release assay (quantiferon-tb gold/t-spot) or ppd skin test
• chest x-ray or chest ct to look for active or healed pulmonary involvement
## Ocular & systemic
• ivfa: characterize retinal vasculitis and capillary non-perfusion
• ac/vitreous pcr for m. tuberculosis (specific but low sensitivity)
• rule out mimics: syphilis (rpr/fta), sarcoid (ace/ct), lyme, and behçet
actionSteps: • consult infectious disease and pulmonology teams for systemic management
• report cases to public health authorities and screen household contacts
• establish baseline vision/color testing before starting ethambutol
• do not treat empirically with steroids alone without anti-tb coverage
treatment: ## Anti-TB therapy (ID directed)
• 4-drug ripe regimen: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (2 months)
• maintenance: rifampin + isoniazid (4–7 months)
## Anti-inflammatory
• oral prednisone (1 mg/kg): used once anti-tb therapy is established to prevent scarring
## Ocular complications
• anti-vegf or prp for retinal neovascularization
• monitor ethambutol toxicity: dose-dependent optic neuropathy risk
followUp: • monthly ophthalmic review during active treatment; quarterly once quiescent
• monitor visual acuity, color vision, and fields while on ethambutol
• coordinate liver enzyme monitoring with the id team
review: • ocular tb often presents as chronic, granulomatous uveitis in patients from endemic areas
• serpiginous-like choroiditis is a high-yield clinical pattern for tb uveitis
• the most dangerous error is missing latent tb before starting immunosuppressants
pearl: choroidal tubercles — creamy-yellow, ill-defined lesions scattered across the fundus — are pathognomonic for miliary tb. in any immunocompromised patient or patient from a high-prevalence area with granulomatous uveitis, always exclude tb before starting tnf-α inhibitors for presumed idiopathic disease.
draw: fundus with small yellow-white choroidal spots, perivascular sheathing, and mutton-fat keratic precipitates

name: Optic Neuritis
symptoms: • typical age 18–45 years; usually unilateral
• vision loss progressing over hours to days (nadir at ~1 week)
• retro-orbital pain, especially with eye movement (>90% of cases)
• acquired loss of color vision (red desaturation)
• uhthoff sign: worsening of symptoms with exercise or increased body temperature
• pulfrich phenomenon: altered perception of moving objects
• atypical: advanced age, bilateral onset, or severe loss without recovery (suspect nmosd/mogad)
findings: ## Clinical examination
• relative afferent pupillary defect (rapd) in unilateral cases
• decreased color vision on ishihara plates
• central, cecocentral, or arcuate visual field defects
## Nerve appearance
• retrobulbar (2/3): normal optic disc appearance (adults)
• papillitis (1/3): swollen optic disc (children/young adults)
• absence of peripapillary hemorrhages is typical for demyelinating on
etiology: ## Demyelinating disease
• multiple sclerosis (ms): frequently the initial manifestation
• nmosd (anti-aqp4) and mogad (anti-mog): critical atypical causes
## Other causes
• viral: measles, mumps, varicella, mononucleosis
• granulomatous: sarcoidosis, syphilis, tb, lyme
• contiguous inflammation: meninges, orbit, or sinuses
redFlags: • lack of pain: present in >90% of typical on; absence suggests ischemia or sarcoid
• vision loss progressing >2 weeks: rule out compressive or infiltrative etiology
• poor recovery at 4–6 weeks: consider nmosd or mogad
• systemic features (rash, arthritis): evaluate for lupus or sarcoidosis
investigations: ## Imaging
• mri brain + orbits with gadolinium and fat suppression (essential to see enhancement)
## Laboratory workup
• anti-aqp4 and anti-mog antibodies: draw on all first-presentation cases
• targeted: ace (sarcoid), rpr/fta-abs (syphilis), lyme titer, esr/cbc
## Functional testing
• automated visual field (hvf 24-2 or 30-2)
• oct rnfl: baseline and monitoring for axonal loss
• csf oligoclonal bands: predictive of ms if mri is inconclusive
actionSteps: • confirm afferent findings: va, color plates, rapd, and perimetry
• order urgent mri brain/orbits with gadolinium and fat suppression
• refer to neurology if demyelinating lesions are present on mri
• strictly avoid standard-dose oral prednisone alone (doubles recurrence rate per ontt)
• initiate iv methylprednisolone 1g/day × 3 days for acute attacks
treatment: ## Acute phase
• iv methylprednisolone 1 g/day × 3 days, followed by oral prednisone taper
• gastric prophylaxis: omeprazole 20 mg po daily
• plasmapheresis: if poor steroid response in suspected nmosd
## Long-term management
• ms disease-modifying therapy (dmt): interferons, glatiramer acetate, ocrelizumab, etc.
• nmosd/mogad: chronic immunosuppression (e.g., rituximab, azathioprine)
followUp: • re-examine at 4–6 weeks, then every 3–6 months
• repeat mri brain annually for clinically isolated syndromes (cis)
• high-risk ms or nmosd: specialized neurology/neuro-ophthalmology care
• prognosis: 72% risk of ms at 15 years if mri is abnormal at onset
review: • optic neuritis is a clinical diagnosis supported by mri and enhancement patterns
• the primary goal of treatment is speeding recovery and preventing future relapse
• atypical features must trigger testing for nmo/mog to avoid devastating vision loss
pearl: ontt (optic neuritis treatment trial): iv steroids speed recovery but don't improve 1-year vision. 15-year data: 50% develop ms if mri abnormal; 25% if normal mri. mri at presentation is most important prognostic test. vep latency remains prolonged even after clinical recovery — useful for diagnosing subclinical or previous optic neuritis.
draw: optic disc swelling (papillitis) with hyperemic blurred margins or normal disc (retrobulbar)

name: Optic Pit
symptoms: • often asymptomatic; incidental finding on routine exam
• painless central blur or metamorphopsia (if maculopathy develops)
• central or paracentral scotoma
• micropsia (objects appearing smaller)
findings: ## Optic disc morphology
• hallmark: small, round/oval, grayish depression within the optic nerve head
• location: typically inferotemporal (~70%); may be central
• associated peripapillary chorioretinal atrophy crescent
• glial membrane may drape over the pit
## Optic pit maculopathy
• occurs in 25–75% of cases, usually in the 2nd–4th decade of life
• inner-retinal schisis-like splitting between the pit and macula
• outer-layer serous macular detachment
• hyporeflective communicating channel between pit and retina on oct
## Visual fields
• enlarged blind spot and arcuate defects corresponding to the pit
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• congenital defect of the optic nerve head involving focal excavation
• fluid source for maculopathy is debated (vitreous, csf, or nerve parenchyma)
• communication channel allows fluid to track from the pit to the retinal layers
## Genetics
• usually unilateral and sporadic; rarely bilateral
redFlags: • optic pit maculopathy is frequently misdiagnosed as central serous chorioretinopathy (csc)
• bilateral pits or associated midline anomalies mandate mri to rule out basal encephalocele
• sudden vision drop: fluid tracking from the disc to the fovea
investigations: ## Imaging (mandatory)
• oct: differentiates from csc; shows pathognomonic inner-retinal schisis and a connection to the disc
• fluorescein angiography (fa): shows late staining of the pit; lacks the "smokestack" leak of csc
## Systemic workup
• neuroimaging (mri brain/orbits): required for bilateral cases or if morning glory disc is present
## Functional testing
• amsler grid and humphrey visual field (hvf)
actionSteps: • perform oct to screen for subretinal fluid or intraretinal schisis
• observe asymptomatic pits with serial imaging
• refer to retina specialist for symptomatic maculopathy (surgical candidate)
• coordinate neurology referral for neuroimaging if bilateral or syndromic
treatment: ## Conservative
• observation for asymptomatic pits; many remain stable for life
## Surgical (definitive)
• pars plana vitrectomy (ppv) with ilm peeling and gas tamponade (sf6 or c3f8)
• face-down positioning required post-operatively
• note: laser photocoagulation at the temporal disc margin is an older, less reliable adjunct
## Visual prognosis
• anatomic closure is successful in ~70–80%; visual recovery is slow (months to years)
followUp: • asymptomatic: oct monitoring every 6 months
• post-operative: frequent visits to monitor anatomic reattachment and iop
• educate patient on daily amsler grid self-monitoring
differentials: • central serous chorioretinopathy (csc) — lacking the disc connection
• acquired pit of the optic nerve (glaucomatous damage)
review: • optic pits are congenital but the vision-threatening maculopathy often presents in young adulthood
• the key diagnostic differentiator is the presence of schisis-like splitting on oct
• surgical treatment focuses on blocking the fluid communication from the disc
pearl: an optic pit with serous macular detachment is often confused with csc — oct reveals retinoschisis-like splitting and a communicating channel to the pit, and vitrectomy is the definitive treatment.
draw: optic disc with an inferotemporal gray pit and a fluid pocket extending toward the macula

name: Orbital Blowout Fracture
symptoms: • pain with eye movement and local orbital tenderness
• binocular diplopia (resolves when one eye is covered)
• eyelid edema, ecchymosis, and periorbital swelling
• crepitus (crackling) after nose blowing (orbital emphysema)
• numbness of the cheek, upper lip, or teeth (v2 distribution)
• nausea or vomiting (suggests oculocardiac reflex)
findings: ## Clinical exam
• infraorbital nerve (v2) hypesthesia: highly specific for floor fractures
• restricted motility: most common in upgaze (inferior rectus) or lateral gaze
• enophthalmos (sunken eye) or hypoglobus: may be masked by initial swelling
• palpable orbital rim step-off deformities
## Pediatric specialty
• white-eyed blowout fracture (webof): minimal external bruising but severe muscle entrapment
• oculocardiac reflex: bradycardia, nausea, and syncope (surgical emergency)
## Associated injuries
• always screen for globe rupture, hyphema, commotio retinae, and retrobulbar hemorrhage
etiology: ## Mechanism
• blunt trauma (e.g., fist, ball, airbag) transmits pressure to the thin orbital walls
• orbital floor (maxilla) and medial wall (ethmoid) are the most frequent sites
## Entrapment
• herniated orbital fat or extraocular muscles become "snagged" in the fracture site
• pediatric "trapdoor" effect: flexible bone snaps back, incarcerating the muscle
redFlags: • pediatric trapdoor fracture: requires emergent repair (24–48h) to prevent muscle ischemia
• retrobulbar hemorrhage: signs include proptosis, tight lids, and increased iop; requires lateral canthotomy
• rapd or sudden vision loss: suggests traumatic optic neuropathy or compartment syndrome
investigations: ## Imaging (mandatory)
• ct orbits + midface (1mm cuts, no contrast): coronal views are best for the floor
## Clinical testing
• forced duction test: used to distinguish mechanical entrapment from muscle edema/palsy
• sensation testing: compare cheek and upper lip sensation bilaterally
• cardiac monitoring: check for bradycardia in symptomatic children
actionSteps: • enforce strict NO NOSE BLOWING precautions to prevent air forced into the orbit
• rule out globe rupture and optic nerve compromise before further manipulation
• identify children with nausea/vomiting for immediate surgical consultation
• schedule elective reassessment for adults at 1–2 weeks once edema subsides
treatment: ## Acute phase
• head elevation, cold compresses, and nasal decongestants (e.g., oxymetazoline)
• prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin/clavulanate) if sinusitis is present
## Surgery (immediate - 24–48h)
• indicated for pediatric trapdoor fractures with oculocardiac reflex or muscle incarceration
## Surgery (delayed - 1–2 weeks)
• indicated for persistent symptomatic diplopia, enophthalmos ≥2mm, or floor fracture >50%
followUp: • reassess at 1 and 2 weeks to evaluate motility and globe position as swelling resolves
• dilated fundus exam: screen for peripheral retinal tears or dialysis once globe is stable
• long-term: monitor for late-onset glaucoma or persistent diplopia
differentials: • cranial nerve palsy (iii, iv, or vi)
review: • pediatric blowout fractures are often deceptively "quiet" (white-eyed) but more urgent
• infraorbital numbness is the clinical hallmark of an orbital floor fracture
• surgical timing is a balance between muscle salvage (early) and edema resolution (delayed)
pearl: in a child with a blowout fracture, a "quiet" eye with vertical restriction and bradycardia/nausea is the trapdoor sign — operate within 24–48 hours to save the inferior rectus.
draw: coronal ct view showing "teardrop sign" (herniated orbital contents into the maxillary sinus)

name: Orbital Cellulitis
symptoms: • acute-onset unilateral eyelid swelling, erythema, and deep-seated pain
• pain with eye movement and diplopia (double vision)
• decreased vision or "washed out" colors (advanced cases)
• fever, headache, and malaise (common systemic features)
• history of preceding sinus infection or upper respiratory symptoms
findings: ## Clinical signature
• hallmark: proptosis and restricted extraocular motility (ophthalmoplegia)
• pain on eye movement: a critical early differentiator from preseptal cellulitis
• chemosis (conjunctival swelling) and eyelid edema
## Optic nerve compromise
• relative afferent pupillary defect (rapd), decreased color vision, or disc edema
• elevated iop due to orbital compartment syndrome
## Systemic & atypical
• black eschar on palate/nasal mucosa: suggests life-threatening mucormycosis
• ams or bilateral involvement: suggests cavernous sinus thrombosis
etiology: ## Sinusitis
• ethmoid sinus (>90% in children) is the most common source of infection
## Pathogens
• s. aureus (including mrsa), s. pneumoniae, and h. influenzae
• polymicrobial and anaerobes common in adults and dental sources
• fungal (mucormycosis/aspergillus): consider in diabetics or immunocompromised
redFlags: • orbital vs preseptal: proptosis, motility restriction, and pain on movement are ONLY in orbital
• optic nerve compression: rapid vision loss or rapd requires emergent decompression
• intracranial extension: altered mental status (ams) or cranial nerve palsies
• mucormycosis: high mortality in diabetics; requires emergent debridement
investigations: ## Imaging (gold standard)
• ct orbits and sinuses with contrast: evaluate for subperiosteal abscess (spa) and sinus source
## Laboratory workup
• cbc with differential, blood cultures (x2), and esr/crp
• blood glucose and hba1c for all adults
## Specialized
• mri orbits/brain: if cavernous sinus thrombosis or intracranial extension is suspected
• nasal endoscopy/biopsy: if fungal infection is suspected
actionSteps: • emergent ct orbits with contrast to identify abscesses or intracranial involvement
• admit for immediate iv broad-spectrum antibiotics
• consult ophthalmology, ent (for sinus drainage), and id
• monitor vision, pupils, and motility every 4–6 hours
treatment: ## Medical management
• iv antibiotics: vancomycin + ceftriaxone ± metronidazole (for anaerobes)
• transition to oral antibiotics once improved; total course 2–3 weeks
## Surgical intervention
• drainage of subperiosteal or orbital abscess if large, progressing, or nerve is threatened
• emergent surgical debridement for suspected fungal (mucor) infection
## Complications
• lateral canthotomy/cantholysis if orbital compartment syndrome (high iop/nerve threat) exists
followUp: • daily hospital monitoring of va, color vision, motility, and proptosis
• repeat ct if no improvement within 48 hours or if clinical deterioration occurs
• long-term monitoring for optic atrophy or residual strabismus
differentials: • preseptal cellulitis (lacks proptosis/motility restriction/pain on movement)
• thyroid eye disease (subacute, bilateral, no fever)
• cavernous sinus thrombosis (bilateral signs, ams, cn palsies)
review: • orbital cellulitis is a sight-threatening and life-threatening emergency
• the primary goal is to rule out abscess and optic nerve compression early
• children with subperiosteal abscesses may respond to iv antibiotics alone, but adults often require surgery
pearl: the preseptal vs orbital distinction is made by proptosis, pain on eye movement, motility restriction, and rapd — all absent in preseptal, present in orbital. ct orbits with contrast is mandatory if any of these are present. in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with periorbital infection, rule out mucormycosis before considering routine orbital cellulitis — delay kills.
draw: ct scan cross-section showing proptosis, fat stranding, and a subperiosteal abscess against the medial orbital wall

name: Orbital Tumors
symptoms: • proptosis (prominent eye) or globe displacement
• diplopia (double vision) and restricted motility
• decreased vision or "washed out" color (compressive neuropathy)
• pain: highly suggestive of malignancy or acute inflammation
• rapidly progressive proptosis: emergent red flag in children (rhabdomyosarcoma)
findings: ## Pediatric presentations
• capillary hemangioma: most common benign pediatric tumor; "strawberry" skin lesion; involutes by age 5–7
• rhabdomyosarcoma: most common primary pediatric malignancy; explosive growth; superonasal location
• dermoid cyst: most common benign pediatric mass; superotemporal, well-circumscribed
## Adult presentations
• cavernous venous malformation: most common benign adult tumor; middle-aged women, slow painless proptosis
• orbital lymphoma: most common primary adult malignancy; "salmon patch" subconjunctival appearance
• optic nerve sheath meningioma: "tram-track" calcification on ct; optociliary shunt vessels
## Metastatic disease
• breast (women) and lung (men) are most common; prostate favors bone (sphenoid)
• scirrhous breast carcinoma: can cause enophthalmos (sunken eye) due to fibrosis
etiology: ## Intraconal
• cavernous venous malformation, optic nerve glioma, meningioma, schwannoma
## Extraconal
• mucocele (sinus origin), dermoid cyst, lacrimal gland tumors (pleomorphic adenoma)
## Systemic/vascular
• lymphoma (malt/emzl), leukemic chloroma, orbital varices, avm
redFlags: • rapid progression in a child: assume rhabdomyosarcoma; biopsy within 24–48 hours
• vision loss + rapd: indicates compressive optic neuropathy requiring urgent debulking
• bony destruction: characteristic of aggressive malignancies (e.g., adenoid cystic ca)
• bilateral lacrimal enlargement: consider igg4-related disease, sarcoidosis, or lymphoma
investigations: ## Imaging (essential)
• ct orbits (axial/coronal): best for bone detail and calcification (meningioma)
• mri orbits with gadolinium & fat suppression: gold standard for soft tissue and nerve
## Clinical workup
• hertel exophthalmometry: to objectively measure proptosis
• vision testing: va, pupils (rapd), color plates, and visual fields
## Biopsy & staging
• incisional biopsy: required for most suspicious masses; fresh tissue needed for lymphoma (flow cytometry)
• systemic staging: pet-ct or ct chest/abd/pelvis for lymphoma and metastases
actionSteps: • obtain urgent mri/ct orbits with fat suppression to localize the mass
• perform emergency biopsy for rapidly growing pediatric masses
• coordinate multidisciplinary care (orbital surgeon, oncology, radiation)
• rule out systemic primary in adults with suspected metastatic disease
treatment: ## Benign lesions
• cavernous malformation: observe if asymptomatic; excise if progressive
• capillary hemangioma: oral propranolol is first-line if vision is threatened
• dermoid: surgical excision with intact capsule (avoids inflammatory rupture)
## Malignant lesions
• rhabdomyosarcoma: chemoradiation (excellent prognosis >90% if localized)
• lymphoma: external beam radiation for localized; rituximab/chemo for systemic
• ons-meningioma: stereotactic radiotherapy for progressive vision loss
## Other
• mucocele: endoscopic sinus drainage and antibiotics
followUp: • urgent: daily/weekly for rapidly progressive or compressive lesions
• routine: every 6–12 months with serial imaging for stable, benign masses
• long-term: systemic surveillance for lymphoma and metastatic disease
• post-radiation: monitor for radiation-induced optic neuropathy or retinopathy
differentials: • thyroid eye disease (most common cause of adult proptosis; usually bilateral)
• carotid-cavernous fistula (bruit, pulsatile proptosis, corkscrew vessels)
review: • directional globe displacement helps localize the tumor (e.g., superior mass pushes globe down)
• in children, always prioritize ruling out rhabdomyosarcoma due to its rapid growth
• adult lymphoma often presents with a characteristic "salmon-colored" conjunctival mass
pearl: a painless proptosis in an adult without inflammation is a tumor until imaged — vascular lesions (cavernous hemangioma) and lacrimal gland masses top the list; ct and mri together determine surgical approach.
draw: axial mri showing a well-circumscribed intraconal mass displacing the optic nerve

name: Papilledema
symptoms: • headache: often positional, worse in the morning or with valsalva
• transient visual obscurations (tvo): seconds-long graying/blackout of vision
• pulsatile tinnitus: "whooshing" sound synchronous with heartbeat
• binocular horizontal diplopia: indicates cn vi palsy (false-localizing sign)
• systemic: nausea, vomiting, or radicular back pain (spinal sheath dilation)
• screening hx: ask about weight gain, tetracyclines, vitamin a/retinoids, or ocp use
findings: ## Clinical signature
• bilateral disc swelling with blurred margins and vessel obscuration
• frisén scale (grade 0–5): quantifies severity based on vessel obscuration
• paton lines: circumferential retinal folds temporal to the disc
• absence of spontaneous venous pulsations (svp): suggests icp >200 mmh₂o
## Hemorrhagic/exudative
• peripapillary flame hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots
• disc hyperemia (acute) or gray/atrophic appearance (chronic)
## Functional changes
• enlarged blind spot: earliest change on formal perimetry
• visual acuity: often 20/20 initially; central vision is the LAST to go
etiology: ## Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
• classically affects obese women of reproductive age (f:m ratio 9:1)
## Secondary causes
• intracranial mass (tumor, abscess, hematoma)
• cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (cvst): suspect in postpartum or ocp users
• meningitis: bacterial, tb, fungal, or neoplastic
## Medication-induced
• tetracyclines, isotretinoin/vitamin a, growth hormone, and steroid withdrawal
redFlags: • rapid vision loss (fulminant iih): can progress to blindness over days
• focal neurologic signs: suggests an intracranial mass rather than iih
• fever + altered mental status: suggests infectious meningitis or abscess
• pregnancy + bilateral disc swelling: mandate urgent mrv to rule out cvst
investigations: ## Vital signs (mandatory)
• blood pressure: rule out malignant hypertension (can mimic papilledema)
## Imaging (urgent)
• mri brain + mrv with gadolinium: gold standard to rule out mass and cvst
• ct head: if mri is unavailable (rules out hemorrhage/large mass/hydrocephalus)
## Lumbar puncture (LP)
• opening pressure: >25 cmh₂o in adults confirms raised icp (perform ONLY after imaging)
## Ocular monitoring
• oct rnfl: quantifies edema and monitors treatment response
• automated perimetry (hvf 24-2): crucial for identifying early field loss
actionSteps: • check bp immediately to rule out hypertensive emergency
• obtain emergency neuroimaging (mri + mrv) before performing an lp
• refer to neurology or neurosurgery if mass, hemorrhage, or cvst is found
• admit patient for observation if vision is deteriorating rapidly
treatment: ## Medical (IIH)
• acetazolamide (first-line): titrated up to 1–2 g/day (as per iihtt trial)
• weight loss: the cornerstone of long-term remission in iih
• topiramate: useful adjunct (weight loss benefit + migraine prophylaxis)
## Surgical (if medical fails)
• optic nerve sheath fenestration: for progressive vision loss
• csf shunting (vp/lp): preferred if refractory headache is the primary symptom
• venous sinus stenting: for confirmed transverse sinus stenosis with gradient
followUp: • serial fundus exam + oct rnfl every 2–4 weeks initially
• humphrey visual field (hvf) every 1–3 months until stable
• coordinate care with neurology to monitor systemic weight and bp targets
differentials: • pseudopapilledema (optic disc drusen): no leakage on ivfa, visible on b-scan
• naion: typically unilateral, sectoral swelling in older adults
• malignant hypertension: systolic >180; check blood pressure!
• papillitis (optic neuritis): associated with rapd and significant vision loss
review: • the frisén scale is used for staging; grade 5 involves total vessel obscuration
• in iih management, visual field loss (not headache) is the primary driver for surgery
• oct rnfl and subfoveal fluid measurements are standard for monitoring resolution
pearl: frisén grading 0–5 scales disc swelling severity. spontaneous venous pulsations (svp) present → icp likely <200 mmh₂o. oct rnfl + subfoveal fluid is the current monitoring standard for treatment response. in iih, visual loss — not headache — drives escalation to surgical management.
draw: bilateral optic disc elevation with blurred margins, peripapillary hemorrhages, and obscured vessels

name: Pathologic/Degenerative Myopia
symptoms: • often asymptomatic until middle adulthood
• decreased central vision or metamorphopsia (if macular cnv or schisis develops)
• floaters or flashes: high risk for retinal breaks or detachment
• severe near-sightedness requiring high-minus corrective lenses
findings: ## Diagnostic thresholds
• refractive error: worse than −6.00 d
• axial length: ≥26.5 mm (mechanical stretching of all ocular coats)
## Posterior pole & macula
• posterior staphyloma: pathologic outpouching of the posterior globe wall
• lacquer cracks: yellow, linear subretinal streaks (mechanical bruch ruptures)
• fuchs spots: hyperpigmented scars from prior hemorrhage or regressed cnv
• chorioretinal atrophy: patchy or diffuse thinning of the retina/choroid
## Disc & periphery
• tilted disc: oblique insertion often with a large white myopic crescent
• peripheral thinning: lattice degeneration and high risk for retinal tears
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• progressive axial elongation leads to mechanical stretching and thinning of the ocular tissues
• bruch membrane breaks (lacquer cracks) allow for choroidal neovascularization (cnv)
## Statistics
• strong genetic component; progression often continues into early adulthood
• fellow-eye risk: >30% lifetime risk of cnv once the first eye is affected
redFlags: • myopic cnv: sudden central distortion/blur; requires urgent anti-vegf
• new lacquer cracks: heralds a high risk for immediate subretinal hemorrhage
• macular schisis or hole: progressive vision loss needing surgical evaluation
• sudden floaters/curtain: suggests rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
investigations: ## Biometry & refraction
• axial length measurement (a-scan or iol master) to track elongation
• cycloplegic refraction for accurate power determination
## Ocular exam
• dilated 360° peripheral exam with scleral depression (screen for tears)
• tonometry: note that standard applanation may underestimate iop in thin scleras
## Imaging
• oct: mandatory for detecting foveoschisis, macular holes, and cnv
• oct-a: useful for identifying cnv within areas of chorioretinal atrophy
actionSteps: • perform annual dilated fundus exams with widefield imaging and oct
• educate patient on daily amsler grid monitoring
• treat symptomatic peripheral retinal breaks with prophylactic laser
• provide polycarbonate safety glasses due to increased risk of globe rupture
treatment: ## Macular complications
• intravitreal anti-vegf: first-line for active myopic cnv; excellent response rate
• vitrectomy: for myopic traction maculopathy or macular holes
## Peripheral disease
• laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy for high-risk retinal breaks/tears
## Glaucoma management
• maintain a low threshold for treatment, as myopic discs are hard to evaluate for cupping
followUp: • annual dilated exam for stable pathologic myopia
• every 3–6 months if lacquer cracks or stable treated cnv are present
• immediate follow-up for any new flashes, floaters, or central visual distortion
differentials: • distinguished by presence of drusen and older age of onset
• "punched-out" scars and peripapillary atrophy without high axial length
• scalloped areas of peripheral atrophy; associated with high ornithine levels
review: • pathologic myopia is a structural disease, not just a refractive error
• the thinning of the choroid and rpe makes these eyes highly susceptible to even minor trauma
• myopic cnv typically requires fewer anti-vegf injections than amd-related cnv
pearl: high myopes need a 360° peripheral exam every visit — lattice, breaks, myopic cnv, and posterior staphyloma all hide in a seemingly quiet fundus.
draw: elongated globe with a posterior staphyloma, tilted disc, and macular lacquer cracks

name: Pediatric Cataract
symptoms: • leukocoria (white pupil): often noticed by parents or on screening
• poor visual attention: inability to track light or toys
• strabismus (eye turn) or nystagmus (shaking eyes)
• asymptomatic: mild opacities may only be found on routine red reflex exam
findings: ## Critical surgical timing
• dense unilateral cataract: remove by 4–6 weeks of age (amblyopia emergency)
• dense bilateral cataracts: remove by 8–10 weeks of age
• delay leads to irreversible deprivation amblyopia and sensory nystagmus
## Systemic associations
• galactosemia: classic "oil-droplet" lens; reversible with early diet change
• torch (rubella): "pearly" nuclear cataract and "salt-and-pepper" retinopathy
• lowe syndrome: cataract, congenital glaucoma, and renal fanconi (males)
## Ocular features
• persistent fetal vasculature (pfv): usually unilateral; elongated ciliary processes
• aphakic glaucoma: risk in 20–30% after infant surgery; requires lifelong monitoring
• rapd: a cataract alone does NOT cause a pupillary defect; implies nerve/retina pathology
etiology: ## Idiopathic & genetic
• most common cause is idiopathic; familial cases are usually autosomal dominant
## Metabolic/syndromic
• galactosemia, trisomy 21, lowe syndrome, and alport syndrome
## Morphology
• zonular (lamellar): most common; "onion skin" appearance with clear/white layers
• anterior polar: small, usually stable, but can cause refractive amblyopia
• posterior lenticonus: progressive posterior protrusion and opacification
## Acquired
• trauma, steroid use, chronic uveitis, or radiation
redFlags: • leukocoria: always exclude retinoblastoma before assuming it is "just" a cataract
• nystagmus: a late sign indicating the fovea has never received a clear image
• unilateral microphthalmos: suggests pfv or intrauterine infection
• rapid progression: can turn a partial cataract into a dense amblyogenic one quickly
investigations: ## Clinical screen
• brückner test: assess for asymmetric or absent red reflex
• retinoscopy: a blunted or absent reflex confirms a visually significant cataract
## Imaging
• b-scan ultrasound: mandatory if the fundus is obscured to rule out retinoblastoma/pfv
## Laboratory (bilateral cases)
• rbc galt activity: screen for galactosemia (mandatory if not yet explained)
• urine amino acids: screen for lowe or alport syndrome
• torch titers: screen for congenital infections (rubella, cmv, etc.)
actionSteps: • confirm visual significance: cataracts ≥3 mm or those obscuring the retina need surgery
• perform b-scan to ensure the posterior segment is normal
• coordinate with a pediatrician for systemic and metabolic workup
• facilitate urgent surgical referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist
treatment: ## Surgical
• lensectomy with anterior vitrectomy: to prevent posterior capsule opacification
• infant aphakia treatment study (iats): contact lenses are preferred over iols in <7 months
## Medical/visual
• pupillary dilation: temporizing measure for small central cataracts
• aggressive amblyopia therapy: patching of the better eye is crucial post-operatively
• aphakic correction: high-power contact lenses or glasses
followUp: ## Post-operative
• lifelong monitoring for aphakic glaucoma (every 3–4 months initially)
• frequent refractive updates: the infant eye grows and changes power rapidly
## Long-term
• monitor for retinal detachment and secondary iol timing if currently aphakic
differentials: • retinopathy of prematurity (rop) with vitreous haze
review: • unilateral cataracts have the highest risk of amblyopia due to competition with the good eye
• bilateral cases often have a better visual prognosis because there is no ocular competition
• metabolic cataracts (galactosemia) are among the few that can be reversed medically
pearl: the visual outcome of a pediatric cataract depends on how quickly you operate — unilateral dense cataract is an amblyopia emergency and should be removed within weeks of detection, not months.
draw: white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in an infant eye compared to a normal red reflex

name: Peripheral Corneal Thinning/Ulceration
symptoms: • acute pain, redness, and severe photophobia (puk and mooren ulcer)
• slow, painless vision blur (terrien marginal degeneration and pmd)
• decreased vision due to high irregular astigmatism
• history of systemic autoimmune disease (ra, gpa, sle)
• history of hepatitis c (linked to mooren-like ulcers)
findings: ## Inflammatory (painful)
• puk: crescent-shaped peripheral stromal thinning with an epithelial defect
• scleritis: associated in 90% of puk cases (eye appears deep red/purple)
• mooren ulcer: painful thinning with a characteristic "undermined" overhanging leading edge; NO scleritis
## Non-inflammatory (painless)
• terrien marginal degeneration: superior thinning; yellow lipid line; intact epithelium
• pellucid marginal degeneration (pmd): inferior (4 to 8 o’clock) thinning; "beer belly" ectasia above thinning
• dellen: localized bowl-shaped depression from focal dryness (e.g., next to a pinguecula)
## Advanced signs
• corneal perforation or descemetocele (bulging basement membrane)
• vascularization or pannus crossing the area of thinning
etiology: ## Systemic vasculitis (PUK)
• rheumatoid arthritis (most common), gpa (wegener), polyarteritis nodosa, and sle
## Autoimmune/infectious
• mooren ulcer: idiopathic autoimmune keratitis; strongly linked to hepatitis c
• staphylococcal hypersensitivity: peripheral infiltrates with a "clear limbal zone"
## Degenerative/ectatic
• terrien marginal degeneration: idiopathic thinning, typically in males
• pellucid marginal degeneration (pmd): non-inflammatory corneal ectasia
## Neurotrophic
• non-inflammatory thinning due to cn v/vii palsy or exposure
redFlags: • scleral involvement: suggests life-threatening systemic vasculitis (gpa/ra)
• rapid "melting" (keratolysis): risk of globe perforation within hours/days
• ra patient with corneal melt: indicates 40% 10-year systemic mortality if untreated
• hepatitis c positive: mooren-like ulcer requires antiviral treatment
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• check corneal sensation: rule out hsv and neurotrophic causes
• slit-lamp: narrow beam to assess depth of thinning and epithelial status
• scleral exam: check for nodules, thinning (blue hue), or posterior scleritis
## Mandatory serology (vasculitis screen)
• cbc, esr/crp, rf, anti-ccp, ana, anca (c-anca/p-anca), and spep
## Infectious screen
• hepatitis c antibody, rpr/fta-abs (syphilis), and quantiferon-tb gold
## Systemic evaluation
• urinalysis and chest ct if gpa is suspected (renal/lung involvement)
actionSteps: • rule out infectious keratitis with cultures if the base is heavily infiltrated
• urgent rheumatology consultation for systemic immunosuppression
• start oral doxycycline and vitamin c to inhibit collagenase and support healing
• provide rigid polycarbonate safety lenses to prevent traumatic perforation
• refer to cornea specialist for possible glue, amnion, or patch graft
treatment: ## Systemic therapy (PUK/mooren)
• high-dose oral steroids (prednisone 1mg/kg/day) with ppi coverage
• steroid-sparing agents: cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, or rituximab
## Topical/adjunctive
• topical cyclosporine (0.05%–2%) and judicious topical steroids
• doxycycline 100mg bid and vitamin c 1g–2g daily (collagenase inhibition)
## Surgical (impending perforation)
• cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive (glue) or amniotic membrane graft
• lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty for severe cases
## Degenerative management
• pmd: specialty scleral lenses or collagen cross-linking (cxl)
followUp: • inflammatory: daily monitoring until epithelium closes and thinning stabilizes
• stable (terrien/pmd): every 6–12 months for refractive management
• monitor iop closely: high risk for steroid-induced ocular hypertension
• co-manage with rheumatology to monitor systemic drug toxicity
differentials: • senile furrow degeneration (non-progressive thinning in elderly)
review: • PUK is often the first sign of a lethal systemic vasculitis; it is a medical emergency
• peripheral corneal thinning can lead to high levels of irregular astigmatism
• differentiate inflammatory causes (puk/mooren) from non-inflammatory (terrien/pmd)
pearl: peripheral ulcerative keratitis with systemic features is rheumatoid arthritis in 50% and gpa (wegener) in the rest — get rheumatology and serologies before the globe perforates.
draw: crescent-shaped peripheral corneal thinning with an overlying epithelial defect and adjacent scleral injection

name: Phakomatoses
symptoms: • often asymptomatic in childhood; identified via routine skin or eye exams
• vision loss: from optic gliomas (nf1), retinal hemangioblastomas (vhl), or macular fluid (sws)
• strabismus or eyelid deformity (s-shaped lid from plexiform neurofibroma)
• prominent birthmarks: café-au-lait spots, port-wine stains, or ash-leaf spots
• hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo (classic for nf2)
• systemic: seizures, intellectual disability, or motor deficits
findings: ## Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
• lisch nodules: tan-brown iris hamartomas (diagnostic in ~95% of adults)
• optic pathway gliomas: pilocytic astrocytomas of the nerve/chiasm
• plexiform neurofibroma: "bag of worms" texture; causes s-shaped ptosis
## Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
• juvenile cataracts: posterior subcapsular or wedge-shaped cortical opacities
• combined hamartomas of the retina and rpe; notably lacks lisch nodules
## Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)
• astrocytic hamartomas: "mulberry-like" calcified or semi-transparent retinal lesions
## Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)
• retinal capillary hemangioblastomas: orange-red lesions with large "feeder" vessels
## Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS)
• "tomato-catsup fundus": diffuse choroidal hemangioma
• ipsilateral glaucoma and episcleral vascular anomalies
etiology: ## Genetic basis
• nf1: autosomal dominant (17q11.2); neurofibromin mutation (ras-mapk pathway)
• nf2: autosomal dominant (22q12); merlin/schwannomin mutation
• tsc: autosomal dominant; tsc1 (hamartin) or tsc2 (tuberin) mutations
• vhl: autosomal dominant (3p25.3); vhl tumor suppressor gene mutation
• sws: sporadic somatic mutation (gnaq); mosaicism, not inherited
redFlags: • retinal capillary hemangioblastoma (vhl): heralds life-threatening renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
• port-wine stain (v1 distribution): indicates high risk for ipsilateral glaucoma and brain angiomas
• optic pathway glioma (opg): requires urgent neuro-oncology monitoring to save vision
• hypertension in vhl: must rule out pheochromocytoma before any surgery
investigations: ## Ocular assessment
• slit-lamp (lisch nodules) and gonioscopy (angle anomalies/vascularity)
• dilated fundoscopy: specifically looking for peripheral hemangiomas or calcified hamartomas
## Neuro-imaging
• mri brain/orbits with contrast: identify gliomas, schwannomas, or calcifications
## Systemic screening
• abdominal ct/mri: screen for renal tumors (vhl/tsc) and adrenal lesions
• skin exam: wood lamp for "ash-leaf" spots in tuberous sclerosis
actionSteps: • perform a thorough skin exam to map marks to specific phakomatosis subtypes
• check intraocular pressure (iop) in all nf1 and sturge-weber cases (high glaucoma risk)
• order mri orbits if any proptosis or vision loss is noted in an nf1 patient
• coordinate visual rehab for any lid lesions obstructing the visual axis
• facilitate genetic counseling for the patient and first-degree relatives
treatment: ## Glaucoma (NF1/SWS)
• topical medical therapy (beta-blockers/pgas); caution with surgery in sws (risk of choroidal effusion)
## Retinal/choroidal lesions
• vhl: laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy for capillary hemangioblastomas
• sws: photodynamic therapy (pdt) or plaque radiotherapy for exudative hemangiomas
## Optic glioma (NF1)
• observation; chemotherapy (carboplatin) or mek inhibitors if vision or mri progresses
## Systemic
• surgical excision of neurofibromas; treatment of seizures in tsc/sws
followUp: • nf1: annual eye exams (age <8) for gliomas; then every 2 years
• vhl: lifelong annual dilated exam and systemic tumor surveillance
• sturge-weber: lifelong glaucoma monitoring (every 6 months initially)
• tsc/nf2: annual evaluations for cataracts and retinal lesions
review: • phakomatoses are neuro-oculo-cutaneous syndromes where skin findings predict internal tumors
• vhl requires the most intense systemic surveillance due to the risk of renal cell carcinoma
• lisch nodules (nf1) are diagnostic markers that do not affect vision, unlike cataracts in nf2
pearl: the "skin is a window to the eye and brain" in phakomatoses — café-au-lait spots, port-wine stains, adenoma sebaceum, and ash-leaf spots each point to a syndrome with predictable ocular and systemic complications.
draw: composite showing lisch nodules on the iris, an ash-leaf spot on the skin, and a port-wine stain in v1 distribution

name: Phlyctenulosis
symptoms: • tearing, irritation, and localized ocular pain
• mild-to-severe photophobia (light sensitivity)
• pediatric blepharospasm: a tearful child unable to open the eye
• history of recurrent "styes" or chalazia
• corneal lesions are significantly more painful than conjunctival ones
findings: ## Characteristic lesion
• the "phlycten": a small, raised, white-to-pink nodule at the limbus
• intense focal wedge of dilated conjunctival vessels pointing toward the lesion
• represent a type iv (delayed) hypersensitivity response
## Corneal migration
• "marching" phlyctenule: may migrate centrally across the cornea
• leaves a "leash" of vessels and a wedge-shaped stromal scar behind it
• can cause permanent vision loss if it crosses the visual axis
## Associated lid disease
• nearly always associated with staphylococcal blepharitis or mgd
• ocular rosacea features (telangiectatic lid margins, recurrent chalazia)
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• immune response to microbial antigens (staph, tb) deposited at the limbus
• the nodule is sterile; it contains no live organisms
## Primary triggers
• staphylococcal antigens: the most common cause in developed nations
• tuberculosis (tb): historically dominant; still critical in immigrants and children
• others: hsv, chlamydia, candida, or intestinal parasites (ascaris/giardia)
redFlags: • central corneal migration: requires prompt steroids to prevent axial scarring
• pediatric/immigrant cases: high suspicion for tuberculosis exposure
• persistent lid disease: recurrent chalazia act as an antigenic reservoir
• corneal melting: rare but suggests a severe inflammatory complication
investigations: ## Slit lamp exam
• evaluate lid margins for anterior blepharitis, collarettes, and mgd
• document the position and any migration of the phlyctenule
## Systemic screening (mandatory if recurrent/pediatric)
• tb testing: ppd skin test and/or igra (quantiferon-tb gold)
• chest x-ray: to rule out active or latent pulmonary tuberculosis
## Specialized
• stool ova & parasites: if parasites are suspected in a child from an endemic region
actionSteps: • initiate topical steroids to quiet the immune nodule and prevent scarring
• treat the underlying lid disease with antibiotics and hygiene
• perform tb screening in all high-risk populations before long-term therapy
• monitor weekly until the lesion and associated "leash" of vessels resolve
treatment: ## For the phlyctenule
• topical steroids: prednisolone acetate 1% or loteprednol 0.5% qid with a taper
## For the lids
• warm compresses and lid scrubs bid to reduce staph antigenic load
• topical antibiotic ointment (erythromycin/bacitracin) to lid margins qhs
## For rosacea/MGD
• oral doxycycline (50–100mg bid) for 6–12 weeks; use erythromycin in children <8y
## Systemic TB
• if positive, refer to infectious disease for antituberculous therapy
followUp: • acute: weekly follow-up until the epithelium is intact and the nodule resolves
• chronic: maintain aggressive lid hygiene to prevent antigenic recurrence
• counseling: explain that recurrence is common if the underlying lid disease is not managed
differentials: • inflamed pinguecula (usually horizontal/interpalpebral, lacks corneal migration)
• pterygium (fibrovascular growth, usually chronic and less inflammatory)
• marginal keratitis (staph infiltrates with a clear zone between lesion and limbus)
• ocular surface squamous neoplasia (ossn) (slower growth, abnormal vasculature)
review: • phlyctenulosis is an "allergic" reaction of the cornea/conjunctiva to a distant infection
• the most common location is at the 2, 4, 8, or 10 o'clock positions on the limbus
• visual prognosis is excellent unless central corneal scarring occurs
pearl: a phlyctenule in a child or immigrant patient is tuberculosis until proven otherwise — check ppd/igra before reaching for the topical steroid.
draw: wedge-shaped conjunctival injection pointing to a small white nodule at the corneal limbus

name: Pigment Dispersion Syndrome/Pigmentary Glaucoma
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Mostly asymptomatic (detected on routine exam).
• Classic: Blurred vision, eye pain, and colored halos after vigorous exercise.
• Occurs primarily in young, myopic (near-sighted) men (age 20–45).
• Typically bilateral but often asymmetric.
• High risk of floaters/flashes due to associated lattice degeneration.
findings: ## Mechanical hallmark
• Reverse pupillary block: Peripheral iris bows posteriorly, rubbing against zonules.
• Concavity: "Swept-back" iris contour seen on UBM or AS-OCT.
## The cardinal signs
• Krukenberg spindle: Vertical band of pigment on the corneal endothelium.
• Iris TIDs: Radial, spoke-like transillumination defects in the mid-periphery.
• Scheie stripe (Zentmayer ring): Pigment on the posterior lens equator (pathognomonic).
## Gonioscopy
• 3–4+ dense, homogeneous trabecular meshwork (TM) pigmentation 360°.
• Sampaolesi line: Pigment band anterior to Schwalbe’s line.
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Friction between the posterior iris pigment epithelium and lens zonules liberates pigment.
• Aqueous flow carries pigment into the anterior chamber, where it clogs the TM.
## Statistics
• ~30–50% of patients with Pigment Dispersion Syndrome (PDS) convert to glaucoma.
• Conversion risk is highest in young males with high baseline IOP.
redFlags: • Post-exercise IOP spike: Sudden blur or pain after running/basketball (pigment bolus).
• Rapid field progression: Common in young patients; requires aggressive management.
• Lattice degeneration: Mandatory 360° peripheral exam to rule out retinal tears/RD.
• Unilateral presentation: Reconsider diagnosis (suspect uveitis or IOL chafe).
investigations: ## Clinical evaluation
• Gonioscopy: To confirm heavy, uniform TM pigmentation.
• Slit-lamp red reflex: To visualize mid-peripheral iris transillumination defects.
• Careful IOP check: Consider pre- and post-exercise measurements if symptomatic.
## Glaucoma staging
• Automated perimetry (HVF) and OCT RNFL/GCC for baseline damage assessment.
## Peripheral retina
• Dilated exam with scleral depression (mandatory for all myopic PDS patients).
actionSteps: • Identify reverse pupillary block and document pigment distribution.
• Educate patient on the risks of exercise-induced IOP spikes.
• Screen for peripheral retinal pathology (lattice/tears).
• Initiate IOP-lowering therapy if glaucomatous damage or high ocular hypertension is present.
treatment: ## Medical management
• Standard drops: Prostaglandin analogs or aqueous suppressants (first-line).
• Pilocarpine (miotics): Theoretically ideal (flattens iris), but poorly tolerated in youths.
## Laser therapy
• SLT (Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty): Highly effective due to heavy pigment; use low energy.
• LPI (Laser Peripheral Iridotomy): No longer routine; may benefit young patients with severe concavity.
## Surgical
• Trabeculectomy or tube shunt for refractory cases failing medical/laser therapy.
followUp: • Annual exams for PDS (no glaucoma) to monitor for conversion.
• Every 3–6 months for confirmed pigmentary glaucoma depending on stability.
• Repeat peripheral retinal exams annually due to high risk of detachment.
differentials: • Pseudoexfoliation (older patients, pigment on anterior lens, patchy TM pigment).
• Uveitis (pigment on endothelium but associated with cells/flare/PI).
• Iris chafe (post-surgical, secondary to sulcus-placed IOL).
• Bilateral acute depigmentation of the iris (BADI).
review: • PDS usually "burns out" in older age as the lens grows and pushes the iris forward.
• Unlike POAG, this condition targets young, active individuals.
• The Scheie stripe is on the posterior lens, distinguishing it from exfoliation material.
pearl: A young myopic male with exercise-triggered blur and a Krukenberg spindle has pigment dispersion — warn him about gym-induced IOP spikes and consider pre-exercise pilocarpine.
draw: Vertical Krukenberg spindle on the cornea and mid-peripheral radial iris transillumination defects

name: Plateau Iris
symptoms: ## Presentation
• Usually asymptomatic (detected on routine gonioscopy).
• Intermittent "brow ache," halos around lights, or blurred vision.
• Acute angle-closure: Sudden severe pain, nausea, and redness.
• Classic: Angle closure symptoms that persist *even after* an LPI has been performed.
findings: ## Core concept
• Angle closure caused by an anatomical variant where the ciliary body is anteriorly rotated.
• Unlike pupillary block, the central anterior chamber (AC) depth is often relatively deep.
## The "unmasked" angle
• Plateau iris syndrome: Angle closure that PERSISTS despite a patent laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI).
• Distinguishes it from primary angle closure where LPI usually "fixes" the narrow angle.
## Clinical signs
• "Double-hump" sign: Seen on indentation gonioscopy; the iris rises over the lens, dips, then rises again over the ciliary processes.
• Flat iris plane: The central iris appears flat rather than bowed forward (bombé).
• Patent LPI: Essential to rule out pupillary block as the primary driver.
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• Anteriorly positioned ciliary processes push the peripheral iris root forward into the trabecular meshwork.
• This mechanical crowding prevents aqueous drainage even if a hole (LPI) exists in the iris.
## Demographics
• Typically younger patients (30s–50s) than standard angle closure.
• Female predominance; usually hyperopic (farsighted) or emmetropic.
redFlags: • Persistent closure after LPI: Mandates UBM imaging to confirm plateau configuration.
• Acute attack despite patent LPI: Diagnostic for plateau iris syndrome.
• Mid-dilation closure: Phenylephrine or tropicamide can bunch the iris into the angle, triggering an attack.
• Progressive PAS: Formation of peripheral anterior synechiae despite a patent LPI.
investigations: ## Gold standard imaging
• Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM): The only way to directly visualize the anteriorly rotated ciliary body pushing the iris.
• Anterior segment OCT: Can show the crowded angle but less effective at seeing the ciliary body.
## Gonioscopy
• Indentation gonioscopy is mandatory to look for the "double-hump" sign and assess for PAS.
## Clinical monitoring
• Serial IOP checks and undilated optic nerve evaluation.
actionSteps: • Perform LPI first to eliminate any possible pupillary block component.
• Repeat gonioscopy after LPI; if the angle remains closed, obtain a UBM.
• Avoid strong mydriatics (dilating drops) until the angle is stabilized.
• Perform argon laser peripheral iridoplasty (ALPI) if syndrome is confirmed.
treatment: ## Step 1: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI)
• Mandatory first step to "unmask" the plateau and relieve any pupillary block.
## Step 2: Argon Laser Peripheral Iridoplasty (ALPI)
• Definitive treatment: Low-energy burns to the peripheral iris contract the tissue, pulling it away from the angle.
## Step 3: Medical & Surgical Adjuncts
• Low-dose pilocarpine (0.5–1%): Keeps the iris "stretched" and out of the angle.
• Lens extraction (cataract surgery): Often curative as it creates more space in the anterior segment.
• ECP (endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation): Can be used during surgery to shrink the ciliary processes.
followUp: • Plateau configuration (anatomical only): Monitor every 6 months with gonioscopy and IOP.
• Plateau syndrome: Frequent follow-up after ALPI; monitor for IOP spikes and PAS progression.
• Fellow eye: Almost always bilateral; requires prophylactic LPI and close observation.
differentials: • Ciliary body cysts (can push the iris forward in a similar pattern).
review: • The central AC is deep, but the peripheral AC is shallow—this is the anatomical hallmark.
• If an LPI doesn't open the angle, think plateau iris.
• UBM is the "secret weapon" for confirming the ciliary body position.
pearl: An angle that stays narrow after a patent iridotomy is plateau iris — UBM shows the anteriorly positioned ciliary processes, and argon laser iridoplasty opens the angle.
draw: UBM cross-section showing anteriorly rotated ciliary body pushing the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork

name: Posterior and Panuveitis
symptoms: • blurred vision and floaters (most common presentation)
• scotomas (blind spots) and metamorphopsia (distorted vision)
• photopsias (flashing lights) frequently present
• dull ache or redness if associated anterior chamber inflammation is present
• severe pain: suggests posterior scleritis or endophthalmitis
findings: ## Core posterior signs
• vitritis: vitreous cells, haze, "snowballs," or "snowbanking"
• retinitis: focal or confluent retinal whitening (e.g., "headlight in fog" for toxo)
• choroiditis: creamy yellow-white placoid or punched-out lesions
• vasculitis: perivascular sheathing ("candle-wax drippings" in sarcoid) or hemorrhages
## Pattern recognition
• behçet: shifting hypopyon, occlusive vasculitis, and oral/genital ulcers
• vkh: bilateral serous detachments, "sunset glow" fundus, and hearing/skin changes
• birdshot: bilateral creamy oval choroidal spots in middle-aged caucasians (hla-a29+)
• arn (acute retinal necrosis): peripheral confluent whitening and rapid progression
• multifocal choroiditis: punched-out scars WITH vitritis (unlike pohs)
## Complications
• cystoid macular edema (cme): the leading cause of permanent vision loss
• optic disc edema, epiretinal membranes, and secondary glaucoma
etiology: ## Infectious (must rule out first)
• toxoplasmosis: most common infectious cause; typically adjacent to an old scar
• syphilis ("the great masquerader") and tuberculosis (tb)
• viral: hsv/vzv (arn/porn) and cmv (suspect hiv/immunocompromised)
## Non-infectious (autoimmune)
• sarcoidosis: granulomatous inflammation; often involves lungs
• vkh syndrome: targets melanocytes (pigmented populations)
• birdshot chorioretinopathy and behçet disease
## Masquerade
• primary vitreoretinal lymphoma: suspect in older patients with refractory vitritis
redFlags: • confluent retinal whitening: suspect arn; emergency antivirals needed to save the eye
• hypopyon in young patient: suspect behçet; high risk of occlusive retinal vasculitis
• bilateral serous detachments: suspect vkh; requires immediate high-dose steroids
• chronic "vitritis" in elderly: must rule out lymphoma before starting steroids
investigations: ## Mandatory screening (pre-steroids)
• syphilis: rpr/vdrl plus treponemal-specific assay (fta-abs)
• tuberculosis: quantiferon-gold/t-spot plus chest x-ray or ct
• sarcoidosis: serum ace, lysozyme, and chest imaging
• hiv testing: mandatory for all patients with opportunistic infections (cmv/porn)
## Imaging
• oct macula: monitor for cme and subretinal fluid
• wide-field fa: assess for retinal vasculitis, ischemia, and disc leakage
• icg angiography: superior for choroidal disease (birdshot/vkh/serpiginous)
## Specialized
• hla typing: a29 (birdshot), b51 (behçet), dr4 (vkh)
• aqueous/vitreous tap: pcr for hsv, vzv, cmv, and toxoplasma
actionSteps: • perform a thorough dilated exam to determine the anatomical pattern of inflammation
• order mandatory infectious screen (syphilis, tb, hiv) before initiating immunosuppression
• use wide-field imaging to evaluate the periphery for retinitis or vasculitis
• coordinate with rheumatology or infectious disease for systemic management
treatment: ## Infectious
• toxoplasmosis: tmp-smx or pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine + folinic acid
• viral (arn): iv acyclovir or oral valacyclovir + intravitreal foscarnet
• syphilis/tb: specific iv/quadruple antibiotic protocols
## Non-infectious
• systemic steroids: prednisone 1mg/kg/day with a slow taper
• steroid-sparing agents: methotrexate, mycophenolate, or anti-tnf (adalimumab)
## Local/adjunct
• periocular or intravitreal steroid implants (ozurdex/yutiq) for refractory/unilateral disease
followUp: • acute: weekly monitoring until inflammation is controlled and meds are tolerated
• chronic: every 3–6 months; monitor for steroid-induced cataracts and glaucoma
• coordinated care: ensure systemic monitoring (cbc/bmp/liver) for patients on immunosuppression
differentials: • primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (older, non-responsive to steroids)
• eales disease and multiple sclerosis (intermediate uveitis pattern)
review: • the presence of vitritis is key; its absence in the context of scars suggests pohs or chronic scars
• regional steroid implants provide excellent control but carry a high risk of glaucoma and cataracts
• always check the skin, mouth, and genitals for systemic clues (behçet, vkh, sarcoid)
pearl: in posterior uveitis, the patient's ancestry often points to the diagnosis: hla-a29 (birdshot, northern european), hla-b51 (behçet, silk road), hla-dr4 (vkh, pigmented populations).
draw: fundus sketch showing creamy choroidal spots (birdshot), a "headlight in fog" retinitis (toxo), and candle-wax vascular sheathing (sarcoid)

name: Posterior Vitreous Detachment
symptoms: • floaters: sudden "shower" of small spots, cobwebs, or a large central "fly"
• photopsias (flashes): typically temporal, brief, and more noticeable in dim light
• blurred vision: often from a floater or hemorrhage crossing the visual axis
• progression: symptoms usually peak over hours to days
findings: ## Clinical hallmarks
• weiss ring: a circular glial opacity floating in the vitreous (torn from the optic nerve)
• shafer's sign ("tobacco dust"): brown rpe pigment granules in the anterior vitreous
• vitreous hemorrhage: ranging from mild haze to dense blood obscuring the retina
## Risk correlations
• shafer's sign: ~70–90% correlation with a retinal tear
• vitreous hemorrhage: ~50–70% risk of an associated retinal tear
• uncomplicated pvd: ~10–15% risk of a retinal tear
## Anatomical profile
• axial myopia (>−6 d) and prior cataract surgery significantly increase risk
• "falling ash" on oct: hyper-reflective dots in the vitreous suggesting a break
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• age-related liquefaction (syneresis) of the vitreous gel leads to shrinkage
• the posterior hyaloid membrane separates from its attachments to the retina
## Timeline
• typically occurs after age 50; the fellow eye usually follows within 6–24 months
redFlags: • curtain or shadow: strongly suggests a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
• pigmented cells (shafer sign): high probability of an occult retinal tear
• multiple new floaters + persistent flashes: indicates high traction on the retina
• dense vitreous hemorrhage: may hide a retinal tear or detachment
investigations: ## The gold standard
• dilated fundus exam with indirect ophthalmoscopy and 360° scleral depression
## Slit lamp
• use 60/90d lens to visualize the hyaloid face and weiss ring
• examine the anterior vitreous with a high-power beam to check for pigment
## Imaging
• b-scan ultrasound: mandatory if the retina cannot be seen due to hemorrhage
• oct: confirms the state of the hyaloid attachment at the macula/disc
actionSteps: • perform meticulous scleral depression of the entire periphery in both eyes
• immediately refer any identified retinal tears for laser or cryotherapy
• educate the patient on "rd warning signs" (curtain, shadow, surge in floaters)
• schedule a mandatory repeat exam at 4–6 weeks to catch delayed tears
treatment: ## Observation
• no treatment needed for an uncomplicated pvd with no tears or detachment
## Surgical/laser
• laser retinopexy: for symptomatic horseshoe tears or retinal dialysis
• pars plana vitrectomy: if dense hemorrhage persists or detachment occurs
followUp: ## "Clean" initial exam
• repeat exam with scleral depression in 4–6 weeks (3% risk of delayed tear)
## Hemorrhage present
• repeat exam in 1–2 weeks to monitor the clearing of blood and ensure no tear
## Urgent re-evaluation
• instruct the patient to return the same day if they notice a "curtain" or "shadow"
review: • a weiss ring is the definitive evidence that the vitreous has detached from the disc
• the location of flashes does not reliably predict the location of a tear
• pvd is a common event, but the "tobacco dust" sign makes it a potential emergency
pearl: ten percent of acute pvds have a retinal tear; fifty percent do if there's vitreous hemorrhage or pigment — scleral depression of the entire periphery is the standard of care, not an optional add-on.
draw: weiss ring floating anterior to the optic nerve with the posterior hyaloid detached from the retina

name: Pregnancy
symptoms: • headaches and blurred vision
• photopsias (flashes) and scotomas (blind spots)
• diplopia (double vision)
• dry eye symptoms: grittiness and irritation
findings: ## Physiologic & reversible
• refractive shift: transient myopic shift (0.5–1.5 D); resolves ~6 weeks postpartum
• cornea: decreased sensitivity and increased thickness (affects contact lens fit)
• intraocular pressure: typically decreases by ~10%
• chloasma: periocular skin pigmentation (melasma)
## Preeclampsia & eclampsia
• hypertensive retinopathy: focal arteriolar narrowing, hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots
• serous retinal detachments: bilateral and bullous; occurs in ~10% of eclamptic patients
• cortical blindness (pres): "brisk pupils without rapd"; suggests occipital lobe edema
## Disease exacerbation
• diabetic retinopathy (dr): rapid progression, especially if severe before conception
• central serous chorioretinopathy (cscr): triggered by third-trimester steroid surge
• tumors: pituitary adenomas and meningiomas may enlarge due to hormonal stimulation
etiology: ## Systemic changes
