• hormonal fluctuations: drive corneal changes and tumor growth
• hypercoagulability: peaks 6 weeks postpartum; increases risk of vein/artery occlusions
• hypertensive spectrum: preeclampsia/eclampsia after 20 weeks gestation
## Pituitary events
• sheehan syndrome: pituitary infarct following severe obstetric hemorrhage
• lymphocytic hypophysitis: autoimmune pituitary inflammation
redFlags: • vision symptoms + high bp (≥140/90): maternal emergency; suspect preeclampsia
• cortical blindness: pupils respond but patient cannot see; suspect eclampsia/pres
• diabetic retinopathy: severe npdr/pdr requires monthly to trimonthly screening
• brimonidine use: strictly contraindicated (neonatal apnea/death risk)
investigations: ## Routine screening
• blood pressure and urinalysis (proteinuria) at every eye visit for pregnant patients
• dilated fundus exam: each trimester for pre-existing diabetics
## Imaging safety
• mri brain/orbits: safe without contrast (gadolinium is category c)
• fa/icg angiography: category c; defer unless essential for vision-threatening disease
• oct: safe and essential for monitoring cme or cscr
actionSteps: • defer new glasses/refractive surgery until at least 6 weeks postpartum
• immediately refer any patient with visual symptoms and hypertension to obstetrics
• coordinate with ob/gyn before starting any topical glaucoma or anti-vegf meds
• avoid exogenous steroids in cscr cases as they can worsen/prolong the detachment
treatment: ## Preeclampsia/eclampsia
• blood pressure control and seizure prophylaxis (magnesium sulfate)
• definitive treatment is delivery of the fetus
## Diabetic retinal disease
• panretinal photocoagulation (prp) is preferred over anti-vegf during pregnancy
## Glaucoma
• punctal occlusion with all drops; beta-blockers are generally safest
• avoid brimonidine; use prostaglandins/cais only if benefits outweigh risks
followUp: ## Diabetic patients
• screen once per trimester (or more if pdr is present)
## Postpartum
• re-evaluate refractive error at 6 weeks for stable prescription
• monitor for postpartum graves’ ophthalmopathy flares
• screen for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis if severe postpartum headaches occur
review: • most ocular changes in pregnancy are benign and resolve after delivery
• stable diabetic retinopathy *before* pregnancy is the best predictor of a quiet course
• eclamptic serous detachments usually resolve completely without surgical intervention
pearl: pregnancy accelerates diabetic retinopathy — screen every trimester, and counsel patients that stable dr before conception is the best predictor of an uneventful pregnancy for the eyes.
draw: fundus showing focal arteriolar narrowing and bilateral bullous serous retinal detachments

name: Preseptal (Periorbital) Cellulitis
symptoms: • tenderness, redness, warmth, and swelling of the eyelid
• fever or chills (more common in children)
## Preceding events
• local skin trauma: abrasions, puncture wounds, or insect bites
• adjacent infection: hordeolum (stye), dacryocystitis, or dental abscess
• recent upper respiratory infection or sinusitis
findings: ## Eyelid / periorbital
• erythema (redness), tense edema, warmth, and significant tenderness
• severe swelling may prevent the patient from opening the eye
## Key negatives (must confirm to rule out orbital cellulitis)
• NO proptosis (bulging of the eye)
• NO pain with eye movement
• NO restriction of extraocular motility (eye moves fully)
• NO optic neuropathy (vision is normal, no rapd)
• globe is white and quiet (minimal conjunctival injection)
etiology: ## Common pathogens
• staphylococcus aureus (including mrsa)
• streptococcus species
• haemophilus influenzae (consider in non-immunized children)
## Specific scenarios
• anaerobes: suspect if there is a foul-smelling discharge or an animal/human bite
• viral: vesicular rash suggests hsv or vzv
redFlags: • any orbital sign: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or pain on motion → orbital cellulitis
• pediatric toxic appearance: high fever or lethargy requires immediate admission
• failed therapy: progression despite 48 hours of oral antibiotics
• decreased vision/rapd: suggests optic nerve compromise from orbital pressure
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• meticulous assessment of motility, proptosis, and pupillary reactions
• use a desmarres retractor if lids are too swollen to see the globe
## Imaging (CT orbits with contrast)
• indicated if: orbital signs present, child is febrile, trauma/foreign body suspected, or no improvement in 48h
## Labs
• cbc with differential and blood cultures (if febrile/toxic)
• gram stain and culture of any open wound drainage
actionSteps: • differentiate from orbital cellulitis immediately via motility and vision checks
• initiate oral antibiotics for mild cases in reliable adults/older children
• admit and start iv antibiotics for children <5 years or any severe/febrile cases
• schedule 24-hour follow-up to ensure therapy is effective
treatment: ## Outpatient (mild disease)
• amoxicillin-clavulanate: 875/125 mg po q12h (adults); 25–45 mg/kg/d (children)
• mrsa coverage: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (tmp-smx) or clindamycin
## Inpatient (severe/pediatric/toxic)
• iv ampicillin-sulbactam or vancomycin + ceftriaxone
## Adjuncts
• warm compresses for symptomatic relief
• duration: typically 7–10 days of total antibiotic therapy
followUp: • recheck in 24–48 hours: if worsening, convert to iv and order ct imaging
• once stable: complete the full 7–10 day course
• dental/ent referral: if a sinus or dental source is suspected
differentials: • allergic eyelid edema (itchy, pale swelling, no warmth/tenderness)
• necrotizing fasciitis (rapidly progressive, dusky/purple skin, crepitus)
review: • preseptal cellulitis is an infection limited to the tissues anterior to the orbital septum
• the clinical "litmus test" is the motility exam—if the eye moves freely and painlessly, the infection is likely preseptal
• children under 5 years old can progress to orbital involvement with terrifying speed
pearl: preseptal vs orbital cellulitis: if the eye moves normally without pain and there is no proptosis, it is preseptal (safer). any doubt → ct orbits. children < 5 years are at higher risk of rapid progression to orbital involvement.
draw: swollen, red eyelid with the globe underneath appearing white and moving normally

name: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
symptoms: • usually asymptomatic until advanced stages ("the silent thief of sight")
• painless, progressive loss of peripheral vision
• central vision typically remains 20/20 until end-stage disease
• bilateral, though frequently asymmetric in severity
• History: always ask about steroid use (nasal, skin, joints) to rule out secondary causes
findings: ## Diagnostic triad
• open, normal-appearing angle on gonioscopy (no closure/pigment/exfoliation)
• characteristic optic nerve cupping (structural damage)
• corresponding visual field defects (functional damage)
## Structural signs (optic nerve)
• vertical cup-to-disc ratio (c:d) >0.6 or asymmetry ≥0.2 between eyes
• isnt rule violation: thinning of the inferior/superior rim first
• drance hemorrhage: splinter hemorrhage at the disc margin; a sign of active progression
• rnfl wedge defects: visible as dark "slits" on red-free exam or oct
## Functional signs (visual fields)
• nasal step, arcuate (bjerrum) scotoma, or paracentral defects
• defects respect the horizontal midline (unlike neuro-defects which respect the vertical)
## Pachymetry (CCT)
• thin corneas (<555 μm) are a major independent risk factor for progression
• thin corneas "under-read" iop, making the measured pressure seem safer than it is
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• increased resistance to aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork
• mechanical and vascular stress leads to retinal ganglion cell apoptosis
## Risk factors
• age >60, african or hispanic ancestry (higher prevalence and earlier onset)
• elevated iop, family history (1st-degree relatives), and high myopia
• systemic: diabetes, hypertension, and low ocular perfusion pressure
redFlags: • progression at "normal" iop: suggests normal-tension glaucoma or nocturnal dips
• optic nerve pallor > cupping: suggests a non-glaucomatous (neurologic) cause
• rapid field loss: warrants immediate reassessment of target iop and compliance
• split fixation: field loss threatening the central 5 degrees; requires urgent surgery
investigations: ## Baseline workup
• applanation tonometry (gold standard) and gonioscopy (to confirm open angle)
• ultrasonic pachymetry to measure central corneal thickness (cct)
## Imaging & perimetry
• oct of the rnfl and ganglion cell complex (gcc) for structural baseline
• humphrey visual field (hvf) 24-2 (or 10-2 if advanced) for functional baseline
• high-quality disc photography to track structural changes over years
## Atypical workup
• if field loss doesn't match the nerve, consider mri orbits/brain or labs (b12, syphilis)
actionSteps: • establish a baseline "peak" iop before starting therapy
• set a target iop (typically 20–30% reduction from baseline)
• initiate first-line therapy: prostaglandin analogs or slt (laser)
• educate the patient on the lifelong nature of the disease and medication adherence
treatment: ## First-line
• topical prostaglandins (latanoprost, bimatoprost) once daily at bedtime
• selective laser trabeculoplasty (slt): proven as an effective first-line alternative to drops
## Medical adjuncts
• beta-blockers (timolol), alpha-agonists (brimonidine), or rho-kinase inhibitors
• carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide/acetazolamide)
## Surgical intervention
• trabeculectomy or tube shunts for uncontrolled progression
• migs (minimally invasive glaucoma surgery) often performed during cataract extraction
followUp: • efficacy check: 4–6 weeks after starting a new medication or laser
• stable disease: monitor every 3–6 months with iop checks and annual dilated exams
• progression monitoring: repeat hvf and oct every 6–12 months (more often if unstable)
• gonioscopy: repeat annually to ensure the angle remains open
differentials: • physiologic cupping (large disc with large cup, but thick rim and normal hvf)
• neuro-ophthalmic mimics (ischemic optic neuropathy, compressive lesions)
review: • iop is the only modifiable risk factor; the disease can progress even at "normal" pressures
• disc hemorrhages are critical to find; they often signal a need to lower the target iop
• oct can detect damage years before it shows up on a visual field test
pearl: normal tension glaucoma (ntg): glaucomatous damage with iop always <21 mm hg. requires same treatment principles — target iop reduction 30% from baseline. disc hemorrhage is an independent predictor of progression. rnfl thinning on oct often precedes visual field loss by years.
draw: optic nerve showing vertical cupping, isnt violation, and a splinter drance hemorrhage

name: Pterygium/Pinguecula
symptoms: • irritation, redness, and foreign body sensation
• blurred vision if the lesion induces astigmatism or blocks the visual axis
• cosmetic concern (yellowish bump or fleshy "wing" on the eye)
• often asymptomatic until inflamed by wind, dust, or uv
findings: ## Location
• interpalpebral fissure: almost always at the 3 or 9 o’clock position
• nasal predominance: UV reflected from the nose concentrates on the nasal limbus
## Pinguecula
• yellow-white, fleshy conjunctival lesion adjacent to the limbus
• key: does NOT cross the limbus or involve the cornea
## Pterygium
• triangular, fibrovascular tissue that crosses the limbus onto the cornea
• stocker’s line: yellow-brown iron line on the cornea ahead of the leading edge (indicates stability)
• induced astigmatism: flattening of the cornea (with-the-rule) as it grows
## Complications
• delle: localized corneal thinning/drying adjacent to an elevated lesion
• inflammation: focal injection and dilated "feeder" vessels
etiology: ## Risk factors
• chronic UV/sunlight exposure (the primary driver)
• environmental irritants: wind, dust, sand, and heat
• epidemiology: most common in equatorial "pterygium belt" regions
redFlags: • rapid growth or atypical location (superior/inferior): suspect ossn or cin
• corkscrew vessels or gelatinous surface: suggests ocular surface squamous neoplasia
• visual axis encroachment: requires surgical intervention to prevent permanent vision loss
• restricted motility: if the "pterygium" tethers the eye, consider symblepharon
investigations: ## Slit lamp exam
• measure the distance from the limbus to the leading head (cap) for monitoring
• check for a stocker line and assess the underlying corneal thickness (rule out delle)
## Topography
• essential for documenting irregular astigmatism caused by corneal distortion
## Histopathology
• mandatory: send every excised specimen to pathology to rule out occult malignancy (ossn)
actionSteps: • prescribe UV-protective sunglasses for all patients (primary prevention)
• use topical lubricants for mild symptoms; manage delle with thick ointment
• refer for surgery if the lesion causes astigmatism, blocks vision, or appears atypical
• use conjunctival autograft (cag) during excision to minimize recurrence risk
treatment: ## Conservative
• preservative-free artificial tears: 4–8x/daily
• mild steroids (e.g., fml or loteprednol): for short-term control of inflamed flares
## Surgical (standard of care)
• excision with conjunctival autograft (cag): graft from the superior bulbar conjunctiva
• cag reduces recurrence from ~40% (bare sclera) to ~5%
• amniotic membrane: used if the patient needs to save conjunctiva for future glaucoma surgery
## Adjuvants
• mitomycin c (mmc): used intraoperatively for high-risk recurrent cases
followUp: • asymptomatic: every 6–12 months with photography to track growth
• post-op: monitor for recurrence (usually occurs within the first 6–12 months)
• lifelong: continue strict UV protection to prevent recurrence or new lesions
differentials: • cin/ossn (look for gelatinous, white, or vascular surface)
• pseudopterygium (adhesion from prior trauma or chemical burn; can occur anywhere)
• phlyctenule (inflammatory nodule; usually responds rapidly to steroids)
review: • a pinguecula is purely conjunctival; once it crosses onto the cornea, it is a pterygium
• delle is treated with moisture, not more steroids, which can worsen thinning
• a stocker line is a sign of a "quiet" pterygium that hasn't moved in a while
pearl: a pterygium that crosses 3–4 mm onto the cornea or induces astigmatism should come off — removal with a conjunctival autograft drops recurrence to ~5% and preserves surface biology.
draw: triangular wing-shaped pterygium encroaching on the nasal cornea with a Stocker iron line at the leading edge

name: Purtscher Retinopathy
symptoms: • sudden, severe decrease in vision (often bilateral)
• history of severe compression injury (chest, head, or lower extremities)
• sudden vision loss 24–48 hours after a major systemic event (pancreatitis, fracture)
findings: ## Classic fundus appearance
• Purtscher flecken: pathognomonic polygonal patches of superficial retinal whitening
• perivascular clearing: a "halo" of normal retina immediately surrounding the vessels within whitened areas
• cotton-wool spots (cws): clustered around the optic nerve and macula
• intraretinal hemorrhages: scattered in the posterior pole
## Additional signs
• macular pseudo–cherry-red spot (due to surrounding retinal edema)
• optic disc edema (late) or relative afferent pupillary defect (rapd)
• serous macular detachment or dilated, tortuous vessels
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• microembolic occlusion of peripapillary retinal arterioles
• mechanical or complement-mediated (c5a) leukoembolization
## Classic causes (true Purtscher)
• trauma: severe blunt chest compression (crush), head trauma, or long-bone fractures (fat embolism)
## Non-traumatic (Purtscher-like)
• acute pancreatitis (most common non-traumatic cause)
• systemic lupus erythematosus (sle) or other vasculitides
• obstetric: childbirth, eclampsia, or amniotic fluid embolism
• hematologic: ttp, hellp syndrome, or chronic renal failure
redFlags: • sudden bilateral vision loss after trauma or childbirth
• multiple posterior pole cotton-wool spots without a history of diabetes or htn
• high lipase/amylase: presence of retinopathy in a patient with abdominal pain is diagnostic for pancreatitis-associated Purtscher
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• dilated fundus exam: look for the "flecken" and perivascular sparing
• oct macula: shows inner retinal hyper-reflectivity (edema/ischemia) in acute phase
• fa (fluorescein angiography): demonstrates arteriolar non-perfusion and leakage
## Systemic workup
• labs: lipase, amylase, cbc, coagulation profile, ana, and complement levels
• imaging: chest ct or mri as indicated by the trauma history
actionSteps: • initiate an immediate systemic workup to identify the underlying trigger (e.g., pancreatitis)
• treat the primary systemic cause; ocular symptoms are a manifestation of the systemic insult
• observe: no proven ocular treatment exists; steroids remain controversial
• monitor vision and oct resolution weekly for the first month
treatment: ## Systemic management
• focus entirely on treating the underlying cause (e.g., stabilize fractures, manage pancreatitis)
## Ocular management
• observation: spontaneous recovery of some vision occurs in ~50% of patients
• steroids: iv methylprednisolone is sometimes used in severe cases but lacks strong evidence
• supportive care: referral for low-vision rehabilitation if permanent scotomas persist
followUp: • acute: weekly for 1 month to monitor for secondary complications (like cme)
• chronic: monthly until the retinopathy resolves (usually 1–3 months)
• document: late-stage optic atrophy or retinal thinning on oct
differentials: • central retinal vein occlusion (crvo) — more widespread hemorrhages, "blood and thunder"
• central retinal artery occlusion (crao) — diffuse whitening, no flecken/sparing
review: • Purtscher flecken are distinct from standard cotton-wool spots due to the clear zone around the vessels
• the prognosis is variable; initial visual acuity is the best predictor of long-term outcome
• always check pancreatic enzymes if no trauma is reported
pearl: Purtscher flecken surrounding the disc and macula after trauma, pancreatitis, or childbirth point to complement-mediated arteriolar occlusion — treat the systemic cause and watch the retina recover.
draw: posterior pole showing polygonal white patches (flecken) clustered around the disc with a 50-micron clear zone adjacent to the retinal vessels

name: Retinal Arterial Macroaneurysm
symptoms: • sudden vision loss: typically due to acute hemorrhage (vitreous or macular)
• gradual blurring: caused by chronic exudation and macular edema
• floaters: if blood breaks through into the vitreous cavity
• systemics: almost universally associated with hypertension
findings: ## Demographics & location
• classic profile: elderly women (70s–80s) with chronic hypertension
• anatomy: saccular dilation of a major retinal artery within the first 3 bifurcations
• superotemporal arcade is the most common site (highest pressure/flow)
## Multi-level hemorrhage (near-pathognomonic)
• blood in ≥3 levels: subretinal, intraretinal, and pre-retinal (sub-hyaloid)
• the hemorrhage is centered at an arterial bifurcation or A/V crossing
## Exudative pattern
• "circinate" ring of hard exudates surrounding the aneurysm
• chronic macular edema mimicking diabetic retinopathy
## Natural history
• most RAMs spontaneously thrombose, fibrose, and involute after a bleeding event
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• mechanical shear stress weakens the arterial wall at points of turbulence
• atherosclerosis and chronic hypertension are the primary drivers
• ~30% of cases have a concurrent retinal vein obstruction
redFlags: • multi-level hemorrhage centered on an artery: suggests RAM over other pathologies
• subfoveal hemorrhage: high risk of permanent photoreceptor toxicity; requires displacement
• multiple macroaneurysms: indicates severely uncontrolled systemic hypertension
• premacular sub-hyaloid hemorrhage: can be drained with YAG to speed recovery
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• dilated exam looking for the "light bulb" arterial dilation and circinate exudates
## Imaging
• OCT: essential for tracking macular edema and subretinal blood volume
• ICG Angiography: superior to FA for seeing the RAM through overlying blood
• IVFA: shows focal hyperfluorescence (the aneurysm) with late leakage
## Systemic workup
• mandatory blood pressure check and referral to PCP for cardiovascular management
actionSteps: • measure blood pressure in-office and ensure medical management of hypertension
• observe asymptomatic or peripheral RAMs as they often self-resolve
• consider pneumatic displacement (gas ± tPA) for acute submacular blood
• use focal laser or anti-VEGF for persistent exudation threatening the fovea
treatment: ## Medical & surgical
• observation: for the majority of cases as they tend to self-thrombose
• anti-VEGF: effective for associated macular edema
• focal laser: gentle argon/yellow laser to the aneurysm; avoid the feeding artery
• displacement: intravitreal gas injection to move blood away from the fovea
• vitrectomy: for dense vitreous hemorrhage or thick sub-ILM macular blood
## Systemic
• primary care coordination for aggressive hypertension and lipid control
followUp: • acute phase: monthly until the hemorrhage clears or the aneurysm fibroses
• chronic: every 3–6 months to monitor for recurrent exudation or CME
• vision rehab: if permanent foveal scarring occurs after a major bleed
differentials: • valsalva retinopathy (similar multi-level blood, but no aneurysm)
• diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms are smaller and venous-side)
• coats disease (massive exudation in young males)
• exudative amd (associated with drusen and subretinal neovascularization)
review: • RAM is one of the few conditions that causes blood in three different retinal layers at once
• laser treatment is risky; excessive power can cause the aneurysm to rupture and bleed
• subretinal blood is toxic to the retina within days—displacement is time-sensitive
pearl: Most macroaneurysms self-thrombose and need no treatment — the exception is submacular hemorrhage, where pneumatic displacement with tPA can rescue central vision.
draw: retinal artery with a focal saccular dilation surrounded by a ring of hard exudates and multi-level hemorrhage

name: Retinal Detachment
symptoms: • photopsias (flashes): peripheral light flickers from vitreoretinal traction
• floaters: sudden "cobwebs" or a "shower of black dots" (suggests hemorrhage)
• peripheral curtain: a dark shadow or veil progressing toward central vision
• central vision loss: occurs once the macula detaches ("macula-off")
• shifting field: in exudative RD, the vision defect may move with head position
findings: ## Rhegmatogenous (RRD) - the most common
• corrugated appearance: opaque, convex retina that undulates with eye movement
• retinal break: horseshoe tear, operculated hole, or dialysis seen on depression
• shafer sign ("tobacco dust"): pigment cells in the anterior vitreous
## Tractional (TRD)
• concave & immobile: retina tented up by fibrovascular membranes (e.g., in diabetes)
• no breaks: unless it is a combined tractional-rhegmatogenous detachment
## Exudative/serous (ERD)
• smooth & bullous: subretinal fluid shifts with gravity and head position
• no breaks: often reveals underlying mass, inflammation, or vascular leakage
## General signs
• intraocular pressure (iop): typically lower in the affected eye
• rapd: may be present in large or total detachments
etiology: ## RRD (breaks)
• liquid vitreous enters subretinal space through a break (PVD, lattice, trauma)
## TRD (tension)
• proliferative membranes pull retina off (Diabetes, Sickle Cell, ROP, PVR)
## ERD (fluid)
• neoplastic: choroidal melanoma or metastasis
• inflammatory: VKH syndrome or posterior scleritis
• vascular: malignant hypertension, preeclampsia, or Coats disease
redFlags: • macula-on rrd: a surgical emergency; must be repaired within 24h to save central vision
• sudden floater shower + flashes: requires urgent dilated exam to find a pre-RD tear
• bilateral serous rd + hearing loss/meningismus: suspect VKH syndrome
• bullous rd in pregnancy: immediate workup for preeclampsia/eclampsia
investigations: ## The gold standard
• dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with 360° scleral depression of both eyes
## Imaging
• b-scan ultrasound: mandatory if the retina is obscured by blood or cataract
• oct macula: confirms "on" vs. "off" status and identifies tractional membranes
## Systemic (for ERD)
• blood pressure and urinalysis (to rule out hypertensive emergencies)
• fluorescein angiography (fa) to localize leakage sites or tumors
actionSteps: • immediate vitreoretinal referral for any suspected rrd or symptomatic tear
• position head so the detachment is dependent (gravity-assisted to stay macula-on)
• ensure patient is npo (nothing by mouth) if urgent surgery is anticipated
• restrict activity: no heavy lifting, velsalva, or air travel (if gas is used)
treatment: ## RRD repair
• pneumatic retinopexy: gas bubble + head positioning (for superior breaks)
• scleral buckle: silicone band around the globe (ideal for young/phakic patients)
• pars plana vitrectomy (ppv): removal of vitreous + gas/oil tamponade + laser
## TRD/ERD management
• trd: vitrectomy with membrane peeling; prp laser for underlying ischemia
• erd: do not operate on the retina; treat the systemic/inflammatory cause
followUp: • post-op: typically day 1, week 1, and month 1; then every 3–6 months
• fellow eye: 10% lifetime risk of RD; prophylactic laser for high-risk lesions
• watch for pvr: the leading cause of surgical failure (scarring/redetachment)
differentials: • retinoschisis: smooth dome, absolute scotoma, no undulating movement
• choroidal detachment: dark brown, solid appearance, lower iop
• vitreous hemorrhage: may occur with or without a detachment
review: • rrd requires a break, trd requires a pull, and erd is a leak
• the shafer sign is essentially pathognomonic for a retinal break in an acute PVD
• macula-on detachments are time-sensitive "emergencies"; macula-off are "urgencies"
pearl: Rhegmatogenous RD requires a full-thickness retinal break; tractional RD is tented by fibrovascular traction; exudative RD shifts with gravity and has no break. Shafer sign (pigmented anterior vitreous cells) is the classic pointer to an occult break. Macula status drives urgency: macula-on RRD should be repaired within 24 h. PVR is the leading cause of surgical failure.
draw: fundus showing a corrugated, detached superior retina with a horseshoe tear at 12 o’clock

name: Retinal Tear / Break
symptoms: • photopsias (flashes): bright, brief flickers typically in the peripheral field
• floaters: sudden appearance of "cobwebs", "hairs", or a "film" that moves with the eye
• blurred vision: may occur if there is associated vitreous hemorrhage
• history: often follows an acute posterior vitreous detachment (pvd)
findings: ## Clinical signs
• shafer sign ("tobacco dust"): brown pigmented RPE cells in the anterior vitreous
• horseshoe tear: flap of retina pulled forward by vitreous traction (high risk)
• operculated hole: a "plug" of retina completely pulled free from the surface
• vitreous hemorrhage: ranging from mild "dust" to dense blood
## Chronic features
• pigmented borders: a ring of pigment around a hole suggests it is old and stable
• subretinal fluid (srf): localized fluid around the break (the start of a detachment)
etiology: ## Mechanism
• vitreoretinal traction: the vitreous gel pulls on areas of firm attachment during a PVD
• lattice degeneration: localized thinning of the retina that is prone to holes or tears
## Risk factors
• high myopia (longer eye = thinner retina), trauma, and previous intraocular surgery
• family or personal history of retinal detachment
redFlags: • shafer sign (pigment): ~90% correlation with a retinal break
• horseshoe tear: extremely high risk of progressing to retinal detachment if untreated
• vitreous hemorrhage + acute pvd: 50–70% risk of an underlying tear
• symptomatic fluid: localized detachment surrounding a fresh tear
investigations: ## Exam protocol
• dilated fundus exam with 360° scleral depression is mandatory for both eyes
• slit lamp: check the anterior vitreous specifically for pigment cells
## Imaging
• b-scan ultrasound: essential if vitreous hemorrhage prevents a clear view of the retina
• wide-field photography: useful for documentation and patient education
actionSteps: • refer to ophthalmology within 24 hours for any symptomatic suspected tear
• perform laser retinopexy or cryotherapy to "spot weld" the retina around the break
• counsel patient on detachment signs: "curtain," "shadow," or sudden vision loss
• schedule follow-up to ensure the laser scar is mature and the break is sealed
treatment: ## Retinopexy
• laser retinopexy: 1–3 rows of confluent burns around the break to create a scar
• cryotherapy: cold probe used if the break is too peripheral or media is too hazy for laser
## Conservative management
• atrophic holes: small, round holes in lattice may often be observed if asymptomatic
• lifestyle: avoid heavy lifting or high-impact activities for 2 weeks post-treatment
followUp: • 1–2 weeks: confirm the laser/cryo has pigmented and is holding the retina down
• 1–3 months: ensure no new breaks have developed (common after the initial event)
• annual: regular dilated exams to monitor for new peripheral pathology
differentials: • lattice degeneration (thinning without a full-thickness break)
• vitreous hemorrhage from other causes (e.g., diabetic retinopathy)
• retinoschisis (splitting of retinal layers; usually less urgent)
review: • the shafer sign is essentially RPE cells "leaking" through a hole into the vitreous
• horseshoe tears are more dangerous than round holes because of persistent traction
• laser treatment does not "fix" the tear but glues the edges down to prevent fluid entry
pearl: "Tobacco dust" (Shafer sign) in the anterior vitreous = retinal tear until proven otherwise. Pigmented cells in the vitreous come from the RPE after a full-thickness break. A symptomatic tear without treatment leads to retinal detachment in ~50% within days to weeks.
draw: peripheral retina showing a horseshoe-shaped tear with the flap pulled toward the center of the eye

name: Retinitis Pigmentosa and Inherited Chorioretinal Dystrophies
symptoms: • nyctalopia (night blindness): the earliest and most consistent symptom
• tunnel vision: progressive loss of peripheral visual field over decades
• photophobia: sensitivity to bright lights, often appearing as cones become involved
• central vision loss: typically occurs late in the disease course
• shimmering lights (photopsias): common in the mid-peripheral field
findings: ## Classic fundus triad
• bone-spicule pigmentation: pigment clumps along vessels in the mid-periphery
• attenuated arterioles: threadlike narrowing of the retinal blood vessels
• waxy disc pallor: a yellowish-pale appearance of the optic nerve head
## Imaging & electrophysiology
• full-field erg: defining test; rod responses are extinguished or severely reduced
• oct: shows loss of the "ellipsoid zone" (photoreceptors) starting from the periphery
• autofuorescence: often shows a "hyperautofluorescent ring" surrounding the macula
## Associated ocular signs
• posterior subcapsular cataract: nearly universal in adult patients
• cystoid macular edema (cme): present in 20–40% of cases; a treatable cause of blurring
• vitreous cells: fine pigmented "dust" often visible even before bone spicules
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• primary degeneration of rod photoreceptors followed by secondary cone loss
## Genetics
• extremely heterogeneous: >100 causative genes identified
• inheritance: autosomal recessive (most common), dominant, or x-linked (most severe)
## Syndromic forms
• usher syndrome: rp + sensorineural hearing loss
• bardet-biedl: rp + obesity + polydactyly + renal issues
• kearns-sayre: rp + external ophthalmoplegia + cardiac heart block (potentially fatal)
redFlags: • mandatory usher screen: every pediatric patient with RP needs audiology testing
• treatable blurring: check for cme on oct; it often responds to topical drops
• kearns-sayre: any patient with ptosis/eye movement limits needs an urgent ekg
• vitamin a safety: avoid in stargardt/abca4 disease as it accelerates vision loss
investigations: ## Clinical & functional
• goldmann visual fields: superior to automated perimetry for tracking the ring scotoma
• baseline erg: to distinguish rp from stationary night blindness
## Laboratory & genetic
• genetic testing: now standard of care to identify candidates for gene therapy
• syphilis serology: "pseudo-rp" can be caused by late-stage syphilis
• metabolic screening: phytanic acid (refsum) or lipid panels if syndromic signs exist
actionSteps: • order comprehensive genetic testing to define the specific mutation
• refer to low-vision rehabilitation and mobility training (orientation/mobility)
• screen for and treat cystoid macular edema (cme) with topical drops
• evaluate family members and provide genetic counseling
treatment: ## Medical management
• topical dorzolamide (cai): first-line treatment for cystoid macular edema
• vitamin a palmitate (15,000 iu): controversial; may slow progression in non-smokers
• gene therapy: voretigene neparvovec (luxturna) is fda-approved for biallelic rpe65
## Surgical & supportive
• cataract surgery: can provide significant improvement if the macula is functional
• tinted lenses: help with photophobia and improve contrast in bright environments
• low-vision aids: magnifiers, telescopes, and digital assistive technology
followUp: • annual: comprehensive exam including oct, visual field, and fundus photography
• cardiology: serial ekgs for patients with kearns-sayre syndrome
• audiology: regular checks for usher syndrome patients with hearing aids/implants
differentials: • congenital rubella (salt-and-pepper fundus, but normal erg)
review: • a normal erg essentially rules out the diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa
• bone spicules are formed by rpe cells migrating into the retina to "wrap" around vessels
• tunnel vision is the classic description of the progressive field loss
pearl: Ring scotoma, bone spicules, attenuated vessels, and waxy disc pallor on exam with extinguished ERG is classic RP — but always obtain genetic testing, because gene therapy for RPE65 (Luxturna) is now a reality.
draw: fundus showing bone-spicule pigment in the mid-periphery, thin vessels, and a waxy-looking optic disc
willsRef: Wills Eye §11.28 (Retinitis Pigmentosa and Inherited Chorioretinal Dystrophies)

name: Retinopathy of Prematurity
symptoms: • asymptomatic in neonates: screening is the only way to detect early stages
• leukocoria (white pupil): seen in advanced stage 4 or 5 retinal detachment
• nystagmus or poor tracking: indicates significant bilateral visual impairment
• high myopia: ex-preemies often develop severe nearsightedness as they grow
findings: ## Screening criteria (AAP/AAO)
• birth weight ≤1500 g OR gestational age ≤30 weeks
• first exam: at 31 weeks postmenstrual age or 4 weeks old (whichever is later)
## ICROP-3 classification (2021)
• zones: I (posterior pole), II (mid-periphery), III (temporal crescent)
• stages: 1 (line) → 2 (ridge) → 3 (fibrovascular growth) → 4/5 (detachment)
• plus disease: dilated/tortuous vessels in ≥2 quadrants (the key treatment trigger)
• aggressive rop: flat, rapidly progressive neovascularization in the posterior zone
## Late sequelae
• macular dragging: temporal displacement of the fovea by scar tissue
• lifelong risk: high myopia, strabismus, and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• phase 1: relative hyperoxia after birth halts normal vessel growth
• phase 2: the avascular retina becomes hypoxic and overproduces vegf
• result: abnormal, fragile new vessels grow at the vascular-avascular junction
## Risk factors
• low birth weight and gestational age (most critical factors)
• supplemental oxygen exposure, sepsis, and frequent blood transfusions
redFlags: • plus disease: indicates high metabolic demand; requires treatment within 72h
• zone i stage 3: high risk of rapid progression to detachment
• stage 4/5 (detachment): requires emergent surgical intervention (vitrectomy/buckle)
• missed screening: the window for effective treatment is extremely narrow
investigations: ## Screening protocol
• dilated fundus exam with scleral depression (use speculum and depressor)
• pupil dilation: combined phenylephrine 1% and cyclopentolate 0.2%
## Documentation
• precise recording of zone, stage, extent (clock hours), and plus status
• retinal imaging: wide-field cameras (e.g., RetCam) for baseline and serial follow-up
actionSteps: • initiate screening for all infants meeting weight or age criteria
• coordinate with the NICU to ensure serial exams until vascularization is complete
• perform laser or anti-VEGF injection for Type 1 ROP within 72 hours
• ensure long-term follow-up for late recurrence, especially after anti-VEGF
treatment: ## Type 1 ROP (requires treatment)
• zone i: any stage with plus, or stage 3 without plus
• zone ii: stage 2 or 3 with plus
## Modalities
• laser photocoagulation: ablate the avascular peripheral retina to stop vegf production
• intravitreal anti-vegf (bevacizumab): often first-line for Zone I disease
• surgery: vitrectomy or scleral buckle for stage 4 and 5 detachments
followUp: • weekly: for immature vascularization in Zone I or stage 1/2 in Zone I
• 1–2 weeks: for regressing ROP or immature vascularization in posterior Zone II
• long-term: yearly exams for life to screen for myopia, amblyopia, and retinal tears
• note: anti-VEGF patients need longer follow-up as recurrence can occur months later
differentials: • fevr (familial exudative vitreoretinopathy) — similar appearance but full-term birth
• coats disease (unilateral, usually older male children)
review: • plus disease is the single most important clinical sign for initiating treatment
• treatment does not fix the vessels; it eliminates the stimulus for abnormal growth
• the "macular drag" can cause a pseudo-exotropia appearance (large angle kappa)
pearl: Three ROP epidemics: 1940s-50s (oxygen), 1970s+ (neonatal advances), 1990s+ (LMICs). ICROP3 (2021) classification: zone + stage + vascular characteristics. Plus disease = dilated tortuous vessels in ≥2 quadrants. Anti-VEGF preferred over laser for Zone I disease (lower recurrence, preserves peripheral vascularization). BEWARE reactivation months to years after anti-VEGF. Screening: BW ≤1500g or GA ≤30 weeks.
draw: retinal map showing the three zones (I, II, III) and a ridge of neovascularization at the junction of vascular and avascular retina

name: Retinoschisis
symptoms: • often asymptomatic: frequently an incidental finding during routine exams
• peripheral field loss: noticed as a "blind spot" rather than a "curtain" (absolute scotoma)
• decreased vision: occurs if the schisis involves the macula (juvenile form)
• floaters: rare, unless associated with a vitreous hemorrhage or secondary RD
findings: ## Degenerative (senile) form
• smooth dome: transparent, immobile elevation usually in the inferotemporal periphery
• snowflakes: white crystalline spots on the inner wall (Müller cell footplates)
• sheathed vessels: retinal vessels within the inner wall often appear white or sclerosed
• absolute scotoma: the area of elevation corresponds to a complete lack of light perception
## Juvenile X-linked form
• spoke-wheel maculopathy: cystic spaces radiating from the fovea in a stellate pattern
• negative erg: preserved a-wave but markedly reduced b-wave
• peripheral schisis: present in ~50% of affected males
## Schisis vs. retinal detachment (RD)
• schisis: smooth/tight surface, immobile, absolute scotoma, no "tobacco dust"
• detachment: corrugated/wrinkled surface, undulates with eye movement, relative scotoma
etiology: ## Degenerative
• idiopathic splitting of the retinal layers (usually at the outer plexiform layer)
• strongly associated with hyperopia and older age
## Juvenile X-linked
• mutation in the RS1 gene (retinoschisin protein) essential for cell-to-cell adhesion
• X-linked recessive inheritance (affects males; females are carriers)
redFlags: • outer-layer breaks: high risk for progressing to a schisis-associated retinal detachment
• vitreous hemorrhage: may occur from bridging vessels in the schisis cavity
• progressive encroachment: if the schisis cavity moves toward the fovea
• "tobacco dust" (Shafer sign): if present, indicates a full-thickness tear and RD
investigations: ## Imaging
• oct: the "gold standard" to visualize the layer of splitting and distinguish from RD
• ivfa: shows NO leakage in juvenile foveal schisis (differentiates from true CME)
• visual field: confirms an absolute scotoma in the area of elevation
## Electrophysiology
• erg: essential for juvenile cases; shows a "negative" waveform
actionSteps: • perform a careful dilated exam with scleral depression to rule out retinal breaks
• use OCT to confirm the diagnosis and establish a baseline of the cavity height
• educate the patient on the symptoms of retinal detachment (flashes/new floaters)
• for juvenile cases, consider topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors for macular cysts
treatment: ## Conservative
• observation: most degenerative cases are stable and never require surgery
## Medical (juvenile)
• topical dorzolamide: may reduce foveal cystic spaces and improve visual acuity
## Surgical
• vitrectomy or scleral buckle: reserved for schisis-associated retinal detachments
• laser demarcation: occasionally used if schisis is progressively nearing the macula
followUp: • routine: every 6–12 months with wide-field imaging or photography
• juvenile: more frequent monitoring in childhood to manage potential amblyopia
• post-surgical: follow typical retinal surgery protocols if detachment occurred
differentials: • rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (the most critical differentiator)
• cystoid macular edema (leakage on FA, unlike juvenile schisis)
review: • retinoschisis is a "split" within the retina; a detachment is a "separation" of the whole retina
• "snowflakes" are pathognomonic for schisis and help identify the inner wall
• because it is a split in the neural tissue, the field loss is absolute and permanent
pearl: Retinoschisis has an absolute scotoma, retinal detachment has a relative one — if you cannot tell clinically, B-scan and OCT usually distinguish them, and schisis rarely needs surgery.
draw: OCT cross-section showing a clear split within the retinal layers (usually OPL) with bridging pillars of tissue

name: Retrobulbar Hemorrhage
symptoms: • severe orbital pain and pressure
• sudden, progressive vision loss
• inability to open eyelids due to extreme swelling
• history of recent trauma, eyelid surgery, or orbital injection
• use of anticoagulants (warfarin, eliquis, aspirin)
findings: ## Orbital compartment syndrome (OCS)
• proptosis: "rock hard" globe with total resistance to retropulsion
• tense eyelids: nearly impossible to evert or open manually
• motility: limited extraocular movement in all fields (frozen globe)
• external: diffuse subconjunctival hemorrhage and chemosis
## Optic nerve & vascular signs
• afferent pupillary defect (rapd) and loss of color vision
• intraocular pressure (iop): often >40–50 mmHg
• fundus: disc swelling or pulsations/occlusion of the central retinal artery
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• the orbit is a fixed bony space; rapid bleeding increases pressure
• orbital compartment syndrome: pressure exceeds perfusion, killing the optic nerve
• ischemic tolerance: permanent damage occurs within ~90 minutes
## Common triggers
• trauma (orbital wall fractures, blunt force)
• surgery (blepharoplasty, sinus surgery, retrobulbar blocks)
• spontaneous: in patients with bleeding disorders or severe hypertension
redFlags: • do not wait for imaging: if vision is failing and the globe is "rock hard," decompress immediately
• iop >40 mmHg + rapd: pathognomonic for urgent surgical decompression
• "teardrop" or "tented" globe on ct: indicates the optic nerve is at maximum stretch
investigations: ## Clinical priority
• visual acuity and rapd check: the most important monitoring tools
• iop measurement: confirm elevation to justify surgical intervention
## Imaging (secondary)
• ct orbit (axial/coronal): useful AFTER decompression to find the source
• look for "tenting" of the posterior globe (posterior angle <130°)
actionSteps: • perform emergent lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis at the bedside
• re-check iop immediately after cantholysis; if still high, perform superior cantholysis
• add medical adjuncts: iv mannitol and acetazolamide to lower pressure
• monitor vision every 15 minutes post-procedure until stabilized
treatment: ## Bedside decompression (canthotomy)
• instruments: hemostat, blunt-tipped scissors (stevens/westcott), and toothed forceps
• 1. canthotomy: cut the lateral canthal angle (skin to conjunctiva)
• 2. cantholysis: identify and cut the inferior crus of the canthal tendon
• indicator of success: the lower eyelid should fully release from the globe
## Medical adjuncts
• head elevation (45°) and ice compresses
• iop drops: timolol, brimonidine, or dorzolamide
• systemic: iv methylprednisolone to reduce orbital soft tissue edema
followUp: • monitor in-hospital for 6–12 hours to ensure the hemorrhage has not re-accumulated
• wound care: antibiotic ointment (erythromycin) to the canthotomy site tid
• repair: the site can be left to heal by secondary intention or repaired in 1–2 weeks
• visual fields: check once stable to assess permanent damage
differentials: • orbital cellulitis (fever, elevated wbc, infectious history)
• orbital emphysema (history of sneezing after sinus fracture; crepitus)
review: • canthotomy is just the "doorway"; the cantholysis (cutting the tendon) is the actual decompression
• as long as the eye is "rock hard," pressure is too high for the optic nerve to survive
• if the iop does not drop after the procedure, you likely missed the tendon
pearl: Retrobulbar hemorrhage = orbital compartment syndrome. Vision loss is permanent within 60–90 minutes if untreated. Lateral canthotomy is a life-of-the-eye procedure that any physician must know how to perform.
draw: diagram showing the lateral canthal tendon with the inferior crus being cut to release the tension of the lower eyelid

name: Ruptured Globe / Open Globe
symptoms: • sudden ocular pain and significant decrease in vision
• fluid loss: feeling of "warm liquid" running down the cheek after trauma
• mechanism: hammering metal-on-metal, projectile (BB/pellet), or blunt force
• note: patient report of vision often underestimates the severity of injury
findings: ## Cardinal signs
• seidel-positive wound: fluorescein stream washing away from a corneal/scleral site
• 360° subconjunctival hemorrhage: "hemorrhagic chemosis" can hide a rupture
• peaked pupil: the iris points toward the site of the full-thickness wound
• chamber depth: shallow AC (anterior rupture) or deep AC (posterior rupture)
## Direct visualization
• uveal prolapse: dark/brown tissue (iris or choroid) protruding through the wound
• hyphema or vitreous hemorrhage: blood filling the anterior or posterior segments
## Occult rupture
• low iop + irregular pupil + blunt trauma: highly suspicious for posterior rupture
etiology: ## Mechanisms of injury
• penetrating/perforating: sharp objects, glass, or high-velocity projectiles
• blunt rupture: severe impact causes the globe to burst at its thinnest points (limbus/equator)
• iatrogenic/surgical: prior surgeries like RK or large-incision cataract surgery weaken the eye
• hammering: classic history for an intraocular foreign body (IOFB)
redFlags: • do not measure iop: any pressure on the globe can express intraocular contents
• do not force eyelids open: if the globe is open, external pressure is catastrophic
• seidel sign: indicates a continuous leak of aqueous from the eye
• 360° blood: always assume a hidden scleral rupture until proven otherwise
investigations: ## Imaging
• ct orbits (thin cuts): the "gold standard" to rule out IOFB and localize the rupture
• mri: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED if there is any chance of a metallic foreign body
• b-scan: generally avoided in the acute phase to prevent pressure on the globe
## Clinical assessment
• assess light perception (LP) and pupil function before any surgical manipulation
actionSteps: • place a rigid shield (Fox shield) immediately—do NOT use a pressure patch
• make the patient NPO (nothing by mouth) for emergent surgical repair
• administer antiemetics: prevent vomiting/Valsalva which increases intraocular pressure
• start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., Vancomycin + Ceftazidime)
treatment: ## Surgical management
• primary repair within 24 hours to significantly reduce the risk of endophthalmitis
• suturing: watertight closure of corneal (10-0 nylon) and scleral (8-0/9-0 silk/nylon) wounds
• uveal tissue: restore viable tissue or excise if severely necrotic/contaminated
## Systemic support
• tetanus prophylaxis based on immunization history
• post-operative antibiotics and close monitoring for signs of infection
followUp: • daily exams for the first week to monitor for endophthalmitis
• monitor for retinal detachment: high risk following any open globe injury
• sympathetic ophthalmia: watch for bilateral inflammation in the weeks/years following trauma
• long-term: visual rehabilitation with specialty lenses or secondary surgeries
differentials: • retrobulbar hemorrhage (proptosis and high IOP, but globe remains intact)
review: • "no pressure, no drops, no iop" is the mantra for any suspected open globe
• iris tissue often plugs a wound, leading to the characteristic "peaked" pupil shape
• ct is essential to rule out an IOFB, which can cause siderosis or endophthalmitis
pearl: In any suspected open globe: cover with a rigid shield, no pressure, NPO, tetanus, IV antibiotics, and to the operating room. Do NOT measure IOP, force open eyelids, or apply topical drops. Seidel-positive wound, 360° subconjunctival hemorrhage, peaked pupil, and deep or shallow AC are the cardinal signs — any one warrants CT and surgical exploration.
draw: eye with a peaked pupil pointing toward a limbal wound with iris prolapse

name: Sarcoidosis
symptoms: • blurred vision and floaters: common in intermediate or posterior involvement
• ocular pain & photophobia: typically seen in acute anterior uveitis flares
• dryness: "gritty" sensation due to lacrimal gland infiltration
• systemic: chronic cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and skin rashes
• neuro: facial drooping (CN VII palsy) or unexplained headaches
findings: ## Anterior segment
• "mutton-fat" kps: large, greasy, yellow-white deposits on the corneal endothelium
• iris nodules: koeppe (pupillary margin) and busacca (iris stroma) nodules
• trabecular meshwork nodules: seen on gonioscopy; may cause "tent-shaped" synechiae
## Posterior segment & vitreous
• "string-of-pearls": inferior vitreous snowballs or opacities in a linear chain
• "candle-wax drippings": segmental, waxy yellow perivasculitis (periphlebitis)
• optic nerve: granulomas on the disc or significant disc edema
## Adnexa
• lacrimal gland enlargement: often bilateral and painless
• conjunctival granulomas: small, yellow-pink "millet-seed" nodules in the fornix
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• multisystem inflammatory disease involving non-caseating granulomas
• the "great mimicker": can present as anterior, intermediate, posterior, or panuveitis
## Demographics
• bimodal peaks: ages 20–40 and 60–70; higher prevalence in African American and Northern European populations
• blau syndrome: a rare pediatric genetic variant (NOD2) with uveitis, rash, and arthritis
redFlags: • neuro-sarcoidosis: optic nerve granulomas or cns involvement require immediate systemic steroids
• cardiac sarcoid: must rule out fatal arrhythmias or heart block with an EKG/cardiology referral
• candle-wax drippings: highly specific for sarcoid vasculitis; suggests active posterior disease
• heerfordt syndrome: the triad of uveitis, parotid swelling, and facial nerve palsy
investigations: ## Laboratory
• serum ace & lysozyme: markers of total granuloma burden; often elevated in active disease
• quantiferon-tb gold: mandatory to rule out TB before starting steroids (mimics sarcoid)
## Imaging
• chest ct (hrct): significantly more sensitive than CXR for hilar lymphadenopathy
• gallium scan: may show the "panda sign" (uptake in lacrimal, parotid, and salivary glands)
## Tissue diagnosis
• biopsy: non-caseating granulomas from conjunctiva or skin is the diagnostic gold standard
actionSteps: • order chest imaging (HRCT preferred) and serum ACE/Lysozyme levels
• screen for TB (QuantiFERON) and Syphilis (RPR/FTA-ABS) to exclude mimics
• initiate aggressive topical steroids and cycloplegia for anterior segment inflammation
• refer to pulmonology and cardiology for systemic staging (EKG, PFTs)
treatment: ## Local therapy
• topical: prednisolone acetate 1% (frequently, e.g., q1h–qid) and cyclopentolate tid
• periocular: sub-Tenon triamcinolone for unilateral macular edema or posterior disease
## Systemic therapy
• oral prednisone: 1 mg/kg/day for severe, bilateral, or neuro-involvement
• steroid-sparing: methotrexate, mycophenolate, or adalimumab (Humira) for chronic control
## Surgical
• monitor for and treat secondary glaucoma and steroid-induced cataracts
followUp: • acute: weekly to ensure inflammation is resolving and iop is stable
• chronic: every 3–6 months once quiet to monitor for cystoid macular edema (cme)
• co-management: shared care with rheumatology for long-term immunosuppression monitoring
differentials: • ocular tuberculosis (caseating granulomas, positive TB test)
• syphilis (the other "great mimicker"; check treponemal antibodies)
• vkh syndrome (bilateral serous detachments, usually non-granulomatous)
review: • if the ACE level is normal but suspicion is high, remember that ACE inhibitors (for HTN) lower ACE levels
• "candle-wax drippings" are formally known as segmental periphlebitis
• sarcoid is a diagnosis of exclusion—you must rule out TB and Syphilis first
pearl: Sarcoid uveitis can involve any ocular structure — granulomatous KPs, candle-wax drippings, segmental vasculitis, and optic-nerve granuloma are all red flags; chest CT and ACE usually seal the diagnosis.
draw: fundus view showing yellow-white waxy exudates (candle-wax) along the retinal veins and mutton-fat KPs on the cornea

name: Scleritis
symptoms: • severe, boring eye pain: often radiates to the forehead, jaw, or sinuses
• nocturnal awakening: the pain is classically severe enough to wake the patient from sleep
• pain with movement: discomfort worsens with eye movement and palpation of the globe
• gradual or acute redness: the eye often develops a deep, violaceous (purple) hue
• tearing and photophobia: common associated symptoms; vision may also be decreased
findings: ## Anterior segment
• deep scleral injection: large, deep vessels that do NOT blanch with 10% phenylephrine
• violaceous hue: a characteristic purple color seen best under natural sunlight
• scleral edema: may be diffuse, sectoral, or manifest as a localized nodule
• immobility: unlike episcleral vessels, scleral vessels cannot be moved with a cotton swab
## Necrotizing features
• scleral thinning: the underlying dark uvea becomes visible through the translucent sclera
• avascular patches: areas where the superficial and deep vascular plexuses are missing
## Posterior scleritis
• t-sign on b-scan: fluid in Tenon’s space and optic nerve sheath thickening
• fundus signs: choroidal folds, disc edema, or an exudative retinal detachment
etiology: ## Systemic associations (~50%)
• rheumatoid arthritis (ra): the most common underlying systemic cause
• gpa (wegener granulomatosis): often associated with more severe, necrotizing forms
• relapsing polychondritis: look for inflamed cartilage (ears or nose)
• inflammatory bowel disease (ibd) and systemic lupus erythematosus (sle)
## Infectious & traumatic
• infectious: herpes zoster, syphilis, tuberculosis, or pseudomonas (post-surgery)
• surgical: history of pterygium surgery with Mitomycin-C or scleral buckle
redFlags: • necrotizing scleritis: a medical emergency with high mortality if systemic vasculitis is present
• scleromalacia perforans: painless scleral melting; classic in long-standing RA
• posterior scleritis: can mimic a choroidal tumor; check for the "T-sign" on B-scan
• phenylephrine failure: if the redness persists after drops, it is scleritis, not episcleritis
investigations: ## The phenylephrine test
• apply 2.5% or 10% phenylephrine; episcleritis blanches, scleritis does not
## Imaging
• b-scan ultrasound: mandatory if posterior scleritis is suspected (look for T-sign)
## Systemic workup (rheumatology panel)
• labs: cbc, esr, crp, rf, anti-ccp, ana, anca (c-ANCA/p-ANCA), ace
• infectious: rpr/fta-abs (syphilis), quantiferon-tb gold, chest x-ray
actionSteps: • differentiate from episcleritis using the phenylephrine blanching test
• initiate systemic nsaids (e.g., indomethacin) for non-necrotizing disease
• refer to ophthalmology and rheumatology for a comprehensive systemic evaluation
• protect the globe: if thinning is severe, prescribe protective eye shields or glasses
treatment: ## Non-necrotizing
• oral nsaids: indomethacin 50 mg tid (with a ppi for stomach protection)
• oral steroids: prednisone (60–80 mg) if nsaids fail or if disease is bilateral
## Necrotizing or refractory
• aggressive immunosuppression: methotrexate, mycophenolate, or biologics (anti-tnfα)
• iv steroids: pulse methylprednisolone for sight-threatening or severe pain
## Contraindications
• avoid subconjunctival steroid injections in necrotizing cases (risk of perforation)
followUp: • weekly: initially to monitor for response and ensure no progression to necrosis
• long-term: periodic monitoring of iop (steroid response) and scleral thickness
• coordination: close communication with a rheumatologist for systemic management
differentials: • episcleritis (blanches with phenylephrine, minimal pain, no bluish hue)
review: • scleritis pain is "boring" (like a drill) and often wakes patients up at 3:00 AM
• the "violaceous hue" is caused by congestion of the deep episcleral vascular plexus
• scleromalacia perforans is unique because it causes severe thinning without pain
pearl: Scleritis is associated with systemic disease in 50% — most commonly rheumatoid arthritis (the most common association), GPA (Wegener granulomatosis), relapsing polychondritis, IBD. Necrotizing scleritis without inflammation (scleromalacia perforans) occurs in long-standing RA with high mortality. Always phenylephrine test: blanches episcleritis (superficial), not scleritis.
draw: eye showing a localized deep purple patch on the sclera with large, non-blanching vessels

name: Sickle Cell Retinopathy (Including Sickle Cell Disease, Anemia, and Trait)
symptoms: • asymptomatic: peripheral lesions are often silent until a complication occurs
• floaters: sudden "cobwebs" or spots usually indicate a vitreous hemorrhage
• flashes & shadows: may signal the onset of a tractional retinal detachment
• systemic: history of painful crises, acute chest syndrome, or joint pain
findings: ## Proliferative (Goldberg staging)
• stage i: peripheral arteriolar occlusions ("silver-wire" vessels)
• stage ii: peripheral a-v anastomoses (loops shunting blood around dead zones)
• stage iii: "sea fan" neovascularization (fan-shaped fronds at the periphery)
• stage iv: vitreous hemorrhage
• stage v: tractional retinal detachment
## Non-proliferative signs
• salmon patch: pink-orange superficial hemorrhage (resolves to leave a scar)
• black sunburst: pigmented chorioretinal scar from an old hemorrhage
• comma vessels: sickle-shaped capillaries in the inferior bulbar conjunctiva
• macular thinning: temporal macular thinning often seen on OCT
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• abnormal hb causes rbcs to sickle in the low-oxygen environment of the peripheral retina
• vessel occlusion → ischemia → vegf release → neovascularization ("sea fans")
## The SC paradox
• hbsc and hb sβ-thal: have more severe eye disease (higher blood viscosity)
• hbss: has more severe systemic crises but less retinopathy (auto-infarction of vessels)
redFlags: • sea fans (stage 3): high risk for hemorrhage; requires prophylactic laser
• hyphema + sickle: medical emergency; avoid systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (cais)
• tractional rd: requires advanced surgical intervention by a retina specialist
• sickle trait (hbas) + trauma: can still develop severe retinopathy and high iop
investigations: ## Ocular imaging
• widefield fluorescein angiography (fa): the gold standard for staging non-perfusion
• oct: used to detect "the maculopathy of sickle cell" (temporal thinning)
## Systemic workup
• hemoglobin electrophoresis: essential to define the specific genotype (SS vs SC)
• cbc and reticulocyte count: to monitor systemic disease activity
actionSteps: • screen sc and sβ-thal patients annually starting at age 10
• perform widefield fa to identify peripheral "sea fans" or areas of non-perfusion
• treat stage 3 disease with peripheral scatter laser photocoagulation
• coordinate care with hematology for systemic optimization (e.g., hydroxyurea)
treatment: ## Proliferative disease
• scatter laser: ablate the ischemic peripheral retina to regress sea fans
• anti-vegf: useful as an adjunct to laser or prior to vitrectomy to reduce bleeding
## Surgical
• vitrectomy: indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional detachment
## Systemic
• hydration and oxygenation: critical during any ocular crisis or surgery
• caution: avoid acetazolamide (diamox) as it promotes sickling via acidosis
followUp: • routine: every 6–12 months for SC/S-Thal; every 1–2 years for SS
• post-laser: check at 1 month to ensure regression of neovascular fronds
• hematology: ensure the patient is on appropriate systemic management
differentials: • diabetic retinopathy (central dot-blot hemorrhages vs peripheral sickle fans)
• talc retinopathy (refractile crystals in the macula of iv drug users)
• fevr (genetic, peripheral non-perfusion in younger patients)
review: • "sea fans" grow at the junction of perfused and non-perfused retina
• sea fans in sickle cell can "auto-infarct," but they usually bleed first
• the comma-shaped conjunctival vessels are a quick clinical "clue" to the diagnosis
pearl: Proliferative sickle retinopathy is paradoxically most common in SC, not SS — screen SC patients yearly from age 10, and sector laser arrests sea fans before they bleed.
draw: peripheral retinal view showing a fan-shaped cluster of new vessels (sea fan) at the edge of an avascular zone
willsRef: Wills Eye §11.20 (Sickle Cell Retinopathy (Including Sickle Cell Disease, Anemia, and Trait))

name: Solar or Photic Retinopathy
symptoms: • blurred vision: typically a sudden drop in central acuity after exposure
• central scotoma: a blind spot or "shimmering" patch in the center of vision
• metamorphopsia: straight lines appearing wavy or distorted (Amsler grid)
• dyschromatopsia: altered color perception, especially in the central field
• bilateralism: usually affects both eyes if exposure was environmental (e.g., eclipse)
findings: ## Acute phase (hours to days)
• yellow-white spot: a tiny, focal opacification at the center of the fovea
• foveal granularity: subtle pigmentary changes surrounding the acute injury
## Chronic phase (weeks to months)
• red foveolar depression: the yellow spot fades, leaving a sharply defined red "pit"
• lamellar hole: a permanent loss of tissue in the outer retinal layers
## OCT (diagnostic hallmark)
• outer retinal disruption: focal loss of the ellipsoid zone (EZ) and interdigitation zone
• outer retinal cavity: a hyporeflective "hole" in the photoreceptor layer
• preservation: the inner retinal layers (closer to the vitreous) remain intact
## Autofluorescence
• hyperautofluorescence initially (RPE stress), followed by a hypoautofluorescent "burn" spot
etiology: ## Mechanism
• photochemical injury: short-wavelength (blue) and near-UV light create free radicals
• focal concentration: the eye's lens acts as a magnifying glass, focusing light on the fovea
## Common exposures
• solar eclipse viewing: looking at the sun without ISO-certified filters
• sungazing: often related to ritual, psychiatric illness, or hallucinogen use
• occupational: arc welding without a shield or professional astronomy
• high-power lasers: recreational laser pointers (especially blue/green) in children
redFlags: • eclipse viewing: any history of unprotected viewing followed by vision loss
• arc welding: "welder’s flash" can involve both the cornea (keratitis) and retina
• persistent scotoma: if visual recovery stalls after 6 months, the damage is likely permanent
• laser pointers: high-wattage non-toy lasers can cause immediate, irreversible burns
investigations: ## History
• specific questioning about sun exposure, eclipse dates, or laser pointer play
## Clinical testing
• amsler grid: to map the location and severity of the central scotoma
• sd-oct: mandatory to visualize the characteristic "punched-out" outer retinal defect
## Electrophysiology
• multifocal erg: can document reduced foveal function even if the fundus looks near-normal
actionSteps: • obtain an OCT to confirm focal disruption of the outer retinal layers
• observe: most patients experience significant spontaneous recovery over 3–6 months
• educate: provide strict counseling on UV protection and the dangers of sun-gazing
• rehabilitate: refer for low-vision aids if a central scotoma interferes with reading
treatment: ## Management
• no proven medical cure: treatment is primarily observational
• steroids: sometimes used in severe acute cases, but evidence for benefit is limited
## Prevention
• use ISO 12312-2 certified eclipse glasses for any solar viewing
• ensure appropriate shade-rated filters for all welding activities
• strictly regulate high-power laser pointers as they are not toys
followUp: • 1 month & 3 months: repeat OCT to track the maturation of the foveal "hole"
• prognosis: vision often recovers to 20/20–20/40, but the scotoma may persist
• long-term: yearly exams to monitor for late-stage RPE changes
differentials: • central serous chorioretinopathy (fluid under the retina, not a tissue defect)
• stargardt disease (bilateral flecks and progressive "beaten bronze" macula)
review: • the damage is photochemical, not thermal—it is essentially a "foveal sunburn"
• visual acuity often returns to near-normal, but the "blind spot" in the center remains
• it is a "punched-out" defect of the photoreceptors, while the RPE may or may not survive
pearl: A foveal "hot spot" after sun-gazing or a laser pointer is solar retinopathy — there is no treatment, prognosis is fair, and prevention (eclipse glasses, welding filters) is the real lesson.
draw: OCT cross-section of the fovea showing a small, discrete break in the bright ellipsoid zone line while the upper layers are normal

name: Staphylococcal Hypersensitivity
symptoms: • mild photophobia and discomfort: usually less severe than infectious ulcers
• localized redness: often sectoral, matching the location of the infiltrate
• lid crusting: "morning mattering" and greasy debris on the lashes
• foreign body sensation: a gritty feeling exacerbated by lid movement
• recurrence: history of multiple "styes" (chalazia) or similar red-eye episodes
findings: ## Marginal infiltrates
• "lucid interval": a clear, uninflamed strip of cornea separates the infiltrate from the limbus (diagnostic hallmark)
• 2, 4, 8, 10 o’clock: infiltrates occur where the eyelid margins rest on the cornea
• appearance: small (0.5–2.0 mm) white-gray subepithelial stromal opacities
• staining: may show overlying punctate staining or a small epithelial defect
## Eyelid disease (mandatory)
• blepharitis: lash-base collarettes (crusts) and telangiectatic lid margins
• mgd: "pouting" or capped meibomian glands with thickened, toothpaste-like secretions
• rosacea: look for facial flushing, telangiectasias on the nose/cheeks, or rhinophyma
## Phlyctenulosis
• a raised, vascularized nodule at the limbus that "walks" toward the central cornea
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• type iii & iv hypersensitivity: it is a sterile immune reaction, NOT an active infection
• mechanism: staphylococcal antigens from the lid diffuse into the peripheral cornea
• the reaction: antigens meet antibodies from limbal vessels, forming immune complexes
• result: recruitment of inflammatory cells (PMNs) into the corneal stroma
redFlags: • infiltrate abutting the limbus: lack of a "lucid interval" suggests infectious keratitis
• hypopyon or severe ac reaction: sterile infiltrates should not have pus in the chamber
• madarosis (loss of lashes): may indicate a more serious lid malignancy (sebaceous cell)
• phlyctenules in children: can be a rare sign of systemic Tuberculosis—rule out TB
investigations: ## Clinical examination
• slit lamp: carefully document the distance between the infiltrate and the limbus
• lid eversion: check for meibomian gland health and presence of chalazia
## Cultures
• only indicated if the diagnosis is ambiguous or the lesion is atypical (e.g., central or touching the limbus)
actionSteps: • initiate aggressive lid hygiene (warm compresses and lid scrubs)
• use a combination topical antibiotic/steroid (e.g., Tobradex) for rapid relief
• apply antibiotic ointment (erythromycin) to the lash line at bedtime
• treat underlying ocular rosacea with systemic doxycycline if necessary
treatment: ## Topical management
• steroid: low-potency (e.g., fluorometholone or loteprednol) to quiet the immune response
• antibiotic: prophylactic cover (e.g., erythromycin ointment) to reduce bacterial load on the lids
## Systemic (for rosacea/MGD)
• doxycycline: 50–100 mg bid; acts by inhibiting bacterial lipases and reducing inflammation
• note: children < 8 years old should use oral erythromycin instead of tetracyclines
## Maintenance
• lifelong lid hygiene is required to prevent "the rule of recurrence"
followUp: • 1 week: to ensure the infiltrate is regressing and the epithelium is intact
• chronic: 3–6 month intervals once the lid disease is under control
• education: emphasize that steroids are for the "flare," but lid hygiene is for "life"
differentials: • infectious marginal keratitis (no lucid interval, more pain, touches the limbus)
• cat-scratch disease or other granulomatous conjunctivitis
• peripheral ulcerative keratitis (puk) associated with RA or GPA
review: • if the infiltrate touches the limbus, it is an infection until proven otherwise
• "collarettes" at the base of the lashes are like a "smoking gun" for staph involvement
• the "lucid interval" exists because the antigen concentration drops off before it reaches the blood supply
pearl: Marginal infiltrates with a clear zone from the limbus are sterile immune responses to staph exotoxins — treat the lid margin, not just the cornea.
draw: diagram showing white infiltrates at 4 and 8 o’clock with a clear space between the white spot and the corneal edge

name: Stargardt Disease (Fundus Flavimaculatus)
symptoms: • central vision loss: progressive decline in childhood or early adulthood (ages 10–20)
• "malingerer" pitfall: vision is often 20/100+ while the fundus still looks near-normal
• reading difficulty: letters disappear or become blurry (central scotoma)
• color vision changes: subtle difficulty distinguishing hues as the fovea atrophies
• light sensitivity: discomfort in bright environments (photophobia)
findings: ## Classic clinical triad
• pisciform flecks: yellow-white "fish-tail" spots at the RPE level in the posterior pole
• beaten-bronze macula: a dull, metallic, mottled sheen at the fovea (earliest sign)
• bull’s-eye maculopathy: a ring of RPE atrophy around a central foveal island
## Diagnostic imaging
• "silent choroid" (ivfa): excess lipofuscin blocks the choroidal flush, creating a dark background
• faf (autofluorescence): flecks are hyperautofluorescent; atrophy is hypoautofluorescent
• oct: loss of the ellipsoid zone and outer nuclear layer at the fovea
## Electrophysiology
• erg: typically normal early on (unlike cone dystrophy), confirming it is a macular disease
• eog: often subnormal (reduced Arden ratio); indicates widespread RPE dysfunction
etiology: ## Genetics & pathophysiology
• inheritance: primarily autosomal recessive (ABCA4 gene mutation)
• mechanism: defective "flippase" protein prevents clearance of vitamin A byproducts
• toxic buildup: accumulation of lipofuscin (A2E) in the RPE leads to cell death
• fundus flavimaculatus: a later-onset variant with widespread flecks and slower vision loss
redFlags: • vitamin a warning: strictly avoid megadose vitamin a or AREDS; it accelerates A2E buildup
• rapid decline: if vision drops significantly, assess for secondary choroidal neovascularization
• family screening: siblings of an affected child have a 25% risk of having the disease
• blue light: theoretical risk of accelerating damage; UV-blocking lenses are recommended
investigations: ## Primary workup
• genetic testing: sequencing the abca4 gene is the definitive diagnostic step
• fundus autofluorescence (faf): the most sensitive non-invasive tool for monitoring flecks
• widefield fa: look for the pathognomonic "midnight fundus" (silent choroid)
## Functional testing
• amsler grid: to monitor for central scotoma and metamorphopsia
• goldmann visual field: to check for central scotomata and peripheral preservation
actionSteps: • perform FAF and OCT to confirm macular atrophy and RPE lipofuscin deposits
• order genetic testing for ABCA4 to guide management and clinical trial eligibility
• counsel the patient and family to avoid high-dose Vitamin A supplements
• refer to a low-vision specialist for magnifiers and educational/occupational aids
treatment: ## Management strategy
• observation: no currently approved treatment to reverse or stop the disease
• protective: use UV-blocking tinted sunglasses (yellow/amber) to reduce phototoxicity
• medical avoidance: ensure the patient is NOT taking AREDS-type multivitamins
## Emerging therapies
• clinical trials: deuterated vitamin A (ALK-001), gene therapy, and stem cell research
• visual rehab: eccentric viewing training to use the "para-foveal" retina for reading
followUp: • annual: comprehensive exam with OCT and FAF to track atrophy progression
• psychosocial: provide resources for visually impaired students/adults
• genetic counseling: discuss inheritance patterns and risks for future offspring
differentials: • chloroquine toxicity (history of Plaquenil use, similar bull’s-eye appearance)
• best disease (autosomal dominant, distinct "egg-yolk" lesion, abnormal EOG)
• fundus albipunctatus (night blindness, stationary flecks, normal vision)
review: • Stargardt is the most common inherited macular dystrophy in pediatric populations
• the "silent choroid" on IVFA is present in about 85% of cases
• children are often called "malingerers" because they cannot see 20/20 but the eye looks normal
pearl: A "beaten-bronze" fovea with peripheral pisciform flecks in an adolescent is Stargardt — ABCA4 is the gene, and vitamin A supplementation may accelerate disease, so avoid it.
draw: fundus showing a ring-like bull’s-eye maculopathy and yellow "fish-tail" flecks in the periphery

name: Strabismus Syndromes
symptoms: • abnormal eye position: usually noted by parents in early infancy or childhood
• compensatory head posture: face turns, chin tilts, or head tilts to maintain single vision
• absence of diplopia: children usually suppress the deviating eye, avoiding double vision
• stable/non-progressive: unlike tumors or neuro diseases, these are typically birth-onset and static
• face turn in duane type i: child turns face TOWARD the affected eye to align the eyes in primary gaze
findings: ## Duane retraction syndrome (DURS)
• pathognomonic sign: globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction
• type i (80%): limited abduction (looks like a VI palsy), esotropic in primary gaze
• type ii: limited adduction; exotropic in primary gaze
• type iii: limited both abduction and adduction
• leash effect: dramatic upshoots or downshoots of the eye during adduction
## Brown syndrome (SO tendon sheath syndrome)
• restricted elevation in adduction: the eye cannot look up and in, but elevation is NORMAL in abduction
• v-pattern: often shows a V-pattern exotropia in upgaze
## Möbius syndrome
• mask-like facies: bilateral CN VII palsy (cannot smile or close eyes tightly)
• horizontal gaze palsy: bilateral CN VI palsy (eyes fixed in or limited horizontally)
## Other syndromes
• marcus gunn jaw-winking: ptosis that improves/elevates when the child opens their mouth or chews
• cfeom: bilateral ptosis with eyes fixed in a downward ("chin-up") gaze
etiology: ## Congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders (CCDDs)
• duane: failure of the CN VI nucleus; the lateral rectus is aberrantly innervated by branches of CN III
• brown: mechanical restriction—the superior oblique tendon is too short or caught in the trochlea
• möbius: developmental failure of the brainstem nuclei (CN VI and VII)
• marcus gunn: "miswiring" between the CN V (jaw muscles) and the CN III (levator muscle)
redFlags: • adult-onset: new "syndrome-like" features in an adult are NEVER congenital; rule out tumor or MG
• positive forced duction: indicates a physical/mechanical restriction (like Brown or Entrapment)
• negative forced duction: indicates an innervational/paretic problem (like Duane or Nerve Palsy)
• progressive worsening: congenital syndromes should be stable; change warrants neuroimaging
investigations: ## Motility testing
• 9 cardinal positions: document exactly where the "block" or "retraction" occurs
• versions vs. ductions: check if the limitation is the same in both eyes or just one
## The "gold standard"
• forced duction test: physically moving the eye with forceps (usually under anesthesia) to find a "tug"
## Refraction
• cycloplegic refraction: must rule out accommodative esotropia (high hyperopia)
actionSteps: • treat amblyopia (patching or atropine) as the first priority—surgery does not fix "lazy eye"
• prescribe full cycloplegic glasses if significant refractive error is found
• document the degree of head tilt/turn; plan surgery if >15° or causing neck pain
• refer to a pediatric ophthalmologist for specialized surgical planning
treatment: ## Surgical rules
• duane syndrome: medial rectus recession to fix face turn; NEVER resect the lateral rectus (worsens retraction)
• brown syndrome: superior oblique tenotomy or expander if the primary gaze is affected
## Ptosis & winking
• marcus gunn: levator excision and frontalis sling if the "wink" is cosmetically severe
• cfeom: frontalis suspension to lift the lids and muscle recessions to center the eyes
followUp: • q3–6 months: during the "plastic" period of vision development (up to age 9) to monitor amblyopia
• post-op: 1 week, 1 month, and 6 months to check for "drift" or overcorrection
• annual: once the child is visually mature and alignment is stable
differentials: • abducens (vi) nerve palsy (no retraction on adduction; usually trauma or viral-onset)
• thyroid eye disease (restrictive, usually older patients)
• orbital blowout fracture (history of trauma, entrapment on forced ductions)
