• myasthenia gravis (variable, tired lids, fluctuating diplopia)
review: • in Duane, the "narrowing" of the eye on adduction is the lateral rectus pulling at the same time as the medial
• the easiest way to tell Brown from a Superior Rectus palsy is that Brown is only limited when looking *in*
• surgery in these cases is about fixing the "head position," not just making the eyes look straight
pearl: The unifying feature of strabismus syndromes is CONGENITAL, NON-PROGRESSIVE aberrant innervation or mechanical restriction. Duane is the most common (~80% type I, limited abduction). The pathognomonic Duane sign is globe retraction + palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction. Brown syndrome has a POSITIVE forced duction (mechanical); Duane has a NEGATIVE forced duction (innervational). NEVER resect the lateral rectus in Duane — it worsens retraction.
draw: diagram showing an eye retracting into the socket and the eyelid closing slightly when the eye looks toward the nose

name: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage
symptoms: • painless red eye: often discovered incidentally in the mirror or by a peer
• asymptomatic: vision is normal, there is no discharge, and no photophobia
• mild irritation: a slight foreign body sensation or "tightness" if the hemorrhage is large
• no itching: helps distinguish it from allergic conjunctivitis
findings: ## Clinical appearance
• blood under conjunctiva: a sharply demarcated, bright-red flat patch
• color evolution: turns yellow, green, or brown over 1–3 weeks (like a bruise)
• posterior margin: if you can see the back edge of the blood, it’s likely local; if not, consider an orbital source
## Warning signs
• 360° bullous hemorrhage: an elevated "bag of blood" after trauma suggests a ruptured globe until proven otherwise
• chemosis: swelling of the conjunctiva over the blood suggests a higher-pressure event or trauma
• recurrent same-site: look for underlying vascular lesions like lymphangiectasia or Kaposi Sarcoma
etiology: ## Valsalva & mechanical
• sudden pressure: coughing, sneezing, vomiting, or straining (lifting/constipation)
• eye rubbing: common in patients with dry eyes or allergies
## Systemic factors
• hypertension: a frequent "silent" trigger for spontaneous vessel rupture
• medications: aspirin, clopidogrel, or anticoagulants (warfarin, apixaban)
• bleeding disorders: thrombocytopenia or clotting factor deficiencies (rare)
redFlags: • 360° bullous hemorrhage + trauma: treat as an open globe; rigid shield and NPO immediately
• bilateral/spontaneous in a child: must rule out non-accidental trauma or leukemia
• recurrent episodes: warrants checking blood pressure and basic coagulation (PT/PTT)
• trauma + restricted motility: rule out orbital fracture or retrobulbar hemorrhage
investigations: ## Primary checks
• blood pressure: the most important systemic vital to check in the office
• slit lamp: confirm the hemorrhage is flat and check for associated trauma (abrasions, hyphema)
## Laboratory (for recurrent/bilateral)
• cbc with smear: to rule out low platelets or leukemia
• coag panel: PT, PTT, and INR (especially if the patient is on Warfarin)
## Imaging
• orbital ct: only if trauma is present or if there is no visible posterior margin of the blood
actionSteps: • reassure the patient: most cases resolve spontaneously in 2 weeks
• measure blood pressure to screen for hypertensive crisis
• screen for Valsalva triggers (e.g., chronic cough or constipation)
• if trauma is involved, perform a dilated fundus exam to rule out internal eye damage
treatment: ## Observation
• spontaneous resolution: no treatment is required; it "clears" like a bruise
• artificial tears: for comfort if the patient feels a "lump" or dryness
## Systemic management
• do NOT stop essential blood thinners, but advise against elective aspirin/NSAIDs
• manage blood pressure if it is found to be elevated
• for 360° bullous trauma: emergent surgery and IV antibiotics
followUp: • none required: if the vision is normal and it is a first-time isolated event
• return if: the blood does not clear, vision changes, or if it happens again
• referral: to a primary care doctor if blood pressure was high or if labs are needed
differentials: • episcleritis (sectoral redness, visible vessels, blanches with phenylephrine)
• kaposi sarcoma (vascular tumor, usually more elevated and purple, seen in HIV/AIDS)
review: • it’s a bruise on the eye; it will get worse (spread out) before it gets better
• always ask about trauma—if the eye is "squishy" or has a 360° red ring, it’s an emergency
• many patients wake up with this because they rubbed their eyes in their sleep
pearl: A spontaneous subconjunctival hemorrhage is almost always benign — the exception is the patient on warfarin or with bilateral recurrences, where you should check BP, INR, and a platelet count.
draw: eye with a discrete patch of bright red blood on the white sclera, vision is normal

name: Subluxed or Dislocated Crystalline Lens
symptoms: • decreased vision: often due to high astigmatism or the eye becoming "aphakic" (no lens)
• monocular diplopia: seeing double with one eye covered; caused by the lens edge splitting the pupil
• fluctuating vision: sight changes as the lens shifts with head position
• ocular pain: may indicate secondary glaucoma if the lens moves forward into the angle
findings: ## Clinical signs
• phacodonesis: quivering of the lens during eye movement (the most sensitive early sign)
• iridodonesis: tremulousness of the iris because the lens is no longer supporting it
• lens edge: the equator of the lens or visible zonules seen through a dilated pupil
• asymmetric ac depth: the anterior chamber is deeper where the lens has recessed
## Genetic localization
• superotemporal (up & out): classic for marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 defect)
• inferonasal (down & in): classic for homocystinuria (cbs deficiency)
• anterior (into ac): suggests weill-marchesani syndrome (microspherophakia)
## Pseudoexfoliation (PXF)
• target pattern: white, flaky material on the lens capsule; a major cause of zonular weakness
etiology: ## Primary causes
• trauma: the #1 cause overall; look for vossius rings or angle recession
• pxf syndrome: the most common non-traumatic cause in elderly patients
• marfan syndrome: autosomal dominant; associated with life-threatening aortic root dilation
• homocystinuria: autosomal recessive; associated with high thromboembolism risk
• weill-marchesani: short stature and small spherical lenses (microspherophakia)
redFlags: • marfan suspicion: mandates an immediate echocardiogram to rule out aortic dissection
• homocystinuria surgery: high risk of fatal clots under general anesthesia; requires hydration
• anterior dislocation: an ophthalmic emergency; can cause acute pupillary-block glaucoma
• posterior dislocation: if the lens falls into the vitreous, it requires a retina specialist (lensectomy)
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• slit lamp: check for phacodonesis before dilation and pxf flakes after dilation
• gonioscopy: evaluate for angle recession (trauma) or sampaolesi line (pxf)
## Systemic workup
• marfan: cardiology referral for aortic root measurement
• homocystinuria: plasma homocysteine and urine nitroprusside tests
• syphilis: rpr/fta-abs (historically associated with "luetic" lens subluxation)
actionSteps: • distinguish between partial (subluxation) and complete (dislocation) displacement
• refer for cardiology/metabolic workup if systemic syndromes are suspected
• manage acute glaucoma if the lens is in the anterior chamber (dilate and reposition supine)
• coordinate with a vitreoretinal surgeon if the lens has migrated posteriorly
treatment: ## Non-surgical
• observation: if vision is stable and there is no inflammation or glaucoma
• optical: aphakic contact lenses or spectacles if the lens is completely out of the visual axis
## Surgical
• lens extraction: required for symptomatic cataracts, uncorrectable diplopia, or glaucoma
• advanced tools: use of capsular tension rings (ctr) or segments to stabilize the new iol
• fixation: scleral-fixated or iris-sutured iols are used when zonular support is absent
followUp: • routine: 6–12 month monitoring for stable subluxation
• urgent: immediate return if sudden pain (angle closure) or new shadows (retinal detachment)
• post-op: standard cataract/vitrectomy follow-up with extra attention to iol stability
differentials: • pseudoexfoliation syndrome (weak zonules but lens usually still central)
• morgagnian cataract (heavy nucleus sinks within the capsular bag)
• simple ectopia lentis (isolated ocular finding without systemic disease)
review: • Marfan zonules are usually "intact" inferiorly, which is why the lens pulls upward
• in Homocystinuria, the zonules are brittle and break entirely, often leading to inferior luxation
• monocular diplopia is the classic symptom of a lens "half-in, half-out" of the pupillary axis
pearl: Superotemporal lens subluxation points to Marfan (zonules intact inferiorly); inferonasal to homocystinuria (zonules disrupted superiorly) — the direction localizes the genetic disease before blood tests return.
draw: slit lamp view of a dilated pupil showing the curved edge of a displaced lens and broken string-like zonules
willsRef: Wills Eye §13.2 (Subluxed or Dislocated Crystalline Lens)

name: Superficial Punctate Keratopathy
symptoms: • foreign body sensation: a gritty, "sand-in-the-eye" feeling
• pain and photophobia: light sensitivity that improves with topical anesthetic
• tearing and redness: reflex tearing in response to surface irritation
• blurred vision: often fluctuates with blinking as the tear film destabilizes
findings: ## Clinical appearance
• punctate epithelial erosions (pee): tiny, pinpoint areas of cell loss
• fluorescein staining: the damaged spots take up green dye under cobalt blue light
• lissamine green/rose bengal: stains devitalized cells (useful in dry eye)
## Staining patterns (the diagnostic key)
• superior (top 1/3): suggests lid pathology (evert for FB), vernal catarrh, or floppy eyelid
• interpalpebral (middle band): suggests aqueous deficiency (dry eye) or neurotrophic causes
• inferior (bottom 1/3): suggests blepharitis, exposure (incomplete closure), or drop toxicity
• diffuse: suggests severe dry eye, chemical injury, or viral infection
etiology: ## Key mechanical triggers
• dry eye syndrome: aqueous deficiency or evaporative loss (MGD)
• exposure: nocturnal lagophthalmos (sleeping with eyes open) or CN VII palsy
• toxicity: preservatives (BAK) in chronic eye drops or toxic antibiotics (gentamicin)
• mechanical: trichiasis (inward lashes), contact lens overwear, or foreign bodies
## Specialized forms
• thygeson spk: coarse, raised, gray-white lesions with a very quiet (white) eye
• ultraviolet (welder's flash): diffuse, extremely painful SPK after UV exposure
redFlags: • reduced corneal sensation: check BEFORE anesthetic; suggests neurotrophic keratitis (post-herpes)
• vertical linear scratches: high suspicion for a foreign body trapped under the upper lid
• contact lens wearer: any SPK in a CL wearer requires a fluoroquinolone to cover Pseudomonas
• non-resolving SPK: rule out Acanthamoeba or medicamentosa (toxicity from the treatment itself)
investigations: ## Slit lamp workup
• staining: note the location—it is the single most helpful clue to the etiology
• lid eversion: mandatory if SPK is superior or linear to rule out a subtarsal foreign body
• corneal sensation: test with a cotton wisp to screen for CN V dysfunction
## Tear film assessment
• tbut: count seconds until the tear film breaks up (normal >10 seconds)
• schirmer test: measure tear production with paper strips if dry eye is suspected
actionSteps: • identify the underlying cause—treating SPK without fixing the trigger will fail
• initiate aggressive lubrication with preservative-free (PF) artificial tears
• address eyelid health: warm compresses for MGD or taping for exposure
• switch chronic preserved drops to preservative-free alternatives if toxicity is suspected
treatment: ## General management
• lubrication: PF artificial tears q1h to q4h; lubricating ointment (e.g., Refresh PM) at bedtime
• antibiotic cover: erythromycin or bacitracin ointment tid if erosions are confluent
## Specific etiologies
• contact lens: stop wear immediately; start prophylactic fluoroquinolone (e.g., moxifloxacin)
• exposure: moisture chambers or nighttime taping/bland ointment
• thygeson: low-dose topical steroids or cyclosporine drops
followUp: • 1–2 weeks: most simple cases of SPK should show significant improvement
• persistent cases: evaluate for punctal plugs, bandage contact lenses, or serum tears
• chronic monitoring: essential for neurotrophic or exposure-related disease
differentials: • adenoviral keratitis (look for follicles and subepithelial infiltrates)
• herpes simplex keratitis (look for true dendrites with terminal bulbs)
• acanthamoeba (extreme pain, ring-shaped infiltrate in contact lens wearers)
• medicamentosa (red eye that gets worse the more drops the patient uses)
review: • "vertical tracking" = foreign body under the eyelid
• "3 and 9 o'clock staining" = exposure or dry eye from the lids not meeting
• "inferior staining" = the drops you gave them are probably hurting them
pearl: SPK is a syndrome, not a diagnosis — always find the cause (dry eye, blepharitis, toxicity, exposure, trichiasis) because treating the epithelium without fixing the trigger is a losing battle.
draw: diagram showing different staining patterns: superior, band-like, and inferior staining on a cornea

name: Superior Limbic Keratoconjunctivitis
symptoms: • red eye and burning: localized primarily to the top of the eye
• foreign body sensation: constant grit or "sand" feeling, worse with blinking
• tearing and photophobia: light sensitivity that fluctuates with the ocular surface state
• frequent blinking: a compensatory move to manage the mechanical friction
• relapsing course: patients often have a history of "flare-ups" lasting months
findings: ## Theodore’s sign (diagnostic key)
• superior bulbar injection: localized redness and thickening of the top conjunctiva
• visibility: the lesion is often HIDDEN by the upper lid; must lift the lid in downgaze to see it
## Surface changes
• superior limbal staining: intense staining with lissamine green or rose bengal
• corneal filaments: small "tails" of mucus and epithelium that pull on the cornea
• superior micropannus: fine blood vessels growing into the top of the cornea
• tarsal papillae: small bumps on the underside of the upper eyelid
## Systemic link
• thyroid association: 30–50% of patients have current or history of thyroid dysfunction
etiology: ## Mechanical friction
• pathophysiology: chronic rubbing between a "tight" upper lid and redundant superior conjunctiva
• result: cellular damage, inflammation, and abnormal keratinization of the surface cells
## Risk factors
• thyroid eye disease: the most significant systemic association (Graves, Hashimoto)
• demographics: most common in middle-aged women
• contact lenses: CL-induced SLK can occur (often a reaction to preservatives or fit)
redFlags: • unexplained redness under upper lid: always check TSH/fT4 for subclinical thyroid disease
• severe filaments: indicates advanced surface breakdown and requires aggressive mucolytics
• persistent pain: if not responding to lubrication, consider secondary neurotrophic changes
• unilateral presentation: rare for SLK; rule out a localized conjunctival tumor or foreign body
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• staining: use lissamine green; it is superior to fluorescein for showing conjunctival damage
• "lid-lift" maneuver: essential to visualize the sectoral superior redness
• lid eversion: to check for tarsal papillae or a hidden foreign body
## Systemic workup
• mandatory labs: TSH, free T4, and TSI (Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulin)
• endocrinology referral: if any thyroid labs are abnormal
actionSteps: • order a full thyroid panel (TSH, free T4) to rule out underlying systemic disease
• utilize mucolytics (Acetylcysteine) if corneal filaments are present
• initiate aggressive preservative-free lubrication and topical cyclosporine
• consider silver nitrate application to the superior conjunctiva for refractory cases
treatment: ## First-line (medical)
• lubrication: preservative-free artificial tears q1-2h and ointment at bedtime
• cyclosporine / lifitegrast: to manage the underlying surface inflammation
• bandage contact lens: can provide a mechanical shield to reduce friction
## Procedural (moderate/severe)
• silver nitrate (0.5%): chemically cauterizes the redundant, inflamed conjunctiva
• acetylcysteine: 10% drops to dissolve painful mucus filaments
## Surgical (refractory)
• conjunctival resection: surgically removing the redundant "loose" conjunctiva
followUp: • acute phase: every 2–4 weeks to monitor filament resolution and staining
• maintenance: 3–6 months once stabilized on topical immunomodulators
• referral: involve endocrinology early if thyroid markers are elevated
differentials: • vernal keratoconjunctivitis (look for giant papillae and history of allergies)
• floppy eyelid syndrome (lax lids, diffuse punctate staining, associated with sleep apnea)
• contact lens-induced keratopathy (resolves with lens cessation)
• tracheoma (conjunctival scarring and different geographic prevalence)
review: • remember: "Lift the lid to find the SLK"
• the friction is like a "carpet burn" on the eye caused by the eyelid moving over it
• silver nitrate works by "tightening" the loose conjunctiva so it doesn’t bunch up during blinks
pearl: Bilateral superior bulbar redness with filaments and tarsal papillae in a middle-aged woman points straight to thyroid disease — check TSH, fT4, and treat the mechanical friction with silver nitrate or conjunctival resection.
draw: diagram showing the upper eyelid being lifted to reveal a sector of bright red conjunctiva at the very top of the eyeball

name: Sympathetic Ophthalmia
symptoms: • bilateral pain and redness: onset in both the "injured" and "uninjured" eye
• photophobia: extreme light sensitivity is often the earliest subjective symptom
• decreased vision: typically bilateral drop in acuity (reading and distance)
• loss of accommodation: difficulty focusing on near objects (early sign)
• history: penetrating trauma or intraocular surgery (especially vitreoretinal) in one eye
findings: ## Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis
• mutton-fat kps: large, greasy-looking inflammatory cells on the corneal back surface
• busacca/koeppe nodules: inflammatory lumps on the iris surface or pupillary margin
• dalen-fuchs nodules: pathognomonic small, yellow-white nodules at the RPE level
• vitritis: significant inflammatory "snow" in the vitreous cavity of both eyes
## Posterior segment
• sunset-glow fundus: chronic orange-red discoloration due to RPE depigmentation
• serous retinal detachment: fluid pooling under the retina (similar to VKH)
• choroidal thickening: diffuse inflammation of the vascular layer (best seen on EDI-OCT)
• optic disc edema: swelling and hyperemia of the optic nerve head
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• autoimmune response: T-cell mediated attack on previously "hidden" uveal (melanocyte) antigens
• mechanism: trauma to one eye ("exciting eye") releases antigens into the bloodstream/lymphatics
• result: the immune system attacks both the exciting eye and the healthy "sympathizing eye"
## Timing
• window: 90% occur within 1 year; most common between 2 weeks and 3 months post-injury
• range: can occur as early as 5 days or as late as several decades after trauma
redFlags: • any uveitis in a healthy eye after fellow-eye trauma: must be SO until proven otherwise
• bilateral serous detachments: a sign of intense choroidal inflammation requiring IV steroids
• 14-day window: if a traumatized eye is blind and unsalvageable, enucleation within 14 days may prevent SO
• relapse on taper: standard for SO; requires long-term (often lifelong) immunosuppression
investigations: ## Imaging workup
• fluorescein angiography (fa): shows pinpoint RPE leaks and late pooling (starry sky appearance)
• icg angiography: hypocyanescent (dark) spots showing multifocal choroidal involvement
• edi-oct: used to measure and track the characteristic thickening of the choroid
## Systemic screening
• chest x-ray / ct: to rule out sarcoidosis or tuberculosis (which mimic SO findings)
• syphilis screen: RPR/FTA-ABS to rule out luetic panuveitis
actionSteps: • obtain a detailed history of any past eye surgeries or penetrating trauma
• initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (oral or IV) immediately
• refer to a uveitis specialist for early "steroid-sparing" immunosuppressant therapy
• counsel on the risks/benefits of enucleating a blind inciting eye if within the 14-day window
treatment: ## Induction
• systemic steroids: high-dose oral Prednisone (1–2 mg/kg/day) or IV Methylprednisolone
• topical steroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Difluprednate q1-2h for anterior control
## Maintenance (steroid-sparing)
• immunomodulators: Methotrexate, Mycophenolate, or Azathioprine to allow steroid taper
• biologics: Anti-TNF agents (e.g., Adalimumab) for refractory or severe cases
## Prevention
• enucleation (not evisceration): only if done within 14 days of trauma in a blind eye
followUp: • acute: daily to weekly to ensure inflammatory control and monitor intraocular pressure
• taper: monthly checks; the goal is to reach <5mg Prednisone while on steroid-sparing agents
• long-term: lifelong monitoring as flares can occur decades after the original injury
differentials: • vkh syndrome (identical ocular signs but NO history of trauma; has neuro/skin findings)
• sarcoidosis (bilateral granulomatous uveitis but with lung/systemic involvement)
• syphilis (the "great masquerader"; can present with panuveitis and RPE changes)
• phacoantigenic uveitis (reaction to lens protein; usually only in the injured eye)
review: • once SO starts, taking out the injured eye does NOT help the healthy one
• evisceration (scooping the eye) leaves uveal tissue behind and does not reliably prevent SO
• the history of "penetrating trauma" is the only way to distinguish SO from VKH clinically
pearl: Sympathetic ophthalmia is the reason to consider enucleation of a blind painful eye within 2 weeks of trauma — once the sympathizing eye inflames, both eyes are at risk for life.
draw: Diagram of two eyes showing trauma to the right eye and subsequent inflammatory cells appearing in both eyes

name: Syphilitic Optic Neuritis
symptoms: • visual loss: acute or subacute, often sudden and severe; more commonly bilateral than MS-related ON
• pain: retro-orbital or periocular discomfort, but typically less prominent than in demyelinating ON
• dyschromatopsia: significant decrease in color vision perception
• systemic signs: secondary syphilis may present with a rash (palms/soles), fever, and malaise
• neurologic: headache or stiff neck may suggest concurrent syphilitic meningitis
findings: ## Clinical presentation
• disc edema (papillitis): often more pronounced than MS-ON, frequently with peripapillary hemorrhages
• rapd: present in unilateral or asymmetric cases
• intraocular inflammation: vitritis and anterior chamber cells are common (hallmark markers for infectious ON)
## Posterior segment signs
• asppc: large, yellowish, damp-looking placoid chorioretinal lesions in the macula
• neuroretinitis: disc edema associated with a macular star (hard exudates)
• retinal vasculitis: dilated, tortuous vessels and perivascular sheathing
## Visual function
• visual fields: central or cecocentral scotomas are typical
etiology: ## Pathogen
• treponema pallidum: spirochetal infection; "The Great Imitator"
• stage: can occur at any stage, but ocular involvement most commonly reflects secondary or early tertiary syphilis
• co-infection: HIV significantly increases the risk and aggressiveness of neurosyphilis/ocular syphilis
redFlags: • steroids alone: never treat presumed ON with steroids without ruling out syphilis; steroids without antibiotics worsen the infection
• hiv status: mandatory testing for all ocular syphilis patients due to high co-infection rates
• vitritis + swollen disc: this combination almost never happens in MS; strongly suspect syphilis or sarcoidosis
• jarisch-herxheimer: systemic flu-like reaction within 24h of starting IV Penicillin
investigations: ## Serology (the essential pair)
• treponemal (confirmatory): FTA-ABS or TP-PA (once positive, usually positive for life)
• non-treponemal (quantitative): RPR or VDRL (used to monitor disease activity and treatment response)
## Neuro workup
• lumbar puncture: mandatory; CSF VDRL, cell count, and protein to assess neurosyphilis
• mri brain/orbits: look for optic nerve enhancement and leptomeningeal involvement
## Ocular baseline
• oct: to monitor the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and macula
actionSteps: • order urgent RPR/VDRL and FTA-ABS/TP-PA in all patients with optic neuritis
• perform mandatory HIV screening and a diagnostic Lumbar Puncture
• treat any ocular syphilis as neurosyphilis, regardless of the CSF result
• admit for IV Aqueous Penicillin G for a 10–14 day course
treatment: ## First-line antibiotics
• aqueous penicillin g: 18–24 million units/day IV (continuous or q4h) for 10–14 days
• penicillin allergy: Ceftriaxone 2g IV/IM daily; however, penicillin desensitization is preferred
## Adjuvants
• corticosteroids: may be added AFTER antibiotics are started to control inflammation, at expert discretion
## Public health
• infectious disease consult and mandatory reporting to local health authorities
followUp: • titer monitoring: RPR/VDRL at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months; expect a fourfold decrease by 1 year
• repeat lp: at 6 months to ensure CSF VDRL normalization and resolution of pleocytosis
• ophthalmology: reassess in 2–4 weeks to monitor visual recovery and optic nerve appearance
differentials: • idiopathic optic neuritis (MS-associated; rarely has vitritis)
• nmosd (typically more severe visual loss, long spinal cord lesions)
• sarcoidosis (also causes vitritis and disc edema; check ACE/Chest CT)
• lyme disease (similar presentation; check Lyme titers)
review: • if the disc is swollen and there are cells in the vitreous, it isn't MS
• ocular syphilis is neurosyphilis—treat with IV meds, not IM injections
• "The Great Imitator" can look like anything from a mild blur to total blindness
pearl: The great imitator. Syphilitic ON is frequently misdiagnosed as MS-related or AION. Steroids without penicillin worsen outcome. Test everyone.
draw: Diagram of a swollen optic disc with small hemorrhages and inflammatory "dots" (cells) in the vitreous jelly in front of it

name: Third Nerve Palsy
symptoms: • binocular diplopia: double vision that resolves when either eye is covered
• ptosis: drooping of the upper eyelid, which may completely cover the eye
• ocular pain: may be severe (aneurysm) or dull/aching (ischemic)
• blurred vision: if the pupil is involved, causing loss of accommodation
findings: ## Motility & position
• "down and out": the eye is deviated outward (exotropia) and downward (hypotropia)
• restricted gaze: inability to look up, down, or inward (adduction)
• ptosis: levator palpebrae weakness
## The pupil rule
• pupil-involving: dilated, fixed, or sluggish; suggests compression (Aneurysm)
• pupil-sparing: normal reactive pupil; favors microvascular ischemia (Diabetes/HTN)
## Aberrant regeneration
• synkinetic movements: e.g., the eyelid lifts when the patient tries to look down or in
• significance: indicates a chronic compressive or traumatic cause; NEVER microvascular
etiology: ## Compressive (surgical emergency)
• p-com aneurysm: posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the nerve
• uncal herniation: brain swelling forcing the temporal lobe onto the nerve
• tumors: cavernous sinus masses or pituitary apoplexy
## Ischemic (medical management)
• microvascular: diabetes, hypertension, or GCA (vasculitis of small vessels)
## Other
• trauma, varicella zoster, or ophthalmoplegic migraine (in children)
redFlags: • painful pupil-involving palsy: a P-Com aneurysm until proven otherwise; requires emergent CTA/MRA
• partial third nerve palsy: any "incomplete" palsy is high-risk and requires full neuroimaging
• progression: a palsy that worsens over several days is highly suggestive of a growing tumor or aneurysm
• age ≥55: check ESR/CRP to rule out Giant Cell Arteritis even if the pupil is spared
investigations: ## Urgent imaging
• cta/mra: emergent head and neck imaging to look for aneurysmal dilation
• mri brain/orbits: with gadolinium to visualize the nerve and rule out mass lesions
## Ocular exam
• pupillary assessment: must be done carefully in a dark room; check for subtle anisocoria
• motility: check all 9 cardinal positions for "hidden" weakness in other nerves
## Lab work
• vasculopathic screen: blood pressure, HbA1c, and lipid panel
• gca screen: ESR, CRP, and platelets in patients over 55
actionSteps: • immediately assess the pupil; if dilated or sluggish, treat as a neurosurgical emergency
• order emergent CTA or MRA to rule out a life-threatening P-Com aneurysm
• monitor for "aberrant regeneration" which points to a non-ischemic cause
• refer to neuro-ophthalmology for stable or resolving microvascular cases
treatment: ## Etiological
• aneurysm: neurosurgical clipping or endovascular coiling
• ischemic: optimization of blood pressure and glucose control; aspirin
## Symptomatic
• diplopia: occlusion patching or Fresnel prisms (once the deviation is stable)
• surgery: strabismus surgery or ptosis repair if the palsy does not resolve after 6 months
followUp: • microvascular: if truly pupil-sparing, observe every 1–2 weeks for the first month
• monitoring: most ischemic cases show improvement within 4–6 weeks and resolve by 3 months
• warning: if the pupil becomes involved later or no recovery occurs by 3 months, order an MRI
differentials: • myasthenia gravis (the "great masquerader"; can mimic any eye movement deficit)
• thyroid eye disease (restrictive, usually causes proptosis or lid retraction)
• internuclear ophthalmoplegia (ino) (lesion in the MLF; affects adduction only)
• parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain lesion; affects upgaze and pupils)
review: • why the pupil rule works: pupillomotor fibers live on the surface of the nerve, so they are hit first by external compression (aneurysm)
• ischemic damage usually happens in the center of the nerve, leaving the surface fibers intact
• always check for ptosis—it can be so severe that the patient doesn't even notice the double vision
pearl: Complete CN III palsy with pupil involvement: posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise — emergent CTA/MRA. Pupil-sparing CN III: likely ischemic (diabetes, HTN). Aberrant regeneration does NOT occur after ischemic CN III.
draw: diagram showing the "down and out" eye position and a droopy eyelid (ptosis)

name: Thygeson Superficial Punctate Keratitis
symptoms: • foreign body sensation: mild-to-moderate "gritty" feeling
• photophobia and tearing: sensitivity to light without significant discharge
• white eye: strikingly, the patient has NO history of a "red eye" during flares
• chronic relapsing: symptoms come and go over months or years, often asymmetrically
findings: ## The "quiet eye" sign (pathognomonic)
• white conjunctiva: the eye looks perfectly calm and uninfljected despite the corneal lesions
• no discharge: distinguishes it from viral or bacterial conjunctivitis
## Characteristic lesions
• coarse opacities: snowflake-like or "stellate" (star-shaped) gray-white intraepithelial dots
• location: scattered predominantly across the central cornea (usually 5–30 lesions)
• raised surface: the dots are slightly elevated and can be "felt" with a fluorescein strip
• variable staining: active lesions stain lightly with fluorescein; older ones barely stain
etiology: ## Idiopathic
• suspected viral or immune link, but no specific pathogen has been proven
• course: a decades-long cycle of exacerbations and remissions
• burnout: the disease eventually resolves on its own without leaving any scars or vision loss
redFlags: • steroid side effects: chronic use of even mild steroids requires monitoring for IOP spikes and cataracts
• corneal thinning/infiltrates: if the cornea starts to thin or look "cloudy" (stromal), reconsider the diagnosis (e.g., HSV or Adenovirus)
• atypical response: failure to improve with low-dose steroids should trigger a referral for a corneal specialist
investigations: ## Slit lamp exam
• identify the classic coarse, snowflake-like epithelial lesions
• confirm the total absence of conjunctival injection or corneal edema
## Clinical history
• absence of prior "pink eye" or cold sores (HSV) helps confirm the diagnosis
actionSteps: • start low-dose topical steroids (e.g., fluorometholone 0.1%) for rapid relief of active flares
• introduce topical cyclosporine early as a steroid-sparing agent for long-term management
• reassure the patient that while the condition is chronic, it does not cause permanent damage
treatment: ## Acute management
• mild steroids: Fluorometholone or Loteprednol qid, then taper slowly as symptoms resolve
• lubrication: preservative-free artificial tears for comfort during minor flares
## Long-term maintenance
• cyclosporine 0.05%: often the preferred treatment to prevent relapses without steroid risk
• avoid: high-potency steroids or unnecessary topical antivirals
followUp: • flare-ups: every 1–3 months to monitor the clearing of lesions and intraocular pressure
• remission: every 6 months to 1 year for routine monitoring
• prognosis: excellent; the goal is symptomatic control until spontaneous "burnout" occurs
differentials: • adenoviral keratitis (presents with red eye, follicles, and subepithelial infiltrates)
• herpes simplex (hsv) (true dendrites with terminal bulbs; usually unilateral)
• dry eye syndrome (staining is usually inferior or band-like, not coarse snowflake dots)
• medicamentosa (toxicity from other eye drops; eye is usually red and irritated)
review: • Thygeson = "The snowflake dots in a white eye"
• if the eye is red, it is almost certainly NOT Thygeson
• the dramatic response to steroids is so characteristic it is practically a diagnostic test
pearl: Thygeson is benign but relapses for years — reassure the patient that the coarse intraepithelial dots come and go, and resist the urge to chase it with strong topical steroids.
draw: slit lamp view of a clear cornea with small white star-shaped dots in the center and a white sclera

name: Toxoplasmosis Retinochoroiditis
symptoms: • blurred vision: often due to vitreous "fog" or a lesion in the macula
• floaters: caused by inflammatory cells in the vitreous jelly
• photophobia and redness: from secondary anterior chamber inflammation
• pain: typically mild, but can be sharp if eye pressure (IOP) is elevated
findings: ## The classic lesion
• "headlight in the fog": a fluffy white focal retinitis obscured by overlying vitritis
• satellite lesion: a new white lesion appearing directly adjacent to an old, pigmented scar
• unilateral: usually affects one eye at a time in immunocompetent patients
## Associated signs
• vitritis: intense inflammatory debris directly over the active area
• kyrieleis arteritis: yellowish plaques along the retinal arteries near the inflammation
• vasculitis: perivascular sheathing (inflammation of the vessels)
• neuroretinitis: optic disc swelling with a "macular star" of hard exudates
## Immunocompromised variant
• punctate outer retinal toxoplasmosis: deep, multiple lesions with very little vitreous haze
etiology: ## Pathogen
• toxoplasma gondii: an intracellular protozoan; cats are the definitive host
## Transmission
• congenital: passed from mother to fetus during a primary pregnancy infection
• acquired: ingestion of oocysts (undercooked meat, contaminated water, or cat feces)
## Reactivation
• cysts remain dormant in old scars and can rupture later in life, especially during pregnancy or immunosuppression
redFlags: • vision-threatening location: any lesion in the macula or near the optic nerve requires immediate systemic therapy
• "headlight in fog": severe vitritis that hides the fundus makes it hard to rule out other infections (like ARN)
• hiv/immunosuppression: lesions may be bilateral, multifocal, or rapidly progressive; requires aggressive workup
• bone marrow suppression: pyrimethamine treatment can drop blood counts; must monitor CBC
investigations: ## Lab work
• serum antibody: IgG (indicates past exposure) or IgM (indicates recent infection)
• rule of thumb: a negative titer in an immunocompetent patient makes toxo very unlikely
## Ocular sampling
• pcr: testing the aqueous or vitreous fluid for T. gondii DNA; highly specific for atypical cases
## Systemic screening
• rule outs: HIV, syphilis (RPR), and TB (QuantiFERON) before starting high-dose steroids
actionSteps: • confirm if the lesion is "vision-threatening" (macula, optic nerve, or large vessel)
• initiate "triple therapy" or TMP-SMX for active, sight-threatening disease
• start oral steroids ONLY after 24–48 hours of antimicrobial coverage
• coordinate with an infectious disease specialist if the patient is immunocompromised
treatment: ## Observation
• small, peripheral lesions in healthy patients may resolve without treatment
## First-line (triple therapy)
• pyrimethamine: (load then daily) + Folinic Acid (to protect bone marrow)
• sulfadiazine: or TMP-SMX (Bactrim DS) as a more accessible alternative
## Adjuvants
• prednisone: to reduce inflammatory damage; must be used alongside antibiotics
• intravitreal: clindamycin/dexamethasone injections for patients who can't take oral meds
## Associated issues
• topical: steroids and cycloplegics for anterior segment "spillover" inflammation
followUp: • weekly: monitor the lesion size, vitreous haze, and intraocular pressure
• labs: weekly CBC if the patient is on Pyrimethamine to check for toxicity
• long-term: TMP-SMX prophylaxis may be used for patients with frequent recurrences
differentials: • cmv retinitis (usually "pizza-pie" appearance, minimal vitritis, seen in advanced AIDS)
• acute retinal necrosis (arn) (rapidly spreading, peripheral, viral etiology)
• syphilitic retinitis (the "great imitator"; always check RPR/FTA-ABS)
• cat-scratch disease (bartonella; look for neuroretinitis and history of cat scratches)
review: • "Headlight in the fog" = Toxo
• "Pizza pie" = CMV
• Never give steroids alone! You could cause the parasite to destroy the entire retina
pearl: Most common cause of infectious retinochoroiditis globally. Classic presentation: active white fluffy lesion adjacent to an old pigmented scar ("satellite lesion"). PCR of aqueous/vitreous most sensitive for atypical cases.
draw: fundus diagram showing a dark pigmented scar with a fuzzy white "fluffy" area right next to it in a hazy vitreous

name: Traumatic Choroidal Rupture
symptoms: • decreased vision: ranging from mild blur to severe central loss (if fovea is involved)
• asymptomatic: peripheral ruptures may only be found on routine exam
• history: significant blunt ocular trauma (e.g., sports injury, airbag, fist)
findings: ## Pathognomonic morphology
• crescent-shaped streak: a yellow-white curvilinear line, typically concentric to the optic disc
• location: most commonly found on the temporal side of the disc
• acute obscuration: the rupture is often HIDDEN by subretinal blood immediately after trauma
## Associated trauma signs
• commotio retinae: a "sheen" or whitening of the retina from photoreceptor shock
• subretinal hemorrhage: blood pooling under the retina
• secondary complications: retinal tears, macular holes, or angle recession (glaucoma risk)
## Late complication
• choroidal neovascular membrane (cnvm): the primary long-term threat; new vessels grow through the crack
etiology: ## Mechanism of injury
• contrecoup effect: blunt force causes sudden compression/expansion of the globe
• tissue failure: the inelastic Bruch membrane and choriocapillaris tear under tangential stress
• types: "Indirect" ruptures (classic concentric shape) are far more common than "Direct" impact-site ruptures
redFlags: • delayed visual loss: a sudden drop in vision months or years later usually means a CNVM has formed
• subfoveal involvement: if the crack passes through the fovea, the prognosis for central vision is poor
• vitreous hemorrhage: may mask a more serious retinal detachment or open globe injury
• metamorphopsia: wavy lines on an Amsler grid indicate subretinal fluid/CNVM
investigations: ## Imaging
• oct macula: essential to identify the rupture and monitor for fluid (CNVM)
• fundus photography: to document the baseline extent of the rupture as blood clears
• fluorescein angiography (fa): used if CNVM is suspected to locate leaking vessels
## Clinical tools
• amsler grid: the most critical tool for home monitoring
actionSteps: • perform a thorough dilated exam to rule out peripheral retinal tears or breaks
• document the rupture once subretinal hemorrhage has cleared (days to weeks later)
• issue an Amsler grid and educate the patient on lifelong daily home monitoring
• refer to a retina specialist immediately if any new metamorphopsia or fluid is detected
treatment: ## Acute phase
• observation: no specific medical or surgical treatment for the rupture itself
• protection: recommend polycarbonate safety lenses for the healthy eye
## Late phase (CNVM management)
• anti-vegf injections: (e.g., Aflibercept, Ranibizumab) to stop vessel growth and leakage
• monitoring: daily Amsler grid use is the standard of care for lifetime surveillance
followUp: • initial: every 1–2 weeks until subretinal blood clears and the full extent is known
• short-term: every 3 months for the first year to monitor for early CNVM formation
• long-term: annual exams for life to screen for late CNVM or angle-recession glaucoma
differentials: • angioid streaks (bilateral, associated with systemic disease like Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum)
• lacquer cracks (seen in high myopia/nearsightedness; not associated with trauma)
• histoplasmosis (presents with "punched-out" spots and peripapillary scarring)
review: • "Crescent moon next to the disc" = Choroidal Rupture
• a clear macula on day 1 does NOT mean the eye is okay; wait for the blood to clear
• the risk of CNVM never truly goes away—it can happen 10 years later
pearl: A crescentic subretinal scar concentric to the disc after trauma is a choroidal rupture — the lifetime risk of secondary CNV approaches 10%, so every patient needs an Amsler grid for life.
draw: diagram showing a yellow-white crescent-shaped line curving around the optic nerve head

name: Traumatic Optic Neuropathy
symptoms: • sudden vision loss: typically occurs immediately following head or facial trauma
• dyschromatopsia: washed-out color vision (especially red desaturation)
• visual field defects: missing "chunks" of vision, often altitudinal (top or bottom half)
• orbital pain: associated with the initial injury or bone fractures
findings: ## The diagnostic signature
• new rapd: a Positive Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect in the setting of trauma
• normal fundus: initially, the optic nerve looks perfectly healthy (posterior indirect TON)
• delayed pallor: the nerve only turns pale (atrophy) 3–6 weeks later as the axons die
## Anterior variants
• nerve head avulsion: a deep hemorrhagic "crater" at the disc; often hidden by blood
• disc edema: may be seen if the injury is very close to the globe (anterior TON)
## Associated trauma
• eom restriction: inability to move the eye due to muscle entrapment or nerve damage
• orbital compartment syndrome: rock-hard eyelids, proptosis, and high eye pressure
etiology: ## Indirect TON (most common)
• deceleration injury: a blow to the forehead transfers energy to the optic canal
• shear forces: the nerve is "tethered" in the bony canal, causing nutrient vessels to tear
• compartment effect: nerve swelling within the rigid bony canal causes secondary damage
## Direct TON
• mechanism: bone fragments, bullets, or foreign bodies physically lacerating or crushing the nerve
## Compressive
• orbital hemorrhage: blood pooling behind the eye (retrobulbar hematoma) choking the nerve
redFlags: • concomitant tbi: high-dose steroids increase mortality in head-injured patients (CRASH trial)
• orbital compartment syndrome: if the eye is "tense" and vision is dropping, perform an emergent lateral canthotomy immediately
• progressive vision loss: while most TON is immediate, worsening vision suggests an expanding hematoma or bony impingement
• bilateral rapd: an RAPD only shows which nerve is *worse*; both nerves could be severely damaged
investigations: ## Clinical bedside
• swinging flashlight test: the single most important test for detecting an RAPD
• color vision: check for "red desaturation" using a red bottle cap or Ishihara plates
## Imaging
• thin-cut ct orbits (1-mm): specifically looking for fractures involving the optic canal or orbital apex
• b-scan ultrasound: to rule out nerve avulsion if the view is blocked by blood
actionSteps: • stabilize the patient (ABC/Trauma protocol) before focusing on the eye
• perform a meticulous pupil exam to document the presence of an RAPD
• obtain urgent thin-cut CT imaging of the brain and orbits
• consult neurosurgery and ENT if bony impingement or intracranial injury is suspected
treatment: ## Current standard
• observation: most cases are managed with "watchful waiting" as there is no proven benefit to surgery or meds for most indirect TON
## Controversial steroids
• methylprednisolone: generally avoided if there is any Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
## Surgical options
• lateral canthotomy: emergent decompression for retrobulbar hemorrhage
• endoscopic decompression: reserved for cases with visible bony fragments "pinching" the nerve in the canal
followUp: • acute: serial exams (vision, pupils, color) every 24 hours to ensure no progression
• recovery: follow-up at 1 month and 3 months to document the final level of optic atrophy
• counseling: many patients experience spontaneous (though often partial) visual recovery
differentials: • vitreous hemorrhage (masks the view, but doesn't usually cause a profound RAPD)
• traumatic macular hole (decreased vision, but the optic nerve/pupils are normal)
• chiasmal injury (bilateral vision loss, often associated with skull base fractures)
review: ## The 3 TON truths
1. If the vision is gone and the nerve looks normal, it's TON until proven otherwise.
2. High-dose steroids can be fatal if the patient also has a head injury.
3. A "normal" pupil in an unconscious patient does not guarantee the eye can see.
pearl: Vision loss with a RAPD after blunt trauma without a visible optic nerve injury is traumatic optic neuropathy — high-dose steroids and decompression remain controversial, and the best evidence is that most recover spontaneously.
draw: Diagram of the optic nerve passing through the narrow bony optic canal in the skull base

name: Anterior Uveitis
symptoms: • acute pain: a deep, aching "boring" pain in the eye
• redness: localized mostly around the iris (ciliary flush)
• photophobia: sensitivity to light; often "consensual" (light in the healthy eye hurts the sick eye)
• blurred vision: from inflammatory debris or secondary swelling (CME)
• chronic floaters: more common in long-standing or recurrent cases
findings: ## Slit lamp findings
• ciliary flush: circumlimbal injection (redness concentrated in a ring around the cornea)
• ac cells & flare: "dust motes" in a sunbeam; 0 to 4+ grading of white cells and protein leakage
• keratic precipitates (kp): inflammatory dots on the corneal back surface; "mutton-fat" (large/greasy) suggests granulomatous disease
• hypopyon: a layered "level" of white blood cells at the bottom of the anterior chamber
## Structural changes
• posterior synechiae: the iris "sticks" to the lens, causing an irregular, non-reactive pupil
• iris nodules: koeppe (pupil margin) or busacca (iris stroma) nodules in granulomatous disease
• band keratopathy: calcium deposits on the cornea from chronic inflammation
etiology: ## Non-infectious (common)
• idiopathic: 30–50% of cases have no identifiable cause
• hla-b27 associated: linked to Ankylosing Spondylitis, IBD, Psoriatic Arthritis, or Reactive Arthritis
• sarcoidosis: often presents with bilateral "mutton-fat" KPs and iris nodules
• jia: chronic, often asymptomatic iritis in children; can lead to blindness if not screened
## Infectious
• herpetic (hsv/vzv): typically unilateral with high eye pressure and iris atrophy
• syphilis/tb: the "great imitators"; can cause any pattern of inflammation
## Special syndromes
• fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (fhic): chronic, low-grade, non-responsive to steroids; different colored eyes
redFlags: • mutton-fat kps: strongly suggests sarcoid, TB, or syphilis—requires systemic workup
• hypopyon: classic for HLA-B27 or Behçet disease; also rules out endophthalmitis
• high iop: common in herpetic uveitis (trabeculitis) or synechial angle closure
• chronic pediatric uveitis: may be completely white and painless (JIA) while still causing damage
investigations: ## Clinical workup
• review of systems: check for back pain, rashes, cough, diarrhea, or ulcers
• dilated fundus exam: essential to ensure there is no posterior involvement (Panuveitis)
## Targeted labs
• hla-b27: if acute/recurrent and unilateral
• syphilis/tb/sarcoid screen: RPR/FTA-ABS, QuantiFERON, and Chest X-ray/ACE
• pcr: of aqueous fluid if viral (HSV/CMV) or toxo is suspected
actionSteps: • initiate topical steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1%) frequently—often every hour initially
• prescribe a cycloplegic (e.g., Cyclopentolate) to stop painful ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae
• monitor intraocular pressure (IOP) closely, as both the disease and the treatment can raise it
• perform a targeted lab workup for recurrent, bilateral, or granulomatous cases
treatment: ## Topical therapy
• steroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Difluprednate 0.05% with a slow, careful taper
• cycloplegics: Cyclopentolate 1% or Atropine 1% for comfort and pupil management
## Systemic/advanced
• immunomodulators: Methotrexate or Biologics (e.g., Adalimumab) for JIA or chronic steroid-requiring cases
• iop control: standard glaucoma drops (avoiding prostaglandins if they worsen inflammation)
followUp: • acute phase: every 1–7 days to monitor the cell count and IOP
• taper phase: gradual reduction only after the eye is completely quiet (zero cells)
• maintenance: periodic checks for complications like cataracts, glaucoma, or macular edema (CME)
differentials: • scleritis (presents with much more severe, "boring" pain and a deeper red hue)
• endophthalmitis (post-surgical or traumatic; severe vision loss and vitritis)
• pigment dispersion syndrome (pigment in the AC can mimic cells; look for iris transillumination)
• masquerade syndromes (lymphoma or leukemia in older or high-risk patients)
review: • "Ciliary flush + AC cells = Uveitis"
• if the eye hurts more when the OTHER eye is exposed to light, that is the "consensual photophobia" sign of iritis
• never stop steroids abruptly; the inflammation will bounce back with a vengeance
pearl: Granulomatous KPs (large, "mutton fat") suggest sarcoidosis, TB, or syphilis. Non-granulomatous (small, fine) KPs suggest HLA-B27 associated disease or herpes.
draw: Diagram of the eye cross-section showing "dots" (cells) floating in the anterior chamber and sticking to the back of the cornea

name: Valsalva Retinopathy
symptoms: • sudden vision loss: painless blur or a "blind spot" appearing immediately after straining
• trigger history: heavy lifting, forceful coughing, vomiting, constipation, or even vigorous wind-instrument playing
• floaters: if the blood breaks through the membranes into the vitreous jelly
findings: ## Classic presentation
• "boat-shaped" hemorrhage: a well-demarcated pool of blood with a flat top (fluid level) when the patient is upright
• location: almost always overlies the macula (the central vision area)
• anatomic planes: blood can be trapped under the ILM (tight, round) or under the hyaloid face (larger, boat-shaped)
## Disease course
• color change: the bright red blood turns yellow or white over several weeks as it breaks down
• quiet retina: no signs of diabetic retinopathy, tears, or leaky vessels elsewhere
etiology: ## Mechanism
• venous pressure spike: straining causes a sudden rise in intraocular venous pressure
• capillary rupture: superficial retinal capillaries "pop" under the sudden stress
• risk factors: uncontrolled hypertension, blood thinners, or clotting disorders
redFlags: • large premacular hemorrhage: if the blood is thick and covers the entire macula, spontaneous clearing can take months
• breakthrough hemorrhage: blood moving into the vitreous (vitreous hemorrhage) can further obscure vision
• recurrence: multiple episodes without a clear trigger suggest an underlying bleeding disorder or severe hypertension
investigations: ## Imaging
• oct macula: the "gold standard" to see exactly which layer the blood is trapped in (sub-ILM vs. sub-hyaloid)
• b-scan ultrasound: used only if the blood is so thick the doctor can't see the retina at all
## Systemic workup
• blood pressure: must be checked at the time of the event
• blood labs: CBC and PT/INR if the patient is on anticoagulants or has easy bruising
actionSteps: • confirm the diagnosis by identifying the characteristic "boat-shaped" blood pool over the macula
• observe small hemorrhages, as most will clear on their own within 1–3 months
• discuss YAG laser membranotomy if the hemorrhage is large and the patient needs rapid vision recovery
• advise the patient to avoid further straining or heavy lifting during the healing phase
treatment: ## Observation
• first-line: most patients recover 20/20 vision without any intervention as the body reabsorbs the blood
## Nd:YAG laser membranotomy
• procedure: a quick laser pulse "pokes a hole" in the membrane holding the blood
• effect: the blood drains out into the bottom of the eye, clearing the central vision almost instantly
## Surgical
• vitrectomy: reserved for cases where the blood doesn't clear after 3 months or if complications arise
followUp: • initial: every 2–4 weeks to monitor the rate of blood reabsorption and check for "settling"
• post-laser: follow-up within 24 hours to ensure the blood is draining correctly and the eye pressure is stable
• long-term: usually none required once the blood has completely cleared and vision returns to baseline
differentials: • ruptured macroaneurysm (usually older patients with hypertension; often more yellowish exudate)
• proliferative diabetic retinopathy (look for laser scars, or bleeding in the other eye)
• terson syndrome (vitreous hemorrhage associated with a subarachnoid brain bleed)
review: • "Strain then blur" = Valsalva Retinopathy
• if the blood has a flat top like a level, it’s in the "sub-hyaloid" space
• if it’s a tight, round dome, it’s likely "sub-ILM"
pearl: A perfectly round preretinal blood blob after weightlifting or labor is Valsalva retinopathy — most resolve in weeks, but Nd:YAG membranotomy drains a large hemorrhage in seconds.
draw: Diagram of a "boat-shaped" hemorrhage over the macula with a clear horizontal fluid level

name: Vitamin A Deficiency
symptoms: • night blindness (nyctalopia): the earliest and most common symptom; difficulty seeing in low light
• dry eyes: a gritty, sandy sensation (xerosis)
• ocular pain: may occur if the cornea begins to break down
• severe vision loss: occurs rapidly if "keratomalacia" (corneal melting) develops
findings: ## WHO staging (xerophthalmia)
• XN (Night Blindness): reversible dysfunction of the rod cells in the retina
• X1B (Bitot Spots): foamy, triangular, silver-gray plaques on the conjunctiva (pathognomonic)
• X2 (Corneal Xerosis): the cornea looks hazy, dry, and "lustreless" like wax paper
• X3B (Keratomalacia): a medical emergency where the cornea physically liquefies and melts
## Ocular surface signs
• white conjunctiva: despite severe dryness, the eye is often not "red" initially
• rapid TBUT: the tear film breaks up almost instantly (often < 5 seconds)
## Fundus signs (XF)
• yellow-white dots: small deep retinal spots in the periphery; reversible with treatment
etiology: ## Primary (dietary)
• lack of vitamin A-rich foods (liver, carrots, leafy greens, eggs)
• leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide
## Secondary (malabsorption)
• bariatric surgery: common in developed countries (gastric bypass)
• gastrointestinal disease: Crohn's, Celiac, or Cystic Fibrosis (pancreatic insufficiency)
• liver disease: alcoholism or cholestasis
redFlags: • foamy spots (Bitot): in a child, this is an emergent warning of impending corneal melt
• keratomalacia: the cornea can perforate within hours; requires immediate high-dose Vitamin A
• measles: Vitamin A deficiency significantly increases measles mortality; treatment is mandatory
• pregnancy: while high-dose Vit A is teratogenic, a corneal threat outweighs fetal risk
investigations: ## Clinical exam
• Slit-lamp exam to stage the disease and check for corneal ulcers
• Schirmer test to quantify severe dryness
## Labs & imaging
• serum retinol: levels are often the last to drop (liver stores must be empty)
• RBP (Retinol Binding Protein): more sensitive for early deficiency
• ERG: can detect rod dysfunction before visible changes appear
actionSteps: • administer immediate high-dose Vitamin A (dosing depends on age and severity)
• treat any secondary bacterial infections with topical antibiotics
• initiate intensive ocular lubrication (preservative-free artificial tears)
• investigate the underlying cause (e.g., refer for malabsorption workup or nutritional counseling)
treatment: ## Systemic replacement (WHO protocol)
• adults/children >1yr: 200,000 IU orally on Days 1, 2, and 14
• children 6-12 months: 100,000 IU on the same schedule
## Ocular management
• frequent lubrication with ointment/tears
• protect the globe if "melting" is present to prevent perforation
followUp: • 1 week: night blindness usually improves within days; xerosis within 2 weeks
• long-term: monitor fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) in patients with chronic malabsorption
• counseling: avoid toxic levels (>10,000 IU/day) in pregnant women unless the cornea is involved
differentials: • Sjögren syndrome (autoimmune dry eye; usually older females)
• congenital stationary night blindness (nyctalopia without the "dryness" findings)
• trachoma (causes scarring and dryness but has characteristic lid findings)
review: • "Nyctalopia + Dryness = Vitamin A Deficiency"
• if you see a foamy triangle on the white of the eye, give Vitamin A immediately
• Vitamin A is the "purple power" for the rods (rhodopsin) and the "glue" for healthy skin/membranes
pearl: Bitot spots and night blindness in a child from a low-resource area or a malabsorbing adult is vitamin A deficiency — keratomalacia melts the cornea within days, so replace vitamin A urgently while working up malabsorption.
draw: Diagram of a Bitot spot (foamy triangle) on the side of the cornea and the WHO xerophthalmia staging chart

name: Vitreomacular Adhesion/Vitreomacular Traction/Macular Hole
symptoms: • blurred vision: central vision "fuzziness" or a significant drop in acuity (typically ~20/200 for a full hole)
• metamorphopsia: straight lines appearing wavy or distorted (e.g., door frames, Amsler grid)
• central scotoma: a gray or black "blind spot" right in the center of the vision
• micropsia: objects appearing smaller in the affected eye
findings: ## The disease spectrum
• VMA (Adhesion): vitreous is "stuck" to the fovea, but the retinal shape is still normal; usually no symptoms
• VMT (Traction): the vitreous pulls on the fovea, "tenting" it up and causing vision loss or distortion
• Full-Thickness Macular Hole (FTMH): a literal round hole in the center of the macula
## Clinical signs
• red spot: a round, well-demarcated red defect at the fovea (the "hole")
• gray cuff: a ring of fluid surrounding the hole
• klein tags: tiny yellow deposits sometimes visible at the base of the hole
• watzke-allen sign: a thin beam of light projected on the fovea appears "broken" to the patient
etiology: ## Primary mechanism
• anomalous pvd: as we age, the vitreous gel shrinks. If it stays "glued" to the fovea while pulling away elsewhere, it creates a tugging force (traction)
• risk factors: more common in women (3:1 ratio), high myopia (nearsightedness), and history of trauma
redFlags: • acute onset: holes present for less than 6 months have a much higher surgical success rate
• large diameter: holes >400 μm are harder to close and may require stricter postoperative positioning
• fellow eye risk: if a hole is present in one eye, there is a ~10-30% risk of the other eye developing one if the vitreous hasn't detached yet
investigations: ## OCT (the gold standard)
• essential for staging the condition and measuring the hole size
• differentiates a "true" hole from a "pseudohole" (which is just a wrinkle in the surface)
## Slit lamp biomicroscopy
• using a high-power lens (90D) to visualize the foveal contour and any overlying "operculum" (a floating piece of retinal tissue)
actionSteps: • perform an OCT to determine if the hole is partial (lamellar) or full-thickness
• refer to a retina specialist for full-thickness holes, as these usually require surgery
• monitor stage 1 "impending" holes closely, as 50% may resolve spontaneously without treatment
• educate the patient on using an Amsler grid to monitor the fellow eye
treatment: ## Surgical (gold standard)
• pars plana vitrectomy (ppv): removing the vitreous gel to relieve traction
• ilm peeling: stripping the thin inner "skin" of the retina to help the hole close
• gas tamponade: a gas bubble is placed in the eye to act as a "bandage" to seal the hole
## Postoperative care
• face-down positioning: historically required for 1-7 days; still recommended for larger holes to keep the bubble against the macula
followUp: • post-op: frequent checks to monitor the gas bubble and intraocular pressure
• recovery: vision improves slowly over months as the gas is replaced by the eye's natural fluid
• monitoring: lifetime surveillance of the fellow eye
differentials: • macular pucker (epiretinal membrane; causes a "pseudohole" appearance)
• solar retinopathy (burn from staring at the sun; can look like a tiny hole)
• cystoid macular edema (fluid bubbles in the retina that can mimic a hole on exam)
review: • VMA = Stuck, VMT = Pulling, FTMH = Hole
• a "pseudohole" is a hole in an overlying membrane, not a hole in the retina itself
• if the patient sees the light beam as "broken," it’s a full-thickness hole
pearl: Face-down positioning: Cochrane review shows NO significant difference in closure rates vs non-face-down for most holes — burden of strict positioning less justified. Large holes (>400μm): 94% face-down vs 84% non-face-down success.
draw: OCT cross-section showing a full-thickness gap in the central foveal dip

name: Vitreous Hemorrhage
symptoms: • sudden, painless vision loss: ranging from a mild "haze" to total darkness
• floaters: black spots, "cobwebs," or "streaks" that move with the eye
• photopsias: flashes of light, especially if the hemorrhage is caused by a retinal tear
findings: ## Clinical presentation
• diminished red reflex: the "orange glow" of the eye is dull or absent when viewed with an ophthalmoscope
• obscured fundus: the doctor cannot see the retina clearly through the pool of blood
• ochre membrane: in chronic cases, the blood turns a pale yellow-tan color as it breaks down
## Associated signs
• rbc in anterior chamber: red blood cells may "spill over" into the front of the eye
• rapd: a mild pupillary defect may be present if the hemorrhage is extremely dense
etiology: ## Proliferative (leaky vessels)
• diabetic retinopathy: the most common cause; fragile new vessels (neovascularization) bleed easily
• vein occlusion (brvo/crvo): back-pressure in the veins leads to bleeding
• wet amd: advanced bleeding from under the retina can break through into the vitreous
## Structural (mechanical tears)
• pvd: the vitreous gel pulling away from the retina can tear a blood vessel
• retinal tear/detachment: a full-thickness rip in the retina often causes immediate bleeding
## Other
• trauma: direct blunt or penetrating injury
• terson syndrome: bleeding in the eye caused by a sudden brain hemorrhage (subarachnoid)
redFlags: • "no view": if the doctor cannot see the retina, a B-scan ultrasound is MANDATORY to rule out a hidden retinal detachment
• flashes & floaters: suggests a retinal tear is the primary cause of the bleed
• trauma: always exclude a "globe rupture" (a hole in the eye wall) if the injury was severe
• monocular patient: if this is the patient's only seeing eye, surgical intervention (vitrectomy) is usually expedited
investigations: ## Imaging
• b-scan ultrasound: the single most important test when the retina is hidden; it "sees through" the blood using sound waves
• ivfa: used once the blood clears slightly to find the "leaky" source
## Clinical exam
• slit lamp exam: check for "nvi" (new vessels on the iris) which suggests advanced diabetes or ischemia
• check the other eye: the "healthy" eye often holds clues to the underlying cause (e.g., diabetic changes)
actionSteps: • perform a B-scan immediately if the fundus is not visible to rule out a retinal detachment
• instruct the patient to sleep with the head of the bed elevated (30–45°) to help blood settle
• advise the patient to avoid heavy lifting, straining, or bending over (which can trigger re-bleeding)
• schedule weekly follow-ups until the blood clears enough for a full laser/surgical plan
treatment: ## Conservative management
• observation: small bleeds often clear on their own over weeks to months
• activity restriction: no strenuous exercise or blood-thinning meds (unless medically necessary)
## Interventional
• laser photocoagulation: to seal retinal tears or "zap" leaky diabetic vessels once they become visible
• anti-vegf injections: to shrink abnormal new vessels in diabetes or AMD
## Surgical
• vitrectomy: surgery to physically remove the bloody gel; indicated for non-clearing bleeds (>2 months) or if a retinal detachment is found
followUp: • weekly b-scans: to ensure the retina remains "attached" while the blood is thick
• post-clearing exam: a "360-degree" peripheral exam with scleral depression is required to find any hidden tears
differentials: • vitritis (white blood cells from inflammation/infection; usually slower onset and painful)
• retinal detachment (can occur without bleeding, but often co-exists)
• asteroid hyalosis (calcium "sparkles" in the vitreous; looks like a snowstorm but vision is usually good)
review: • "Painless sudden blur = Vitreous Hemorrhage"
• step 1: Can I see the retina? If NO, get a B-scan.
• step 2: Is the retina attached? If NO, get to surgery.
• blood turns from red to "ochre" (yellow) as it gets old
pearl: The most important question in vitreous hemorrhage: is there a retinal detachment hiding behind the blood? B-scan ultrasound is mandatory when the fundus is not visible. Never delay if detachment is suspected.
draw: Diagram of an eye with red "clouds" in the vitreous cavity obscuring the view of the retina

name: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada Syndrome
symptoms: • sudden vision loss: typically bilateral and profound
• prodrome: flu-like symptoms, severe headache, and a stiff neck (meningismus)
• auditory: tinnitus (ringing in ears), muffled hearing, or vertigo
• sensitivity: photophobia and eye pain
• skin/hair: patches of white hair (poliosis) or skin (vitiligo) appearing later
findings: ## Phase 1: prodromal (the "brain" phase)
• mimicry: looks like viral meningitis; patient has fever, headache, and ear pain
## Phase 2: acute uveitic (the "eye" phase)
• serous retinal detachments: pathognomonic multiple "pockets" of fluid lifting the retina
• panuveitis: inflammation in the front (cells/flare) and back (vitritis) of the eye
• thickened choroid: the vascular layer under the retina becomes massively swollen
## Phase 3: convalescent (the "skin" phase)
• sunset-glow fundus: the retina turns a striking orange-red due to loss of pigment
• sugiura sign: whitening of the perilimbal conjunctiva
• poliosis/vitiligo: whitening of eyelashes, eyebrows, or skin patches
## Phase 4: chronic recurrent
• dalen-fuchs nodules: small yellow-white spots in the peripheral retina
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• autoimmune attack: T-cells mistakenly attack melanocytes (pigment-producing cells)
• targets: anywhere pigment is found—the uvea (eye), inner ear, meninges (brain cover), and skin
## Risk factors
• ancestry: most common in Asian, Hispanic, Middle Eastern, and Native American populations
• genetics: strongly associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04:05
redFlags: • headache + vision loss: bilateral serous detachments with a headache is VKH until proven otherwise; requires immediate IV steroids
• stiff neck: indicates meningeal involvement; requires neuro-consult and potentially an LP
• rapid recurrence: stopping steroids too early (before 6 months) almost guarantees a relapse
• sunset-glow: indicates the disease has entered a chronic stage and needs long-term immunosuppression
investigations: ## Imaging
• oct macula: shows "septated" pockets of subretinal fluid (looks like bridges over water)
• fluorescein angiography (fa): "starry sky" appearance—pinpoint leaking dots across the retina
• icg angiography: shows multiple dark spots (hypocyanescent) representing choroidal inflammation
## Systemic workup
• lumbar puncture: CSF pleocytosis (elevated white cells) supports the diagnosis
• rule-outs: must exclude Syphilis, TB, and Sarcoid before starting heavy steroids
actionSteps: • initiate high-dose IV corticosteroids immediately to "cool down" the acute attack
• perform baseline OCT and EDI-OCT to measure choroidal thickness
• coordinate with Neurology (for meningitis signs) and Audiology (for hearing loss)
• start a steroid-sparing agent (e.g., Mycophenolate) early to avoid long-term steroid side effects
treatment: ## Acute phase
• iv methylprednisolone: 1g daily for 3 days to save vision
• oral prednisone: 1–2 mg/kg/day with an extremely slow taper (over 6+ months)
## Long-term control
• steroid-sparing therapy: Mycophenolate Mofetil or Methotrexate to prevent the "sunset-glow" stage
• biologics: Anti-TNF agents (Adalimumab) for refractory cases
followUp: • acute: weekly exams to ensure the subretinal fluid is resolving
• maintenance: monthly checks for 1–2 years; this is a chronic, relapsing-remitting disease
• monitoring: watch for secondary glaucoma and cataracts from chronic inflammation
differentials: • sympathetic ophthalmia (identical presentation, but requires a history of eye trauma/surgery)
• posterior scleritis (usually unilateral and very painful; shows a "T-sign" on ultrasound)
• central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) (fluid pockets but NO inflammation or headache)
review: ## The VKH "pigment" rule
• the immune system "sees" pigment and attacks it in the eye (uveitis), ear (hearing loss), brain (headache), and skin (vitiligo)
• if they have a headache and "pockets" of fluid in both eyes, it's an emergency
pearl: Bilateral multifocal serous retinal detachments in a pigmented patient with headache and tinnitus is VKH — ICG shows dark dots, and aggressive long-term steroids prevent the sunset-glow fundus.
draw: Diagram of multifocal serous retinal detachments (fluid pockets) on OCT cross-section

name: Wet Age-Related Macular Degeneration
symptoms: • metamorphopsia: straight lines (like door frames or blinds) appearing wavy or distorted
• central scotoma: a gray, black, or "fuzzy" spot in the center of the vision
• decreased vision: rapid or subacute drop in the ability to read or recognize faces
• photopsias: brief flashes of light in the central visual field
findings: ## Clinical presentation
• subretinal fluid (srf): pockets of clear fluid under the retina causing a "dome" elevation
• intraretinal hemorrhage: small "dots" or "blotches" of blood within the retinal layers
• retinal exudates: yellowish lipid deposits (hard exudates) from leaking vessels
• rpe detachment (ped): a localized elevation of the pigment layer (RPE)
• disciform scar: a late-stage white/gray fibrous scar resulting in permanent vision loss
## Risk factors
• demographics: age >55, Caucasian ancestry, and light-colored eyes (blue/green)
• lifestyle: smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor
• fellow-eye risk: 10–12% annual risk of the second eye "turning wet"
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• choroidal neovascularization (cnv): abnormal, fragile blood vessels grow from the choroid through Bruch’s membrane into the retina
• vegf drive: damaged retinal cells release Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) which triggers this "leaky" vessel growth
• genetics: high association with complement pathway dysregulation (CFH Y402H and ARMS2 genes)
redFlags: • sudden distortion: any new waviness on an Amsler grid is an emergency—refer to retina the same day
• submacular hemorrhage: a large pool of blood under the fovea can cause rapid, irreversible damage
• non-responders: if fluid persists after 3 monthly "loading" injections, a switch in medication may be needed
• rpe tear: a physical rip in the pigment layer following an injection; requires careful monitoring
investigations: ## OCT (the gold standard)
• used at every visit to detect microscopic fluid and track response to injections
## Fluorescein angiography (FA)
• an injected dye test used to classify the CNV as "classic" (bright/distinct) or "occult" (fuzzy/leaky)
## OCTA
• a newer, non-invasive "no-needle" way to visualize the abnormal blood vessel network
## ICG angiography
• helpful for seeing through blood or detecting specific variants like Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy (PCV)
actionSteps: • obtain an OCT macula immediately to confirm the presence of fluid or blood
• refer to a retina specialist within the same week for the first anti-VEGF injection
• start AREDS2 vitamins for the fellow eye if it has intermediate dry AMD
• provide an Amsler grid for daily home monitoring and explain the "wavy line" rule
treatment: ## Intravitreal anti-VEGF (mainstay)
• agents: Aflibercept (Eylea), Ranibizumab (Lucentis), Bevacizumab (Avastin), or Brolucizumab (Beovu)
• protocol: typically starts with 3 monthly "loading" doses, followed by a "Treat-and-Extend" schedule
## Support measures
• smoking cessation: essential to slow disease progression
• areds2 supplements: reduces the risk of the "dry" eye turning "wet"
• low vision aids: magnifiers and high-contrast tools for those with permanent scarring
followUp: • acute: every 4 weeks during the loading phase
• maintenance: the interval is slowly extended (e.g., to 6, 8, or 12 weeks) as long as the retina stays "dry"
• monitoring: lifetime follow-up is required; if injections stop, the "wet" vessels almost always return
differentials: • ocular histoplasmosis (presents with CNV but also peripheral "punched-out" spots)
• angioid streaks (cracks in Bruch’s membrane that can bleed)
• central serous chorioretinopathy (cscr) (fluid in younger patients, usually no blood)
• myopic CNV (bleeding caused by high nearsightedness, not age)
review: • "Wavy lines = Wet AMD until proven otherwise"
• the injections don't "cure" the disease; they "mop up" the leakage the vessels produce
• AREDS2 vitamins are for the *good* eye (or the dry eye) to prevent the wet stage
pearl: Metamorphopsia (wavy lines) = wet AMD until proven otherwise. The Amsler grid is the best home screening tool. Every month of delay before anti-VEGF costs the patient central vision.
draw: OCT cross-section showing a dome of subretinal fluid and intraretinal cysts over a thickened RPE

name: Wilson Disease
symptoms: • ocular: typically asymptomatic; vision is rarely affected
• hepatic: jaundice, abdominal swelling (ascites), or unexplained liver failure
• neurologic: "wing-beating" tremors, difficulty speaking (dysarthria), or clumsy gait
• psychiatric: sudden personality changes, depression, or declining school/work performance
findings: ## Ocular pathognomonics
• kayser–fleischer (kf) ring: a golden-brown or green copper deposit in the peripheral cornea (Descemet’s membrane)
• sunflower cataract: copper deposits under the lens capsule in a "rosette" or "petal" pattern; does not affect vision
## Systemic signs
• cirrhosis: liver scarring from chronic copper toxicity
• risus sardonicus: a fixed, vacuous smile caused by facial muscle spasms
• face of the giant panda: a classic "sign" seen on brain MRI (midbrain changes)
etiology: ## Pathophysiology
• genetic: autosomal recessive mutation in the ATP7B gene (Chromosome 13)
• mechanism: the liver cannot excrete copper into bile; "free" copper spills into the blood and settles in the brain, eyes, and kidneys
• demographics: typically presents between ages 5 and 40
redFlags: • kf ring + neuropsychiatric symptoms: essentially diagnostic for Wilson disease; requires immediate systemic workup
• acute liver failure + hemolytic anemia: a near-certain sign of Wilson disease in young patients
• hidden rings: early KF rings start under the upper eyelid—if you suspect Wilson, you MUST perform gonioscopy to see the top of the cornea
investigations: ## Ocular exam
• slit-lamp exam: to find the KF ring or sunflower cataract
• gonioscopy: essential for spotting early copper deposition hiding under the lids
## Systemic labs (Leipzig criteria)
• serum ceruloplasmin: typically very low (<20 mg/dL)
• 24-hour urinary copper: significantly elevated
• liver biopsy: the "gold standard" to measure copper concentration in tissue
actionSteps: • look for the KF ring in any young patient with unexplained liver or neurologic issues
• refer to a Hepatologist or Neurologist for systemic chelation therapy
• screen all first-degree relatives (siblings have a 25% chance of also having the disease)
• use the KF ring as a "compliance marker"—it should fade if the patient is taking their medication correctly
treatment: ## Systemic chelation
• penicillamine or trientine: drugs that "grab" copper and help the body pee it out
• zinc salts: blocks the intestines from absorbing copper in the first place
## Advanced
• liver transplant: curative, as the new liver will have the correct machinery to process copper
followUp: • regular slit-lamp exams: the KF ring usually begins to fade after 6–12 months of successful treatment
• lifelong monitoring: treatment must never be stopped; untreated Wilson disease is fatal
differentials: • arcus senilis (white/gray lipid ring; common in elderly, but requires a lipid check in the young)
• primary biliary cholangitis (can cause "pseudo-KF rings" due to chronic bile backup)
• chalcosis (copper in the eye from a foreign body like a brass shard)
review: • "Brown ring + Tremor = Wilson Disease"
• the KF ring is in the cornea; the Sunflower Cataract is in the lens
• if the ring doesn't go away with treatment, the patient probably isn't taking their pills
pearl: A golden-brown ring around the cornea in a young patient with liver or neurologic disease is the Kayser-Fleischer ring — slit-lamp gonioscopy confirms, and serum ceruloplasmin is the diagnostic test.
draw: Diagram of a Kayser-Fleischer ring circling the iris and a "Sunflower Cataract" rosette in the pupil

name: Infantile Esotropia
symptoms: Inward turning of one or both eyes noted before 6 months of age.
Parents often report the child 'crosses' their eyes constantly.
Usually no other systemic or neurological symptoms if isolated.
findings: ## Clinical Presentation
• Large angle esotropia (typically >30 prism diopters).
• Cross-fixation (using right eye to look left, and left eye to look right).
• Alternate fixation often preserves equal visual acuity in both eyes.
## Associated Motor Signs
• Inferior oblique overaction (IOOA) develops in 70% of cases by age 2.
• Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD) develops in 50-90% of cases by age 3.
• Latent nystagmus (nystagmus that appears or worsens when one eye is covered).
## Refractive Error
• Usually normal for age (mild hyperopia, +1.00 to +2.00 D). Not fully corrected by glasses.
etiology: • Idiopathic failure of binocular vision development in the occipital cortex.
• Not caused by excessive accommodation (unlike accommodative esotropia).
redFlags: • MUST rule out Leukocoria (Retinoblastoma, Cataract).
• MUST rule out neurological causes if nystagmus is constant or developmental milestones are delayed.
investigations: • Cycloplegic refraction to rule out significant hyperopia.
• Dilated fundus exam to rule out sensory deprivation (retinoblastoma, optic nerve hypoplasia, toxoplasmosis scar).
• Prism and Alternate Cover Test (PACT) for near and distance.
actionSteps: • Cycloplegic refraction.
• Treat any amblyopia with patching first.
• Surgical correction once vision is equalized.
treatment: • Bilateral Medial Rectus Recession (BMR) is the standard surgical treatment.
• Goal is surgical alignment within 10 prism diopters of orthotropia by age 2 to promote peripheral binocular fusion.
• Botulinum toxin injection (Botox) to medial recti is an alternative in some centers.
followUp: • Monitor for development of amblyopia, IOOA, and DVD for years after initial alignment.
pearl: Infantile esotropia is a classic triad of large angle ET, cross-fixation, and normal hyperopia. Always check the fundus to rule out sensory esotropia from retinoblastoma.

name: Accommodative Esotropia
symptoms: • Inward turning of one eye, usually starting between age 2 and 3 years.
• Initially intermittent, worse when tired, sick, or looking closely at near objects (e.g., coloring, screens).
• May become constant if left untreated.
findings: ## Clinical Presentation
• Variable angle of esotropia.
• Moderate to high uncorrected hyperopia (typically +2.00 D to +6.00 D or more).
• High AC/A ratio in some variants (near deviation is significantly larger than distance deviation).
## Amblyopia
• High risk of developing strabismic and/or refractive amblyopia if the deviation becomes constant in one eye.
etiology: • Driven by the accommodative convergence reflex.
• Due to uncorrected hyperopia, the child must accommodate excessively to clear retinal images. This excessive accommodation triggers excessive convergence, crossing the eyes.
redFlags: • Acute onset of large angle esotropia without hyperopia requires neurological workup (rule out brain tumor/Arnold-Chiari).
investigations: • Mandatory cycloplegic refraction (Cyclopentolate 1% or Atropine) to uncover the full amount of hyperopia.
• Measurement of deviation at distance and near with and without full hyperopic correction.
actionSteps: • Prescribe the FULL cycloplegic hyperopic refraction.
• Re-evaluate in 6-8 weeks.
treatment: • Full hyperopic spectacle correction is the primary treatment.
• Bifocals (Executive or flat-top) if a high AC/A ratio is present (eyes are straight at distance with glasses, but still cross at near).
• Amblyopia treatment (patching/atropine) if vision is unequal.
• Surgery ONLY for the residual non-accommodative portion (the angle that remains while wearing full glasses).
followUp: • Every 3-4 months initially to monitor alignment and visual acuity, then every 6 months.
pearl: Never operate on the accommodative portion of an esotropia. If glasses fully straighten the eyes, surgery is strictly contraindicated.
